ground_truth_answer:
Too bad you picked this as your first booby trap scenario! The SSR means exactly what it says...?  Is there a reason to think otherwise? Yes, unfortunately. 

The reason to think otherwise is that there is no definition of "booby trap activation" anywhere in the rule book. The author of the SSR is making up a concept, perhaps trying to conserve space on the scenario card (?) to add a nearly pointless SSR. Searching the ASLRB, there are (B28.9) "booby trap resolution", "booby trap attacks", and "booby trap capability", also "booby trap trigger (D15.54)" but no such thing as "booby trap activation".  The SSR lazily cites no rules to help clear things up, even though there is plenty of space on the scenario card.

This forces us to conjecture what the hell the designer wanted when he wrote this. I would personally lean towards MR's view on this, but JR V has an equally valid argument, because no-one knows what the designer really meant here, so we are forced to offer opinions. 

Since it's a matter of opinion due to poor SSR wording, I'd roll it off with the opponent if they disagree. But here is the silly thing... such a minor nuance is a bit over the top! Why are these booby traps in this scenario not effective under all circumstances possible? Is the scenario that finely tuned that the balance is in question without this scenario special rule? Which is, in any event, unclear? I can't possibly this scenario outcome hangs on a dime such as this! I can only imagine some weird playtest outcome caused one side to win when they otherwise "didn't deserve to" according to the views of the designer. Who knows? 

Maybe use this: poorly worded and nearly useless SSR are to be ignored. Play on.

query:
Set DC versus AFV.: Hi all.

We know that for a Placed/Thrown DC to attack an armored vehicle, that must be pre-designated as its target. But what about a Set DC (other than a Japanese A-T set DC)? Can it destroy the AFV, or will it only affect vulnerable PRC?

Thanks in advance.
title: Set DC versus AFV.
raw_question:
Hi all.

We know that for a Placed/Thrown DC to attack an armored vehicle, that must be pre-designated as its target. But what about a Set DC (other than a Japanese A-T set DC)? Can it destroy the AFV, or will it only affect vulnerable PRC?

Thanks in advance.
ground_truth_answer:
A23.5 "In order for a DC attack (as with any ordnance Direct Fire vs a Location containing an AFV in combination with unarmored targets) to affect an AFV, it must be predesignated as being made against the AFV."

A23.71 " A detonated Set DC is resolved on the 36+ FP column of the IFT (or with 18 FP [the 16 FP column] vs concealed units) with a -3 DRM and no TEM including vs the vulnerable PRC of an AFV (with +2 CE DRM)." 

A DC can't be declared as set against a vehicle (and it is unlikely that there would be an enemy vehicle in the Location when it is set anyway). The only effect will be general collateral vs. PRC and/or possible indirect effects vs. terrain.

An A-T Set DC can affect a vehicle [G1.6121].

query: Landing Craft vehicle unloading costs: A LCM(3) (4 MP movement allotment) beached across a not-exposed reef hexside last friendly MPh. At the start of this friendly MPh it unloads its Passenger Sherman. The cost for the Sherman is 1 MP to Start, 4 MP to unload to unload (25% of its MP allotment (FRU) = 13 * 0.25 = 3.25 MP, FRU to 4 MP) and 3 MP to wade in the reef hex (2 MP + 1 MP COT for waterproofed, fully-tracked)  for a total of 8 MP. What is the cost for the LC? Is it 1 MP (25%) to unload, 2 MP (1 MP spent while the Sherman started plus 25% to unload) or 3 MP (the Sherman spent 61.5% of its MP allotment in unloading, and the LC must expend a corresponding percentage of its MP allotment)?
title: Landing Craft vehicle unloading costs
raw_question: A LCM(3) (4 MP movement allotment) beached across a not-exposed reef hexside last friendly MPh. At the start of this friendly MPh it unloads its Passenger Sherman. The cost for the Sherman is 1 MP to Start, 4 MP to unload to unload (25% of its MP allotment (FRU) = 13 * 0.25 = 3.25 MP, FRU to 4 MP) and 3 MP to wade in the reef hex (2 MP + 1 MP COT for waterproofed, fully-tracked)  for a total of 8 MP. What is the cost for the LC? Is it 1 MP (25%) to unload, 2 MP (1 MP spent while the Sherman started plus 25% to unload) or 3 MP (the Sherman spent 61.5% of its MP allotment in unloading, and the LC must expend a corresponding percentage of its MP allotment)?
ground_truth_answer:
The LCM(3) is a landing craft. I'd say LC rules apply, particularly this one quoted below. This rule does address the aforementioned uncertainty about the 25% MP expenditure. What I don't know is why an LTV4 is being cited here in reference to the question, instead of the data for LCM(3) and landing craft? I guess the unloading procedure could be similar for the lighter vehicles that the LTV4 can carry per chapter G, but it can't carry the Shermans. 

As for the cost, I agree that more than 50% of the total cost of the vehicle to leave the LC is used, but less than 75%, so that would mean 3/4 of the points are spent. I don't think this is staggered incrementally but is totalled up. 

[ EDIT -- USA Vehicle note 51 speaks of MP allotment and movement allotment in the same paragraph. Note that while MF and MP are defined in the index as "measures of movement capability" (no mention of "allotment"), MF allotment is adequately described in A4.11 and MP allotment is not so adequately described in D1.1. There is NO general definition of movement allotment, though it is used in A4.1, D12.5, USA Vehicle Note 51, Korean Vehicle Note 25. We can deduce that movement allotment really means MF allotment or MP allotment, depending on the unit type. IMO "movement allotment" should be added to the Index and defined. ]

12.4 (UN)LOADING: Except as stated otherwise, normal Vehicle—not Boat—(un)loading rules (D6.4-.5; D8.5) apply to LC and their Passengers. A LC Passenger may unload into an enemy-occupied hex. If a LC is Aground (or is Beached across a hexside that is not within its VCA), units may unload from it only into its hex, and do so by expending 25% (FRU) of their MF/MP allotment (plus COT MP if it is a vehicle). There is no D2.14 penalty cost for the presence of the LC in the Location, but Overstacking will apply when a vehicle [EXC: motorcycle] is in the same Location as a LC but is not a Passenger on one. A unit wishing to load onto an Aground LC must be in (or enter, expending that Location's COT to do so—plus, if it is a vehicle, one extra MP for the presence of the LC; D2.14) that LC's Location, then expend 25% (FRU) of its MF/MP allotment (plus, if it is a vehicle, one MP as the LC's COT and one MP to Stop).

query:
Does the "No Quarter" declaration allow use Low Crawl to units adjacent to the enemy?: Hi all.

As stated in the question, I have a doubt regarding rules A20.21 and A20.3. If one side has declared No Quarter, can an enemy unit use Low Crawl if it is adjacent to that side at the start of its Rout Phase? Or does the prohibition under rule A20.21 still take precedence?

Thanks in advance.
title: Does the "No Quarter" declaration allow use Low Crawl to units adjacent to the enemy?
raw_question:
Hi all.

As stated in the question, I have a doubt regarding rules A20.21 and A20.3. If one side has declared No Quarter, can an enemy unit use Low Crawl if it is adjacent to that side at the start of its Rout Phase? Or does the prohibition under rule A20.21 still take precedence?

Thanks in advance.
ground_truth_answer:
Why are you equating Low Crawl with being ADJACENT????

10.52 LOW CRAWL: Low Crawl is a rout of one Location which requires 
the entire MF allotment of the routing unit (but is still considered a form of 
Assault Movement should the routing unit enter a FFE Blast Area). A rout-
ing unit using Low Crawl cannot be Interdicted. Low Crawl cannot be used 
to enter Marsh or a Water Obstacle, or in any stream unless dry. Low Crawl 
cannot be used to exit an enemy-occupied Location [EXC: Night (E1.54)]. 
All other Rout provisions apply unchanged to Low Crawl, e.g., rout must still 
be towards the nearest woods/building Location within 6 MF.

Nothing in 10.52 requires a unit that wants to Low Crawl be ADJACENT to an enemy unit (Known or otherwise).

A Routing Unit has these options:
* If not subject to possible surrender, it designates its Rout target (nearest woods/building within 6 MF) and:
1) Routs using its 6 MF (3 for Wounded Leader, etc). towards that target; if moving into Open Ground it may be subject to Interdiction (A10.53; A10.531).
2) Declares Low Crawl and only Routs a single hex, AGAIN TOWARDS THE ROUT TARGET.

*If No Quarter has NOT been declared and it begins the Rout phase adjacent to a KEU and cannot Rout in any way to avoid Interdiction, it Surrenders to that adjacent KEU.

*If No Quarter HAS been declared and it begins the Rout phase adjacent to a KEU and cannot Rout in any way to avoid Interdiction, it does NOT Surrender and may either Rout using its 6 MF (taking the Interdiction MC(s)) or Low Crawl one hex and avoiding all Interdiction rolls.

Note that if the broken unit begins the Rout phase adjacent to a KEU, but has a VALID Rout path that does _not_ subject it to Interdiction, it does ** NOT ** Surrender and can Rout via the first bullet above (either using full 6 MF or Low Crawling one hex ... but both still must be towards it's designated Rout target).

query: Gullies: If a squad advances into crest status from IN a gully does it lose concealment? And what is the TEM be for units in crest status?
title: Gullies
raw_question: If a squad advances into crest status from IN a gully does it lose concealment? And what is the TEM be for units in crest status?
ground_truth_answer:
It depends...

If a unit can see it through a non-Crest hexside or that have LOS into the gully (per B20.92), then I would say 'yes', as it is in Open Ground per A10.531.  But if the only units that can see it must cross a Crest hexside, then it gets the Crest TEM (B27.3 via B20.92) of +4 versus OVR or OBA and +2 versus non-CC, FT attacks.

query: Unknown enemy units: Can an unknown enemy unit(Concealed or IN a depression hex) be fired upon? In other words does there have to be a LOS to the units or can a hex be fired on even though it would be considered "empty' ?
title: Unknown enemy units
raw_question: Can an unknown enemy unit(Concealed or IN a depression hex) be fired upon? In other words does there have to be a LOS to the units or can a hex be fired on even though it would be considered "empty' ?
ground_truth_answer: There is another way of "attacking" when the only target in the hex is out-of-LOS: WP. The WP counter will generally "fall" to the ground level Location [C8.52]. When a WP counter is placed in a Location, all units in that Location must take a WP NMC regardless of whether they were hit or not (and if not in LOS with no other units that are in LOS the units not in LOS could not be hit) [A24.31].

query: RB 1 SSR 3 question: RB 1 SSR 3 states that Russian MMC must take a NMC after German reinforcements are setup. It states that a unit loses its concealment "only" if it loses its good order status. Does this mean that failure of the NMC only strips concealment or is the unit subject to breaking, ELR, casualty reduction also?
title: RB 1 SSR 3 question
raw_question: RB 1 SSR 3 states that Russian MMC must take a NMC after German reinforcements are setup. It states that a unit loses its concealment "only" if it loses its good order status. Does this mean that failure of the NMC only strips concealment or is the unit subject to breaking, ELR, casualty reduction also?
ground_truth_answer:
RB 1 SSR 3 states that Russian MMC must take a NMC after German reinforcements are setup. It states that a unit loses its concealment "only" if it loses its good order status. Does this mean that failure of the NMC only strips concealment or is the unit subject to breaking, ELR, casualty reduction also? 

RB1 SSR3 "Each such unit loses its concealment (if any) only if the NMC causes it to lose Good Order status, regardless of enemy LOS."
Could be read as: ""Each such unit loses its concealment (if any) as the sole consequence if the NMC causes it to lose Good Order status, regardless of enemy LOS.",
or could be read as: ""Each such unit loses its concealment (if any) just in the case when the NMC causes it to lose Good Order status, regardless of enemy LOS."

I can see reading this two ways, as you suggest. In one way the "only" is attached to the loss of concealment clause, i.e. the sole consequence of losing its Good Order is to lose concealment. But that means that the sole consequence of failing the NMC is to lose concealment, i.e. not only does failing the NMC not HoB, ELR or casualty reduce, it also does not break. If that is the case then the unit never breaks (or goes berserk) and so always remains Good Order after the NMC and so never becomes unconcealed. That seems unlikely. So I have to conclude the intention was the second interpretation, i.e. the NMC causes all normal effects including breaking, HoB, ELR and Casualty MC. If after that MC it is no longer Good Order, then it loses concealment. So for instance if the result of the NMC is HoB with hero creation and battle hardening then the unit does not lose concealment, but if the result is HoB, berserk then it does lose concealment.

title: Routing... again!
raw_question:
The DM unit in G11 must rout.  Can it ignore G9?  The American in D10 is not visible from its current location, but will be visible upon the routing unit entering G10.  I think that all the info necessary to answer the question can be seen in the pic, but just in case...  G10 is not interdictable due to the WP in G11 and the CX unit in E11 and the orchard in E10.
As a follow up, if G9 can be ignored, the routing unit would like to go to the building with the leader in H7.  G8 cannot be interdicted by the overstacked units in I11.

ground_truth_answer:
If I read you correctly:

While in G11, I9 was ignore-able (owing to the no-farther-from-I11 allowable EXC).

I9 is too far away to be considered in G11. It is four MF, vs. three MF for G9 & F9. F9 is ignorable but G9 is not. Klas's trick is to choose F9 anyway, knowing that the rout to F9 will be prevented once the unit reaches G10 by D3. 

While in G10, you seemingly imply I9 is no longer ignore-able (owing to I11 LOS having been lost?).

The way A10.51 is written, a unit allowing ignoring of a hex has to be Known, but unlike routing toward KEUs where the condition is either currently Known or Known at some point during this rout, ignoring due to Known unit does not mention units seen during the rout but no longer in LOS. The two are different; one uses memory, the other does not.

I could imagine this being overturned in a q&a, i.e. that what is ignorable is based both on current LOS and on memory, but I could also imagine it being sustained as it seems to be written. I would give it 60-40 likely sustained, but that is merely my guess.

While in H9 (w/I11 back in LOS and thus Known -- again) I9 (initially ignore-able, owing to I11) is no longer ignore-able (even though it was at the beginning)?

While in H9 the broken unit has no reason to re-figure its rout. If it had a reason to re-figure its rout then I9 would be ignorable, but it can't start the re-figuring process. Re-figuring is not something that can be done whenever you want. You have to be prevented from reaching your previously designated rout target to re-figure. The q&a you give below says that.

That certainly is chaotic -- okay, thematically, perhaps -- is it also Correct?
A10.51 A broken unit starts to rout toward the
nearest building/woods hex, but during its rout
the building/woods hex is not farther from a
Known enemy unit than its present hex. Can the
broken unit now choose to ignore the building/-
woods? Or must it continue to rout toward that
target?
A. It must continue (assuming it is otherwise able
to). [An97; Mw]
Does knowledge of the I11I9 range (and EXC) not persist from the start of the Rout move?  Upon entry of G10, does I9 indeed fall off the initial list of ignore-able Rout Targets?

query: Desperation Morale: What does "taking the possibility of cowering into account" mean in rule 10.62 ?
title: Desperation Morale
raw_question: What does "taking the possibility of cowering into account" mean in rule 10.62 ?
ground_truth_answer:
What does "taking the possibility of cowering into account" mean in rule 10.62 ? 
Take all thirty-six possible DRs, from 1,1 to 6,6. Look up the result on the IFT for that FP (applying the DRM for the attack) for all the thirty-six DRs. If a particular DR is a doubles, and the attack might cower, use the result from the IFT column for the cower, not the original IFT column. At the end of the exercise you will have thirty-six possible results. If any of them is a NMC or better, the broken unit is marked with a DM.

As a practical matter it is sufficient to look at the result on a DR of three if the attack can cower or on a DR of two if the attack can't cower. If the result is a NMC or better, broken units will be marked DM by the attack.

In both cases this is regardless of the actual IFT DR.

ground_truth_answer:
I have probably played this wrong for more than 30 years: The rules say: "...a routing unit must move to the nearest (in MF calculated at
the start of its RtPh) building or woods hex...". Can this be a hex to which the unit has no LOS? I cannot understand the design idea behind that.
The rout target does not need to be in LOS.

My explanation is that the unit is somewhat aware of its position and surroundings on the battlefield. It has probably scouted the area the vicinity enough to know that there are a few buildings in that direction and a woods line in the other. In the game the unit may have moved in LOS of the hex that later becomes its target. So if you really, really want to be sure the rout is to a place the unit "knows about" (even disregarding hypothetical, extra-scenario scouting or movement) you would have to track every hex seen by every unit. That's a nightmare. And although you may envision the rout as a pell-mell, headlong flight, it could instead sometimes represent a more cautious and calculated movement, trying to find a place to regroup. Limiting the unit's knowledge, either past or future, to just what it has in LOS right this second is probably as bad a simulation, and possibly worse, as how the rules work.

HI guys. I've reviewed several threads on these issues but I want to make sure I've understood them correctly. Could I get some confirmation on the following?

If accuracy isn't achieved, the AR can deviate by up to 6 hexes if that result is rolled on the white die. But if you later  try to Correct it, the maximum deviation is one hex for every three you modify it.

OBA FP isn't halved against HIP units. And somehow your opponent must inform you of the effects on it (e.g., if the unit is eliminated or must take an MC). Provided it's affected, of course.

If OBA scores a CH on a unit in Woods, does it receive both the -1 Airburst and the -1 TEM (for a total of -2)? And if the unit were in a Foxhole, would the total be -5? Or does only the -1 Airburst apply?"

What if the CH was from a mortar on the board? Would it be -1 (airburst only), -2 (airburst+TEM), or -3 (airburst+Foxhole)?

Thanks in advance.
ground_truth_answer:
If accuracy isn't achieved, the AR can deviate by up to 6 hexes if that result is rolled on the white die. But if you later  try to Correct it, the maximum deviation is one hex for every three you modify it.
Technically the AR is placed first, accuracy is rolled and and if not accurate, based on the Extent-of-Error DR the resulting SR or FFE is placed relative to the AR, i.e. the AR is not moved. Purely a technical point; you can move the AR then place the SR/FFE on it if you like with little harm.
OBA FP isn't halved against HIP units. And somehow your opponent must inform you of the effects on it (e.g., if the unit is eliminated or must take an MC). Provided it's affected, of course.
Correct, but this is not special for OBA. You can fire against HIP units too with IFT fire or ordnance fire, and your opponent has to evaluate the effects.
If OBA scores a CH on a unit in Woods, does it receive both the -1 Airburst and the -1 TEM (for a total of -2)? And if the unit were in a Foxhole, would the total be -5? Or does only the -1 Airburst apply?"
Only positive TEM are reversed [C3.71] (with certain exceptions, e.g. pillbox); negative TEM still apply normally. So an air burst is just -1. A CH against a foxhole would have a -5 DRM. 
What if the CH was from a mortar on the board? Would it be -1 (airburst only), -2 (airburst+TEM), or -3 (airburst+Foxhole)?
Using the same principles, the DRM is -3.

ground_truth_answer:
A7.35 "Usage limitations for each type of SW are listed on the SW Chart." Per note B, which applies to halfsquads and crews, "B. May fire one SW but at cost of inherent FP." This unfortunately is murky as to its exact meaning because of SFF & FPF. However it is generally understood that once a halfsquad uses a SW during a player turn, it may use no other, although, depending on the type of SW it used, it can switch to its inherent instead for SFF & possibly for FPF. 

EX: a halfsquad fires a BAZ as first fire. It also possesses a LMG. It can now fire its inherent as SFF & FPF. It can't use the LMG for SFF/FPF.
EX: a halfsquad fires a MMG as first fire. It also possesses a LMG. It can now fire its inherent as SFF (or it could use the MMG), but it *must* use the MMG for FPF. It can't use the LMG for SFF/FPF, even if the MMG malfunctions. If the MMG malfunctions the halfsquad can use its inherent for FPF.

ground_truth_answer:
As per previous the TCA change is done in conjunction with some other expenditure. It is not an expenditure in itself. However changing VCA *is* an expenditure in itself, and the "traditional" way to burn MP (besides expending more MP than necessary or stopping and delaying, etc.) is to change VCA over and over. There is a risk that you change your VCA from front to side to a threat, so watch out. You also can't do this in bypass.

This is by official rule.  Or you can play with laid back people who just say "Sure, you can retro your initial movement into the hex to expend the extra MPs and do you TCA upon entry of the hex."  It all depends on how competitive you want to be (though if you ever go to tournaments, it would be strongly recommended to stick closely to the exact written rules ...).

My group is full of 50+ Grognards who don't have infinite free time and are in it for a combination of competitiveness, comradery, and catching up with each other ... so we couldn't care less if you asked to 'correct' your MP expenditure, even if we had declared fire on the vehicle, etc.  It's a game, after all ... it's about enjoying the time playing and feeling like you beat your opponent through your skill (read: VASL dice gods), not through a minor-speed-of-play issue (read: we do this to also prevent people from spending 15 minutes trying to think out their entire movement as these minor oopsies are easy to 'fix' ...  but we don't generally allow things like completely re-doing a movement from multiple hexes back, etc.).

ground_truth_answer:
A8.14 discusses broken or spent units but based upon A8.3, units that spend 2 or more MF (it doesn't say good order or broken) could still be fired upon.  Is a "follow-up attack" different than Subsequent First Fire?  I'm not sure I'm understanding if there's a difference between the two rules given that A8.14 mentions broken/spent units specifically.

SFF is an mode of attack based on the attacker's state. A unit or MG/IFE that is marked with a First Fire counter can use SFF (subject to all the limitations for SFF of course) [A8.3]. Depending on previous history in the turn (e.g. the DEFENDER had fired on other targets prior to this one or had fired on this target on a different expenditure) the first attack against a particular target on this expenditure might be SFF.

The possibility of follow-up attacks are based on the MF spent by the moving unit and are independent of whether SFF is used. If a moving infantry unit moved into brush up a hill (four MF) and the DEFENDER fired a MG, if the DEFENDER was lucky with ROF none of the attacks would be SFF. If the MG was unlucky with ROF the first attack might be First Fire, the second might be SFF and (if the DEFENDER were ADJACENT) the remaining two attacks would be FPF. 

The two are only indirectly related, and then only by normal play, not by rules. A SFF attack might or might not be a follow-up attack. A follow-up attack might or might not be SFF. Often a follow-up attack will be SFF, but that is only because inherent FP doesn't get ROF and ROF from MGs is more likely to fail than not.

Also, I'm assuming (I hope safely) that a unit that moves through grain (at 1.5 MF) isn't subject to SFF because they haven't spent 2 or more MF (since FRD should apply).  So, if a unit moved only hex and it was a grain hex (in season, of course), only one defensive fire attempt could be made against it.

Correct, unless there was some other reason the MF were increased, e.g. gaining elevation, entering concealment terrain at night, etc.

ground_truth_answer:
I believe an AFV entering a gutted factory via a vehicular-sized entrance is subject to a +1 Bog DRM for debris plus another +1 Bog DRM for factory hex ( probably also ground pressure ) because the benefit of treating the entrance as Open Ground is negated if the entrance is roofless, as per my understanding of B23.742.
There is a somewhat-related q&a:

B23.1, O1.2, O5.42 - In Red Barricades what is the MP cost for a fully tracked vehicle to enter a roofless factory hex from outside of the factory? Note this is not a VSE. Is it ½ of its MP for entering a building, ¼ of its MP for entering debris, or ¾ of its MP for entering a building and entering debris?
A. One-half of its MP.

The person who asked apparently thinks that a vehicle-sized entrance makes a difference because such a hex was excluded from the question. If being a vehicle-sized entrance is different then the cost to enter a vehicle-sized entrance hex would be ¼ MP allotment because for movement purposes the hex still uses Open Ground MP costs as its base. I don't see any rule that says that a vehicle-sized entrance becomes an ordinary factory hex if it is filled with debris due to being roofless, so I would be inclined to say that it does not become an ordinary factory hex. Unfortunately the answer to the q&a does not cover what happens to a vehicle-sized entrance in a roofless factory, so it sounds necessary to request another q&a for that case.

A11.22, "Provided it has not already been eliminated/captured/pinned, any Infantry/Cavalry unit which rolls an Original 2 CC DR may withdraw from CC/Melee immediately thereafter in the same CCPh without being attacked, even if it did not eliminate the defenders."

query: Hola!  Rooftops and rubble:do you check for rubble on the rooftop or not?: C24.1
title: Hola!  Rooftops and rubble:do you check for rubble on the rooftop or not?
ground_truth_answer:
Perhaps a multi-level building hit by a KIA with OBA or Area target type (with rooftops not playable).  Would you then roll for the rooftop 'as if the rooftop was a non rooftop level as per B23.86?
A multi-level building hit by OBA is more complicated. Unless it is an interior building hex [B23.32] all Locations are hit by OBA. If the result is potential rubble, one or more Locations selected by Random Selection have to make the rubble dr [A24.11]. If rooftops are in play they would be included in the Random Selection. If the result for the rubble dr on an in-play rooftop is rubble, the full-level below would be rubbled instead and the rooftop Location would cease to exist. If the hex is an interior building hex only the top full level and rooftop would be involved in the Random Selection per B23.32.

query:
quick summary of Journal 16 rules changes: VBM related: This is a quick summary and comments on the rules changes in ASL Journal 16 related to VBM.

1) The most important is that a vehicle (in bypass) has to be in the same Location to invoke A7.212. Being at ground level but subject to TPBF from an upper level no longer does. This of course usually prevents/ends firelanes from the ground-level Location but at least allows DFF from the upper levels until ROF runs out. 
2) Ending the MPh in bypass no longer automatically strips concealment of DEFENDERs in the ground-level obstacle Location. Instead passing a PAATC will allow units in the bypassed obstacle to keep concealment [A12.42]. 
3) Regular ambush CC DRM is now in addition to street fighting ambush DRM rather than in lieu of it [A11.8].

The first still leaves the bypass vehicle as the closest enemy unit and so prevents SFF/FPF out of the hex even from upper levels. In addition if the hex is a single-hex, multi-level building the upper levels will be subject to upper-level encirclement by the appearance of a vehicle in bypass at ground level. The second fixes a strange rule that always left me scratching my head. It was never clear (to me at least) why a vehicle in bypass automatically stripped concealment when one in-hex did not. Although the third sounds impressive, unless infantry advance in there won't be ambush rolls (unless a HIP unit turns up) [A11.4].
title: quick summary of Journal 16 rules changes: VBM related
raw_question:
This is a quick summary and comments on the rules changes in ASL Journal 16 related to VBM.

1) The most important is that a vehicle (in bypass) has to be in the same Location to invoke A7.212. Being at ground level but subject to TPBF from an upper level no longer does. This of course usually prevents/ends firelanes from the ground-level Location but at least allows DFF from the upper levels until ROF runs out. 
2) Ending the MPh in bypass no longer automatically strips concealment of DEFENDERs in the ground-level obstacle Location. Instead passing a PAATC will allow units in the bypassed obstacle to keep concealment [A12.42]. 
3) Regular ambush CC DRM is now in addition to street fighting ambush DRM rather than in lieu of it [A11.8].

The first still leaves the bypass vehicle as the closest enemy unit and so prevents SFF/FPF out of the hex even from upper levels. In addition if the hex is a single-hex, multi-level building the upper levels will be subject to upper-level encirclement by the appearance of a vehicle in bypass at ground level. The second fixes a strange rule that always left me scratching my head. It was never clear (to me at least) why a vehicle in bypass automatically stripped concealment when one in-hex did not. Although the third sounds impressive, unless infantry advance in there won't be ambush rolls (unless a HIP unit turns up) [A11.4].
ground_truth_answer:
Thoughts on changes to tactics:

If the DEFENDER is at ground level, VBM freeze works as it always did during that first MPh, with the exception of additional risk to to vehicle due to the street fighting DRM counting for CC-RF for SFF & FPF. I suspect I played this point wrong (but in line with the Journal 16 changes) so for me it does not change my calculus. If you played this correctly it does increase the importance of minimizing your exposure by making sure you spend the fewest MP possible in the DEFENDER's hex by bleeding off MP prior to entry of VBM. But that was probably true before the Journal 16 because if you didn't then by the D2.4 requirement to spend all MP if possible the bypassing vehicle might have to stop in-hex in order to Delay [D2.17] (making it Stopped and thus even more vulnerable to CC-RF), continue bypass or overshoot the bypass hex and be required to exit.

If the DEFENDER is on an upper level, VBM freeze is no longer possible. DFF from upper levels is now allowed even though there is a TPBF opportunity to ground level. The best a bypassing vehicle can do in such a situation is restrict SFF & FPF by being the closest (zero-hex range) enemy target. This is not a bad thing to do but it does allow an upper-level DEFENDER to use all its non-SFF/FPF fire, including ROF, outside its own hex even if there is an enemy vehicle in bypass at ground level.

This in turn suggests some changes to play. First against an upper-level DEFENDER the ATTACKER might consider delaying moving into the hex in bypass until after the the DEFENDER has become marked with a First-Fire counter. The DEFENDER is going to be able to fire outside the hex anyway, and those attacks may have a result that eliminates the need to freeze (now with "SFF freeze") the DEFENDER. The DEFENDER may cower, or it may malfunction its MG, etc. That would leave the ATTACKER free to use the vehicle that was held back for "SFF freeze" for other purposes. Plus because the DEFENDER would now be marked with a First-Fire counter, its FP would now be halved and the risk from fire from above would be reduced. CT AFVs can perform "SFF freeze" while BU, which reduces the risk to them from small arms/MGs to zero if they wait until the DEFENDER is marked with a First-Fire counter. If the situation allows it, the ATTACKER might consider moving to range one rather than in bypass at range zero. This will still "SFF freeze" an upper-level DEFENDER for ranges > one, plus for OT AFVs may avoid the risk of being treated as an unarmored vehicle [D5.311] even to the point of allowing them to BU (but note that an OT AFV is still vulnerable as a soft vehicle at range one against a DEFENDER at level two).

Alternately the ATTACKER might enter bypass of the hex before the upper-level DEFENDER is marked with a First-Fire counter and try for a vehicular Smoke dispenser. Vehicles with high Smoke Dispenser usage numbers in most cases should be able to nullify an upper-level DEFENDER nearly as effectively as VBM freeze. When shrouded in Smoke the DEFENDER no longer qualifies for FFMO and gets the extra hindrance for firing out of Smoke at level one (or level zero). At level two the DEFENDER won't be firing out of Smoke but will still be firing through Smoke to lower levels. Even if the vehicle doesn't have a high (or even any) Smoke Dispenser usage number it can try to Vehicular Smoke Grenades [D13.35] for the same effect. If Smoke is successfully placed the vehicle might then move on to do other things, including BFF at other enemy units. If not the ATTACKER has the option of either remaining in-hex (subject to figuring out how to spend the remainder of its MPs per D2.4) or try again with another vehicle if available.

query:

Per a recent q&a a unit in a foxhole that assault moves out to an ADJACENT Location using a combined expenditure into an enemy unit is A12.15 pushed back INTO the foxhole with no opportunity for the enemy to fire while out of the foxhole. Assume a CPVA unit has gotten adjacent concealed, and because of previous fire your unit in the foxhole is not concealed. You are rightly concerned about the ambush next turn. You can fire (here at six FP, add one if night), but that does not guarantee a result. Or you could instead bump-scout using a combined expenditure. That's guaranteed to strip concealment. The enemy can fire first of course (as DFF or DFPh) but you get the +2 TEM from the foxhole (+3 including night LV) and no FFMO or FFNAM. If the moving unit survives it can fire in the AFPh (using assault fire here) at the now-unconcealed unit. And you can use Opportunity Fire for units not actually performing the bump-scout.

This applies for a variety of nationalities, not just the CPVA and Americans I show here. I use them as example because I am in the middle of 210 "This Is Where We Stand", with the CPVA pushing up the hill against my Americans. The Good Order CPVA are all stealthy [W7.9], so avoiding ambush is a really good idea. Of course if the concealed target has more than one unit you might not strip concealment from all units, and if the target is a dummy, you might be in an awkward position after the move.

Per a recent q&a a unit in a foxhole that assault moves out to an ADJACENT Location using a combined expenditure into an enemy unit is A12.15 pushed back INTO the foxhole with no opportunity for the enemy to fire while out of the foxhole. Assume a CPVA unit has gotten adjacent concealed, and because of previous fire your unit in the foxhole is not concealed. You are rightly concerned about the ambush next turn. You can fire (here at six FP, add one if night), but that does not guarantee a result. Or you could instead bump-scout using a combined expenditure. That's guaranteed to strip concealment. The enemy can fire first of course (as DFF or DFPh) but you get the +2 TEM from the foxhole (+3 including night LV) and no FFMO or FFNAM. If the moving unit survives it can fire in the AFPh (using assault fire here) at the now-unconcealed unit. And you can use Opportunity Fire for units not actually performing the bump-scout.

This applies for a variety of nationalities, not just the CPVA and Americans I show here. I use them as example because I am in the middle of 210 "This Is Where We Stand", with the CPVA pushing up the hill against my Americans. The Good Order CPVA are all stealthy [W7.9], so avoiding ambush is a really good idea. Of course if the concealed target has more than one unit you might not strip concealment from all units, and if the target is a dummy, you might be in an awkward position after the move.
ground_truth_answer:
Not clear on how the Marines still get the foxhole TEM. A12.15 A unit forced back to an entrenchment/shellhole Location can derive no TEM benefit therefrom vs any ensuing Defensive First Fire, although it can for any Defensive Final Fire or subsequent attacks.

This is an interesting observation, but my best guess is this is not fixed for the Journal 16 changes. I could be wrong here, though. Per q&a, 
12.15 & B27.4 An American squad is in a Foxhole in Open Ground adjacent to a Concealed German unit in Woods. During the MPh:
(1) The American squad uses non-Assault Movement to exit the Foxhole for 1 MF and then attempts to enter the Woods.
(2) The American squad uses non-Assault Movement to exit the Foxhole for 1 MF, then attempts Smoke Grenade placement for 1 MF, and then attempts to enter the Woods.
(3) The American squad makes one combined expenditure of MF using Assault Movement to exit the Foxhole and enter the Woods.
In all cases the American squad is forced back into its initial hex via A12.15. In the above cases, is the American squad under the Foxhole for Defensive Final Fire?
A. Case 3 only.
If the answer to any of the above is yes, can the American squad—on returning to its initial hex—decline being placed back in the Foxhole?
A. No option exists.

 

Since the unit was under the foxhole my assumption was that it was given the +2 TEM. But the q&a specifically asks about DFPh. So it is possible that the unit is subject to FFMO despite being in a foxhole, in which case my idea is invalid. I will submit for a q&a, I think.

query: Leader in a multi hex FG: Please help with an example.  1 leader in a multi hex FG , how is his leadership applied to the squads  firing with him as part of the FG . I understand his leadership does not apply to the other hexes. Thank you
title: Leader in a multi hex FG
raw_question: Please help with an example.  1 leader in a multi hex FG , how is his leadership applied to the squads  firing with him as part of the FG . I understand his leadership does not apply to the other hexes. Thank you
ground_truth_answer:
A7.53, A7.531 & A7.9 An 8-1 leader and squad
w/ LMG are in a Location; another friendly squad
is in an Adjacent Location. Absent Leader
Direction, each squad is subject to Cowering. All
of these units have LOS to a target. They declare
an attack on that target as a firegroup. To prevent
Cowering in his Location, may the leader be
declared as directing the fire of the squad and
LMG in his location (even though he may not
apply his DRM to the attack – A7.531)?
A. No.
If not, suppose there were another 8-1 and it were
stacked with the other squad, such that both
Locations of the FG featured a –1 leader directing
the FG attack. A7.531 allows a -1 leadership
attack DRM in this case. Because this would be
an attack directed by two leaders (as opposed to a
leader – A7.9, 1st sentence), would the attack be
subject to Cowering?
A. No. 
Upshot:  A Leader in just one hex of a multi-hex FG cannot direct that FG if any other hex of FG is w/out it's own directing Leader.

ground_truth_answer:
Am a little embarrassed to ask about this, but we're not totally certain we've been playing the illustrated situation correctly:

Rule A8.3 SUBSEQUENT FIRST FIRE states in part that "The same unit/weapon can never fire on a moving unit in the same Location more times than the number of MF/MP expended... in that Location during that MPh."   In our game, the German SQ in J9, having totally missed with his Defensive First Fire at F10 (w/ DRM -2 for FFMO & FFNAM), wishes to follow up immediately by using Subsequent First Fire, also into F10.  Can he do so?

The Americans did expend 3 MF to get to hex F10, but given that 2 of those MF were expended crossing the bocage, are they or are they not considered to have expended all 3MF in the F10 Location?  If they didn't expend the extra 2 MF in that Location, then my understanding is that no immediate Subsequent First Fire back into F10 should be allowed.
The cost to cross a wall/hedge is an addition to the COT [B9.4], resulting in an increased MF cost for that expenditure. That addition is not made as a separate expenditure (unlike, say, exiting a foxhole or placing a DC/smoke grenade), so the unit performs its move then receives DFF for all MF spent in that expenditure at any point to which the LOS can be traced. Similarly extra MF for entering SMOKE add to the COT for the expenditure and are not separate expenditures. Once the movement action is complete the unit may be fired on as many times as the unit spent MF in that expenditure.

As a slightly different example an infantry unit spending two MF in bypass, say in H10 when there is SMOKE present, can be fired on two times at any of the two or three vertices that are used by that bypass. The unit does not spend one MF at each vertex for a single-hexside bypass nor expend two-thirds of a MF at each vertex for a two-hexside bypass. The firing unit could fire at different vertices if it wanted (e.g. it turns out that LOS to one vertex was blocked, and the DEFENDER wanted to try LOS to a different vertex), but it is not required to switch the vertex for a single expenditure.

ground_truth_answer:
I like the consistency in the Perry Sez answer: when Infantry are changing hexes, they're moving and can be seen through gaps in a wall. This aligns well with note B in the A12.121 Concealment Loss/Gain Table.
One reason I had my doubts is A.3, which says that says the term "move" is used only for the MPh, and rules which want to address more than that use "move/Advance." But when the original question arose I looked at A.3 more carefully, and it says
Whenever a rule refers to a non-vehicular unit's inability to move, it refers only to movement in the MPh. If a unit's advance capability during the APh is also restricted, the rule will specifically prohibit both movement and advance.
When I reviewed the rule in the context of the original question I realized that A.3 covered a very specific subset of rules and was not the general-purpose rule I had imagined it to be. That said it does raise the point that in the ASLRB the word "move" may or may not be restricted to translation in the MPh. There is no formal definition of, "move," as being "all counter translation" or just "counter translation during the MPh." Because of this ambiguity one can come to have doubts about the specific use of "move" that is intended in a given context.

That changes the calculation but you still don't necessarily need a double-acquisition. The maximum DRM for moderate dust is +3 [F11.72]. For the most part the nuance would never matter. Per B2.1 with Journal 11 errata installed, other terrain in the hex no longer exists when shellholes are placed. As far as I know geomorphic maps don't have terrain other than open ground with shellholes. When there are shellholes they tend to be in places where there is no lower level from which to move into them. Sword & Flame broke this by having shellholes in terrain other than open ground, and also by having hexes where you could easily move/advance up a level into foxholes.
Such is the nature of a living set of rules!

A.1 DICE: The rules often require use of a colored die to differentiate
it from the other die in use. A set of four dice of different colors is included
in ASL Module 1: BEYOND VALOR. A white die and one of the colored
dice are rolled simultaneously and summed normally for most purposes, but
occasionally the colored dr will take on added significance either by itself or in
comparison to the white dr. Players may also find it beneficial to get in the habit of
rolling three dice, and using the third colored die as an automatic “subsequent dr”
for any situation requiring one (such as 5.132, 7 .309, 9.74, 11.13, 11.501, 24.1).
The term “dr” refers to die roll while the term “DR” in all CAPITAL letters
refers to Dice Roll. The term Original DR/dr refers to one before the addition

ground_truth_answer:
Not really seeing what issue there is with these two - can you elaborate perhaps?Prior to J16:
--If an A11.4 Ambush occurred in CC, then the A11.4 Ambush DRM would apply but the A11.8 Street Fighting Ambush DRM could not apply.
--If no A11.4 Ambush occurred in CC and the requirements for Street Fighting were met, then the A11.8 Street Fighting Ambush DRM would apply.
The word "Ambush" was overloaded: it could mean normal Ambush, or it could mean Street Fighting Ambush, but the two were mutually exclusive so it sort of worked.

Now we have a rule change and the two Ambushes can potentially occur together. This creates an ambiguity that previously was avoided (because previously the two were mutually exclusive).

D7.21 CC REACTION FIRE: Each Infantry/Cavalry DEFENDER unit that is unbroken, unpinned and neither Unarmed (A20.5) nor in Melee may attempt CC Reaction Fire, using the CC-vs-vehicle rules (A11.5, etc.; see also 7.211-.213) [EXC: Ambush is NA unless using Street Fighting; 7.211].
The EXC, as written, can be read as saying that (a) if "Street Fighting" conditions are met, then ordinary Ambush is also possible;
or it can be read as saying that (b) ordinary Ambush DRM is always impossible but the Street Fighting Ambush DRM may be possible.

ASOP 8.12B: Resolve Ambush if advance into CC (not Melee) was into woods/building/jungle/bamboo/kunai (A11.4; G.6) and/or by/vs “?” (automatic ATTACKER Ambush for Street Fighting; A11.8) {night Ambush dr; E1.77}.
Here, "automatic ATTACKER Ambush for Street Fighting" likewise now has two potential meanings: (a) that whenever Street Fighting conditions are met, the ATTACKER also automatically qualifies for ordinary Ambush DRM, or (b) that ordinary Ambush may or may not occur, but the Street Fighting Ambush DRM can separately apply.

I recommend that the wording be improved to avoid this kind of confusion.
--The EXC could read: A11.4 Ambush is NA but Street Fighting is permissible; 7.211.
--The ASOP parenthetical could simply read: Street Fighting; A11.8.

I know what these two phrases mean and how to interpret them, but that's only because I know the history of how Street Fighting previously worked. I also know that these two phrases were originally worded to describe the old mechanic, but I think they were allowed to remain as they are because, if you squint, they still sort of work.

A new player will not have that history, and IMO may be quite confused. I sure would be.

ground_truth_answer:
So yellow (sunlight) and green make blue😆
It's just crazy for being where I found it. I had an unpunched Partisan years ago. 
CMYK is a subtractive color system, that is colors are taken away from white. To generate green (for Axis Minor) you would use cyan and yellow. If the yellow ink faded and no longer subtracted, that would leave only the cyan ink, which is a kind of blue. Mixed with more white from the faded yellow areas that might produce a light blue.

It would take a long time for such fading to take place, I would think. I don't think sitting out in the parking lot for a day or two would be long enough, and you'd expect a cardboard counter to have water damage if it spent a long time outdoors. Perhaps it was sitting in a car under the windshield for a long time and finally got dislodged.
And thats the crazy part.  I had Partisans module quite a few years ago.  Never punched it since I then got the newer updated module when I was first getting into ASL from SK.  There is no reason for that one counter to be in the center of the driveway leading up to our shop.  It had to have been recent because there is no water damage as you say.   Maybe a bird picked up elsewheres and dropped it as it flew overhead.  No idea.

A  concealed squad moves into an open ground hex in the LOS of an enemy squad, but there's a hinderence hex between them. Does the moving squad lose concealment?
The hindrance means the concealed squad is no subject to FFMO, and is therefore not moving in the open. Therefore, the concealed squad maintains concealment if it is an Assault Move, and loses concealment otherwise.

Do the Brits get to attempt to rout out in the Rout Phase as they are not held in melee?

query: Infantry OVR TC DRM for foxholes: An Infantry OVR requires a TC, to which a DRM for TEM applies [A4.15]. B27.3, "Any unit beneath a foxhole counter is entitled to a +4 TEM against any OVR [EXC: an OVR using only FT armament] or OBA attack, or a +2 TEM to any other type of attack." What is the DRM for the TC vs. a SMC in an foxhole, +2 or +4?
title: Infantry OVR TC DRM for foxholes
raw_question: An Infantry OVR requires a TC, to which a DRM for TEM applies [A4.15]. B27.3, "Any unit beneath a foxhole counter is entitled to a +4 TEM against any OVR [EXC: an OVR using only FT armament] or OBA attack, or a +2 TEM to any other type of attack." What is the DRM for the TC vs. a SMC in an foxhole, +2 or +4?
ground_truth_answer:
I'm failing to communicate, apparently.

The Infantry OVR TC TEM modifier has nothing to do w/CC, per se -- like most any ASL TC, it is a test vs unit morale to answer an abstract Q, in this case, Willingness or not to move into [a place] occupied by a known enemy SMC.

Terrain affects that willingness, e.g., going into a wood building, say, would likely be more intimidating than vs a guy in a Foxhole in Open Ground.

Apply an Infantry OVR TC Foxhole TEM modifier?  Why?

I've given the plausible why not.
...perhaps you can cite/quote a rule.

A unit in an entrenchment gets either a +2 TEM or +4 TEM (unless attacked by a FT), so as far as I can see those are the only possible answers, i.e. the Infantry OVR NTC DRM against a unit in a foxhole is either two or four, unless you claim that *all* TEM is zero for CC and therefore the NTC DRM is zero for all terrain, foxholes or not.
I can see your logic.

You omit, however, the EXC re CC, in B27.3.

 Any unit beneath a foxhole counter is entitled to a +4 TEM against any
OVR [EXC: an OVR using only FT armament] or OBA attack, or a +2 TEM
to any other type of attack including on-board mortar fire [EXC: CC, FT]. A
foxhole TEM is not cumulative with that of other positive TEM in the same
hex but is applicable in combination with the negative TEM of an Air Burst
(13.3).

Arguably, an Infantry OVR is an "other type of attack."  It happens that one of is resolution mechanics is potential CC.

As you argue, CC is "always" resolved w/out TEM ... so, why the EXC re Foxhole TEM in B27.3, if not to address the corner case Infantry OVR TC DRM?

[Given the history of the Infantry OVR rule (as related in Footnote A3) I find it easy to believe a reference, from the B27.2 CC EXC, to A4.15 was maybe overlooked?]

 4.15 INFANTRY OVR: The inclusion of an Infantry OVR rule was a source of
heated debate among our playtesters—many of whom opposed it as an unnecessary
complication. Others pointed out the End Game problem of using SMC as unrealistic
sacrifices to “block” movement into hexes required for Victory Conditions. The result-
ing rule is an attempt to deal both with the artificial time constraints of the Game Turn
and to give lone SMC the option of giving way before overwhelming force rather than
risk sure elimination or capture.
It seems to me there was no intent to grant an Infantry OVR TC Foxhole TEM DRM advantage to an SMC facing a potential Infantry OVR.

As a corner case, this matter is seldom visited.  TBH, IDK the intent.  But I best-guess as per the evidence and my argument as given above.  YMMV.

I've nothing more.  Peace.

This is not specific, but I'm sort-of reading that you feel the DRM is +2. What you wrote originally was, "the Foxhole itself adds no DRM re the A4.15 Infantry OVR Task Check." If you say, "+2," that might or might not be correct, but it is at least reasonable. If you say the foxhole "adds no DRM re the A4.15 OVR Task Check," I find no support for neither two TEMs of a foxhole applying, and I cannot see any way that could be the right answer.

Regarding whether Infantry OVR is an "other type of attack," I will say that B27.3 does not say the +4 applies only to vehicle OVR, and as per above the index entry for OVR includes both Infantry and vehicular OVR. Whether that has unintentional consequences or not I can't say. But I am leaning toward reading the rules-as-written as saying the TC would get a +4 DRM without a clarification.

ground_truth_answer:
... the last sentence of 2.9 has puzzled me ...
Does it mean that 90% of your units must be set up with a Leader ie an SMC ? 
Also the words “ if the nationality is capable of Deployment” - why are they in play if not?

ASL rule 2.9"] Up to 10% (FRU) of the squads that set up on-board, and up to 10% (FRU) of the squads that enter in a given turn, may be freely Deployed (without leader/TC) prior to setup, if the nationality is capable of Deployment.

In ASL, Deployment means exchanging a full squad for two half squads of the same type.

Some nationalities cannot Deploy.  See rules sections A25 and G18.

Most can.

If you are playing one of the nationalities which can Deploy, and you start with 1 to 10 squads, one of them can be exchanged for two half squads when you are setting up.   You don't have to do this, but you can.

If you have 11 to 20 squads, you can exchange one or two squads for two or four half squads if you decide to Deploy.

And so on.

You can also do this with each turn's reinforcements if you like.

So rule A2.9 allows automatic Deployment upon setting up at start forces and reinforcements.

To Deploy during play, a squad needs to be stacked with a Leader and pass a Task Check during the Rally Phase of its player turn (A1.31).

The automatic Deployment on setup does not require the presence of a Leader or a Task Check.

title: Desperation Morale
raw_question:
If 2 FP attacks a broken unit in a stone building and rolls a 2 resulting in a NMC which the unit then passes, is the broken unit now DM?

I ask this because if the attacker cowers, then there is not an opportunity for a NMC result on the 1 FP column.

10.62 DESPERATION MORALE (DM): DM is a condition
which afflicts any unit during the Player Turn it breaks (even if it
breaks voluntarily) or any already broken unit which is subsequently attacked by CC/WP, or enough FP (taking the possibility of Cowering into account) to possibly inflict at least a NMC result on the target
ground_truth_answer:
Put another way, there are thirty-six possible DRs on the IFT. Write them all down. For all those DR combinations, write next to it the result you would have gotten on the IFT for this particular attack. For a given combination if cowering would have applied (because the attacking firegroup was susceptible) then write down the adjusted result. If any of the results you wrote was a NMC or better, the target is marked with DM. If all the results you wrote are PTC or NE, the broken target is not marked with DM.

If the firing comes from a fire group susceptible to cowering, does it have to be accounted for the different combinations or Random Selection, including rolling doubles in the RS? The rules of ASL should take this possibility into account, lest they are viewed as somewhat shaggy.
The random selection for marking the unit for cowering does not affect the FP for the attack, if that is what you are thinking. When the firegroup cowers the attack FP drops two columns if Inexperienced Personnel are participating, even if those units are not selected by any Random Selection. Otherwise the firegroup attack FP drops one column, again independent of who is selected by any Random Selection. There is no need to consider the Random Selection when looking at the possible results.

ground_truth_answer:
But I still have two questions: From the above, can we deduce that "normally" the bocage hexside and its "conversion" into a "Single-Story house" produces one more blind hex in addition to those an observer at a one higher level would normally have? For example, three blind hexes seven hexagons away? Or—as I think—does it only produce that one hex?

There should be no more blind hexes for bocage than for other obstacles. But perhaps what is meant by "range" is confusing? In any event here is a bocage and a building at seven-hex range from a second-level hill. 

LOS is clear from 00M5 to 00T3 & 00T5 because those are the obstacle hexes. 00U3 is the first blind hex for the building, and 00V3 is the second blind hex. Likewise 00U6 is the first blind hex from the bocage, and 00V5 is a second blind hex. All of hexrow W would be visible to a unit on the second-level hill of 00M5.

BTW, as I said I understand the issue of "converting to a Single-Story house", but I don't understand what it's meant to represent in the real world. What could it mean if, being at different heights, you could see the hex immediately after the bocage but not the next one?

Any units in 00T5 would be at the roots of the line of trees on top of the bocage. As the unit on the hill raised its eyes to look farther it would be looking through the branches and leaves of those trees to see beyond, so LOS would be blocked until it raised its eyes beyond the top of those trees. That gives a number of blind hexes, i.e. hexes where the LOS has to pass through the branches and leaves of trees planted on the bocage mound.

ground_truth_answer:
My question is, when can a routing unit follow a path that is not the shortest in MF (with the intent of avoiding Interdiction) to reach its destination hex? I'm a little confused by the wording in 10.51 that says "[a unit] need not take the shortest route, but as long as it follows the shortest path in MF otherwise (my italics) it may enter a shellhole / entrenchment / pillbox to avoid Interdiction...". But can the unit enter other terrain to get to its destination hex if this causes it to not take the shortest route?

For example, I have a unit that must Rout and the only valid destination is a Woods hex two hexes away; the shortest path to the destination is 3MF, into an Open hex and then into the Woods, but it would be subject to Interdiction in the Open hex in this case. But it can also get to the Woods hex through a Grain hex, but that makes the total path cost 3.5MF. Can it go through the grain to void Interdiction?
This will depend in a couple of ways. First the alternate rout path must be legal, e.g. it can't involve moving closer to known, armed enemy unit or ADJACENT to one. In your example if the path through open ground did not involve moving closer but the path through grain did, the path through grain could not be used. Second if not using shellholes/entrenchments and/or if using shellholes/entrenchments but not following the otherwise shortest path, the broken unit must reach its rout target. Continuing with your example if the broken unit has enough MF to reach the rout target through open ground but not through the grain then the path through grain could not be used. Because you have put the rout target so close that is not the case for your example unless the routing unit were a broken, wounded leader. In your example a broken wounded leader would be forced to use the open ground because that is the only way it could reach the woods. If both the open ground hex and the grain hex contained foxholes, the broken, wounded leader could rout into the foxhole in open ground even though that would prevent it from reaching the woods but it could not rout into the foxhole in the grain. A broken MMC could rout through the foxhole in either hex unless it was a walking-wounded MMC (a feature of some campaign games).

ground_truth_answer:
A stack contains only concealed units and dummy counters.  Sniper attack is a 1-2 and that hex is selected.  Regardless of which unit is selected by Random Selection, do all units lose concealment and elimination of dummies? OR does only the selected unit lose concealment? 

Only the unit attacked, but it must be in LOS of a Good Order enemy unit within 16 hexes.  

It's not clear from the RB itself but if you look at the Concealment Loss/Gain table, under Note A, you'll find  '...or is attacked by a Sniper dr (A14.3)....'

The table applies to individual units; the stack itself isn't attacked by the A14.3 dr (barring an unfortunate random selection roll), only a unit within it.

JR,
I could be misreading this, but per A14.23 if there are dummy counters and real, it would seem the dummies are eliminated and the real units are then subject to random selection, or am I missing something.  Here is the rule in question:

14.23 CONCEALED TARGETS: If the eligible possible targets include
both concealed and unconcealed units, treat the concealed stack as one pos-
sible target (regardless of how many units it actually contains) for Random
Selection purposes. Then, if a concealed stack is chosen as the sniper’s tar-
get (either per the above Random Selection or if all units are concealed), the
sniper player’s opponent must declare the number (only) of eligible possible
targets that stack contains. If it contains none (i.e., is a Dummy stack), it is

Yeah, I do not think the Dummies are removed, unless it is only Dummies.
1. Concealed stack is chosen as Sniper target.
2. Number of targets announced. 
3. If zero targets, remove the Dummy stack. Otherwise, do nothing with the Dummies.
4. If at least one target, roll Random Selection on the targets.

ground_truth_answer:
One of the many, many things in ASL I can’t get my hands around is infantry with small arms fire (non-ordnance) vs. an unarmored vehicle using the star row on the IFT. What DRMs, if any, come into play (e.g., terrain, hindrances, vehicle size, moving or not moving)?       

Any DRM that appear on the IFT and apply to vehicles. This is perhaps not spelled out as directly as it could be, but A7.308 says that such attacks "are resolved on the ★ Vehicle line of the IFT using the same IFT DR (after any applicable modification) for any Personnel target in the same Location."

Some ways in which the IFT DRM differ from TH DR and also from IFT DRM vs. Infantry: FFMO & FFNAM to not apply (because those apply to Infantry only), an overstacking DRM does not apply [A5.132] and neither target size or moving are DRM for the IFT (nor affect FP). TEM generally applies, although for instance shellholes apply to Infantry only. Hindrances apply (always, I believe). 

Great answer, but also lends me an opportunity to wax philosophical regarding "rules."

In a few years, we will have progressed to the point where we realize that asking humans to read rules to play a game, especially very long and complex rulebooks, will be as outdated as the horse and carriage. Or as outdated as asking them to write a C++ or Java program to achive some goal. Yes, I said it. 

What's needed for ASL really is countless examples of play, saying what can be done, and which tables to use. And flowcharts, much like the great routing flowchart from Texas ASL.

In this case, you realize "I want to shoot at that jeep / truck with a unit riding in it, what are my options, and what do I do? And how are the effects adjudicated and applied?" You don't want to read rules. You want a clear example showing a number of options, and telling you how to resolve based on the options chosen.

Rules are for computers (just like programs are), not people.

You guys will see that in just a few years (especially with the advances in AI) I will be proven right.

Getting a ruleset as massive as ASL's "correct and complete and usable" is a nearly impossible and certainly gargantuan task. Especially the "usable" part.

I see the error in your statement. It becomes quite obvious when you realize that your question is "Should I shoot at etc etc".

As already mentioned, if the vehicle was a moving target [C.8] it is not a TEM until at the end of the following APh [D9.3] Also a burning wreck does not give a +1 TEM [D9.3]. The TEM of a non-burning wreck would be cumulative with SMOKE in the hex, but a burning wreck provides no TEM, only Smoke.

You can always place one trench in a barbed wire or roadblock hex, which allows infantry units to move freely through those obstacles, whether friendly or enemy troops (if they manage to enter the trench). Correct?

For this one trench is typically not enough. A trench in a wire hex allows a unit to move under the wire to under the trench if it is moving from trench-to-trench [B27.54], e.g. from under an adjacent trench, from a bunker or from a lower-level Location to a friendly-controlled trench [B27.6]. If the unit is not moving trench-to-trench it enters above the wire. Unless there is a bunker or a lower-level Location to a friendly-controlled trench, you need two trenches to enable trench-to-trench movement.

One could have two trenches, one on each side of a roadblock, to allow infantry to move "under" that roadblock without crossing the roadblock by moving trench-to-trench [B27.54]. A single trench is not enough.

Unlike something like a foxhole, the protection a unit gets from crest status is directional. If the target is shot from the front (with some other conditions) it gets a +2 TEM. Similarly, from the first floor of G3 you would also see B0 (since the crest of C1 is only 4 hexes away).

Even if it were five hexes away (e.g. as you suggested above the building moved from G3-H3 to H3-I4) a unit at building level one (in H3, absolute level three) could see B0 over C1 because the number of blind hexes behind a crest line in reduced by one [B10.23] for being a crest line, and the viewer is two full levels above the obstacle [B6.42]. The full blind hex calculation is: C1 has one blind hex to level zero behind it (its top is one level higher than the target) plus one for range to obstacle from H3 [A6.41] minus one for being a crest line [B10.23] minus one for the viewer being two full levels above the obstacle height [B6.42], for a net zero blind hexes.

In contract if C1 were a woods at level zero and LOS were traced from level one G3 again, the calculation would be one blind hex not increased by range and decreased by extra full level to zero but always a minimum of one blind hex per B6.42.

I arrived late but that's what I wanted to say regarding the half level obstacles: "I understand why M6 is visible from H3: L5 has a height of 1.5 (because of the houses in the hex) while M6 is only level 1 but a half-level obstacle never creates blind hexes". L5 is not a level one-and-a-half obstacle. It is only a level one obstacle [B23.21]. A building has to be multi-hex [B23.22], have a large white hex center [B31.3] or a steeple [B31.1] to be higher than level one. Though you are correct that if L5 were a level 1.5 obstacle it would still not block LOS from H3 to M6. As you say, relative to M6 a level one-and-a-half obstacle in L5 would only be a half level above M6, and that would not be a large enough difference to form a blind hex.

query:
Marked with a counter vs. being in a state: This originally came to me via a direct message. Although the rules are fairly casual about it, being marked with a counter is not necessarily equivalent to being in a particular state. I was asked recently about a unit that fired its MG in the PFPh, kept ROF and didn't fire its inherent. If you follow the mechanics it is not marked with a Prep Fire counter. Can it move? Can it fire again in the AFPh? Per A4.1, "During his MPh, the ATTACKER may move all, some, or none of his Infantry units provided they did not fire during the PFPh." For game purposes the marking with the Prep Fire counter is a reminder, not a rule. Most players will mark such a unit with the appropriate counter anyway, just to avoid confusion. A7.1, "no unit can fire its inherent FP/SW/Gun in more than one fire phase (A.15) per Player Turn." A.15 allows a unit to fire in both the enemy MPh as DFF and in the friendly DFPh. So no fire in the AFPh, whether you choose to mark the unit or not.

A.12, "All counters printed on a white background can be used by any nationality and are often informational or memory devices only." The rules don't explain this in any more detail nor say which are purely memory devices only and which are not, but it is my belief that Prep Fire counters are among the memory devices. A unit that fires in the PFPh can't move not because it is marked with the counter, but because of A4.1. Many of the rules are written casually as if being marked with a particular counter is equivalent to its state, but it's not necessarily true.

Without concealment on the part of some unit present, unless another circumstance such as Streefighting applies, this isn't an ambush situation so no need to roll for it. Street Fighting A11.8: The second to last statement in A11.8 reads like this -

"Any vehicle in stationary Bypass or using VBM is also subject to Street Fighting rules from any Infantry in the Bypassed obstacle of their hex."  

Underline added for emphasis

3.  And the Infantry is not stated to be in a building (simply a "bypassed obstacle")

title: Street Fighting A11.8
raw_question:
The second to last statement in A11.8 reads like this -

"Any vehicle in stationary Bypass or using VBM is also subject to Street Fighting rules from any Infantry in the Bypassed obstacle of their hex."  

Underline added for emphasis

I note the following about this sentence -

2. The subject vehicle is NOT stated to be in a road hex straddled by buildings
3.  And the Infantry is not stated to be in a building (simply a "bypassed obstacle")

So, when I read this sentence, it implies to me that any Infantry in an obstacle bypassable by a vehicle (building/woods/light jungle/et. al.), even a single hex stand of woods out in the middle of an open field, can invoke "Street Fighting" to conduct "CC Reaction Fire" in its DFF and/or gain the "Street Fighting Ambush" drm in its CC phase against an enemy vehicle bypassing the hex it occupies (regardless of the presence of buildings/road).

What say the gurus?
ground_truth_answer:
Why would the squad be frozen, JR? It doesn't say in 11.8 "...and following any CC attack returned to the same locations they came from."
"VBM Sleaze Freeze" is an action by the vehicle owner during his MPh. It refers to the tactic of moving a vehicle into a Location containing enemy units, which prevents the enemy units from using DFF outside the Location due to A7.212. After he has driven his vehicle in and ended its MPh in the Location, the enemy units are "frozen" i.e. they can't make DFF attacks outside their own Location. This can be done by entering the Location proper, but against enemy units in woods/buildings this is often done by entering the hex in Bypass. The vehicle is still in the same Location, invoking A7.212, but it doesn't have to pay the usually high MPs to enter the terrain and doesn't have to take a Bog check.

There are a number of counter-moves to VBM sleaze freeze. Obviously the units in the Location can use CC-RF, and if the vehicle has used Bypass the vehicle is subject to "street fighting ambush" even though it is not in a road Location with buildings on either side, the point of the comment on the matter. And my reply was that also CC-RF did benefit from the -1 street-fighting-ambush DRM, if the vehicle did not stop that DRM would be combined with the +2 non-stopped DRM. Another possible tactic is to fire at the vehicle (even if it is a BU, CT vehicle) before it enters the Location so as to leave Residual. Other ways to avoid VBM sleaze freeze include having some kind of ordnance or other AT capability in the to-be-frozen Location or nearby, e.g. PF, MOL, MG, a true A-T Gun, etc. Because a bypassing vehicle has a wider side armor facing these can often benefit from hitting the side armor and not the front. None of these countermeasures will guarantee that VBM sleaze freeze is ineffective, but they do give a risk to the maneuver. 

VBM sleaze freeze does not refer to the enemy entering the vehicle's Location using proper street fighting, which is when friendly infantry enter a road Location between two buildings.

Also the leader bonus MF are the last MF spent. You can't say you are spending the leader bonus MF first to avoid losing them something bad happens to the leader.

That may be true in effect, but it is not stated that way in A4.12. The rule paragraph begins "Any Good Order MMC which begins the MPh/APh and ends its MPh/APh stacked with a leader of the same nationality in the same Location..." So, if (and only if) the MMC begins and ends the phase stacked with the leader, it has 2 extra MF to spend. If the leader were KIA'd in the 4th hex of a 6 hex open ground path planned to be traversed by the stack, the MMC couldn't move to the next hex in the path. If the leader KIA were to occur in the 6th hex of the path, then they all "got there."

ground_truth_answer: C1.7 FIRE MISSION: A Fire Mission consists of the entire time between Battery Access chit draws in which a FFE is on board. There are seven types of Fire Missions. The first is the HE Concentration and the second the SMOKE Concentration (1.71), the Blast Area for both of which is defined in 1.32. The other types are Harassing Fire (1.72), IR (E1.93), Barrage (E12.1), SMOKE Barrage (E12.51) and Creeping Barrage (E12.7). A Fire Mission cannot be of more than one type; e.g. if a battery uses a HE Concentration in its FFE:1 stage, it cannot switch to Harassing Fire or SMOKE, etc., in its FFE:2 stage.

If you are feeling lucky, Ordnance Are Fire can be entertaining. But there's no acquisition.
Ordnance Area Fire *may* result in acquisition. It depends on the cause for Area Fire and the target type. The most common cause of Area Fire is probably concealment, and if you use the Area Target Type or the attack strips concealment, acquisition is gained [C6.57]. Okay, now you have got me. Thinking about acq markers sitting in the middle of the street because the dasher ran out of LoS.
The second step of a dash need not be out-of-LOS [A4.63]. It only needs to be not Open Ground. If it is out-of-LOS and the dash unit does not pin or break on some attack then of course the acquisition would remain in the street, but if the second step is in LOS and/or the dashing unit pins or breaks, the acquisition will be effective.

raw_question:
During the MPh, if an attacking vehicle receives a Motion Status (it entered a new hex/hexside during that Player Turn) but spends one MP to stop, does it immediately cancel the Motion status, hence the Case C⁴ Motion Firer DRM?
As from C 5.35 it seems so.

C 5.35 CASE C4; MOTION FIRER: A Motion/Non-Stopped vehicle which is moving and wishes to fire without stopping first, must add the applicable DRM of Case C⁴ to its To Hit DR.

However the confusing part comes from D 2.13

ground_truth_answer:
During the MPh, if an attacking vehicle receives a Motion Status (it entered a new hex/hexside during that Player Turn) but spends one MP to stop, does it immediately cancel the Motion status, hence the Case C⁴ Motion Firer DRM?

"Motion status" [D2.4] is a technical term for a vehicle not during its MPh that has not expended a Stop MP since its last Start MP and has not become Bogged/Immobilized. It is a state the vehicle is in only outside its own MPh. So for instance a vehicle that begins its MPh stopped, expends a Start MP, moves one hex (for example), then expends a Stop MP is never in Motion status. Between when the Start MP is spent and when the Stop MP is spent it is "non-Stopped." If it uses BFF during its MPh it would use case C⁴ when non-Stopped and not use it when Stopped. When using BFF a vehicle is never in Motion because BFF occurs during its MPh. For your example you only mention states during the vehicle's MPh, and Motion status is not defined during that vehicle's MPh.

As from C 5.35 it seems so.

C 5.35 CASE C4; MOTION FIRER: A Motion/Non-Stopped vehicle which is moving and wishes to fire without stopping first, must add the applicable DRM of Case C⁴ to its To Hit DR.

However the confusing part comes from D 2.13

D 2.13 STOPPING: A vehicle must expend one additional MP in its current hex to stop movement...Even though stopped, the vehicle is considered a moving target if it entered a new hex/hexside during that Player Turn or began its MPh in Motion.

So the same vehicle would be considered as a stopped vehicle when firing, but as a moving target against a Defensive Fire? A stopped firer, but moving target?
Yes a vehicle that has expended a Stop MP would be considered a Stopped vehicle, i.e. one that C⁴ does not apply to. But BFF would still be  subject to the other case C DRM (C, C¹ or C², which then invoke case B). The vehicle might be a C.8 Moving Target while being a D3.3 Stopped firer.

There are at least four pairs of technical terms used in ASL for various aspects  "moving." First is "Motion"/"not in Motion".  This is something that is defined only outside the vehicle's MPh. Second is "Stopped"/"not Stopped". This is something that is defined only during the vehicle's MPh. Third is "Moving Target"/"not Moving Target". These are defined both in and not in the vehicle's MPh. Finally there is "moving"/"not moving". "Moving" in this sense is not formally defined but seems to mean something like, "currently conducting its MPh." These four pairs of "moving" terms are only somewhat interrelated, and it is possible for a unit to be in the movement-related state for one of them but not in the movement-related state for another. For example the example vehicle that I described above that spent a start MP,, moved a hex then spent a Stop MP would be a C.8 Moving Target until the beginning of the RtPh but would be a Stopped vehicle for the remainder of its MPh and a "not in Motion" vehicle after its MPh.

It is a mistake to try to relate the ASL technical terms to the non-technical meaning of those words. Doing so only leads to confusion. Within the context of the rules you have to stick to the defined (or in the case of "moving," undefined but implied) technical meaning.
