When firing on the ITT the vehicle is not specifically targeted, so any attack would be a general collateral attack. Even though the vehicle can't be affected [C3.32], if the vehicle is hit any PRC on the vehicle are attacked as a general collateral attack. The vehicle would not only have to be targeted first, but it would also have to be specifically targeted. Specific collateral attacks occur when one vehicle is specifically targeted (and other units in the Location/hex are not). The most common case would be using the VTT, but LATW using their own TH Table (e.g. BAZ, PF, PSK) may also be specifically targeting the vehicle, and FTs can specifically target an AFV [A22.6.12].

For the purposes of the effects the two different types of collateral are the same. The difference is which units are attacked and which units are not attacked.

query:
Assault Movement: There have been a number of posts I have read recently that suggest some players are misinformed about Assault Movement. Since Assault Movement is bread-and-butter ASL―it is not very common that you would play a scenario without using Assault Movement at some point—I thought it might be a good idea to go through the mechanics.

Mechanics
All movement is done by picking the unit or stack to move, declaring and executing an expenditure and waiting for the completion of DFF. After the completion of an expenditure, if the unit/stack can continue making expenditures and wants to, the player may repeat the process until no more expenditures are allowed or desired. This does not change with Assault Movement. Assault Movement adds a few restrictions. With Assault Movement the unit/stack cannot become or have been PRC, at most one of the MF expenditures can be for a change of Location (hex in ASLSK), and the total MF expended must be strictly less than than the unit's available MF, with bonuses such as road movement or leadership bonus included, but disallowing Double Time. The declaration for Assault Movement has to be done before expending any MF, and the effects (e.g. no FFNAM) remain in effect until the end of the move unless Assault Movement is voided, e.g. going berserk or breaking. Assault Movement cannot be cancelled voluntarily.

Some Observations
A unit using Assault Movement can make any number of MF expenditures in any order as long as it does not violate the restrictions for Assault Movement. For example it can recover SW, place DC or smoke grenades or enter/leave entrenchments, possibly in addition to changing Location.

The expenditures do not have to pre-designated. A unit can wait to see the result of the recovery dr before declaring it will place the DC it is trying to recover. Likewise a unit might move into one Location in a subsequent expenditure if it successfully places a smoke grenade but into a different one (or end its MPh) if it does not. In both cases the player could wait until he sees the results of the first expenditure before making (or not making) the second.

Costs for making an expenditure or the total move do not change when using Assault Movement. The MF spent in Assault Movement are *not* ALL, nor (automatically) one-less-than-all nor any fixed number.

Although changing Locations using Assault Movement does not cause concealment loss unless done in A10.531 Open Ground, declaring Assault Movement does not negate concealment loss caused by expenditures made for anything besides movement. Making an expenditure for smoke grenade placement, recovery or DC placement for example cause concealment loss even if done as part of Assault Movement.

A Quick Example
A MMC in a foxhole moving as a stack with an unwounded leader can expend one MF to recover a DC in its entrenchment (one MF), place smoke grenades in its own Location (one MF), exit its foxhole (one MF), enter the adjacent Open Ground hex (one MF) and enter the foxhole in it (one MF). Each expenditure would be done separately, and each would allow intervening DFF.

Last Observation
A unit can't declare Assault Movement then get one extra MF by declaring Late Double Time. Nice try.

Does anyone who may be lurking have insight into why the ASL design team decided that it was beyond the capability of an unassisted American 1st line squad to toss smoke grenades into the adjacent street hex (2MF) and then move into that hex (2MF) as Assault Movement?
I'm guessing it was just a game design decision that made an interesting game mechanic. ASL is all about making tough decisions, all the time. If a lone MMC could place Smoke into an adjacent hex and still have 2 MF left using Assault Movement, we would see tons more Smoke attempts every turn. If you'd fail, you would still have 2 MF left to maybe move to an adjacent building location. As opposed to now, if you fail, now there's no Smoke in the street and you have 1 MF left... what are you going to do now then? Just stay in place? Risk it and Assault Move into the street anyway?

Reasonable. But let's not forget there's always a 1/6 chance of ending your movement phase immediately anyway if you roll the dreaded 6. (To my mind, just another rule to discourage making smoke all the time.)

If you had two squads and one has an 8 morale, and a decent smoke exponent, you could try:

1. declare assault move and move the 6-6-8 (or whatever) into the street for 1 MF
2. survive DFF at -1 FFMO (this is iffy, but not as iffy as -2 FFMO + FFNAM)
3. spend 1 MF to attempt to place smoke in your own (middle of the street) hex (possibly provoking SFF*)
4. don't roll a 6
5. if successful, whistle to the 6-6-6 squad you were originally stacked with to assault move into the street with you (2 MF), under cover of the smoke

* If the smoke grenade placement 1 MF expenditure provokes SFF and is successful, is the incoming SFF shot affected by the +2 Smoke DRM? (That is, does the SFF shot come before or after the smoke appears?) In either case, can the defender decide whether to fire only after seeing the result of the smoke grenade attempt?

ground_truth_answer:
"Immobilized" is not a factor. There is a q&a that could be applied here:
A7.4 & D5.4
Is an abandoned vehicle still a unit? If it is a unit, is a previously friendly vehicle which was abandoned still a friendly unit, thus preventing another friendly unit to fire on it? If it is not a unit, may an abandoned vehicle be fired upon?
A. An Abandoned vehicle is a unit, but it is neither friendly nor enemy and can be attacked by either side.

Since it is not an enemy unit, it would presumably not be an enemy AFV, and so D2.6 would not apply.

A squad wants to move from the plain Trench hex into the Bunker in the adjacent hex. Can it move directly (either by regular movement or Assault Movement) into the Pillbox\Bunker, or must it spend a separate movement point in the Bunker's Trench first (potentially undergoing DFF in the Trench) before safely arriving in the Bunker (where, if the only defensive firers are outside the CA of the Pillbox, it would be immune to DFF)?

The uncertainty in my mind arises from the wording in B30.8 (even though B30.33 is quite clear that the MF expenditure to enter/exit the Pillbox is a separate expenditure), which applies to a Bunker even if only in an Accessible hex to a Trench. In that case, there could be a Trench hex adjacent to the Pillbox hex, and it would still be a Bunker and "a unit may move... between a bunker and such a trench as if the bunker were also a trench." If that implies a move between the adjacent trench hex and the Pillbox in one go, it seems weird that if the Pillbox also has a trench in its own hex, it's a separate expenditure.

The meta here is the annoying habit the ASL rules have of treating seemingly similar terrain features differently. Imagine explaining to a new player that, even though when he moves from an Open Ground hex to an adjacent hex containing a tiny single-story wooden house in the center, he is immediately in the wooden house for DFF purposes, but when he moves from a trench hex to an adjacent trench hex that also has a Pillbox in it, he must traverse another part of the hex (namely the trench) first before being "inside" the pillbox.

ground_truth_answer:
Imagine Trench A (in hex A) is adjacent to Trench B (in hex B) and in the Trench B hex there is a Pillbox, which is then a Bunker. But now, imagine that there is an unpossessed SW in Trench B.

1. Can a squad in Trench A move directly into the Bunker in hex B using assault movement, without undergoing DFF in hex B except when already inside the Bunker? The consensus here seems to be: yes.

As above, yes.

2a. Can a non-CX 1st line squad in Trench A move into the Bunker in hex B using assault movement, while also spending 1 MF to pick up the SW in Trench B along the way? (It certainly has enough MF to do so: 1 + 1 + 1.)

2b. If yes to 2a, would the moving squad be subject to DFF in trench B?

No, the unit may not make such a move as Assault Move. There are a number of problems here. In order to recover the SW the moving unit would have to enter the trench Location [A4.44]. In your proposed move it would then move to the Pillbox/bunker, which is a second Location [B30.1] in the hex. That would not be possible using Assault Movement, which allows a change of at most one Location [A4.46].

This could be done as normal movement (and FFNAM does not apply for movement in a trench [B27.54]), but each of the moves (into the trench, recovery, into the pillbox) would be a separate MF expenditure. Each MF expenditure would allow DFF [A8.1]. 

Looking beyond what you are asking I think you may be under the impression that Assault Movement somehow fundamentally changes the way movement is conducted. The mechanics of movement do not change for Assault Movement; the unit makes separate MF expenditures and awaits DFF as normal. Assault Movement means that at most one of those MF expenditures can be for Location change. For example a squad stacked with a leader might use Assault Movement and expend one MF to place Smoke grenades in their own Location (expenditure one), expend one MF to leave a Foxhole (expenditure two), expend one MF to enter the ADJACENT Open Ground hex (expenditure three), attempt to recover a one PP SW in the new Location (expenditure four) and finally enter a Foxhole in the new hex (expenditure five). Each of these expenditures would be announced and performed separately and would allow DFF before the moving player continued. As far as movement mechanics are concerned, the only difference is that the unit can only make one MF expenditure to enter a new Location.

In the game, I was quite sure that 1 was correct (despite my not arguing the point too hard with my opponent). I also thought both 2a and 2b were true, and so I told my opponent (after discussing this possibility with him) that I wanted to move directly into the bunker, without stopping along the way to attempt to recover the SW. But, as stated elsewhere, my opponent did not agree with point 1, so even making the more conservative move, I never got into that bunker.

A concealed German squad advances into a Location occupied by an unconcealed US squad. The German chooses not to attack in CC, staying concealed. The US squad attacks in CC, no effect. 

It is now the next turn and the US MPh. If the US squad does not move from the Location, does this automatically remove the German squad’s concealment? 

I have an inkling that because the US squad legally ended its MPh in the same Location as the German squad, this strips concealment…as with a Berserk unit charging into an enemy’s Location, a vehicle in bypass, and possibly other cases. I tried to find a relevant rule, no joy.

You may be thinking of A8.312, where a unit is required to attack an enemy MMC that enters its Location during the MPh. In this case A8.312 does not apply because the German unit did not enter during the MPh. The loss of concealment is not inherently due to the entry but rather due to the required attack. If the only unit with LOS is, say, the Berserk unit performing a charge, concealment would not be lost because the Berserk unit is not Good Order and so can't force concealment loss. In your situation the German would remain concealed until something else  happened. 

The only time I can think of where the presence of an enemy unit strips concealment at the end of the MPh is a vehicle bypassing and ending its MPh in the hex [A12.42].

query: Placing smoke with OBA, Ordnance: When placing smoke with OBA, Ordnance you only have to roll on the To Hit Table/Area (Mortar, SMOKE)-row with range up to the hex where you want to place it, correct? No further roll needed, I suppose?
title: Placing smoke with OBA, Ordnance
raw_question: When placing smoke with OBA, Ordnance you only have to roll on the To Hit Table/Area (Mortar, SMOKE)-row with range up to the hex where you want to place it, correct? No further roll needed, I suppose?
ground_truth_answer:
With regard to DRM for firing SMOKE you are getting into an area where game mechanics meet reality. From a pure "reality" standpoint, there's no reason why a SMOKE round would be affected by a moving vehicle or a concealed unit in the area. The firing unit would decide that a SMOKE round is needed in a particular place and fire it. But from game perspective the "coincidental" fact that there is a concealed unit in that hex sounds suspiciously like the player is using his game knowledge (i.e. the existence of a large stack under a "?" counter) that the real life firing unit would not have. Likewise with a moving vehicle the fact that the game holds the counter in a hex for the enemy player turn means the player is using the game mechanics (i.e. the existence of player turns) to try to hobble a target unit for much longer than the few seconds that it would take the moving vehicle to drive through that SMOKE. There's no way for the rules to determine whether the real unit would have made those SMOKE placement attempts that the player made or not. Since this is a game and not a simulation the solution is to allow the attempts but penalize them by applying DRM for trying to hit units. The rules basically assume the player is up to no good and using his knowledge from the game mechanics that the real life firing unit would not be able to use.

You can compare, for instance, firing SMOKE at a hex with a concealed unit vs firing at a hex with a HIP unit. In the latter case the player's information matches that of the firing unit and there is no game penalty. In the former case it seems suspicious that the player has selected the hex with the concealed unit, and it is possible and perhaps likely that he is using information the real unit would not have.

Another place where game mechanics meet reality is OBA. The player has to make an extra chit draw when there is a reason the player would choose a hex for OBA but there is no reason the real observer would choose that hex [C1.21].

query:
HoB - Surrender Question: 7-0 German Leader rolls a 12 for his HoB DR. However, there is a Berserk Russian in the same hex. What is the result? NQ has not been declared. It is the Russian MPh.

title: HoB - Surrender Question
raw_question:
7-0 German Leader rolls a 12 for his HoB DR. However, there is a Berserk Russian in the same hex. What is the result? NQ has not been declared. It is the Russian MPh.

I “think” the 7-0 leader breaks and is disrupted and will rout in the next RtPh.
ground_truth_answer:
I agree with JR V.

A.7 GOOD ORDER: This term refers to a Personnel unit/inherent crew which is not broken, berserk, captured, stunned, shocked, or held in Melee. ...

A15.5 SURRENDER: A Final Heat of Battle DR ≥ 12 causes the affected unit to become broken if it is not already, and Disrupted (19.12), and to Surrender immediately to any ADJACENT Known Good Order armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry as if they shared the same Location. If no such enemy unit is ADJACENT, the unit is only Disrupted instead [EXC: Units subject to No Quarter, Japanese, Gurkhas, Partisans, Fanatics, and Commissars never surrender by the RtPh method nor do SS vs Russians (20.21); nor do they become Disrupted whether thusly ADJACENT or not. They instead become berserk on a Final Heat of Battle DR ≥ 12].
Is the German leader SS?

A19.12 DISRUPTION: ... Unless rallied by a leader first, a Disrupted unit will surrender at the start of any RtPh it begins ADJACENT to, or during any phase it occupies the same Location as, a Good Order armed Known enemy Personnel unit not in Melee [EXC: No Quarter 20.3]. ...

A10.5 ROUTING: During the RtPh a broken unit not in Melee may not remain in the same Open Ground hex in the Normal Range (10.532) and LOS of a Known non-Melee enemy unit/its-SW/Gun, nor—regardless of terrain—may it end a RtPh ADJACENT to or in the same Location with a Known enemy unit that is both unbroken and armed [EXC: Night; E1.54]. ... Broken units must rout away (ATTACKER first—one unit at a time [EXC: Voluntary Rout; 10.711]) during that RtPh or be eliminated for Failure to Rout [EXC: Surrender; 20.21]. ...

A10.51 DIRECTION:  ... A routing unit may never move ADJACENT to a Known enemy unit, unless in doing so it is leaving that enemy unit’s Location. ...

A20.21 RtPh: Any broken Infantry unit during its RtPh that is both ADJACENT to Known, Good Order, armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry and unable to rout away from it or only able to rout while being subject to Interdiction or resorting to Low Crawl (regardless of how it actually routs or if the possible unconcealed Interdictor is Known to it), will surrender to that enemy unit as its prisoner instead, (captor’s choice of unit receiving surrender if more than one unit qualifies) after first abandoning all its SW [EXC: if pinned; 10.53 & G5.5]. A stack of broken units in a Location surrenders simultaneously and must be accepted or rejected (20.3) as a stack. If there are not enough Guards for all such surrendering units, the excess units (captor’s choice) are freed as Unarmed (20.5). Surrendering units are not subject to FFE or minefield attacks. If the only adjacent armed enemy unit is in-Melee/berserk/vehicular, the broken unit must rout away (even if Disrupted) or be eliminated for Failure to Rout—such elimination does not incur No Quarter penalties. If the broken unit is also Disrupted, Encircled, or surrendering due to a Heat of Battle DR (15.5), it will instead rout to that enemy unit as its prisoner even if it had a legal rout path not requiring Interdiction or Low Crawl. Partisans (25.24), Gurkhas (25.43), Commissars (25.22), SS troops facing Russians (25.11), Fanatics (10.8), Japanese and units faced with No Quarter (20.3) never surrender via the RtPh method; they always use Low Crawl or risk Interdiction to avoid surrender. If unable to do any of these, they are eliminated rather than surrender.

----------------------------------

BTW, I think A20.21 is written out of order, and can lead to wrong conclusions. The fifth sentence is meant to be read in opposition to the first sentence. And it appears that the fourth sentence can be negated by the fifth sentence, but I doubt that's intended. I believe this rule would be improved if written in this order:

A20.21 RtPh: Any broken Infantry unit during its RtPh that is both ADJACENT to Known, Good Order, armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry and unable to rout away from it or only able to rout while being subject to Interdiction or resorting to Low Crawl (regardless of how it actually routs or if the possible unconcealed Interdictor is Known to it), will surrender to that enemy unit as its prisoner instead, (captor’s choice of unit receiving surrender if more than one unit qualifies) after first abandoning all its SW [EXC: if pinned; 10.53 & G5.5]. If the broken unit is also Disrupted, Encircled, or surrendering due to a Heat of Battle DR (15.5), it will instead rout to that enemy unit as its prisoner even if it had a legal rout path not requiring Interdiction or Low Crawl.  if the only adjacent armed enemy unit is in-Melee/berserk/vehicular, the broken unit must rout away (even if Disrupted) or be eliminated for Failure to Rout—such elimination does not incur No Quarter penalties. Partisans (25.24), Gurkhas (25.43), Commissars (25.22), SS troops facing Russians (25.11), Fanatics (10.8), Japanese and units faced with No Quarter (20.3) never surrender via the RtPh method; they always use Low Crawl or risk Interdiction to avoid surrender. If unable to do any of these, they are eliminated rather than surrender. A stack of broken units in a Location surrenders simultaneously and must be accepted or rejected (20.3) as a stack. If there are not enough Guards for all such surrendering units, the excess units (captor’s choice) are freed as Unarmed (20.5). Surrendering units are not subject to FFE or minefield attacks.

For clarity, here is my reordered paragraph with subsidiary clauses removed:

A20.21 RtPh: Any broken Infantry unit that is ADJACENT to Known, Good Order, armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry and unable to rout away--or only able to rout while subject to Interdiction or resorting to Low Crawl--will surrender to that enemy unit. If the broken unit is also Disrupted, Encircled, or surrendering due to Heat of Battle, it will rout to that enemy unit even if it had a legal rout path. But if the only adjacent enemy unit is in-Melee/berserk/vehicular, the broken unit must rout away (even if Disrupted) or be eliminated for Failure to Rout.

moving target for To Hit/Effects purposes only if during the current Play-
er Turn it has entered a new hex, or used VBM (D2.3), or began its MPh in

ground_truth_answer:
We had a US HS that had Wall Advantage (WA), but what then overrun by a German StuG and pinned (not broken).  The StuG then moved across the wall and stopped.  We weren't sure if the US unit loses WA due to the OVR and, if they did, whether the StuG then gains WA when it moves across because the US unit was Pinned and both units were able to attempt to claim WA.

Or if the OVR doesn't remove WA (or the Pin doesn't)?

Note: there is NO in-hex TEM for the US HS ...
A unit cannot claim WA when it is "in a Location containing a non-hidden, non-prisoner enemy [EXC: "broken" vehicle (A12.1)] unit" [B9.32]. If it has WA when such an enemy unit enters its Location it must forfeit WA [B9.322]. When the StuG enters the Location neither unit can have WA for this same reason, OVR or not. The OVR is conducted and the DEFENDER becomes Pinned in the non-WA state. A Pinned unit may neither voluntarily claim nor forfeit WA [B9.322], but in this case WA is mandatory. When the StuG exits the hex the DEFENDER has first right to claim WA so the Pinned unit reclaims WA if otherwise allowed.  Even if the DEFENDER weren't Pinned, when the StuG exits the hex the DEFENDER cannot claim WA because it is not one of the five times that allow WA to be claimed by the DEFENDER. As it exited the StuG did not forfeit any WA, which would be the only way for the DEFENDER to claim it. On the other hand this being the StuG's MPh the StuG could claim WA as it enters the next hex assuming it is otherwise allowed.

The -1 penalty is for an immobile vehicle. Per the index immobile is, "any vehicle which is Abandoned, Bogged, Immobilized, Shocked, or Stunned." Note that "immobile" and "immobilized" are not the same thing, although a vehicle that is immobilized is immobile.

You did not mention this but I will throw it in. When a vehicle attacks infantry its MGs and/or IFE are used in ratio against the infantry's CCV, not against the printed FP. This is different from how infantry attack each other. So if a Pz IV with a five FP CMG attacks a Soviet 6-2-8, the attack is at five (CMG FP) to five (squad CCV) i.e. 1:1, not five to six.

A 50mm mortar fires at wooden building containing an enemy Gun with a crew and rolls a Critical Hit of 1,1.  It must use Area Target Type, so is not targeting the gun, it is targeting the hex.  The To Kill DR will be on the IFT Table, column 12, with a -2DRM.

As I understand it, a Gun can be a target, but it is not a unit.

As it happens, my TK DR was also a 1,1 so I think both the gun and the crew have been vaporised, but I would love someone to explain to me what the correct method should be.

Is this something that has come up many times before and I have just never seen it?  Or is it just very late and I'm not thinking straight.
ground_truth_answer:
See C11.4 (and see C3.71 for the same): "A CH automatically destroys both the Gun and its manning Infantry." You don't even need to roll for effect on the IFT, both are gone from this world.
I did read those, but because I was using ATT I didn't think it applied: I was not firing at the gun, but at the hex.  Which is why I fell into the "Random Selection" hole.
When you use ITT or ATT you are really firing at all eligible targets in the Location or Hex. For ITT in C3.32 it says that all PRC and non-AFV "in-LOS enemy units in that Location can be hit." Similarly C3.33 says, all "(including friendly) non-Aerial units in the target hex can be hit ." The text of the rules is somewhat casual about the difference between "firing at a hex," "firing at a Location" and firing at eligible targets in that hex or Location. They should be considered the same.

Similarly the rules are somewhat confusing about "firing at a Gun" and "firing at the crew manning a Gun." These again are equivalent, i.e. anything that attacks the Gun also attacks the crew of that Gun and vice-versa. For instance if inherent FP is fired at a manned Gun and its crew, if the result is a KIA then A9.74, RANDOM SW/GUN DESTRUCTION, will apply. As an aside this is also true of possessed SW, but there is no rule like C11.4 for possessed SW resulting in automatic destruction.

query: Broken infantry after overrun: Hi, I'm struggling through Khamsin desert scenario and trying to learn the effects of overruns. I'm not sure what happens to an infantry unit that was broken due to overrun and the overrunning vehicle remained in the hex. Does the infantry unit survive the Rout Phase and stay in place? Does it fight in CC phase? Can someone explain, please?
title: Broken infantry after overrun
raw_question: Hi, I'm struggling through Khamsin desert scenario and trying to learn the effects of overruns. I'm not sure what happens to an infantry unit that was broken due to overrun and the overrunning vehicle remained in the hex. Does the infantry unit survive the Rout Phase and stay in place? Does it fight in CC phase? Can someone explain, please?
ground_truth_answer:
Just apply A10.5 and A10.51.
A broken unit can get ADJACENT to a KEU only if it is leaving that KEU's Location. So the broken unit can rout away from the vehicle, notwithstanding other constraints of not getting nearer to other enemy units, etc. Note that if the broken unit ends its rout ADJACENT to the vehicle it will be eliminated for FtR, so Low Crawl is not an option. That means that the unit will be probably interdicted by other enemies, if able to.

This situation can happen with vehicles and also when berserk units or cavalry enter an enemy location during movement.

If by some situation at the start of the CCPh a broken unit is in the same Location as enemy units, the broken unit cannot fight and cannot escape. It has to wait for a Melee to be created and then it must Witdraw from Melee.

title: Night Rules +1 Attack Modifier
raw_question:
Is the +1 modifier for Night attacks applicable to Fortifications (Foxholes etc) on higher ground.
Height Advantage and the Night modifier are not both applied where a unit is outside any fortification but as the choice of Height Advantage still exists instead of use of the Foxhole modifier, I think the Night modifier would not be applied.

ground_truth_answer:
Height Advantage and the Night modifier are not both applied where a unit is outside any fortification but as the choice of Height Advantage still exists instead of use of the Foxhole modifier, I think the Night modifier would not be applied.
If a unit has height advantage [B10.31] or its possibility, that *usually* means the night LV DRM cannot apply. The unit is on terrain that is above the firer, and in most cases terrain that is one full level above the firer, which negates Night LV [E1.7]. Hillocks, where the target is ½ level above firer, explicitly denies height advantage [F6.51]. But the other case where a unit can be ½ level above the firer, rooftops, allows height advantage [B23.81]. So for rooftops it is possible to get both Night LV and Height Advantage.

But it is important to understand that Night LV denial is not keyed to the level of the *target unit*. It depends on the height of the *terrain*. The unit can be at any (legal of course) height in that terrain, and it will not affect whether Night LV applies or not. A unit in a level zero woods/orchard or the ground level of a building will not get the Night LV hindrance when fired on by an enemy unit also at level zero. The existence or absence of Fortifications and the target's status as in or out of any Fortification will not change whether Night LV applies, perhaps primarily because Fortifications do not increase the level of the terrain.

query:
Abandoned bulldozers: I recently played FT292, "Engineer Hill." It features an Abandoned, armored bulldozer. This is my attempt at a summary of the rules for such a thing.

The reason it is not obvious how such a thing should work in ASL is because bulldozers do not have crews; they have Inherent Drivers [G15.11]. Per D5.1 an Inherent Driver "never leaves the vehicle" [D5.1]. It is not possible to create an Abandoned Bulldozer by dismounting the Driver during the course of play if you start with a manned one. However per G15.111 an *unarmored* bulldozer can have its Inherent Driver killed (by small arms/MG fire), leaving it Abandoned. Presumably an armored bulldozer could have its Inherent Driver killed and become Abandoned by being attacked with sufficient elevation advantage so it is treated as unarmored [D5.311]. Abandoned bulldozers are possible, just not by using D5.4 (in general; see below about A21.21).

In this scenario the Americans start with two heroes in the same hex as the Abandoned bulldozer. The Japanese VC include CVP, a bulldozer is worth four CVP out of twenty needed for the scenario (eight CVP if captured), so the Americans would like to save the bulldozer if possible, and if not possible then to make sure it ends up destroyed. They might just attack it and be done, but there is a fair chance that they will want to insert one of the heroes as the new Driver.

Remanning a bulldozer (or other Abandoned vehicle which take an Inherent Driver)

D5.42 says, "An Infantry unit may enter an Abandoned vehicle to become its Inherent crew only if it occupies that vehicle's Location at the start of its MPh (not APh) and expends all of its MF to do so." But a bulldozer does not have an Inherent crew, only an Inherent Driver. Disregarding the reality argument that the two ought to be pretty much the same, it is not clear that D5.42 allows a unit to become (if a SMC) (or possibly install if a MMC) an Inherent Driver in the MPh. If it were allowed by D5.42, would the unit (which might be a MMC) be removed to become the Inherent Driver? Would a MMC instead re-crew the vehicle expending all its MF and not be able to move elsewhere? From what I read a unit can re-man a vehicle only if it becomes the Inherent crew, not the Inherent Driver. But that could easily be wrong.

Although I think these are questions that should have answers, in this particular scenario they are probably not important. The Japanese move first, and Abandoned vehicles can be "captured" (re-manned) in the CCPh [A21.2]. The Japanese do not have enough MF to enter the hex with the bulldozer, so in most playings it can be "captured" by one of the two American heroes in the Japanese first player turn CCPh. It will probably then attempt to drive away in the American player turn, which at least prevents it from being lost with double CVP. 

Attacking an Abandoned bulldozer

Per a q&a, "An Abandoned vehicle is a unit, but it is neither friendly nor enemy and can be attacked by either side." In case the Americans want to destroy the Abandoned instead of capturing/re-manning it they can.

Getting a SMC back out after putting it in as Inherent Driver.

If the Americans do decide to try to save the bulldozer by re-manning it, they may want to get the hero back out of it. A21.21 says, "If the vehicle was captured by a SMC, that SMC is removed until the vehicle takes on a new crew (D5.42) or is Abandoned." It is not clear if A21.21 allows all vehicles (including those with just inherent drivers) to be abandoned, apparently overriding D5.1, or it just says that new inherent driver can be installed for those vehicles that can be Abandoned and are. Likewise it says the SMC can be removed once a new crew is installed per D5.42, but one of the requirements for using D5.42 is that the vehicle is Abandoned. Perhaps A21.21 says D5.42 can also be used if the vehicle is not abandoned but rather has a SMC Temporary Driver. After a while of parsing and re-parsing these rules I think I will punt and say that a SMC Temporary Driver can Abandon a vehicle that only has an Inherent Driver despite D5.1, and can also leave the vehicle at the same time a MMC installs a new (permanent) Inherent Driver or a different SMC becomes Temporary Driver per A21.21.

These are my understandings of how Abandoned bulldozers should be handled. If anyone thinks I have misunderstood something or if I have missed some aspect, let me know.

ground_truth_answer:
So I've managed to pull off a nirvana situation where I have two heroes manning a MMG along with a 10-2 leader in the hex (and another MMC+MMG).  My understanding is that this gives us a 12 -4 (German MMGs with the MMC being a 4-6-7) out to 12 hexes, with a ROF 2.  But is there a restriction on the hero being able to apply his DRM if he is sharing manning a MG with another hero?

Edit: Sub shots would be 8 factors with ROF 2, for completeness
Twelve FP down four (plus any other DRM, e.g. TEM, hindrance, etc.) is correct for a MMG manned by two heros and a second MMG manned by a 4-6-7 directed by a -2 leader from range two out to range twelve. Range zero and range one would be more of course. Heroic DRM are cumulative, unlike leadership DRM, and one leadership DRM in addition to the heroic DRMs can also be added. The hero "firing" the MG (i.e. its possessor) and the hero "assisting" both use their heroic DRM out to the normal range of MG.

ESB / Mechanical Reliability / Motion Attempt: I just want to make sure I interpret the rules correctly. Reading D2.5 (ESB) and D2.51 (MR), its seems these rules are for vehicles during IT's MPh. Motion Attempt (D2.401) is a rule for vehicles during IT's DFPh. Yes?

Scenario is BoF14: Cocktails For Molotov (I'm enjoying this one). The situation is: A stopped Russian BT-5 M34 (red MP) facing west on 51R5 and another stopped facing Northeast in 51S5. A stack of Polish 7-0/457 w/DC is in 51S7 with a burning Russian BA-6 in 51S6. It's the Polish MPh and is willing to attack the AFV in 51R5 going through the burning wreck and attack from it's rear. Both Russian AFV's have had the Polish stack in it's LOS. So in reading D2.401, neither AFV can make a Motion attempt in order to change it's VCA/TCA. Am I correct or am I missing something?

If the AFV's were allowed to make a Motion attempt, would an MR still be required?
title: ESB / Mechanical Reliability / Motion Attempt
raw_question:
I just want to make sure I interpret the rules correctly. Reading D2.5 (ESB) and D2.51 (MR), its seems these rules are for vehicles during IT's MPh. Motion Attempt (D2.401) is a rule for vehicles during IT's DFPh. Yes?

A stack of Polish 7-0/457 w/DC is in 51S7 with a burning Russian BA-6 in 51S6. It's the Polish MPh and is willing to attack the AFV in 51R5 going through the burning wreck and attack from it's rear. Both Russian AFV's have had the Polish stack in it's LOS. So in reading D2.401, neither AFV can make a Motion attempt in order to change it's VCA/TCA. Am I correct or am I missing something?

If the AFV's were allowed to make a Motion attempt, would an MR still be required?
ground_truth_answer:
I think this is the situation as you described it:

Getting warm in here

Yes, barring other information, a Motion Attempt would be the best option for the BTs, but since that's off the table they should turn their VCAs during Defensive First Fire to face the oncoming Polish infantry.  It will add another +1 DRM to your shot over just turning the turret, but the Poles will then suffer the +1 DRM for placing the DC through the front hull facing (C7.346).  

Also, it wasn't clear who possessed the DC, the leader or the squad.  Three reasons to give DCs to leaders are:

- Leaders have six MF, giving you a few more options when operating with a DC.

- Leaders are elite, so the DC doesn't suffer a lowered malfunction number (B23.2).  It's rarely an issue in my experience but this case is an exception - the DC TK is high enough that any roll eliminates the BT, assuming a successful placement (final DR of 8 or less), unless the DC malfunctions.  With the squad, that occurs on a ten or higher, but only on boxcars with the leader.

- Most importantly in this particular situation, leaders don't need to take a PAATC to place a DC on an enemy AFV, so that's one less DR you have to sweat.

There are also good reasons *not* to give a DC to a leader - placing a demo charge is dangerous work and your leaders usually have a host of other responsibilities as well.

Good luck!

query:
SW MG Bore Sighting at Night vs NVR: So I just ran into a complicated "analysis paralysis" inducing ASL rules quandary.  Usually I can "Sherlock Holmes" my way through the ASL rules to figure this stuff out, but this one is not quite showing me the solution.  While I am soloing my current scenario (KGP1) and could just "go with my gut," I can imagine that if I was in a face-to-face game this issue could raise an argument between players on rules interpretation, so I would like to see what some of the "expert gurus" think of this.

First off, just the facts -

A9.22 tells us that NVR does not affect the placement of a MG Fire Lane (i.e., a termination point for the MG Fire Lane at Night can be placed beyond NVR provided there would be a LOS not blocked by Obstacle during Daytime)

Nothing in the KGP1 SSRs or the overarching KG SSRs tell you that you can't Bore Sight, but KG CG SSR 12 reveals that the Design Intent is that no Bore Sighting is allowed in KGP with the EXCEPTION of SW MG in Night scenarios (thus my interpretation that the American Scenario Defenders in KGP1 should be able to Bore Sight their SW MMG/HMG).

E1.71 provides an EXCEPTION to Fire Lanes that I want to learn to exploit along the lines of a MMG/HMG may place a Fire Lane at Night (provided a starshell/IR has been fired during the scenario) without firing at a particular moving enemy unit TO a Bore Sighted location.

Chapter C Bore Sighting rules make no mentions of NVR or rule E1.71 and only refer to "LOS"

Now to my question/quandary -

In a nutshell, is Bore Sighting as described above limited by NVR?  or is NVR irrelevant to Bore Sighting in this situation given that Fire Lanes are allowed beyond NVR? 

What "my gut" tells me (and here comes the danger of a "realism argument") is that the Bore Sighted location can be beyond NVR because the defenses (historically in this scenario) were set up before Night fell.

Otherwise, what is the point of E1.71 Exception???

TIA for your participation in solving this "analysis paralysis" inducing quandary.

P.S. - Side note re: scenario KGP1 - The scenario card pre and post battle descriptions are remiss in not defining which "midnight" they are talking about.  So I researched the official published U.S. Army history of this battle (available online) and found that the "midnight" of this battle is midnight of 12/20/44 going into 12/21/44 (NOT midnight 12/19/44 going into 12/20/44).  This is VERY IMPORTANT because that means the German AFVs in scenario KGP1 ARE subject to Fuel Shortage!)

query:
Halftrack passengers, STUN and disembark: Assume the following situation during the German Movement Phase:
A SPW 251/1 with a 8-3-8 Passenger squad moves ADJACENT to a Russian 6-2-8+LMG using its 8th MP. The Russian squad fires 16FP, resulting in a 1MC versus the CE crew and Passenger.
The 8-3-8 passes the 1MC valiantly, but the SPW crew rolls an “8” and is stunned. 
Question 1: Is it correct to put the whole stack, including the 8-3-8, beneath a BU counter (as per D5.33-34)?
Question 2: Can the 8-3-8 disembark?
Question 3: Can the 8-3-8 take the LMG of the SPW (D6.631)?
Question 4: Will the 8-3-8 be attacked by a 6FP Residual?
Question 5: Does the 8-3-8 have 2MF in total because the stun result vs. the SPW crew stops the AFV without the need to spend a MP to stop (D5.34)?
Question 6: At the end of the turn, the Stun marker will be flipped to the +1 side. But the BU counter remains in place, correct?
title: Halftrack passengers, STUN and disembark
raw_question:
Assume the following situation during the German Movement Phase:
A SPW 251/1 with a 8-3-8 Passenger squad moves ADJACENT to a Russian 6-2-8+LMG using its 8th MP. The Russian squad fires 16FP, resulting in a 1MC versus the CE crew and Passenger.
The 8-3-8 passes the 1MC valiantly, but the SPW crew rolls an “8” and is stunned. 
Question 1: Is it correct to put the whole stack, including the 8-3-8, beneath a BU counter (as per D5.33-34)?
Question 2: Can the 8-3-8 disembark?
Question 3: Can the 8-3-8 take the LMG of the SPW (D6.631)?
Question 4: Will the 8-3-8 be attacked by a 6FP Residual?
Question 5: Does the 8-3-8 have 2MF in total because the stun result vs. the SPW crew stops the AFV without the need to spend a MP to stop (D5.34)?
Question 6: At the end of the turn, the Stun marker will be flipped to the +1 side. But the BU counter remains in place, correct?
ground_truth_answer:
This strikes me as in violation of the whole rationale behind a vehicle needing to "expend" all of its MP if it moves at all in a MPh. The expenditure of delay MP represents the inevitable ticking of the clock since the vehicle's whereabouts need to be known and its status accounted for in any given time slice. If a vehicle moves and uses half of its MP and is then stunned (and forced to stop), it makes no sense under that stated rationale that the remaining MP would not be "considered spent" in Delay, for Defensive Fire purposes (as the original poster asked). If it's the way you state here JRV, then there is a space-time discontinuity, which does not happen in our universe (except maybe in a black hole).
Although a vehicle *usually* has to expend all its MP, there are cases where it does not. D2.4, "A vehicle may end its MPh in Motion without expending all of its MP only if it has insufficient MP remaining to enter the next hex it wishes to enter." So if a vehicle is currently not stopped and has, say, four MP left, and the next hex it wants to enter is up a hill (four MP plus COT), it may end in Motion without expending the last four MP. Although this appears to conflict with D2.1, "A vehicle which ends its MPh with MP remaining is assumed to use all those MP in that hex," there is a q&a:

D2.1 & D2.4
Assume the AFV enters the bypass Location from B2 and announces a MP expenditure of 2. As it does so, presume it has MPs remaining. May the AFV declare a desire to enter into D2 for more MPs than it has left, remain in C2 and place a Motion Counter?
A. No.
Assume the AFV has less than Half its MPs left. May it declare a desire to enter into D1, have insufficient MPs left, remain in C2 and place a motion counter?
A. No.
Follow up, to enter D1, it would have to continue to bypass around to the C2/D2 hexside. Assuming it has done so and now has less than half MPs left, may it now declare a desire to enter D1 without bypass and stay in C2 with a motion counter in accordance with D2.4?
A. Not if it has enough MP to enter in bypass. 
Is an AFV required to enter a new hex/hexside if it is able to before falling back on D2.4?
A. It must be unable to enter the hex in its VCA (or RVCA if moving in reverse) it desires to enter.
Does D2.4 only kick in if the AFV has no movement options left that do not require ESB?
A. No; see above.
When you say “It must be unable to enter the hex in its VCA (or RVCA if moving in reverse) it desires to enter” what happens to the remaining MPs?
A. Those MP disappear (D2.4).

Also when a vehicle Bogs it "must end its MPh immediately" [D8.21]. There is a q&a that says it is still subject to DFF, but it is not clarified whether this is just for the expenditure that caused the Bog, or whether it is considered to also be liable for DFF for MP that remain beyond that. I would be interested in seeing a q&a that clarified this, but only out of curiosity right now. If a vehicle moves into LOS for one MP but Bogs, can the defender wait for four MP in LOS and fire in that MPh, or must it wait for the DFPh?

It has never been clear to me what the purpose is for trying to account for all vehicle MP most of the time but not all. It is possible that it was done to make it harder to VBM freeze, forcing the vehicle either to stop so it can spend delay MPs or enter with no MPs left to exit, i.e. to commit to the VBM freeze rather than allowing it to see what happens and possibly move on. Or it may be to cover the case when a HIP Gun pops out and fires on the expenditure, missing but keeping ROF; the moving vehicle can't terminate its vulnerability to further attacks just by declaring its MPh at end, which is in contrast to what infantry may do. Anyway it doesn't seem to be a desire to perform simulation of physical reality; MP available disappear in some cases, just as MF are always allowed to do.

query:
Residual FP and placement of DC: A 8.22, 2nd bullet point states: "Residual FP does not attack until any activity that a MF/MP expenditure allowed is completed (e.g., placing SMOKE grenades, SW Recovery, Searching, firing a Smoke Dispenser, etc.) [EXC: entering a vehicle; (un)hooking; D5.43]."

Assume a squad equipped with a DC enters a hex containing a 4 FP residual FP and survives the attack unpinned. It then spends another 2 MF to place the DC in an adjacent woods hex. According to the rule above, the squad would be attacked by the residual again but only after completing the placement of the DC. Does this mean the DC will attack in the AFPh regardless of the result of the second residual attack?
title: Residual FP and placement of DC
raw_question:
A 8.22, 2nd bullet point states: "Residual FP does not attack until any activity that a MF/MP expenditure allowed is completed (e.g., placing SMOKE grenades, SW Recovery, Searching, firing a Smoke Dispenser, etc.) [EXC: entering a vehicle; (un)hooking; D5.43]."

Assume a squad equipped with a DC enters a hex containing a 4 FP residual FP and survives the attack unpinned. It then spends another 2 MF to place the DC in an adjacent woods hex. According to the rule above, the squad would be attacked by the residual again but only after completing the placement of the DC. Does this mean the DC will attack in the AFPh regardless of the result of the second residual attack?
ground_truth_answer:
Thanks so much for the clarification! So, if the first attack vs. the squad entering the hex is "normal" FP and the second attack (for the 2MF placement) is residual, will a PIN (or better) result vs. the squad actually cancel the placement of the DC? Because my understanding of the second bullet point of A 8.22 is that the attack only happens AFTER the activity is completed.

Yes, anything that happens to the squad as a result of the placement MF expenditure (pinned, broken, etc.) will cancel the DC attack.

See rule A23.3 that covers DC placement where it states  -

"Should the Placing unit survive (unbroken and unpinned, even if newly berserk) all enemy Defensive First Fire, Subsequent First Fire, and FPF in the Placement Hex (including any resulting from the expenditure of MF in the Placement of that DC), the weapon is considered operably Placed. Thereafter, the Placing unit may move away or suffer adverse results with no effect to the DC. However, if the Placing unit is broken, pinned, or eliminated before or during Placement, the DC is not operably Placed, remains with the Placing unit (or in the Placing unit’s Location if the unit is eliminated), and may not attack—
although it is still usable for future Recovery/Placement attempts."

query: Rout Question: Can a DM broken unit rout to the nearest building/woods hex even if it is out of his LOS?
title: Rout Question
raw_question: Can a DM broken unit rout to the nearest building/woods hex even if it is out of his LOS?
ground_truth_answer:
I have a different rout question. I'm just learning ASL so apologies if this is basic. 

The closest building/woods hex to a DM broken unit on the flank is actually forward, two hexes away, not closer to any enemy unit. However, routing to that hex would expose the unit to interdiction or low crawl and forcing it to surrender or be eliminated. The next closest rout target is back where the unit came from, three hexes away and not subject to interdiction, out of view of the enemy.
Is the routing unit forced to select the first hex and surrender?
Yes. Although you may have a sense of "forward" and "backward", the routing units and the rules do not.

Note that the distances to potential rout targets for priority are measured in MF not hexes [A10.51]. I have assumed the potential rout targets in your hypothetical still have the same priority by MF.

Thanks for the quick response. My careful reading of the rules got me to your answer, but it seemed counterintuitive (heh) so I wanted to check before I learned it wrong. And your assumption is correct; the priority holds using MF.

Your situation is why understanding the rout rules is so important. Knowing where is safe to rout from will only improve your game.

query: Bunker Advantages?: Team - please give me some pointers on the advantage of placing a pillbox and a trench counter in the same hex. I am unsure of the tactical advantages. Thank you in advance for any comments on the subject.
title: Bunker Advantages?
raw_question: Team - please give me some pointers on the advantage of placing a pillbox and a trench counter in the same hex. I am unsure of the tactical advantages. Thank you in advance for any comments on the subject.
ground_truth_answer:
Team - please give me some pointers on the advantage of placing a pillbox and a trench counter in the same hex. I am unsure of the tactical advantages. Thank you in advance for any comments on the subject.
The only time I have done that is to allow a weapon, usually an HMG, 360 degree fire with the option to duck into the pillbox. Another reason could be protection for more units - 1 unit in a pillbox, 2 more units in the trench.

As an aside, because the pillbox is a separate Location, the stacking limits for a pillbox and its outside (here a trench) are independent. There could be up to three squad squad equivalents inside a large-enough pillbox and another three squad equivalents outside the pillbox, perhaps in a trench, with no overstacking.

These are certainly among the most likely reasons. A pillbox's CA is limited, and at some point the enemy will often try to go around. If the terrain is suitable then putting the trench in an adjacent hex might be acceptable, and if the terrain is not suitable (e.g. a solitary hill hex like like 2F7) then you might choose to put the pillbox and the trench in the same hex. In the other case units, especially crews, are vulnerable to CC in a pillbox, so a Gun crew in a pillbox might be safer with a friendly unit outside. As long as there are friendly units outside units in the pillbox can't be attacked. As mentioned before the presence of a trench outside does create cover for enemy units, but if the enemy can send in infantry for a 2:1 or similar CC attack against a crew, they may take the trade of outside units attacking next turn even if the terrain outside the pillbox is open ground.

That said my first preference would be to have the pillbox and the trench in separate hexes. But I will not say they are never in the same hex.

query:
Rooftop height of a factory?: So section B is confusing us ...

We have a unit that wants to advance to the rooftop of a factory in the RB "The Last Bid" scenario where the factory has a printed stairwell, so it is a "level 2.5 obstacle to LOS".

The Soviets have a unit on lvl 2 of a building.

The question is... does the rooftop person lose concealment because they do not have "height advantage" over the lvl 2 unit?  Some of us are arguing that even though the factory is a 2.5 level obstacle, the unit on the rooftop is magically treated as being on level 3.

Some of us are arguing that since the factory is a 2.5 level obstacle and "half levels" are mythical in ASL, the rooftop unit must be treated as being on level 2.

We're confused....
title: Rooftop height of a factory?
raw_question:
So section B is confusing us ...

We have a unit that wants to advance to the rooftop of a factory in the RB "The Last Bid" scenario where the factory has a printed stairwell, so it is a "level 2.5 obstacle to LOS".

The Soviets have a unit on lvl 2 of a building.

The question is... does the rooftop person lose concealment because they do not have "height advantage" over the lvl 2 unit?  Some of us are arguing that even though the factory is a 2.5 level obstacle, the unit on the rooftop is magically treated as being on level 3.

Some of us are arguing that since the factory is a 2.5 level obstacle and "half levels" are mythical in ASL, the rooftop unit must be treated as being on level 2.

We're confused....
ground_truth_answer:
Half levels are not "mythical." They exist just like full levels. They are not considered when calculating blind hexes [A6.21], but otherwise they otherwise an elevation a unit can be at. If you are going to play with hillocks and/or embankment RRs (e.g. Hatten, Festung Budapest, desert), you will find yourself facing half-level terrain.

Normal two-story houses and multi-story buildings are one-and-a-half [B23.22] and two-and-a-half [B23.23] level obstacles respectively. If rooftops are not in play then the highest Location a unit can be in them is at level one or level two, despite there being another half-level of building obstacle above the unit. If rooftops are in play there is an additional Location at the full height of the building, i.e. a rooftop Location at level one-and-a-half or two-and-a-half.

Factories are exactly the same except that if rooftops are not in play, there is only a ground level Location. When rooftops are in play there is another Location at the obstacle height. This last is not fully stated in the aslrb. B23.88 alludes to what is meant by describing "quasi-Locations" at level one (and level two for a 2.5 level factory) where DFF can be targeted and RFP placed. But if you took B23.8 literally, "Rooftops are treated the same as another building floor level at the next higher half-level elevation," rooftops in a factory would be at level one-half. That is clearly absurd; the rooftop Location is at the obstacle height.

With regard to concealment, B23.82, "A unit can remain hidden or concealed on a rooftop only if there are no Good Order enemy ground units within 16 hexes of it that are at the same or higher level with a LOS to it." For a unit on a low factory (level one-and-a-half), it can remain HIP/concealed only if all Good Order enemy ground units with LOS and within sixteen hexes are at level one or lower.

query:
Smoke grenades & residual FP: 8.22 says that a unit can only be attacked by residual FP once per location. It also states that an exception is when the residual FP there is increased, further MF/MP expenditure in that location can subject it to another attack. I get this exception. So in this case, attempting smoke grenade placement would cause another attack.

The other exception is when the unit is subject to more negative or less positive DRMs. Since 8.22 also says that smoke grenade attempts are considered a non-simultaneous expenditure of MF (e.g., in addition to the cost to move into the location), would an attempt to use those smoke grenades subject the unit to another residual FP attack there? As the grenades if placed would not be causing more negative DRM to the target unit (but adding to its defense), am I right that there wouldn't be another residual FP attack? Even if the placement attempt failed, that too wouldn't change the DRM picture, right?
title: Smoke grenades & residual FP
raw_question:
8.22 says that a unit can only be attacked by residual FP once per location. It also states that an exception is when the residual FP there is increased, further MF/MP expenditure in that location can subject it to another attack. I get this exception. So in this case, attempting smoke grenade placement would cause another attack.

The other exception is when the unit is subject to more negative or less positive DRMs. Since 8.22 also says that smoke grenade attempts are considered a non-simultaneous expenditure of MF (e.g., in addition to the cost to move into the location), would an attempt to use those smoke grenades subject the unit to another residual FP attack there? As the grenades if placed would not be causing more negative DRM to the target unit (but adding to its defense), am I right that there wouldn't be another residual FP attack? Even if the placement attempt failed, that too wouldn't change the DRM picture, right?
ground_truth_answer:
As Marti and Robin comment, but I'll add some clarification that I /think/ are correct....

If you started your MPh in the hex and another unit first entered your hex, drawing fire (and placing a residual fire marker), if you then attempted to place smoke grenades anywhere (expending 1 or 2 MFs) you would be subject to the residual fire attack because you were expending MFs in that location and had not yet been subject to it.

Furthermore, if that squad was moving and entered a new hex, was fired on and a residual fire marker was placed, and THEN they attempted a smoke grenade placement at 1 or 2 MFs, they would ALSO be subject to a residual fire attack (as they had not yet been attacked by that residual fire).

Conversely, if a residual fire marker was in a hex and a squad entered that hex (and was attacked by the residual fire marker), THEN attempted to place smoke grenades from that hex, they would NOT be subject to an additional residual fire attack as they had already been attacked once by the residual fire and none of the exceptions for a second attack by that residual fire apply.

query: What does the bracketed [9] after the H# on C8.31 chart refer to?: See question in thread title (I am at a loss at the moment to figuring out/remembering what is up with the bracketed 9) -
title: What does the bracketed [9] after the H# on C8.31 chart refer to?
raw_question: See question in thread title (I am at a loss at the moment to figuring out/remembering what is up with the bracketed 9) -
ground_truth_answer:
It's called Ballistics  (which is a science of physics unto itself) 

It is all about ratios between length of barrel, strength of propellant charge, twist rate of rifling, muzzle velocity attained, weight of shell (heavier weight more affected by gravity), aerodynamics of shell (fat heavy HE shell versus light APCR tungsten core dart {which can actually, counterintuitively, reduce range due to instability of the dart versus wind/air resistance), etc., etc.

For example, an air rifle chambered in  .177 caliber pellet can fire that pellet at higher velocity and longer range than a similar air rifle chambered in .22 caliber.  However, due to the projectile's mass, a .22 caliber pellet releases much more kinetic energy upon its target on impact (albeit with a shorter effective range and less muzzle velocity than the .177 caliber pellet).  That is why it is considered inhumane to hunt rabbits or squirrels with a .177 caliber air rifle.  Instead you need to use .22 or .25 caliber air rifle to humanely take out a rabbit or squirrel (proper shot placement on target is also key).  A .177 caliber air rifle is only considered humane when used to take out rats and small birds.

When I find time later, I will post some more data on the Pak36 versus Pak38 versus Pak40 (from my hard copy encyclopedia that I referenced above) to further illustrate the ballistics involved.

query:
Do you have to declare a pre-registered hex?: Mostly a hypothetical question, but consider a scenario where you have several potential pre-reg hexes for your OBA, some offensive and some defensive.  You don't really want your opponent to know where your pre-reg hex is because the ability to call down FFE immediately with a 1-4 accuracy can definitely catch people out in the open.

At some point, however, you want to drop a SR on that hex.  Are you able to roll for accuracy first without announcing that it is a pre-reg hex?  Assuming German or American and no hindrance, that means on a 1-2 it would be accurate regardless and on a 5-6 it would miss, regardless (though I suppose you'd have to announce that the extent of error was halved, so a 5-6 would still give away the pre-reg unless you rolled a 1 on the distance scatter).  On a 3-4, you'd obviously have to announce and reveal the pre-reg to show that the SR landed in the hex.

Basically, what is the general way that people play pre-reg hexes?  In the past, we've always just say "I'm placing an AR in hex XXXX, which is the pre-reg hex, so need a 1-4 for accuracy".  But there has almost never been a need for deception as the pre-reg has been in a scenario where one side is the clear attacker and one the clear defender.  We're currently starting The Last Bid and both sides will likely be defending and attacking, so I could see the desire to keep the opponent guessing as to the exact pre-reg hex location.

Nothing in the rules (including Artillery flow chart) seem to detail the announcement sequencing, which makes me think you could place the AR and, as long as you're not immediately converting to a FFE:1, just roll for accuracy.  Then if you roll a 3 or 4, you'd announce that it is accurate as that is the pre-reg hex.  On a 5-6, you'd roll for scatter and if you rolled a 2+ on distance, announce that the extent of error is halved as its the pre-reg hex.

Just curious what people thought and if the decision would be different in a friendly game versus a tournament setting?

query: FFE1 & FFE2: Is it legal to call in a Fire Mission (HE or Smoke) for FFE1 and then correct it for FFE2 so it strikes again up to 3 hexs away (using the same HE or Smoke of course)?
title: FFE1 & FFE2
raw_question: Is it legal to call in a Fire Mission (HE or Smoke) for FFE1 and then correct it for FFE2 so it strikes again up to 3 hexs away (using the same HE or Smoke of course)?
ground_truth_answer:
Is it legal to call in a Fire Mission (HE or Smoke) for FFE1 and then correct it for FFE2 so it strikes again up to 3 hexs away (using the same HE or Smoke of course)?
In the same phase? No. In a later turn? Sure. The OBA flow chart is probably the best rules reference for this.

The procedure for FFE placement got changed very early in the ASL rules. In the original OBA the FFE:1 stayed on board for a turn before flipping to an FFE:2. Currently in a single phase you announce conversion of a SR or FFE:C, the FFE:1 is put on board, evaluated and flipped to an FFE:2. The FFE:1 as used currently is probably unnecessary, a legacy from when the rules were different.

query:
Narrow streets?: Can a Squad moving along a Narrow Street end it's Movement on a Narrow Street hex, or is it forced into one of the buildings along the road?
Example talks about Bypass Movement, but is that mandatory for Narrow Street Movement?
title: Narrow streets?
raw_question:
Can a Squad moving along a Narrow Street end it's Movement on a Narrow Street hex, or is it forced into one of the buildings along the road?
Example talks about Bypass Movement, but is that mandatory for Narrow Street Movement?
ground_truth_answer:
Can a Squad moving along a Narrow Street end it's Movement on a Narrow Street hex, or is it forced into one of the buildings along the road?

This is a distinction without a difference. A unit moving in bypass is always in one of the two hexes (really Locations) of the hexside on which it is bypassing. Per A4.32, "Infantry may not voluntarily end its move using Bypass." The narrow street rules do not change this. Bypass does not create a separate Location, and Infantry may not end their MPh in Bypass.

title: Breach TEM?
raw_question:
You can tell how far along I am in the rulebook with all my questions:-)

In B23.711 Breach, it states attacking a Row house wall with "Normal" TEM, but further on in the same sentence it states it will attack any Units within at "Full" TEM. 
Is there a difference?
ground_truth_answer: Since neither "normal TEM" nor "full TEM" are defined as formal terms, I think we have to assume the rulebook is being chatty and not trying to define formal terms on-the-sly. Per B23.921 the TEM for a Fortified building is +3 for wood, +4 for stone, and there is only one TEM so any phrasing such as "normal TEM" or "full TEM" refers to that one TEM. With ASLRB experience it is not unnatural to look for a formal definition for terms such as "normal TEM" and "full TEM," but in this case there just isn't any such formal definition. That's unfortunately the trap the ASLRB sets for itself when it is trying to be both formal and chatty.

Per A10.62, a DM is placed on "any already broken unit which is subsequently attacked by ... enough FP (taking the possibility of Cowering into account) to possibly inflict at least a NMC result on the target." ground_truth_answer:
So B9.34 Indirect Fire infers that the TEM of a Wall or Hedge is reduced by one if using Indirect Fire, such as Mortars. 

Indirect fire is only OBA and Mortars. It is possible for other guns to fire as Area Target Type, in which case the full TEM of the wall would apply and the wall wouldn't affect the to-hit roll (C3.331). Counting as Indirect Fire is one of the main differences between a mortar and an INF or ART gun of the same size.

According to G1.424 DC Hero Use, "A DC Hero is treated the same as a T-H Hero except as stated otherwise...A DC Hero must declare as his Designated Target (and hence during his MPh must Banzai Charge) the enemy unit/Gun/Fortification that allowed his creation."

My opponent attempted to advance a DC Hero into a tank's location after declaring it as his Designated Target. I argued that the DC Hero can ONLY conduct a Banzai Charge during it's Movement Phase. It cannot wait until it's Advance Phase to move. However, a T-H Hero has the option to do either.  Is this correct?  If so, what is the advantage to using one versus the other?  

Thanks in advance for the help and apologies for missing anything obvious but this one had us wrapped around the axle for some reason.
ground_truth_answer:
Ok, I see that a DC Hero can not be placed at set up. However, going back to the question as to whether a TH Hero can use a DC, what am I missing from this of reasoning: 
* A TH Hero can be set up in '44-'45 (G1.422)
* A DC can be transferred to him during the RPh (G1.423)

You are speaking of transfer per A4.431. In order to transfer the SW to a HIP unit the HIP unit would have to become un-HIP (and probably lose concealment per A12.141). 

A12.14 & A12.3
For clarification of the above Perry Sez answer, the third question and answer, “must” a unit sacrifice its hidden status and come out concealed in order to perform the types of activities listed?
A. To perform the listed activity, they must not be HIP.

Among the examples for activities that require loss of HIP is "transfer a weapon in the APh." Since the list give is not exhaustive, I conclude that transfer of a weapon during the RPh also requires a HIP unit to lose HIP. You can provide a q&a that allows it, but for now it seems to me to be unlikely that such a q&a would be forthcoming.

G1.425, "A T-H Hero who loses HIP status involuntarily (see 1.422) is immediately eliminated unless his HIP loss occurs either during the enemy MPh and he makes an immediate Reaction Fire attack (D7.2) or during a CCPh in which he is a DEFENDER in the same Location with an enemy unit (A11.19)," and G1.422, "When his HIP is lost, all rules for T-H Heroes go into effect for him [EXC: he might be eliminated immediately; 1.425 ]." Transferring a DC to a HIP T-H Hero would immediately eliminate it (and the DC).

* The TH Hero thus armed can then make a Banzai Charge in the MPh, or he can advance into an AFV in the APh, etc. (G1.423)
* Following which, "Any  unbroken Japanese Infantry unit possessing a DC may, in lieu of Placing it in the normal manner (A23.3; 1.612), 
detonate it immediately during or at the end of its own MPh in the same manner as a DC Hero (and consequently is eliminated as per 1.425)." (G1.424)

The rule you quote here only allows detonation of a DC during the T-H Hero's MPh, and on that point I agree. But it could not detonate it in the CCPh or APh by this rule. The q&a given additionally also says it may not detonate the DC in the CCPh. You can detonate a DC possessed by a T-H Hero any time, so long as it's during that unit's MPh. So even if you still say that a HIP T-H Hero can somehow end up with a DC, it can only detonate it during its MPh.

query: RR embankment: If a target is on a RR Embankment and your firing at it from two hexes away, does a wreck between the attacker and the target cause a +1 Hindrance?
title: RR embankment
raw_question: If a target is on a RR Embankment and your firing at it from two hexes away, does a wreck between the attacker and the target cause a +1 Hindrance?
ground_truth_answer:
We will need to make some assumptions to answer your question. Assumption 1: the unit firing is at level zero relative to a level ½ RR Embankment. Assumption 2: the wreck is either at level zero or level ½. If so then as above, F6.52, "A "half-level" Hindrance (as defined in 4.51), whether on a hillock or not, can affect LOS/LOF to/from/across a hillock hex only if both the firer's and target's elevations are within a half-level of, and the elevation of at least one of those units is ≤ that of, the Hindrance's Base Level." F4.51 says a wreck is a "half-level" Hindrance. With the two assumptions the wreck is within a half-level of that hindrance and also at least one of target or firer is ≤ the level of the hindrance.

If the assumptions are broken then the wreck may not be a hindrance. In particular if the firer is at level ½ (presumably also on the embankment RR, the wreck is at level zero and of course the target is still at level ½, the wreck is not a hindrance.

1. No. The only actions allowed by an off-board unit are deployment and movement [A2.52]. Furthermore there has to be LOS to place smoke grenades [A24.1, definition of ADJACENT] and that does not exist from offboard to on-board [A2.51].

A firelane down a non-alternate hexgrain is more likely to have the initial attack trace its LOS through the hexside center, but again in the A9.222EX if the MMG is making its initial attack at a target using bypass of BB5 on the AA5 side, the MMG might trace its LOS to either of the vertices of the hexside instead of to the center.

There are two questions there. Question 1: is the Berserk German squad *required* to spend another MF to enter the foxhole, or can it just end its MPh after entering the hex? The latter. The German unit has entered the Location with its target per A15.43 and so need not move farther. The foxhole is not a separate Location [B27.13]. Second question, in order to be entitled to the +2 TEM for the foxhole would the German unit have to explicitly expend an extra MF, or would it "fall into" the foxhole in the same way that units "fall into" shellholes? The former. Unlike shellholes units are not put under foxholes without expending an extra MF in the MPh, RtPh or APh [B27.4]. Since a berserk unit can't rout and can't rout or advance, it would have to move under the foxhole in the MPh. Side note: it would be subject to any residual FP from the TPBF attack it received.

Bonus question: can a berserk unit expend one MF to enter an entrenchment once it reaches its target Location? I believe so. There are q&a saying that it may not place smoke grenades but nothing saying that entering an entrenchment is not allowed.

 If not, when he TPB Fires in the AFPh, would the Pinned American Squad get the +2 TEM of the Foxhole?
The American squad would be entitled to the +2 TEM of the foxhole regardless of whether the German unit entered the foxhole with it or not.

ground_truth_answer:
But doesn't hindrance affect only same level Los ? 
A24.2, "All Direct Fire and on-board mortar fire traced into, through, within, or out of (see 24.8) a SMOKE Location is affected by a Hindrance DRM." Note this is different from and overrides A6.7, "All same-level Direct Fire and spotting attempts traced through (not just into or out of) an effective LOS Hindrance hex are modified by a +1 DRM." Also in A24.4, "Conventional smoke is treated as a two level Hindrance to LOS and does not Hinder LOS occurring above that elevation." A two-level hindrance (from level zero) does not hinder that occurs entirely at level two, so squad A & squad C see each other the A24.4EX. In my mind I imagine SMOKE as rising to the ankles of units on level two, which lets me remember that fire at the same level would not be hindered but fire down from level two would be hindered.

One thing that is not well-explained is whether a between-levels LOS goes through a multi-level SMOKE Hindrance Location or not. I don't believe there is anything that spells this out but my understanding is that if turning the SMOKE into an obstacle would block LOS then the SMOKE is a hindrance. That covers most situations. It does leave the case where there is SMOKE starting from a level higher than the ground level, e.g. Drifting SMOKE or blaze/grenades in the upper level of a building but *not* SMOKE ammunition, grenades or blaze in a hex with a crest line. For same-level LOS or LOS from the base level of the SMOKE to a lower level it should be obvious whether the LOS is "beneath" the SMOKE but for LOS which starts higher than the base level of the SMOKE and ends lower I don't know of a rule that covers the situation in general. But it is rare to have SMOKE at an upper level in a hex but not at a lower level. There is this q&a:

A24.61 When applying the phrase in A24.61 that drifting smoke is “...never a Hindrance at levels below the Location of the original SMOKE source.” is it necessary that both the firer and target are below the location of the original SMOKE source? For example, assuming original SMOKE in 2L7 has dispersed and drifted to level 2 of 2M8 and 2N8, would fire from 2O8 to 2M10 be hindered by the smoke?
A. No. No. See the A24.61 Example and turn it upside down.

This covers one of the "easy" cases (LOS from the base level to a lower level), and although reassuring that nothing too crazy is going on it does not answer a more complicated question like 2P8 level three (SSR a building in the hex) to 2M9.

When a SMOKE source (ground-level blaze, primary SMOKE ammunition or grenade, but not Drifting SMOKE) is in a hex with a crest line B10.1 applies. The SMOKE rises from the lower elevation in the lower part of the hex and from the upper elevation in the higher part of the hex.

Also per C8.52 SMOKE ammunition which hits the upper level of a building but not the ground level (which presumably is masked or has hindrances that apply ), the SMOKE counter falls to ground level anyway unless the building hex is interior.

To my mind residual FP does not represent continued fire on the target. Otherwise residual FP would be removed when an attacker makes a SFF/FPF attack. Residual represents the noise and mayhem from the original attack. An ASL MPh takes actions that are in reality simultaneous or nearly so and spreads them out in a sequence. When one unit moves then a second one moves through the same Location, these units are in that same Location at roughly the same time. The second unit is not in exactly in the same place at the same time but it is close enough to be affected by the original attack, possibly only psychologically, e.g. they see bodies lying everywhere and get scared.

ground_truth_answer:
After your roll a to hit DR for ordnance using special ammo such as Smoke (WP, APCR, etc.), there are two numbers you have to look at. The first is the depletion number per C8. This is the number next to the abbreviation on the back of the counter, e.g. for "s8" the abbreviation "s" means "smoke" and "8" is the depletion number. If the TH DR is ≤ the depletion number the weapon successfully fired that type of ammo. Proceed to next step. If you rolled > the depletion number the weapon not have that type of ammo (is depleted) and is considered not to have fired for any purpose unless it malfunctioned. If the TH DR equaled the depletion number the attack is completed below but the weapon is out of that type of ammo for further attacks.

Now you have to add the TH DRM to the TH DR and compare the result to the value on the TH table for the range on the Area Target Type. If the TH DR + TH DRM ≤ the TH value, you have hit with that ammo.

As mentioned above only MTRs can maintain ROF while using the ATT. But Smoke (or other special ammo) can be fired as intensive fire as otherwise allowed, e.g. don't deplete the ammo, 

A unit may not move in the MPh if it fired in the PFPh, regardless of whether ROF is maintained [A3.3].

That simple. I guess I’m starting to overthink. So many rules and exceptions to remember.

If the vehicle was In Motion, infantry in the hex would *not* be in Melee (unless there was some other enemy unit to cause Melee) [A11.15]. The MMC would still have to pass a PAATC to attack using CC-RF.

The +2 DRM is for non-stopped, not Motion. Motion is a state that only has meaning outside the unit's MPh. Technical detail but it is useful to understand the difference between Motion and non-stopped. A Motion vehicle is always non-stopped, but during its MPh a non-stopped vehicle is not In Motion.

Alternately you could attack the halftrack crew with TPBF, +2 CE DRM and -1 leader even though the vehicle is BU because it is OT [A7.211].

Even if the vehicle had been stopped and held the infantry in Melee, once it started the infantry would have been released but they would still have to take a PAATC. Melee does not free infantry from PAATC requirements. All attacks in the CCPh have no PAATC requirements. You only take a PAATC in the (enemy) MPh when making a CC-RF, when an enemy unit enters and you want to retain concealment or during the APh when Advancing into a Location with an unconcealed enemy vehicle.
