Situation 1: no AR or SR/FFE2/FFEC on map - This is easy.  During the PFPh, the observer can either attempt to establish radio contact and battery access (hereafter "Contact+Access") or move during the movement phase.  They can't do both.  They are allowed to advance assuming all other requirements are met.

Situation 2: an SR/FFE2/FFEC is already on the map - This is the one that confuses me.  During the PFPh, I get that the observer can remain in their hex, maintain Contact+Access and do 'OBA stuff'.  They then cannot move during the MPh, but can still advance if otherwise able.  But what if they want to move???

Do they still roll to maintain contact?  If they don't, is this a 'voluntarily loss of contact' and the SR/FFE2/FFEC is removed from the map (cancelled?)?  Just uncertain how an observer moves around and how that movement impacts any on-map OBA stuff...

Rolling for radio contact is a prep fire "action," and as such it places a Prep counter on the unit (at least in your mind; the actual Prep counter need not be placed if the Observer is concealed/HIP per C1.6) just like any other attack, as you say. C1.22 gives us:

"Voluntary loss of Contact (i.e., failure to roll for Contact/Maintenance or voluntary rout; 1.6) causes the immediate loss of Access and Cancellation of the Fire Mission (if any). However, failing to roll for Contact/Maintenance is considered voluntary loss of Contact only if the Observer has no LOS to the SR's/FFE's Blast Height."

This does twist around the meaning of "voluntary" until it is hard to recognize, but in essence it says if the Observer does not roll for contact, battery access is lost and the current OBA counter only goes away if the Observer does not have LOS to current OBA counter's Blast Height. If the Observer *does* have LOS to the Blast Height, it is free to decline to roll during the PFPh/DFPh (and possibly move during the friendly MPh) and the current OBA counter will continue in the OBA progression (SR will remain SR, but FFE:2 will attack and become FFE:C) in its current hex. Note that the Observer can still Rout in the RtPh or Advance in the APh without immediate impact on OBA.

As a final point if the Observer does decline to roll, in the next phase it wants to perform OBA actions it will no longer have the DRM for maintaining radio contact. I will guess that is obvious, but I bring it up for completeness.

ground_truth_answer:
At scenario setup, if you set up a squad in a foxhole that's located behind a hedge, does it become HIP?  If the foxhole is not put on the board because it's out of LOS and can't be fired on until an enemy unit gets adjacent to it, how does it work with a Concealed squad at setup if it's in said foxhole?
The foxhole is not out of LOS to an enemy unit that has LOS to the hex at the same level through a wall/hedge hexside [B9.21]. The foxhole sets up HIP because A12.33 says *all* Fortifications set up HIP. This is regardless of whether the in-hex terrain is concealment terrain or not.

The foxhole would be revealed at the end of setup «just prior to placing non-OB "?"» [A12.33], again assuming an enemy unit within sixteen hexes has LOS to the hex through a wall/hedge hexside (or, of course, if not through a wall/hedge hexside).

A HIP foxhole does not grant HIP to its contents. This is in contrast to a pillbox [B30.7] or a cave [rules cite available on request].

Despite the fact that the foxhole itself is not out of sight through a wall/hedge hexside to an enemy unit at the same level, units in it are out of LOS [B9.21]. There is a q&a on this:
A12.33 & B9.21 Since LOS is reciprocal, B9.21 seems to imply that a hidden entrenchment directly behind a wall/hedge cannot be seen across that wall/hedge by a non-adjacent, same-level unit. Is this correct?
A. No – the required LOS to the entrenchment's Location is all that is necessary to reveal it. 
[An93b; An96; Mw]

If the foxhole behind a wall/hedge is not revealed (PTO, night, long range viewer only, etc.) and that foxhole contains potential targets, this is a problem that is not addressed the rules. I believe the current fashion is to allow the attack but then if there is any effect to say that the target is out-of-LOS. So far as I know there is no officially-sanctioned solution to this problem.

query: Vehicles and ROF: I thought I knew this one. A vehicle that Prep Fires and keeps it ROF can then move in the Movement Phase, right?
title: Vehicles and ROF
raw_question: I thought I knew this one. A vehicle that Prep Fires and keeps it ROF can then move in the Movement Phase, right?
ground_truth_answer:
To be clear, if you fire your MA in one hex and fail to retain ROF, you cannot fire your MGs in another hex [D3.3, D3.51]. 
My understanding here is that the non-MA weapons have to be fired in the first hex the MA fires in, regardless of whether it maintains ROF or not.

D3.51 "Once any vehicular weapon fires, its other weapons may fire in that phase only from that same hex [EXC: OVR; and MA retaining a Multiple ROF may fire again from another hex if the previous shot(s) were Bounding First Fire]."

The MA may fire again in a different hex if it retains ROF, but the MGs and other non-MA weapons are only allowed in the first hex from which *any* fire occurred.

This also means, as best I read it, that the MA must fire from that first fire-hex and retain ROF; you can't fire the MGs in the first hex but not the MA then move to another hex and fire the MA even if the MA has a ROF listed for it. It must fire from that first hex and retain ROF to be able to fire from a hex other than the first fire-hex.

I'm not clear on what difficulty you are having. The blast height of the SR (and more generally any FFE) rises two levels from the base level of the hex [C1.32]. There is no EXC for a Water Obstacle hex, so the blast height rises from level minus-one to level one, i.e. if the observer could see a unit at level one in the hex, the observer can see the blast height of the SR/FFE in that hex. When selecting an alternate target HIP fortifications *may* be revealed by the owning player [A14.21] at his option. If the target player prefers the unit in the foxhole to be targeted, he need only remain mum. query:
A general question about CX paragraph wording: Gentlemen,

I am going through full ALS game rules for the first time (advancing from ASLsk), and have a following general question about the CX rules paragraph. >> I am wondering if I am missing something obvious or perhaps it is just the paragraph that is worded in an unnecessarily convoluted way?

"4.51 COUNTER EXHAUSTION (CX): CX units must add one to any labor task or attack DR they make or direct (+1 to To Hit DR for ordnance; +1 to IFT DR for all others). CX units must add one to any inherent SW (ATMM, MOL, PF) or SMOKE Grenade Availability Check dr they make. CX units must also add one to any CC attack they make, and deduct one from any CC attack made against them. CX units must add one to their Search/Recovery dr (12.152; 4.44), and Ambush Status dr (11.4), and may not advance into Difficult Terrain (4.72). A unit’s CX counter is removed if the unit breaks; or in its next Player Turn as soon as it: has completed all of its Prep Fire, or is designated as an Opportunity Firer, or moves (unless due to a Minimum Move or Deep Stream Entry it becomes CX again), or becomes TI; or at the conclusion of its next MPh—whichever comes first." 

until now all, more or less, clear. But then this:

"A CX counter is removed at the start of a MPh and does not affect that unit during that MPh other than prohibiting its use of Double Time during that MPh."

So, if it is removed at the start of a MPh, how the following could happen: "[...]or at the conclusion of its next MPh—whichever comes first."?
title: A general question about CX paragraph wording
raw_question:
Gentlemen,

I am going through full ALS game rules for the first time (advancing from ASLsk), and have a following general question about the CX rules paragraph. >> I am wondering if I am missing something obvious or perhaps it is just the paragraph that is worded in an unnecessarily convoluted way?

"4.51 COUNTER EXHAUSTION (CX): CX units must add one to any labor task or attack DR they make or direct (+1 to To Hit DR for ordnance; +1 to IFT DR for all others). CX units must add one to any inherent SW (ATMM, MOL, PF) or SMOKE Grenade Availability Check dr they make. CX units must also add one to any CC attack they make, and deduct one from any CC attack made against them. CX units must add one to their Search/Recovery dr (12.152; 4.44), and Ambush Status dr (11.4), and may not advance into Difficult Terrain (4.72). A unit’s CX counter is removed if the unit breaks; or in its next Player Turn as soon as it: has completed all of its Prep Fire, or is designated as an Opportunity Firer, or moves (unless due to a Minimum Move or Deep Stream Entry it becomes CX again), or becomes TI; or at the conclusion of its next MPh—whichever comes first." 

until now all, more or less, clear. But then this:

"A CX counter is removed at the start of a MPh and does not affect that unit during that MPh other than prohibiting its use of Double Time during that MPh."

So, if it is removed at the start of a MPh, how the following could happen: "[...]or at the conclusion of its next MPh—whichever comes first."?
ground_truth_answer:
The last part of the rule is really to pick up a situation where a CX unit does nothing during its MPh.  

Normally the CX counter is removed when the unit moves - ie at the start of that unit's MPh.

But if the unit does nothing during its MPh, then that the moment the unit moves won't ever arrive.

In that situation, the conclusion of the unit's MPh will happen first (ie before it breaks, Prep Fires, is designated for Opp Fire, or moves).  

Not a common occurrence, but something which can happen.  It could probably have been worded in a slightly less cumbersome way (in the example I gave, the start and end of the unit's MPh effectively are the same moment).

ground_truth_answer:
As above, B27.44, "A unit may move/advance beneath a foxhole if otherwise able to enter that Location even if an enemy unit exists in that foxhole. The capacity of a foxhole counter is per side; i.e., two opposing squads can both occupy a 1S foxhole during CC."

The extra bit of text, "during CC," seems to be there just to confuse the reader. The intention seems to be that two opposing squads can both occupy a 1S foxhole at any time. If the friendly and squads in the same foxhole can't eliminate each other in CC, they remain in the foxhole in Melee. They might not have a Melee too, e.g. one squad entered during the MPh as part of a Human Wave, one or both squads are concealed, etc.

query: D5.5: An Immobilized AFV takes a hull hit. the final To Kill number is 5. The AFV survives the hit. Is the crew subject to TC ?
title: D5.5
raw_question: An Immobilized AFV takes a hull hit. the final To Kill number is 5. The AFV survives the hit. Is the crew subject to TC ?
ground_truth_answer: That gave me time to look up the rule. Per D5.5 an Immobilization Task Check is needed only if that hit "would have destroyed or Shocked it with an Original TK or IFT DR of 5." In this case if the TK DR is four or less, the vehicle is destroyed. If the TK DR is five or higher, a five would be a double-secret Immobilization and anything else would be no effect, so there is no Immobilization TC. If the hit had been on the turret with a TK of five, that would cause an Immobilization TC.

query: Can an ATR fire twice in Movement Phase: An ATR is a SW, but can it be fired in First Fire and then in Subsequent First Fire? Like using Intensive Fire for an MG/Gun?
title: Can an ATR fire twice in Movement Phase
raw_question: An ATR is a SW, but can it be fired in First Fire and then in Subsequent First Fire? Like using Intensive Fire for an MG/Gun?
ground_truth_answer:
Not all ATRs are SW. One sort-of exception is if the ATR is a vehicle MA, e.g. the British Morris CS9 Armoured Car or the Carrier B, it may use Intensive Fire. Per a q&a:

"C5.6 May a vehicular-mounted MG/ATR/light-MTR use Intensive Fire?
A. Yes, if it is MA. Such a weapon is considered a Gun (C2.1). [An93a; An95w; An96; Mw]"

This is probably not what was intended for the question. A vehicle-mounted ATR can't still can't use SFF (unless there is one that has IFE), which is disallowed by rule as above.

One final thing to observe is that Intensive Fire is not Subsequent First Fire and vice-versa. IF is an ordnance attack; SFF is a non-ordnance attack.

Yes, I played SL (a lot) when I was younger,  but what brought the question forward is the example below D7.22: “…., and the tank expends another MP to enter D3 where it is safe from Street Fighting since all ADJACENT Russian units are marked with First Fire counters”.

The question brewed up because the Russian in D2 is in the woods and ADJACENT. The wording of the example makes it sound like *only* the FF counter prevents it from CC Reaction Fire.

Anyway, I over thought the example. The rules are clear on it. 

In the D7.22 example it does sound as if the only reason the unit in C3 can't use CCRF/Street Fighting is because it is marked with a First Fire counter. I wonder if the writer of the example misunderstood the rules, because A11.8 clearly says a unit using street fighting has to be *in* a building. It's also possible the rules did not require the street-fighting unit itself to be in a building at the time the example was written but changed at some point without updating the example. We'll probably never know. However in this case the moving vehicle is between two buildings so at least that part of the street fighting requirements are met and are unlikely to happen with a woods-road, although it is possible I imagine.

After a squad performs a street fight vs a AFV,does the AFV get to attack back
against the squad? And if so,in which hex would that attack take place in?
This depends on in which phase the street fighting occurs. During the MPh as CCRF per D7.211, "CC Reaction Fire occurs during the MPh when no vehicle CC attacks (of any kind, including "sN"; A11.622) are allowed" [D7.213]. This is repeated in A11.8, "Reaction Fire is identical to Street Fighting CC procedures except that the vehicle may not attack back; i.e., it has no CC attack options during Reaction Fire (although Crew Small Arms still applies)." During the CCPh normal CC occurs, including the vehicle being able to attack back. The attacks take place in the hex with the vehicle.

query:
C.4 vs. C3.33:  Direct Rules Contradiction?: Maybe we're just confused about possible differences between the concepts of Area Fire and Area Target Type, but these two rules seem contradictory to me: 

-- According to C.4:  "ORDNANCE AREA FIRE:  Ordnance Area Fire never halves the FP effect of any hit.  Instead, any shot affected by any provision of Area Fire caused by the target's status uses the Case K To Hit DRM (6.2)..."

-- But according to C3.33:  "AREA TARGET TYPE:  The Area Target Type must be used at all times by mortars and whenever ordnance [EXC:  LATW] attempts to fire SMOKE; otherwise it may be selected when firing HE...  All units hit by HE are attacked on the IFT using a single DR and half the FP of the firing ordnance;..."

So which is it?  My Marder wishes to use Area Target Type to fire at a Stone Building with Concealed troops inside.  Seems like Case K applies, so at Range 5 my To Hit is 7 while my To Hit dice roll incurs a +2 for Case K.  We prefer to use the IIFT, so if I hit, then do I get a 75L full strength 14FP result (with +3 on the damage DR for the Stone Building), or a half strength 7FP result (again with the +3 for the Stone Building)?
title: C.4 vs. C3.33:  Direct Rules Contradiction?
raw_question:
Maybe we're just confused about possible differences between the concepts of Area Fire and Area Target Type, but these two rules seem contradictory to me: 

-- According to C.4:  "ORDNANCE AREA FIRE:  Ordnance Area Fire never halves the FP effect of any hit.  Instead, any shot affected by any provision of Area Fire caused by the target's status uses the Case K To Hit DRM (6.2)..."

-- But according to C3.33:  "AREA TARGET TYPE:  The Area Target Type must be used at all times by mortars and whenever ordnance [EXC:  LATW] attempts to fire SMOKE; otherwise it may be selected when firing HE...  All units hit by HE are attacked on the IFT using a single DR and half the FP of the firing ordnance;..."

So which is it?  My Marder wishes to use Area Target Type to fire at a Stone Building with Concealed troops inside.  Seems like Case K applies, so at Range 5 my To Hit is 7 while my To Hit dice roll incurs a +2 for Case K.  We prefer to use the IIFT, so if I hit, then do I get a 75L full strength 14FP result (with +3 on the damage DR for the Stone Building), or a half strength 7FP result (again with the +3 for the Stone Building)?
ground_truth_answer:
As above, Area Fire and Area Target Type are not the same thing. One place to see this is in the two separate entries in the index.

Because they are not the same, for any given ordnance attack it is possible that one or the other, both or neither apply to the attack. A BAZ firing out of a shallow stream uses Area Fire [B20.6] but not Area Target Type (it is an LATW that uses its own TH Table [C13.42]). A Mortar firing from open ground to an unconcealed target in open ground uses Area Target Type but not Area Fire. Per A7.23 concealment is a form of Area Fire so a German PaK 40 choosing the Area Target Type when firing against a concealed target would be using both Area Fire (i.e. it has a +2 TH DRM) and Area Target Type (i.e. its effects FP is halved from its normal FP). And a Pz IV firing at an unconcealed T-34 using the Vehicle Target Type would not be using either Area Fire nor Area Target Type.

query: Rout or surrender?: Will the russian surrender, or what routning options do he have?
title: Rout or surrender?
raw_question: Will the russian surrender, or what routning options do he have?
ground_truth_answer:
Am I missing something?  G6 cannot be seen by the German unit.  That means the Russian does not have to surrender.  The Russian can still low crawl to G7, without having to surrender.  A possible route path to G9 might go through G6 using 5 movement points (G6 to G7 to G8 to G9).

20.21 RtPh: Any broken Infantry unit during its RtPh that is both ADJACENT to Known, Good Order, armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry and unable to rout away from it or only able to rout while being subject to Interdiction or resorting to Low Crawl (regardless of how it actually routs or if the possible unconcealed Interdictor is Known to it), will surrender to that enemy unit as its prisoner instead, (captor's choice of unit receiving surrender if more than one unit qualifies) after first abandoning all its SW [EXC: if pinned; 10.53 & G5.5].

The fact that G6 cannot be seen, negates the only clause.  But, we get further clarification from the words in parentheses "regardless of how it actually routs . . ."  If the Russian unit was to rout to G6, it would no longer be ADJACENT to the German unit.  20.21 would no longer apply.  A route path to G6 to G7 to G8 to G9, is a possible rout path.  Low crawl to G7 is allowed because there is an another option that would not leave the Russian unit both ADJACENT to the German unit, and unable to move away without being subject to interdiction.  

So, what rule makes the Russian surrender?

A20.21 forces it to surrender.

The unit has to rout to G9. That is its only rout target. It cannot Low Crawl to G6 because it would not have moved closer to G9, but that is actually not important. However per q&a:

A10.51 If a DM broken unit that must rout is within six MF of the nearest woods/building, must it attempt to reach the woods/building in a single RtPh?
A. Yes, unless it uses Low Crawl, but it need not take the shortest route (in hexes/MF) to do so. Even if it uses Low Crawl, however, it must still do so toward that woods/building (i.e., at no time may it increase the hex range between itself and that woods/building, and must end that RtPh closer to it than it was at the start of the phase).
So its choices are:
  1) Low Crawl to G7.
  2) Rout normally through G7 to G9, facing interdiction in G7 & G8.
  3) Rout normally through G6 to G9, facing interdiction in G7 & G8.

Referring to A20.21, the unit's only choices are to use Low Crawl or face interdiction. It surrenders.

The unit does not have to be subject to interdiction as it moves from ADJACENT to the KEU. It just has to face interdiction somewhere on all the paths it might take. A q&a regarding this:
A20.21 Assume that No Quarter is not in effect and that a broken unit is ADJACENT to a Known, Good Order, armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry, with a Building hex 3 hexes away which is its only possible rout target. If the broken unit would have to suffer Interdiction in the second hex it enters, can it still rout? Or is it captured even though it would no longer be ADJACENT to the enemy unit where it would suffer Interdiction?
A. No. Yes. [Compil3; Letter222]

The unit need not even have LOS to the (unconcealed) unit that will interdict it. Assume that the German halfsquad is in SMOKE but there is another unconcealed German squad in E8 able to interdict G8. The broken unit still surrenders. If the German in E8 were concealed it would have to reveal itself at rout start to force surrender.

The unit manning the Gun has to be unbroken. So the "Normal Range" for any unit/weapon as would force a broken unit in A10.531 Open Ground to rout is its maximum range or sixteen hexes, whichever is less.

query: Routing movement: Recently in a game on a bocage filled board, I had to rout a broken unit. The unit had no LOS to a building or woods. I routed to other terrain. Now my question is does a routing unit have to use all 6 movement factors? I could not find any rule on this.
title: Routing movement
raw_question: Recently in a game on a bocage filled board, I had to rout a broken unit. The unit had no LOS to a building or woods. I routed to other terrain. Now my question is does a routing unit have to use all 6 movement factors? I could not find any rule on this.
ground_truth_answer:
Note that a lot of the rout rules, IMO, are 'fuzzy' and (as such) subject to potential abuse.  I.e. if a unit is 2 hexes away from a building (Open ground separating them), can they rout AROUND that open ground hex (moving first away from the building, but then back towards it), provided they can still reach it with 6 MF?  Or must they take the direct path (3 total MF), but be subject to Interdiction in the Open Ground hex?

A10.51 "As long as it reaches that hex during a single RtPh, it need not use the shortest route, but as long as it follows the shortest path in MF otherwise"

So the unit can in this case avoid the open ground.

If you have no valid rout target, can you designate a hex that allows your unit to "Rout forward", assuming they are not routing towards a KEU?  This is fairly clear 'yes', but can be quite odd-looking in some situations.

A hex need not be woods/building to be a valid rout target. Woods/building are *preferred*  but if not available or if ignorable and ignored, the rout target can be of another kind.

That said, a rout target, woods, building or otherwise, can be "forward" in some sense that is outside the rout rules. The rout rules don't concern themselves with whether the player can create a better situation out a rout than might otherwise be expected.

A lot of times we find ourselves making 'gentleman agreements' with respect to routing in the spirit of the rule versus trying to find ways to abuse the (albeit, limited) control you have over a broken unit that is routing.

You are of course free to do this if you want. I play the rout rules as written, and I will on occasion make a silk purse out of a sow's ear, but not often. As far as I know the rout rules are not "fuzzy" but sometimes a canny player can see multiple options for routing and choose the better of them. Likewise since you know the rout rules you can have a leader "pre-positioned" in likely rout targets before units break. I do this all the time. The line between good play and abuse is fairly narrow one.

One thing that did was changed in the routing rules is that Voluntary Break [A10.41] used to be allowed always. In the 1996 ASL Annual an erratum added that the unit had to be within LOS and normal range of an unbroken enemy unit. Without that Voluntary Break was subject to abuse. But routing "forward?" How would you ever define "forward?"

If you are using the first edition ASLRB you may be missing substantial revisions to the WA rules...yes, it looks as though mandatory WA was introduced with v2. A unit in a hex with no in-hex TEM *must* claim WA as of v2. I really can't answer any questions regarding attempting to play with v1 rules. The rules were very different, and my knowledge is based on v2. The answers above are based on v2 rules, not v1.

If you have more questions you may want to preface them with the version of the rules you are using. query: Support weapons: Guys, if a unit routs can I choose to drop its sw
title: Support weapons
raw_question: Guys, if a unit routs can I choose to drop its sw
ground_truth_answer:
No. It must carry up to its IPC and it must drop the SW that weigh more than their IPC.
A10.4 : ... A broken unit may not portage anything in excess of its IPC, and prior to rout must abandon any items in excess of its IPC in its current Location—but must rout with any SW ≤ its IPC limits if it possessed such items when it broke.

In other words, you don't have a lot of control on brokies.
Footnote 6 of chapter A4.43 rule on Posession gives some design insight on that limitation.
Broken units are not allowed to transfer or drop their weapons because allowing them to do so expands the omniscient player’s control over broken units that he should have little or no control of.

ground_truth_answer:
BTW, as a teachable moment, a tank that wants to fire in its PFPh but can't may be interested in using BFF. BFF does not occur as part of a MP expenditure but rather either "between" MP expenditures or after the last MP expenditure or before the first MP expenditure. The last case is the material one here. The vehicle can fire *before* any MP expenditure, almost like it fired in the PFPh. That means it isn't subject to DFF because there was no MP expenditure by the vehicle to target it with DFF.

Almost. A vehicle that announces a BFF attack before expending any MP can be challenged by the rarely-used DEFENDER Gun Duel [[C5.33]. The target of the attack (only) can claim the right to use DFF against the vehicle that is attempting to BFF before expending any MP. But units other than the target can't intervene. 

It's hard to come up with a case where this is super-useful, but it is a fun bit of trivia.

ground_truth_answer:
Per Chapter D footnote 5 the Mechanical Reliability DR is a game mechanic meant to represent not the literal seizure of the engine or similar but rather an abstract notion that in reality probably meant the vehicle was not even present on the battlefield. As such the game designer wants to keep the number of such DRs made to a "reasonable" level, and so decided to only make the DR on start DRs or Motion attempts. You have to view it more as an abstract game mechanic than a literal representation of the physics of engines or drive trains.

Amazing what one learns by reading the footnotes! Although in this case I think the note is just being too smart:

A more realistic rule would be to simply make a dr at the start of a scenario which a vehicle with poor mechanical reliability would have to pass in order to be included in the scenario. The drawback to such a system is that play balance can be destroyed before the game even begins.

Destroyed is a very strong word, and who knows if it would more more realistic! (ASLRB words, not mine). Designers can set the balance according to the rule itself. My impression is that the DR riffs quite well with the idea that the engine might seize up when you start it. 

How the actual odds of stalling relate to the odds of rolling boxcars is left for optional homework.😀

A broken MMP Guard has a DM marker and it is attacked by its prisoners during CCPh.
Both units remain so they are now in Melee (I guess).
As I understand it, unarmed units do not force DM status.
Is the DM marker removed in the next RPh or is it not as the unit is in Melee?
I think as written the DM counter is removed in the RPh as long as some outside condition does not leave it on (e.g. being ADJACENT to an armed enemy unit, being in Open Ground [A10.531] and in normal range of KEU, etc.). Terrain also plays a factor. If the occupied hex is building or woods, the DM counter must be removed. Otherwise it is the players choice.

ground_truth_answer:
During the MPh a stack of an MMP with an MG fires its MG (not the IFP) without ROF and is marked First Fire. No more fires during the MPh.
In the DFPh, can the MMP fire without the constraints of the First Fire marker on the MG (to a non-adjacent hex)?
I'm going to assume you mean "MMC" instead of "MMP." MMP can always fire because they control the rules and can change them as they desire.

This depends on if the MMC is a squad or not. If it is a squad per A7.351 it does not give up its inherent FP when it fires exactly one SW. This fire capability is independent from its use of that SW. Per A.15 a unit may fire in both enemy MPh and DFPh without being considered as having fired in two phases. The "first fire" counter is regrettable in that when placed it is ambiguous for a squad as to whether just one SW capability has been used or both fire capabilities. Per a q&a these are used independently:

"A8.4 During the defensive fire phase, a squad & MMG want to make fire attacks. The squad (only) is marked with a def first fire counter. Is it legal for the squad to fire his MMG at full FP vs a non-ADJACENT unit and then (provided it didn’t cower) have the squad use final fire at an ADJACENT unit? Would the answer be different if the situation was reversed? (MMG only is marked with a first fire counter, squad fires at non adjacent unit and then MMG final fires at adjacent unit.)"
A. Yes. No."

Various third party producers and now MMP have printed "First Fire SW" and "First Fire Inherent" counters that fix the flaw and allow squads to be marked unambiguously.

Due to health reasons, I only play ASL solo. My method for anything hidden is to identify alternate locations, the exact number depends on the map, avenues of approach, etc. I then assigned probabilities to each location, usually uniform but sometimes variable depending on the likelihood I think appropriate. The probabilities for the locations must total 100%. As an example of variable probabilities for three locations I might have them be a d6:1-3, d6:4-5, and d6:6. Uniform would be d6:1-2, 3-4, 5-6.

When a location comes into an enemy LOS, I roll. If the roll passes (say, a roll of 2 on a d6:1-3), the hidden unit appears - if that's what's supposed to happen. It may just mean that the hidden unit can take a shot and then reveal itself. But the hidden thing is there. Usually, a ? is placed.

If the roll fails, the hidden thing is in one of the remaining locations. I adjust probabilities for those locations so they total 100% and play on.

I used this method for hidden squads, vehicles, fortifications, and so on. I've found over the years that this method works really well. It keeps some tension in the game as to what's where and makes solo play more enjoyable. 
That's what I had in mind as well, Rick. You can perhaps alter the chance of finding a hidden fortification when you first find nothing. The 1-3 yes can then become a 1-4 yes after 2 or 3 buildings.

My opponent Fired on a Concealed Squad in a Foxhole with the +2 DRM for shooting at Concealed units.  He hit.  So its still Area Fire, which is then halved on the IFT Column. So now the +2 for the Foxhole comes in as a DRM on the IFT roll to see if any result would remove the Concealment, correct?

Just want to make sure we played this right.

My opponent Fired on a Concealed Squad in a Foxhole with the +2 DRM for shooting at Concealed units.  He hit.  So its still Area Fire, which is then halved on the IFT Column. So now the +2 for the Foxhole comes in as a DRM on the IFT roll to see if any result would remove the Concealment, correct?
ground_truth_answer:
My opponent Fired on a Concealed Squad in a Foxhole with the +2 DRM for shooting at Concealed units.  He hit.  So its still Area Fire, which is then halved on the IFT Column. So now the +2 for the Foxhole comes in as a DRM on the IFT roll to see if any result would remove the Concealment, correct?
First this sounds as if the firing unit is attacking with ordnance. If that is correct, the firing unit has to choose a Target Type, or if he fails to declare a target type, C.9 will be engaged and the Target Type will be chosen by rule.

You can use any of the three Target Types against any target, concealed or not. There are advantages and disadvantages to each. First the Target Type determines what is hit. The Vehicle Target Type targets exactly one vehicle. So if you use the Vehicle Target Type against a unit in a foxhole you probably aren't going to hit anything. But there is no rules reason you couldn't declare the attack as such. In a situation such as you have you will probably choose the Infantry or Area Target Type instead.

If you choose the Infantry Target Type there is a +2 TH DRM for concealed (Case K) as well as a +2 TH DRM for foxhole TEM (Case Q). If there is any acquisition that applies only to unconcealed units. Plus any other TH DRM, e.g. target size, armor leader, point-blank range, etc. If hit the target is attacked at the ordnance's *full* FP, i.e. not halved [C.4]. If the target loses concealment (or if there is another, unconcealed target in the Location), then acquisition is placed/improved.

If you choose the Area Target Type there is a +2 TH DRM for concealed (Case K). The +2 DRM for TEM is taken on the effects DR [C6.2, C3.331]. Plus any other TH DRM as applicable, but note that point-blank range is n/a for Area Target Type. If hit the target is attacked at half FP for Area Target Type but not halved again for concealment The penalty for concealment is the TH DRM. The +2 DRM for TEM (foxhole) now applies to the effects DR. Regardless of whether there was any hit or effect, acquisition is placed/improved.

To emphasize per C.4 FP is *not* halved for ordnance for concealment. Concealment is a TH DRM for ordnance instead.

query: Firepower 1 halved: When a unit has Firepower 1 and it's halved again, does it still retain firepower?
title: Firepower 1 halved
raw_question: When a unit has Firepower 1 and it's halved again, does it still retain firepower?
ground_truth_answer:
When a unit has Firepower 1 and it's halved again, does it still retain firepower?
To expand on previous answers, it probably depends on why this is important to you. If a unit/firegroup wants to attack on the IFT, and it does not have at least one FP, its attack would not be sufficient to use any column on the IFT table (attacks use the column equal to or to the left of their total FP [A7.3]) and so the attack would automatically fail. It's an interesting question whether this automatically failing attack would still get a LOS string (which might matter if you had something, say ordnance, that also wanted to attack); I would say it would as long as the attack was not entirely out of range, but I don't think the rules cover this exact situation. But if a unit that by itself had < one FP firegrouped with another unit or units, and their combined strength was ≥ one FP, then the attack would be performed normally, and in that sense the unit's FP is "retained." If you have eight pinned 1-2-7 vehicle crews firing at a concealed target in the AFPh without using opportunity fire, their total FP is one, and they have a legitimate attack on the IFT. In CC it is the ratio of FP that is important, so for example a unit with fractional FP can still attack other units in Close Combat. For example a unit with ½ FP for attack (say a pinned SMC alone) could attack another unit with one FP (say an enemy 1-2-7 vehicle crew) at ½-to-1 or 1-to-2 odds. In the context of Rout a unit with < one FP (e.g. a pinned 1-2-7 vehicle crew) is still an armed unit and so can't be routed towards [A10.51] but could not interdict [A10.532]. In sum it depends on the context of your question to say whether the unit "retains firepower."
In this case it was a single unit whose already reduced firepower of 1 was again halved due to area fire and could not be combined with other units in a FG. No shot possible then, I suppose.

This is an interesting question when there is a AFV and a non-vehicle (e.g. a Gun) that are vulnerable to the ammunition being fired by the LATW, say. HEAT. But having finally looked at it, the answer makes sense. If no Target Type is announced then C.9 applies, but most often the situation never arises. In the future I will try to remember to get my opponent to specify his Target Type before he rolls his TH DR where this applies.

title: Assault Move and Concealment
raw_question: Almost sure the answer is no, but need to verify.  You cannot Assault Move into a Foxhole from and Adjacent hex and maintain Concealment, even if said Foxhole is in an Orchard, correct?  Spending 2MF before moving only works for Routing into a Foxhole to avoid Interdiction, correct?
ground_truth_answer:
Almost sure the answer is no, but need to verify.  You cannot Assault Move into a Foxhole from and Adjacent hex and maintain Concealment, even if said Foxhole is in an Orchard, correct?  Spending 2MF before moving only works for Routing into a Foxhole to avoid Interdiction, correct?

As long as it doesn't move in Open Ground (relative to some enemy unit, so the A10.531 definition of Open Ground, not the terrain type) and doesn't perform some other sort of action (e.g. recovery, throw smoke grenades, etc.), assault move allows a unit to maintain concealment. A unit will maintain concealment if it assault moves out of an entrenchment into its own orchard hex then into an adjacent orchard hex.

You can do this as assault movement because inside an entrenchment and outside are the same Location. You cannot exit a pillbox and then move to an adjacent location as assault movement because that's two Locations (unless there is a trench/bunker situation).

I'm not sure what "spending 2MF before moving" means. It only costs one MF to exit an entrenchment (EXC: A-T ditch). Also I consider all use of MF in the MPh as "moving." So recovery, throwing smoke grenades, using stairs, entering/exiting crest or entrenchment, etc. is all "moving" to me. This is not a formal definition, so perhaps you think of it a different way.

Question two:
 What happens if an Infantry unit Advances into a hex with a Concealed AFV?  Its unknown, so I wouldn't think a PAATC is required.  Or would a PAATC be required to then engage it in the CC round or since its Concealed, does it get all the benefits that a Concealed enemy Infantry unit would gain if I advanced into its hex?
Per A11.16 PAATC only applies for an unconcealed vehicle. Note that the vehicle might not be Known (to the advancing unit) because, perhaps, it is out of los in bypass, but what matters for PAATC is whether the vehicle is concealed.

Once in the Location no PAATC is made in the CCPh. You would roll for ambush, which you would do anyway because it's a woods hex. The tank would get +2 for vehicle and -2 for concealed.

CC is sequential because of the vehicle. If there is no ambush the vehicle would retain concealment and the enemy infantry would attack first. Because the target is concealed, that gives a -1 to the CCV for the infantry's attack.

ground_truth_answer:
Can Baddington see the wreck?

I have my doubts because of F6.43.  It requires a unit to be "higher than the topmost height of an intervening hillock hex" (I interpolate:  a hillock summit is a hillock hex (F6.6)) "in order to have a LOS past that hillock hex to an elevation one or more full levels lower than that hillock hex's topmost height".

In the image, Baddington is at level 1/2.  The intervening hillock hex is the hillock summit, the topmost height of which is level 1.  The wreck is at level 0.

I think Baddington would need to be at level 1 1/2 or higher to see the wreck through the hillock summit.

Is that right?

As far as I understand the hillock rules a unit "behind" a hillock (i.e. adjacent to and at the base level of the hillock and ½ level below the top of the hillock) cannot see beyond that hillock to a lower elevation. Per F6.43, "A  unit must be higher than the topmost height of an intervening hillock hex in order to have a LOS past that hillock hex to [a target hex] elevation one or more full levels lower than that hillock hex's topmost height," where I have introduced the phrases "viewing" and "a target hex" to give the two hexes names for clarity. In your EX the hillock is at level one and the target is at level zero, i.e. the target hex is one full level below the topmost height of the hillock, and the viewing unit is *not* higher than the intervening hillock, so there is no LOS. 

The fact that the viewing unit is on a hillock itself and the intervening hillock is actually a hillock summit is covered by F6.6, "A Hillock Summit is treated as a normal hillock that rises from Level ½ instead of from Level 0," i.e. we can reason about such a situation as if the hillock summit was just a regular hillock. 

As you say the viewing unit would have to be above that hillock to see past the hillock (summit) to a level at least one full level below the summit. Technically that could be any amount above (a quarter level, a sixty-fourth), but since the smallest interval we have had to date is a half level, as of today the viewer would have to be at level one-and-a-half to see the wreck.

Question:  Does the +4 for shooting out of the Smoke combine with the +2 TEM for the Foxhole for a +6 total and negate the possibility of shot according to B.10?
There are many kinds of DRMs on the IFT. Hindrances [A6.7] are those DRM that are marked as such on the terrain chart "LOS Obstacle/Hindrance" column and/or in the body of the rules. SMOKE is a hindrance per A24.2. On the terrain chart you will find that entrenchments are not an obstacle or a hindrance, i.e. they have "—" listed in the LOS Obstacle/Hindrance column, but have a TEM (under the TEM/Indirect column) of +2/+4, i.e. it is an IFT DRM but not a hindrance. CX is not listed on the terrain chart nor is it indicated as a hindrance in the rules so it is an IFT DRM but not a hindrance either. As noted above B.10 does not use any IFT DRM but those that are hindrances.

Hillocks are often called "thick walls," and that captures the behavior for units at ground level. You can see over them if you are ADJACENT but if not you can't see past them. When both units are on them, it's as if they don't exist, and that's also true of all other half-level (wall, hedge) obstacles at ground level. When one unit is on one and the other unit off, it's complicated. A unit on one can see over the hillock it is on, completely over another half-level obstacle (although a unit immediately behind a wall/hedge still gets the benefits) and just behind another half-level obstacle but not beyond that.

An AFV is not vulnerable to OVR, but its vulnerable PRC will be attacked "collaterally," i.e. as if they were the target of the attack [D7.12]. Effectively a N FP up two attack.

B23.87 "Infantry expend two MF (for a 1½-level Factory) or three MF (for a 2½-level Factory) to ascend to the Rooftop or vice-versa."

The rooftop is another Location above the standard building levels, so it costs one MF to move from level zero to level one, one MF to move from level one to level two and one MF to move from level two to the rooftop level.

As for whether a particular unit possessing particular PP with a particular CX status can make a move or advance, this is all standard rules based on available MF, MF cost, and CX status. There is nothing different for accessing a rooftop, including a factory rooftop.

For movement if the MF cost is less than available MF and a move of only one Location is made, the unit may assault move (or normal move at its option). If the MF cost is equal to MF available the unit must use non-assault movement. If the move is greater than available MF and the unit has at least one MF available, it may make a minimum move [A4.134]. Double Time [A4.5] can be used with all the standard gains and provisos.

For advance if the MF cost is less than available MF and less than four MF, the unit may advance normally. If the MF cost is greater-than-or-equal-to available MF or greater than-or-equal-to four MF and the unit has at least one available MF and is not CX, it may make an Advance vs Difficult Terrain [A4.72].

query: Yet another slope question: Can these two squads see each other? Does hex T32 have any effect on LOS?
title: Yet another slope question
raw_question: Can these two squads see each other? Does hex T32 have any effect on LOS?
ground_truth_answer:
Sorry for "resurrecting" this thread, but I want to fully understand the image situation and the slope role (I assume the US unit is at level 0 and the German one is at level 1).

I understand that the units can be seen because, while the slope raises the observer slightly it doesn't raise it enough (it's not a full level) to create a blind hex which would otherwise be created even if the German unit were at level two, since in this case there is always at least one. Is that correct or am I missing something?
You have this somewhat backwards. Raising the German higher either reduces blind hexes or keeps them the same. If there were a blind hex when the German was a full level above the S32 obstacle there would also be one when it is ¾ of a level higher (or a half level higher, e.g. on an EmRR). 

To clarify the KGP map colors, the German is on level six; the American is on level five [KGP SSR1]. This does not matter because all calculations for blind hexes are the same when the relative elevations are the same.

A unit viewing across a slope hexside is treated as if at level ¾ above the hex level, i.e. level 6¾. Because the German is (treated as if) at a height > than S32, T32 and U32, it can see over those hexes to a lower elevation [A6.4]. The German will not be "plateau-ed" by those hexes. So now it is a matter of calculating blind hexes. Level-six hex U32 creates one blind hex for a viewer at level 6¾ to level 5, which is T32, so not interesting. T32 creates one blind hex, which is S32, so not interesting. That leaves hex S32. An non-crest-line obstacle in S32 would create one blind hex, so if S32 were a woods or building, hex R31 would be blind. However S32 *is* a crest line. A crest line has to be at least five hexes away to create one or more blind hexes [B10.23], so the number of blind hexes for S32 is zero. There is a minimum of one blind hex for *non-crest-line* obstacles, but S32 is a crest-line obstacle so that minimum does not apply.

query: Shellholes confusion: Let’s say an infantry unit begins the Movement Phase in a hex adjacent to a shellhole hex.  The units moves into the hex and decides to “enter” the shellhole and ends its movement. Is the unit subject to FFMO/FFNAM?
title: Shellholes confusion
raw_question: Let’s say an infantry unit begins the Movement Phase in a hex adjacent to a shellhole hex.  The units moves into the hex and decides to “enter” the shellhole and ends its movement. Is the unit subject to FFMO/FFNAM?
ground_truth_answer:
My conceptualization of shellholes vs foxholes is that a shellhole does not represent a single hole in a corner of a hex (unless it is a *monster* shellhole as might be generated by, say, a sixteen inch shell). Instead shellhole terrain represents multiple shellholes that cover a random and substantial portion of a hex. Think Paschendaele.

https://collection.nam.ac.uk/images/960/103000-103999/103603.jpg

Thus you can enter the hex and zig-zag around the shellholes, but when the music stops there's always one to fall into. But this also explains why shellholes are hard to create. Unless you are using a terrific big weapon, it takes much more than one shell to pockmark an entire hex.

In contrast foxholes are small holes that are set up in a militarily significant and therefore non-random part of the hex. A bit like wire, the abstraction for foxholes says that where ever your unit is in the hex, it's not near the foxhole you want to use. Murphy's Law for Foxholes. So you have to move around in the hex to get into that foxhole, i.e. spend one MF to enter. And again a bit like wire Murphy's Law for Foxholes says that when you want to leave the hex, the foxhole is not near where you want to go, so you have to spend a MF in the hex to "exit" the foxhole.

query:
Critical hits for Infantry Target Type 3.7 (C9): Is it correct that you have to throw an extra dr of 1 or ≤ half of the 
Modified TH# after scoring a critical hit for Infantry Target Type?
Is this only on an original TH DR of 2 or also on a final TH DR < half the Modified TH#?
title: Critical hits for Infantry Target Type 3.7 (C9)
raw_question:
Is it correct that you have to throw an extra dr of 1 or ≤ half of the 
Modified TH# after scoring a critical hit for Infantry Target Type?
Is this only on an original TH DR of 2 or also on a final TH DR < half the Modified TH#?
ground_truth_answer:
There are four possible situations here: the unit is hit by WP but not in the Location where the WP counter is placed, the unit is not hit but in the Location where the WP counter is placed, the unit is both hit and in the Location where the counter is placed, and the unit is neither hit nor in the Location where the counter is placed. In the first three the unit must take a WP NMC; in the last there is no WP NMC. The unit may be subject to a CH if it is hit but not if it is not hit.

JRV, I'm not following the bolded one above?  Do you mean a unit at ground level in, say a Pillbox, where WP hits units outside the Pillbox?  Or do you mean a unit at level 1 or 2 (for example) with WP hitting a unit at Ground level in the same hex?  I.e. I'm confused how it can be hit and subject to the NMC if not in the same Location as where the WP is placed.

Consider a level two building. Level two has an unconcealed unit. Level one has a concealed (but not HIP) unit. The LOS to level zero has six grain hexes, and there is a unit in it, HIP, concealed or unconcealed. The firing unit is not a MTR and fires WP at range, say, eight hexes. Because this is not a cave the ATT is used. The ATT could in theory hit all three levels but because LOS is blocked to the ground level (six grain hexes), it can't be hit. The Base TH number for ATT at range eight is seven, modified by case C4.4 (SMOKE ammunition range ≤ 12 hexes) to nine. The DRM are +0 vs the level two unit and +2 vs. the level one unit. On a TH DR of nine or eight the top unit is hit but not the middle unit. By C8.52 the WP counter is placed at ground level, i.e. level zero. The level two unit and the ground unit both take WP NMCs, the first because it was hit and the second because a WP counter was placed in its Location. The level one unit was neither hit nor had a WP counter placed in its Location and so does not take a WP NMC. If the TH DR had been seven or less, both the top and middle (concealed) units would be hit, and all three would take a WP NMC. On a snakeeyes (critical hit) the top and middle would be eligible for CH effects but not the unit at ground level because, being out of LOS, it was not hit; its WP NMC was "indirect" by the counter being placed at ground level.

If the attacking unit had been a mortar then on a TH DR of seven or less the unit at ground level would also be hit [C3.33], and it could potentially be subject to a critical hit. If the TH DR of eight or nine the middle unit would not be hit, and so the out-of-LOS unit would also *not* be hit.

If instead of a concealed the level one unit had been HIP, the cases for the non-mortar attack remain the same. For the mortar now a TH DR of eight or nine hits the level two unit and also the ground level unit (because the hardest-to-hit-non-HIP target has been hit) but not the level one unit because it is not out-of-LOS and its final TH DR with the +2 TH DRM for concealment (HIP) is > nine.

Pillboxes are actually a tricky, special case that goes beyond what we have covered so far. Per B30.34 they may never contain SMOKE and thus never get the WP NMC except when a WP gets a CH and the placing/firing unit "is ADJACENT-to/within-the-CA-of the pillbox." 

24.31 CASUALTIES: The chemical agents in WP caused discomfort and 
could result in demoralization/casualties. All units (including friendly ones) 
except a non-CE, CT AFV in a Location with a WP counter must take a 
NMC when the WP is placed (by any means) [EXC: non-moving units in 
First Fire] in that Location (not when it drifts or they move into it) or when 
hit by ordnance WP [EXC: if the WP does not rise to that elevation (24.4)]. 

Is it because of the blue text?  I guess I was thinking that still modified 'in a Location' (red text), i.e. the unit must be in the Location of the WP counter and takes the NMC either when the counter is placed (e.g. infantry WP grenades) /or/ when they are Hit (which could potentially cover a unit out of LOS or HiP if 'Hit' due to a variety of reasons).

As far as I know the blue text is a separate case. When the unit is in a Location where a WP counter is placed it takes a WP NMC. When the unit is hit it takes a WP NMC. These two cases overlap but it is possible to have one apply but not the other.

Side comment: Don't mortars have the ability to Hit all levels of a building that they have LOS to + the ground level?  Or something like that?  I vaguely recall reading something about multiple levels of a building being subject to being Hit sometime, but for the life of me can't find what I was thinking ...

The ability for a mortar to hit units that are not in LOS is covered in C3.33.

Does he still eliminate my Squad? Or, does he have to choose to stay in order to cause my elimination, but also take whatever I roll?
ground_truth_answer:
I think we played it that he either withdraws (only) or kills + takes the return fire...but not sure if that is 100% correct, as we had a similar question when this came up in one of our Hatten matches.
You are mixing Ambush [A11.41] rules with Infiltration rules [A11.22]. With Ambush you have the choice to either withdraw immediately with no attack or to attack and possibly be attacked. query: MG TH and ROF: I used a MMG to attack a moving AFV with a TH attemt and got ROF. Can I late in the MPh use the MMG to First Fire, Subsequent First Fire and Final Protective Fire vs a moving Infanrty unit or can I only use the MMG as ordnance?

ground_truth_answer:
Yes you can.
You also could attempt another TH DR.

If you lost ROF, you still could Subsequent First Fire/Final Protective Fire (vs infantry, an unarmored vehicle or an AFV with vulnerable PRC).
If marked with First Fire (not Final Fire), the MG could even fire during the DFPh at an ADJACENT target (at halved FP, doubled for PBF, etc.).
You could not, however, if ROF is lost, fire the MG as ordnance again, as SW don't use Intensive Fire (and a MG that would fire on the IFT at half FP may not fire as ordnance).

query: When Does Defilade Exist?: If a unit is on a level 1 hex and draws LOS to a level ground hex, when, if ever, do intervening level 1 hexes of the same hill block LOS? The rules use the term "blind hexes" rather than defilade but they're extremely unclear.
title: When Does Defilade Exist?
raw_question: If a unit is on a level 1 hex and draws LOS to a level ground hex, when, if ever, do intervening level 1 hexes of the same hill block LOS? The rules use the term "blind hexes" rather than defilade but they're extremely unclear.
ground_truth_answer:
A unit only can see over an obstacle to a lower level only if they are at a higher level than the obstacle.
So a unit at level one cannot see a unit at level 0 if a level 1 obstacle is between them.
Blind hexes are considered when the obstacle is lower than the higher unit.

See A6.2 example :

EX: Woods are a level 1 obstacle to LOS. If the firing unit is beneath level 1, it cannot see through ground-level woods to a target hex at level 1 or lower. The target unit would have to be at an elevation > the top of the obstacle to possibly establish a LOS to a hex at ground level beyond that obstacle.

Defilade is not a notion in ASL and you should not introduce it in your analysis.

That's the great irony of ASL. It tries so very hard to be a weeds up, hyper-detailed simulation of real world combat but then utterly fails to include fundamental, real world, military 101 concepts such as "defilade" which are intuitive to so many of us. 😆 

Anyway, I truly appreciate your attempt at an answer, but I still have absolutely no idea as to whether or not a unit on level 1 ground can see a unit at level 0 if there is intervening level 1 ground forming the same hill. It sounds like the intervening hex would block LOS but I'm not entirely sure since the rules also reference X number of intervening hexes to block LOS.  🤔

query:
A11.62: AFV CC ATTACKS vs INFANTRY: Question regarding: “An AFV may combine any CMG(+1 DRM on a Narrow Street), RMG, halftrack Passenger`s FP, and AAMG FP into one or more combined CC attacks or use them separately in different CC attack”

Why isn`t IFE FP of turreted MA less or equal to 15 mm mentioned in the sentence of combined CC attacks?
title: A11.62: AFV CC ATTACKS vs INFANTRY
raw_question:
Question regarding: “An AFV may combine any CMG(+1 DRM on a Narrow Street), RMG, halftrack Passenger`s FP, and AAMG FP into one or more combined CC attacks or use them separately in different CC attack”

Why isn`t IFE FP of turreted MA less or equal to 15 mm mentioned in the sentence of combined CC attacks?
ground_truth_answer:
Because you can't.
A11.62, "An AFV usually attacks Infantry/Cavalry on the CCT only with its AAMG FP (which usually is usable only if the AFV is CE, or is fired by a Heroic Rider; 15.23) and/or its CMG factor (unless that CMG can fire only through the VCA as signified on the counter by "CMG: VCA only"; D1.82) and/or the IFE FP of turreted MA ≤ 15mm."

Edit--I probably misunderstood the reply. On review I don't think  is saying that you can't attack, just that the FP can't combine. I'm leaving the post in case he meant you can't attack, but like I said that was probably not what he meant.

query: Street fighting: Do a Infantry unit that cc-reaction fire or CC attacks an AFV in bypass of a Wood get the Street fighting DRM?
title: Street fighting
raw_question: Do a Infantry unit that cc-reaction fire or CC attacks an AFV in bypass of a Wood get the Street fighting DRM?
ground_truth_answer: The street fighting DRM adds to the dangers of VBM sleaze freeze. The moving vehicle usually wants to avoid stopping in the hex, i.e. remain in Motion [D2.4]. This means it has to plan its expenditures carefully. The defender should watch to make sure that the moving vehicle has spent all its MPs or does not have enough MPs to enter a next hex. If it has not, then the vehicle is required to spend more MP, which may force the choice of stopping or exiting the hex. It can also enter a new bypass hexside but can only expend "extra" MP on entering a new hex, not in continuing on in bypass. Even if the vehicle has not muffed this, the defending unit can (assuming it passes its PAATC) attack at least twice using CC-RF with +2 for non-stopped and -1 for bypass "street fighting". For a squad that means a better than one-in-six chance of at least immobilizing the vehicle, assuming no other DRM apply. If the vehicle has some other vulnerability (e.g. an open-topped halftrack), the odds go up. And if the vehicle is forced to stop or does so voluntarily, the odds become fairly high that something bad will happen. This may still "neutralize" the defender because if it's using CC-RF, it's not shooting at other units, but at least the neutralization comes with a price.

query: Burning wreck in woods-road hex: If the burning wreck is on the road and not in the Wood, can it then spread to become a Blaze in that hex?
title: Burning wreck in woods-road hex
raw_question: If the burning wreck is on the road and not in the Wood, can it then spread to become a Blaze in that hex?
ground_truth_answer: B25.6 "Every Player Turn after the first Player Turn in which it appears, a Blaze may spread to any adjacent Burnable Terrain Location (including from the ground floor of a Factory hex to its Rooftop Location or to Burnable Terrain in the same Location in the case of a Burning Wreck) at the end of each AFPh." The road and the woods are the same Location. Similarly a burning wreck in bypass can also spread to the obstacle(s) that is bypassed [B25.6]. I think the "not directly attached" DRM will apply.

query:
PAATC and Bypass: This scenario we are playing is bringing up all kinds of new situations.  I have a stationary tank in Bypass along side a building.  I also have a half squad in that building.  My opponents has a Squad and a half-Squad wanting to Advance into said building.  I believe he has to pass a PAATC first due to the tank in the hex, even though its in Bypass,  correct?

If correct, and he passes the PAATC, whats the mechanic for resolving?  Is Ambush amongst the troops rolled for?  Is there sequential Combat with the tank first?
title: PAATC and Bypass
raw_question:
This scenario we are playing is bringing up all kinds of new situations.  I have a stationary tank in Bypass along side a building.  I also have a half squad in that building.  My opponents has a Squad and a half-Squad wanting to Advance into said building.  I believe he has to pass a PAATC first due to the tank in the hex, even though its in Bypass,  correct?

If correct, and he passes the PAATC, whats the mechanic for resolving?  Is Ambush amongst the troops rolled for?  Is there sequential Combat with the tank first?
ground_truth_answer:
This is my understanding:
(1) Yes, he has to pass PAATCs to Advance in. (A11.6)
(2) When he Advances in, you both roll for Ambush. (A11.4)
(3) If there is no Ambush, then he gets Street Fighting Ambush DRM. (A11.8, second sentence, penultimate sentence)
(4) It is a sequential CC, due to the vehicle, with him making the first attack. (A11.31) [EDIT: As noted by JR V, this is assuming regular Ambush does not occur: see his answer for what happens if regular Ambush does occur.]

query: FG and Cowering: Same scenario as below.  My opponent Prep fired with a 3-hex FG, one containing an MMG and a Leader.  He rolled Snakes. So, since the other two adjacent hex's with squads had no Leaders, the Fire Group Cowers.  My opponent is of the opinion that since the Leader was in with the MMG, that the MMG kept rate and therefore can fire again since the Leader was in its hex.  I don't believe this correct.   It was a Fire group that Cowered as a whole, so the Leader I believe is irrelevant, correct?
title: FG and Cowering
raw_question: Same scenario as below.  My opponent Prep fired with a 3-hex FG, one containing an MMG and a Leader.  He rolled Snakes. So, since the other two adjacent hex's with squads had no Leaders, the Fire Group Cowers.  My opponent is of the opinion that since the Leader was in with the MMG, that the MMG kept rate and therefore can fire again since the Leader was in its hex.  I don't believe this correct.   It was a Fire group that Cowered as a whole, so the Leader I believe is irrelevant, correct?
ground_truth_answer:
I was under the impression that a leader can direct a multilocation firegroup (per 7.53), but they will not get the leadership DRM unless a leader (with that DRM) is in every hex (per 7.531).   
This is a common misunderstanding:
A7.53, A7.531 & A7.9 An 8-1 leader and squad w/ LMG are in a Location; another friendly squad is in an Adjacent Location. Absent Leader Direction, each squad is subject to Cowering. All of these units have LOS to a target. They declare an attack on that target as a firegroup. To prevent Cowering in his Location, may the leader be
declared as directing the fire of the squad and LMG in his location (even though he may not apply his DRM to the attack – A7.531)?
A. No.
If not, suppose there were another 8-1 and it were stacked with the other squad, such that both Locations of the FG featured a –1 leader directing
the FG attack. A7.531 allows a -1 leadership attack DRM in this case. Because this would be an attack directed by two leaders (as opposed to a leader – A7.9, 1st sentence), would the attack be subject to Cowering?
A. No.

Rout and Withdraw with a side dish of Vehicle Freeze: Too many threads to pull for my opponent and myself to untangle.  I'm playing the Russians, he is playing the SS.  I broke an SS Squad in a building.  I proceeded to drive one of my T-34's and stop in the building hex with the SS in VBM.  So this makes it impossible for Broken SS Squad to Rout in the Rout Phase, correct?

I then advanced a CX'd Half Squad into the building.  Does CC Occur, with Ambush Die-rolls?  And is it still possible for the SS to Withdraw with T-34 in its hex?
title: Rout and Withdraw with a side dish of Vehicle Freeze
raw_question:
Too many threads to pull for my opponent and myself to untangle.  I'm playing the Russians, he is playing the SS.  I broke an SS Squad in a building.  I proceeded to drive one of my T-34's and stop in the building hex with the SS in VBM.  So this makes it impossible for Broken SS Squad to Rout in the Rout Phase, correct?

I then advanced a CX'd Half Squad into the building.  Does CC Occur, with Ambush Die-rolls?  And is it still possible for the SS to Withdraw with T-34 in its hex?
ground_truth_answer:
So the Sleeze Freeze does not work on Broken units?

Sleaze Freeze usually refers to preventing units from firing out of the Location [A7.212]. A broken unit with an enemy unit in its Location (bypass or not, vehicle or not) is doubly-unable to fire out. It is limited by A7.212, *and* it is broken. "Sleaze Freeze" is not usually a reference to freezing movement, although if the enemy vehicle stops and the units end up in Melee after the CCPh, the enemy vehicle can also stop movement. Since a Melee won't form until after the RtPh, a broken unit will either rout away or be eliminated for failure to rout before a Melee forms.

Firing to reveal HIP AFVs and Guns: Playing ASL24 "The Mad Minute", where several AFVs and Guns are likely HIP in the woods between board 12 and 16.
As I'm quite sure they will be hiding in the woods, I would like to reveal them with my AFVs before sending infantry and halftracks. I don't want to drive with my own AFVs into the woods, because I risk bog and other unpleasant surprises, so the best option is to shoot at several locations?

As they are no known units, can I only use ATT, or is it also allowed to fire with VTT or ITT, using case K for concealed target?
When would the HIP units be revealed? Case A of the A12.121 Concealment Loss Table states: "If it: ... is attacked resulting in at least a PTC". So the IFT result of my ATT attack on a HIP Gun must be at least a PTC to reveal it?
For vehicles I saw: "If it: ... is a vehicle hit by ordnance". So a HIP AFV is already revealed when the TH-attempt was successful?
title: Firing to reveal HIP AFVs and Guns
raw_question:
Playing ASL24 "The Mad Minute", where several AFVs and Guns are likely HIP in the woods between board 12 and 16.
As I'm quite sure they will be hiding in the woods, I would like to reveal them with my AFVs before sending infantry and halftracks. I don't want to drive with my own AFVs into the woods, because I risk bog and other unpleasant surprises, so the best option is to shoot at several locations?

As they are no known units, can I only use ATT, or is it also allowed to fire with VTT or ITT, using case K for concealed target?
When would the HIP units be revealed? Case A of the A12.121 Concealment Loss Table states: "If it: ... is attacked resulting in at least a PTC". So the IFT result of my ATT attack on a HIP Gun must be at least a PTC to reveal it?
For vehicles I saw: "If it: ... is a vehicle hit by ordnance". So a HIP AFV is already revealed when the TH-attempt was successful?
ground_truth_answer:
Note that if you are uncertain if you are shooting at hidden/concealed vehicles or guns - one trick is to not declare the Target Type.

C.9 UNDECLARED ORDNANCE TARGET TYPE: Any time ordnance capable of fire on more than one Target Type of the C3 To Hit Table makes a To Hit DR without first specifying the Target Type being used, the Target Type used for that To Hit DR is the topmost one listed on the To Hit Table that can legally be used vs a target in that hex by that firer (i.e., Vehicle, Infantry or Area in that order).

C2.21 choose the ammo type for you, if you don't specify: "In the absence of a declaration to the contrary, it is otherwise always assumed to be firing HE vs unarmored targets or AP vs armored targets, provided that ammunition type is available, is not Special Ammunition (i.e., has no Depletion #; 8.8), and is allowed on the applicable Target Type of the To Hit Table."When a unit fires a weapon, the firer knows--and deliberately chooses--which type of round he slides into the tube.

When there's no visible target in the hex (e.g., maybe HIP units, maybe not), it seems that the Infantry Target Type should be the default selection, as it's the first target type that can affect what the firer knows and sees to be in the hex: i.e., terrain only. Arguing for a quantum-physics transmutation of the bullet based on what it ends up hitting is foreign to the straightforward way that ASL works. If the firer is trying to hit a vehicle, he should have to specify VTT ahead of time; otherwise (assuming he has HE), he should get ITT.

C.9 is meant to handle cases where target type is obvious or the firer forgets to state it before he rolls; I doubt it was meant for the suggested tactic, which IMO would lessen this great gaming system. Please, MMP, consider patching this one.

C.9 UNDECLARED ORDNANCE TARGET TYPE: Any time ordnance capable of fire on more than one Target Type of the C3 To Hit Table makes a To Hit DR without first specifying the Target Type being used, the Target Type used for that To Hit DR is the topmost one listed on the To Hit Table that can legally be used vs a known target in that hex by that firer (i.e., Vehicle, Infantry or Area in that order, and assigns terrain as the target in the absence of other known targets).

query:
Wall Advantage and Fire Lanes: The Russian unit wants to put a Fire Lane towards O10. What effect, if any, does it have that he does not have Wall Advantage?

TIA.
title: Wall Advantage and Fire Lanes
raw_question:
The Russian unit wants to put a Fire Lane towards O10. What effect, if any, does it have that he does not have Wall Advantage?

TIA.
ground_truth_answer:
One way to 'zen' it is that if you are close enough to the wall that you /could/ have gotten wall advantage (i.e. are in the hex adjacent to the wall), it doesn't mean the enemy with wall advantage is directly adjacent the wall and your guys are 40 m away at the far edge of the hex (in this situation, one would like to think the wall would block LOS; e.g. to O10, because the unit isn't adjacent the wall and that is how non-adjacent walls work).  But instead, think of your guys are also up close to the wall, but are more pre-occupied with the guys that have wall advantage to be exceptionally concerned with using the wall to their advantage when firing at someone else (or, conversely, are close enough to the wall that the other people being fired at don't really gain any benefit from it unless they can get even closer; i.e. also claim wall advantage).

Remember that a unit can still get wall TEM even if it doesn't have wall advantage.  So they are still 'close' to the wall, relatively speaking.  So a German in O10 firing at the MMG would have to add +2 for the wall TEM (see B9.31).  So clearly the Soviets have some wall benefits...just not versus the German HS.

query: Crest status gully TEM: Does crest status in a Gully still afford a +2 TEM for fire crossing the crest hexsides?
title: Crest status gully TEM
raw_question: Does crest status in a Gully still afford a +2 TEM for fire crossing the crest hexsides?
ground_truth_answer: Despite being in the "Stream" section of the rules, B20.9 says, "Crest status can be gained by Infantry in any Depression hex." Per the index Depressions are, "Gully, Stream, Sunken Road." And Wadis are also covered per F5.12. B20.9 allows crest in all Depression hexes; since there is no separate rules section for Depressions, it was stuck in "Streams," probably pretty arbitrarily. I have always been a bit surprised it is not in "Gully," but there you go.

ground_truth_answer:
B11.1 Hill hexsides overprinting a darker, serrated, brownish-black color are cliff hexsides representing near-vertical hillsides. ground_truth_answer:
In this scenario's case the SSR says only the AT Mines can be HIP, no other fortifications (trenches and pillbox).
As a technical point, Prepared Fire Zones are not "Fortifications" as defined in the Index, although in common parlance they are certainly fortification-like. But in game terms they are an independent thing. Any rule or SSR applying to "Fortifications" does not apply to PFZs. For that reason SSR2 does not apply, but then neither does A12.33 [Fortification HIP].

Thanks for the clarification!

ground_truth_answer:
There are many occasions when a broken unit will rout away from an enemy unit in its Location. One of the funniest things to watch is a berserk unit chasing a broken unit all over the board. Human waves can also lead to this, but if in the middle of the wave the broken unit may have nowhere to rout. 

For your case probably the best use for the AFV would not be for OVR but rather to form one half of a surrounding pair to eliminate for Failure to Rout. The tank moves to one side of the hex (it can remain in Motion), and another unit stands on the opposite side. The broken unit will either surrender or be eliminated. Leaders are good units to use for the other side as they often don't have much to do, although another AFV or a MMC will do. An OVR can lead to irritating results like HoB or Immob on the vehicle since it has no weapons to malf. With elimination for FTR there's not even a slight chance of a bad result.

query:

title: MTR fire against Passengers in OT vehicle/LC (2)

Area fire against an AFV is resolved according to C 1.55. Let's say an OT AFV is targeted and hit by a 81* MTR Area Fire. How is the Collateral Attack supposed to be resolved against the Infantry Passengers in the AFV?

ground_truth_answer:
Vulnerable is defined in the ASL index: "Vulnerable PRC (any PRC subject to a specified attack if their vehicle is not eliminated/shocked/stunned [Riders are still vulnerable]; all CE PRC are Vulnerable, as are all units conveyed by an unarmored vehicle and those in an AFV that for a particular reason is treated as unarmored [for that attack]): [Near Miss also affects Specific Collateral Attack vs Vulnerable PRC: E7.421]"

LC are covered in G12.672. Per G12.123 Passengers are *always* BU through an armored facing except large guns and vehicles and so ordinarily would not be vulnerable. G12.672 overrides that. However if the LC is considered armored for the attack the collateral is at half FP [G12.672]. The CE DRM does not seem to apply to Passengers, although I have inferred that from the G12.672 EXs. For an armored LC hit with the Area Target Type or by OBA on the eight FP column the collateral would be at four FP flat, or possibly up two for an AFV passenger (i.e. the passenger itself is also an AFV) or up one for Infantry if there is a passenger AFV.

title: LC Inherent MG use timing
raw_question:
I'm going into details here but…

G 12.5 NON-CC ATTACKS FROM/BY LC: The Inherent weapon(s) of a LC may Prep Fire only if the LC is Fast Aground and Inherently crewed.

Why the "Fast" prerequisite? Being "Fast Aground" assumes the LC previously attempted to remove its Aground (and thus its Bogged) status in a previous MPh and didn't make it, basically. Why a LC couldn't use its MG when being "simply" Aground? 

And why the following:
G 12.211 FAST AGROUND: An otherwise-Mobile LC may attempt to remove its Aground (and thus its Bogged) status at the start of its MPh, provided it has not fired during its PFPh.

How could the LC have fired during the PFPh if it wasn't Fast Aground. This is confusing.
ground_truth_answer:
When aground but not fast aground the LC might try to unbeach [G12.3] itself. But this is not required, and units might unload (in hex) instead, going "over the side." Per D6.5, "Passenger/Riders may leave a vehicle that fired in the preceding PFPh and expended no MP in this MPh, although they could not leave the vehicle's Location during that MPh," so without G12.5 the LC could fire while the passengers unload. The rule prevents the LC from firing in the PFPh while the Passengers unload. The LC might even just sit there, for instance if unloading would result in much carnage on its contents and its fire support would help other units. I assume this is done for "reality reasons" (e.g. the crew was busy with the disembarkation) but I don't know for certain.

As to the apparently unnecessary phrase in G12.211 I have no idea, but it does not create a conflict so I'll just let it roll.

PU move from one Shallow water hex to the next paying 3MF. This is not considered as an Hazardous movement.

ground_truth_answer: The question is perhaps better phrased, "what happens when they are out of the LC?" I suppose this depends on how the scenario defines the water hexes. In order to invoke E5.532 Shallow Water the hexes would have to be defined as "fordable" per E5.53. Most scenarios that use LC won't define water obstacle hexes as "fordable;" typically they will use OCEAN hexes per G13.1. Some scenarios might not have OCEAN hexes or even a mix of both, but "fordable" hexes would be river hexes or ponds. See the G13.12 EX. If in OCEAN hexes, units are wading per G13.42. As G13.42 says, "Wading—not Fording—rules apply in shallow-OCEAN." Also for both boats and LC, units can unload in a hex other than the one the boat/LC is in when the boat/LC is beached across a hexside.
