I /think/ we did everything correctly, but wanted to run the following things past the powers_that_be and see if we screwed anything up.

Soviet turn 2, during DPh the GE leader manning the radio rolls for battery contact (succeeds), then draws a chit (black).  So they place an AR on a hex with lots of Soviets nearby, where they can see both the ground level of the hex and many of the Soviets.  A '1' is rolled for accuracy, so we replace the AR with an SR and that ends the DPh for the Leader+Radio.

Correct?

The Leader survives all Advancing Fire and during the German turn 3 Prep Fire Phase rolls to maintain battery contact (+1 due to Bttn MORs), succeeding.  They then declare that they are correcting the SR 1 hex and converting to FFE.  We place a red AR in the corrected hex and roll for accuracy (a 2, so accurate).  We immediately place a FFE:1 in the hex and resolve a 16 factor attack on all seven hexes (woods being at -1 DRM; grain and open at +0 DRM).  We roll a KIA on a grain hex, so make a Kindling roll needing >10 (EC = no DRM).  After resolving the FFE:1, we leave it as a FFE:1 and that ends the Leader+Radio's Prep Fire.

Correct?

During Soviet DPh during the German MPh, a sniper wounds the Leader with the radio.  Since only a light wound, this has no impact on battery access, etc.  Correct?

During the GE MPh, we have a ht w/ a loaded 75L AT Gun on a lvl3 hex.  The crew, previously broken and now rallied, is 4 MFs away.  We move the crew to the ht hex, where it is fired on at a net +1 (+1 for height advantage, +1 for the ht Hindrance, -1 for FFNAM).  It survives all the fire against it.  We then have the ht start its movement by attempting to lay smoke grenades (fails), which costs it 0 MPs.  It then expends 8 MPs to unhook (C10.12) the gun. This appears to be valid even though the crew used its entire 4 MFs to move to this hex, as nothing in C10.111 talks about the crew needing to expend MFs ... only that the towing vehicle expends 1/2 its MP allotment (8 MPs for the ht).  The ht/crew/gun all survive fire and the gun is now allowed to be placed unhooked at any CA in this hex.

Can it fire during the AFPH?  If 'yes', does it have any DRMs associated with it (given that it never moved to a new hex ... the ht and gun began the MPH stopped in that hex)?  I think the answer is "Yes, it can fire ... and 'only Case B, +2 DRM' to its fire".  Correct?

During the German MPh, a HMG manned by a squad needed to Dash across a Road to avoid the oncoming Soviet horde.  This cost 3 MFs (road + forest), which was the exact amount the squad has (4 PP HMG). If Smoke has been laid in the road hex, he could have still Dashed ... but would have had to declare CX at the start of the move.  Correct?
ground_truth_answer:
This is a place where the rules could use a rewrite, since its apparent that C10.1 expects you'll always have the crew for the gun inside the vehicle that's towing it. Note that all the references to 'crew' in C10.1 and subsections are Infantry (or Passenger) crew, not Inherent vehicle crew (well... maybe if you've got a Bren carrier towing something...). So, normally, the ht would go along, stop, and unload+unhook, with the Gun crew taking possession of the Gun, who would become TI (C10.12). As usual with loading/unloading procedures, the crew would be expending MF as part of the ht's MPh. 

So... without riding in the vehicle, most likely, the (future) Gun crew would have to start in the hex, the ht comes up, unhooks, the crew goes TI (forgoing its normal MPh) and gets possession of the Gun (and there needs to be a crew for the Gun to unhook). (See here)

And since the crew will be TI, no it can't fire in AFPh (since TI prohibits fire).

We missed the TI part, agree completely on that.  Not sure I agree with the argument for the crew moving.  One of the reasons is that C10.11 explicitly mentions movement wrt hooking up the Gun
10.11 HOOKING UP: A Stopped vehicle not in Bypass may hook up a 
Gun (if the vehicle’s T# ≤ the Gun’s M#) by spending half (FRU) of its 
MP/MF allotment [EXC: if the Gun’s M# is circled (e.g., M 6 ), the vehi-
cle must expend two-thirds (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment] in that Gun’s 
hex (in addition to any required MP/MF cost to enter the hex), provided a 
crew (as per 10.111) is on foot in that hex. This expenditure does not itself 
qualify that vehicle as a moving target, but does allow Defensive First Fire 
opportunities against it (that Gun shares its target status and is destroyed 
or missed depending on the fate of the vehicle). That Gun is then placed on 
top of that vehicle to indicate that it is in tow. Neither that Gun, its crew, nor 
that vehicle/its PRC can fire during that PFPh/MPh and all are TI for the 
rest of that Player Turn. That crew may also load into that towing vehicle 
at no extra MP/MF cost as it hooks up that Gun, but if it expends > half 
its MF allotment in pushing/entering that Gun’s hex, that Gun cannot then 
be hooked up by that unit in that MPh. A non-QSU Gun (10.23) must first 
be limbered (10.21) before it can be hooked up. See 10.31 for pushing and 
hooking up a Gun in the same MPh.  (emphasis added)

But C10.12 has absolutely no similar mention...
10.12 UNHOOKING: A Stopped vehicle not in Bypass may unhook a 
Gun only by spending half (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment [EXC: if the 
Gun’s M# is circled (e.g., M 6 ), the vehicle must expend two-thirds (FRU) 
of its MP/MF allotment] under the otherwise same conditions as were 
necessary for hooking up (10.11). That Gun’s crew may disembark from 
that vehicle at no extra MP/MF cost as part of that unhooking procedure, 
but that crew and Gun must remain TI in that hex [EXC: that vehicle may 
expend its remaining MP/MF]. After being unhooked, certain Guns must 
still be unlimbered (10.21) before they can be fired. Neither the crew nor 
the vehicle/PRC may fire during that PFPh/MPh prior to unhooking. A 
Gun’s CA may be changed simultaneously as it is (un)hooked.

This made us feel that the omission of that language was intentional and that a crew could move TO the vehicles hex and assist in unhooking the gun, provided the ht can expend the requisite MPs.

-K

An AFV can’t voluntarily offload its MG/MA, unless allowed by the vehicle notes.

query:
When do you get Gunshield DRM (or 'what is a manning crew'): So we had this come up in our current game of Hill 621 as the GE crew was unloading from the HT to set up the 75L AT gun.

Two Soviet MMGs had long range (exactly 16 hexes) fire at the crew and while the crew had Height Advantage, we weren't sure if they could (instead) claim the +2 Gun Shield TEM?

They were unhooking the gun and not in position to fire the gun...so does that qualify them as 'manning crew' per the Gun Shield rule (C11.5)?  Ultimately, we ruled 'no' and a IFT roll of '5' against them broke them regardless of whether it would have been a +1 or +2 DRM, but we did want to ask to know for the future.

Questions were:
1) Is there a definition of 'manning crew' for the purpose of Guns?

2) Do crews/squads unhooking a gun gain the Gun Shield DRM?

3) Do crews/squads PUSHING a gun gain the Gun Shield DRM (even though this is treated as Hazardous movement, nothing in the Hazardous Movement rules talk about not gaining a Gunshield DRM if the fire came through that CA).

2) Do crews/squads unhooking a gun gain the Gun Shield DRM?

ground_truth_answer:
Two Soviet MMGs had long range (exactly 16 hexes) fire at the crew and while the crew had Height Advantage, we weren't sure if they could (instead) claim the +2 Gun Shield TEM?

Gunshield is a DRM, not a TEM.

They were unhooking the gun and not in position to fire the gun...so does that qualify them as 'manning crew' per the Gun Shield rule (C11.5)?

No, they are not "manning the gun" until they have finished unloading/unhooking.  While they are in the act of unloading/unhooking they are just moving.

11.5 GUNSHIELDS: ... Infantry moving to a Gun or pushing it while being attacked by Defensive First Fire is not entitled to any protective DRM from its gunshield ... 

The "to a Gun" phrase above is effectively redundant.

 1) Is there a definition of 'manning crew' for the purpose of Guns?

Not in the rules that I know of, but it's pretty clearly covered by common sense.  What is a manning crew?  It's a unit that possesses the gun.  A unit that doesn't possess the gun clearly isn't manning it.  (The EXC would be in the case of 2 SMC combining to operate the weapon per A21.13; only one of the SMC can possess the gun, but the two SMC together would be the "manning crew".)

2) Do crews/squads unhooking a gun gain the Gun Shield DRM?

No, as above.  A squad (or HS, or any number of SMC) in any case will never qualify for the gunshield DRM -- only crews qualify.

3) Do crews/squads PUSHING a gun gain the Gun Shield DRM (even though this is treated as Hazardous movement, nothing in the Hazardous Movement rules talk about not gaining a Gunshield DRM if the fire came through that CA).

No.  This is stated explicitly in C11.5, as above.

Since there is nothing in the rules to cover this, I would assume both sides setup under the rules as attackers (cloaking etc) and there is no scenario defender.

Thoughts?
title: A Bridge too Far ASL game rule question

In the A Bridge too far, CG1 game, there is a second night turn, 18N. If both the British & the German players select an attack chit then a dual assault develops.

ground_truth_answer: Why do you say "there is nothing in the rules to cover this"?  R9.62133 specifically tells you to look at CG24, which in turn specifically tells you that "the side(s) selecting the Attack chit in a night scenario is considered the Scenario Attacker (E1.4; ...)".  Note the plural; they've already taken into account the possibility of a Dual Attack.  The rule then goes on in some detail about how to treat this; you can ignore everything referring to the Scenario Defender, because there isn't one.

Questions from our last session: In no particular order:

(1) Can a MOR can go back and forth between spotted and non-spotted fire in same phase.  E.g. first shot during enemy MPh was with a spotter; kept ROF; later in same MPh, a unit moved into its LOS (but not the Spotters), can the MOR fire at it?  We ruled 'yes', that the Spotter rules say /may fire/ and not /must fire/; e.g. Spotters merely add to what the Mortar can fire at versus changing its possible targets to a different subset.

(2) Does a stunned vehicle lose its acquisition? We ruled 'yes', but since vehicle died shortly thereafter was a moot point.

(3) Does an OT vehicle lose its acquisition if it goes BU? We rules 'no', but - as above - vehicle died shortly thereafter so was moot to us

(4) If a unit has to rout (e.g. starts adj to enemy) and the nearest building is 6 MFs away, with an orchard adjacent THEN a road/open ground hex that is subject to interdiction by enemy units, can the routing unit stop in the orchard hex (only expending 1 MF) or must they move through the open ground (road) to reach the building?  Alternatively, can they declare a low crawl to the adjacent orchard hex even if their initial hex wasn't open ground and that orchard would not be subject to any interdiction? We ruled that the Low Crawl rules never state that one can only do this to avoid Interdiction or only in Open Ground hexes, so a Rout of 1 hex by using Low Crawl to the adjacent orchard was considered valid ... but we were not sure because it kind of goes against the spirit of "must use all MFs to get to the nearest building/woods" and "routing units are not in the control of the player".

(5) GE Player turn.  They move a CE ht up adjacent to a broken US unit and stops. The US unit goes DM (adjacent, Known armed enemy) and must Rout during the Rout Phase.  Can the ht interdict the Routing unit if it moves to a non-adjacent, Open Ground hex?  Or is the ht considered to still be a "Moving" vehicle, and hence subject to half FP, which prevents it from Interdicting?  We ruled that it could NOT interdict, but the only rules we found talked about the ht still being a moving /TARGET/ for the rest of the player turn, not that it was consider a moving vehicle, per se, for Interdiction purposes.  E.g. a moving vehicle becomes a +1 Hindrance after the AFPh; i.e. is no longer "moving", per se, but there is nothing in the Interdiction rules or (from what we could find) vehicle movement rules that clarify when a stopped vehicle is truly considered 'stopped'.  We think we are correct given that the "moving target" language does say entire Player Turn ... but wasn't sure if there was something more explicit that we missed...

query:
ASL concepts - Halftracks: edit(1): replaced "HT" with 'ht' to be correct with ASLRB abbreviations
edit(2): updated per corrections below, in bold+italics 

Not really a 'how to use them' post (though I certainly welcome comments to that effect), but more a summary of how we understand Halftracks (hts) to make sure we are getting those rules correct (can't think about /how/ to use something if we don't actually understand the underlying rules on them first!).

The following will be predicated on the GE SPW 251/1 ht

In no particular order, what understand about hts are:
* armored  hts are AFVs because they are armored. If unarmored, they are NOT AFVs.

* As AFVs, they have smoke grenades (D13.35). If BU, the placement roll is a '1'; otherwise it is a '2'.

* A Passenger can remove the MG as they dismount (D6.631) if the vehicle notes allow it, or the crew can while abandoning, which is a MG of the same or less factors (so a LMG in the case of the SPW 251/1). This costs no additional MPs/MFs.  Scrounging of the MG from a non-burning Wreck can also be done, but is always a LMG (D10.52).

* hts can be part of a FG if using non-FT, non-IFE, non-ordnance (D6.64).  Hatten in Flames modifies this slightly, FWIW, to allow the GE IFE hts to also form FGs.

* CE Passengers in a ht can form a FG with other CE Passengers or Infantry/Cavalry (D6.64)

* CE Infantry Leaders may apply their Leadership DRM to a FG including the ht and Passengers, but cannot modify the hts fire if fired alone. This includes an OVR if the Passengers participate (D6.65). A Leader must have LOS to the target to direct fire and cannot aid other units in the hex if the ht has entered a new hex/hexside or is in Motion. This implies that if a FG is formed between units in a Motion ht and other Infantry in the same hex, no Leadership applies unless the other units also have the same or better Leader.

* A CE Armor Leader in a ht may apply their Leadership as above, but cannot modify the /Passenger/ fire if the Passengers fire alone.

* Up to 4 SMC can be carried at 0 PP (D6.1).

* BU Passengers are immune to small arms fire unless the target has height advantage greater than range to ht or if subject to TPBF in the same hex as the firer, regardless of elevation difference. Excessive height advantage can reduce the +2 CE DRM to less. Most likely scenarios are: Lvl 1 at adjacent ht = no fire (1 vs 1).  Lvl 2 at adjacent ht = fire at +2 DRM (2 vs 1). Lvl 1 at same hex ht = Fire at +2 DRM.  Lvl 2 at same hex ht = Fire at +1 DRM.

* ht Passengers are halved in FP for movement, but not just for being Mounted (D6.63).

* Non-vehicle MGs can attempt to kill a ht via a To Hit procedure and a '4' TK#.  It can be Stunned even if BU this way (A9.61). Vehicle MGs that are Main Armaments can also do this, but non-MA vehicle MGs may not (D3.54).  This *IS* modified by the Case D to kill per the example in C7.24.

* Armored Assault (D9.31) is a way to move infantry and vehicles simultaneously AND provide the +1 TEM of the vehicle to these infantry even though the ht was moving.  The ht does /not/ need to end in the same hex as the infantry, but can move no further than what those infantry /could/ have moved (assuming, presumably, CX and/or leadership).  The ht movement is done as if the infantry were accompanying it, even if they got broken, pinned, stopped moving, etc.

* hts are /tracked/ vehicles, along with Fully Tracked.  This is important for some ECs/terrain/weather conditions; e.g. Ground Snow affects "untracked" vehicles, which is not explicitly defined in the rules, but seems intuitively to mean: non-half tracked or non-fully tracked (exception being sledges).  But hts have their own MP costs versus Fully Tracked and cannot enter buildings, etc.

* Apparently throwing a DC from a moving ht is a 'nirvana-esque' ASL experience that is on everyone's bucket list...  We don't really know the 'hows' and 'whys' to perform this task, though...

* hts are excellent for VBM "Freeze" (VBF) if one does not care if the ht will have a high risk of dying - the concept of getting a Motion ht into someone's hex to prevent them from being able to fire outside their hex (A7.211 and A7.212).  This also breaks any FL originating from that hex. hts VBF all elevations in its hex even if BU, because they are either in their Location (ground level) or are subject to being attacked with TPBF (higher elevations).

* Passengers can embark for 1 MF and 1/4 MPs of the ht (4 for the SPW 251/1). Passengers can debark a Stopped ht for the same.  Passengers lose 1 MF for every 1/4 MPs (4 MPs for SPW 251/1) spent.

* hts, being AFVs, provide a +1 TEM versus FLs /if/ they were/are not moving/Motion (D9.3; D9.4).

* hts can tow guns if marked with a T#.

* hts are Known, armed enemy units, so can dictate enemy Rout paths even if BU.

* Broken units IN a ht are safe from needing to Rout (even if ADJACENT or same hex) or Failure to Rout

* hts can be used to provide a place for units to Rout under them per D6.1 (though if ADJACENT, those units would still have to continue routing is our interpretation).

* A CE ht can also interdict (A10.53), provided it is not in Motion or subject to any other DRM/halving (A10.532).

-----
I think that is pretty much everything re: hts.  Let us know if we missed anything or if there are key uses that hts are valuable for.

Stairwell under rubble: Hello,

1. Is it possible for a unit to change level if the only stairwell in the building is under rubble ?

2. Can I set up a unit in a level in a building whose only staircase is under rubble ?

Thank you for your answers.
title: Stairwell under rubble
raw_question:
Hello,

1. Is it possible for a unit to change level if the only stairwell in the building is under rubble ?

2. Can I set up a unit in a level in a building whose only staircase is under rubble ?

Thank you for your answers.
ground_truth_answer:
The stairwell still exists under the rubble....

B24.4:
" Stairwell movement to or from a rubble level also costs three MF, not the normal one MF cost for changing levels via a stairwell."

So e.g., in a two story house (B23.22) if Level 1 is rubbled, you can still use the inherent stairwell to/from ground level, but it costs 3 MF.

query:
CC Reaction walkthrough/questions: We had a couple situations last session where we felt CC Reaction came into play, but weren't 100% certain if we did things correct.  So let me describe the situation and how we resolved it and people can correct what we did wrong...

Hatten in Flames scenario 2: Bertoldo the Brave.  GE Turn 3 MPh.  A BU AAMG HT starts up and moves towards a building with some US squads at ground lvl with a MMG and a US squad on lvl 1 with a MMG.  There are two leaders at ground lvl (8-0 and a 9-1).  (situation due to the 8-0 and the MMG squad having to rout to this building and then rallying during the Rally phase of turn 3).

The MMGs had fired at other units earlier in the turn (both losing ROF), but the squad on the 1st lvl and a separate 6-6-6 and the 8-0 leader on the ground lvl had yet to fire).  As the HT moves towards their hex, /if/ the MMGs had not already fired (or if they had kept ROF and the HT was in their CA), they could have tried to fire at it as a To Hit roll, perhaps establishing a FL with the ground lvl MMG.  But since they had already fired, they could not affect the HT so it moved into their hex.

Had the HT entered their hex from a road with a building on one of the other sides, we could have declared a Street Fighting CC Reaction, but they entered from a non-road hex.  So we could not CC Reaction them in the adjacent hex, nor did we have any LATW to Non-CC Reaction or DFF them in the adjacent hex.  So the HT enters their hex and declares bypass and remains in Motion.  They do NOT declare an Overrun.

We then allowed the ground floor squad and 8-0 leader (both not marked with any First or Final Fire markers) to attempt CC Reaction.  The squad succeeded in its PAATC roll and the Leader does not need to make one.  We immediately resolved the CC attack against the HT, rolling a '7' and missing a result by one :(.

A second HT then did the same thing to another building hex manned by a HMG.  The HMG proceeded to roll an '11' on its TH roll, failing miserably to kill the HT as it moved up, but the squad was not marked DFF (only the HMG).  Since there were still two Panthers that had yet to move, the adjacent M18 held its fire and the HT entered the HMGs hex (with a 9-1 leader and a 5-4-6 squad).  They declared CC Reaction, which was allowed as the provision against doing so with SWs marked First Fire is only if attempting Street Fighting.  We resolved the CC and rolled another '7', but this time we felt it was an Immobilization on the HT given the -1 leadership DRM (5 CCV for squad +1 CCV for leader -2 drm for OT vehicle +2 drm for motion -1 drm for leadership).

The biggest questions we had were:
1) Reaction Fire is only vs vehicles in YOUR hex, unless you are doing Street Fighting, correct?  This is even with Non-CC Reaction Fire (i.e. LATW or a Gun).  If we had a bazooka, we could have just used regular DFF against the HT in an adjacent hex.

2) Is Reaction Fire even allowed against a BYPASSING vehicle?  Or is Reaction Fire only allowed vs Overrunning vehicles?

3) In both our situations, the squads are marked CC (as the vehicle did not die).  Come the CCPh, is there /another/ round of CC between the vehicle and the squad?

4) We were correct in that the vehicle does NOT get to CC back against the squads during CC Reaction, right?

5) If the vehicle and squads were to CC each other, would a BU HT with only a 4 AAMG be able to attack the squad in CC at all?  If it was CE, it would have 4 factors to attack with, correct?  If it was CE and in Motion, would it still have 4 or would it have 2 factors due to halving for Motion?

query:
Intensive Fire Questions: We were confused by the Intensive Fire rules and who a unit is allowed to target with their Intensive Fire.  Our understanding is as follows ... please correct where appropriate:

Prep Fire: A Gun may Fire, exhaust its ROF, then (if not a 'non-IF' gun) fire one more shot as IF at any target in LOS.

Advancing Fire: IF is not allowed during AFPh.

Defensive Fire: If during the DFPh, a gun may exhaust its ROF (or if already marked First Fire/Final Fire) may gain one additional shot as IF, but ONLY at same or adjacent hex targets.

query:
Vehicles in buildings Question: Please confirm that we understand this correctly and/or add anything we missed.

Vehicles can enter or set up in buildings provided they can legally enter them during their MPh; e.g. open top vehicles, HTs, etc. cannot.

Vehicles must be BU to enter a building, but may CE once in a building.

Entry of a building is 1/2 total MPs and a bog check.  Expending more than 1/2 MPs doesn't change the bog check requirements.

Change of the VCA in a building incurs a bog check and is double DRM if done while firing.

Change of a TCA in a building is a double DRM if done while firing.

Vehicles in a building are NOT Hulldown, but qualify for a TH DRM of the TEM of the building (+2 or +3 for wood/stone, respectively).

If entering a wooden building, some (all?) vehicles have a chance to fall into the cellar.

I want to say there is a chance that a building collapses/turns to rubble when a vehicle enters it, but I can't seem to find the rule ... so I may be remembering something from another game or a SSR or something.

----------------------
The big thing is that a tank in a building, for example, is exchanging a hull-down "miss me if you hit the hull" defensive feature for a "harder to land a shell on me" TEM DRM.  As long as they do not have to change their CA, their return fire is unaffected by being in the building and, as such, being in a building can certainly offer advantages to inferior tanks facing superior ones.

We are not sure which is better ... HD versus a +3 TEM.  Part of me thinks HD since that can simply erase a Hit whereas part of the TEM can be erased due to ACQ over multiple shots.  But if you're able to take out the other tank before they can get the multiple shots, then maybe the DRM is better...

-K

ground_truth_answer:
Vehicles in a building are NOT Hulldown, but qualify for a TH DRM of the TEM of the building (+2 or +3 for wood/stone, respectively).

A vehicle in any Location can claim the TEM or HD (if otherwise eligible); but you can't claim both.  However, that would only be even possible if the reason for HD is a successful HD Maneuver Attempt (D4.22); D4.21 specifies that if you can be HD from a wall/bocage hexside, you are -- i.e., if your vehicle is in a building behind a wall, you are HD (and the building provides no TEM).

If entering a wooden building, some (all?) vehicles have a chance to fall into the cellar.

All buildings (not just wooden) [EXC: Factories], and certainly can affect all vehicles able to actually drive into a non-Factory building.  And there's no wreck stacking limit in a cellar -- a famous story from many years ago described a particularly unlucky player sending an entire platoon of tanks into the same cellar in the same MPh. :)

I want to say there is a chance that a building collapses/turns to rubble when a vehicle enters it, but I can't seem to find the rule

B23.41, right after the Black Hole of Calcutta cellar rule. 🙂 Note that the mechanics of this rule means that it's impossible to rubble a multi-level stone building by this method.

ground_truth_answer:
An example. A vehicle has moved and ends with the remaining movement points in the last hex. In the defensive fire phase, a gun shoot him.

For the modifiers to apply, the vehicle is "in motion" or stopped.

You can't end a vehicle's MPh with remaining Movement Points. You have to spend them all.

The modifiers for "Moving Vehicluar Target" apply if during the current Player Turn the target 
- has entered a new hex, or
- used VBM (D2.3), or 
- began its MPh in Motion (D2.4), or 
- is currently in Motion.

So, "has moved" is insufficient information to determine whether the +2 apply or not.
You are right. I have not explained well. I mean the vehicle expends the remaining movement points in the hex and with the last one stops.

FT unit -1 IFT modifier applies to whole stack?: Hi, I'm just trying to get into ASL and I have a question that may turn out to be nonsense so apologies in advance :-)

The rules say that when firing at a unit carrying a flamethrower a -1 modifier is applied on the IFT result. But if there is a stack of units and one of them has a FT, does the -1 modifer apply to a roll against all the units in the stack?

title: FT unit -1 IFT modifier applies to whole stack?
raw_question:
Hi, I'm just trying to get into ASL and I have a question that may turn out to be nonsense so apologies in advance :-)

The rules say that when firing at a unit carrying a flamethrower a -1 modifier is applied on the IFT result. But if there is a stack of units and one of them has a FT, does the -1 modifer apply to a roll against all the units in the stack?

Thanks!
ground_truth_answer:
It can be (very) dangerous to stack other units with a unit thar has a FT (probably like in real life)....if one e.g., gets a K/# vs the other units, the FT-toting unit might get a KIA (due to the extra -1 DRM).
Even worse ... if the stack gets a 1KIA against it, the FT unit will cop a 2KIA all on his own, effectively making it a 2KIA for the whole stack (since without the FT the 1KIA would "only" be a random selection amongst all the units in the stack).

When a unit possesses a FT, that unit generally attracts a lot of enemy attention, including fire. As such, I try to avoid stacking with that unit.

query:
Improbably vs Critical Hits: Can someone confirm that we played this correctly.

Rules at question are: C3.6 and C3.7.

We had a FL established by a MMG in a wooden building in Bertero in Flames scenario (Hatten in Flames, Scen. 2). The German player drove up a BU Panther at about 4 hex range and fired during its movement phase (after stopping).  He rolled a '2'.

We judged the TH# to be 8 (Infantry 0-6 range).
We judged the DRMs to be: +4 (moving, slow-turret); +1 (BU); +2 (TEM); +1 (an orchard Hindrance), for a net DRM of +8.

This fell under Improbable Hits, 3.6.  Meaning a subsequent dr was needed to secure an actual hit (with dr=1 being critical and 2-3 = regular).  He rolled a dr=4, so we judged this to be a 'miss'.

BUT...3.7 has "A CH also occurs while using the Infantry Target Type whenever the Final TH DR is < half the Modified TH# (not our situation), or on an Original TH DR of 2 followed by a subsequent dr of 1 or <=half of the Modified TH#".

Noting that this sentence does NOT have any reference to 3.6 (but the previous sentence in 3.7 does).  This would mean that even though the Panther needed a '0' DR to Hit, there is some implication that a '2' DR followed by a 1-4 dr (<= half of 8) would score a critical hit.  There would be NO chance of a regular Hit...either one misses or critical hits.

This didn't seem to make sense to us, so we ruled that 3.6 took precedence ... but we weren't sure if we ruled this correctly.

We judged the DRMs to be: +4 (moving, slow-turret); +1 (BU); +2 (TEM); +1 (an orchard Hindrance), for a net DRM of +8.

This fell under Improbable Hits, 3.6.  Meaning a subsequent dr was needed to secure an actual hit (with dr=1 being critical and 2-3 = regular).  He rolled a dr=4, so we judged this to be a 'miss'.

BUT...3.7 has "A CH also occurs while using the Infantry Target Type whenever the Final TH DR is < half the Modified TH# (not our situation), or on an Original TH DR of 2 followed by a subsequent dr of 1 or <=half of the Modified TH#".

Noting that this sentence does NOT have any reference to 3.6 (but the previous sentence in 3.7 does).  This would mean that even though the Panther needed a '0' DR to Hit, there is some implication that a '2' DR followed by a 1-4 dr (<= half of 8) would score a critical hit.  There would be NO chance of a regular Hit...either one misses or critical hits.

This didn't seem to make sense to us, so we ruled that 3.6 took precedence ... but we weren't sure if we ruled this correctly.
ground_truth_answer:
Great.  That is what we thought ... that C3.7 only applies when C3.6 doesn't.  Note that the reference in 3.7 to 3.6 appears to be referring to the sentence that only talks about IFF HE/WP and Vehicle type CHs, which is why we were confused:

3.7 CRITICAL HITS (CH): A CH is a hit so well placed that it increases 
the chance of causing damage on the resulting IFT Effects or TK DR. 
Even if the target is HD (3.9), a CH occurs on an Original 2 DR during the 
resolution of a HE (or WP; see 3.76) FFE (1.53), or on an Original TH DR 
of 2 on the Area/Vehicle Target Type or on a LATW TH Table. [EXC: De-
liberate Immobilization (5.72). If only the lowest Final TH DR possible for 
that shot would achieve a hit, a CH occurs only on a subsequent dr of 1 
following that hit; a 2-6 results in a normal hull hit (or a normal turret hit 
vs a HD vehicle); if the lowest Final TH DR possible for that shot would 
be a miss, 3.6 applies.] A CH also occurs while using the Infantry Target 
Type whenever the Final TH DR is < half the Modified TH# (3.3), or on 
an Original TH DR of 2 followed by a subsequent dr of 1 or ≤ half of the 
Modified TH#. MG (including all 12.7mm [.50-cal] and aircraft MG, but 
not 15mm) TK attacks have no CH possibility, since this effect is factored 
into their Basic TK# and Range modifiers. The effects of a HE FFE CH 
are resolved using the same Original 2 DR that caused it.

IMO, if 3.6 is supposed to modify CHs versus Infantry (which certainly appears to be the intent given the wording in C3.6), the 'Exception" clause in 3.7 really should be moved to either the very end of this paragraph or immediately after the "A CH also occurs while ..." sentence.

This makes it clearer that the Exception applies to both of these sentences.  Right now, we had confusion whether the exception only applied to the HE FFE, 2 TH roll on vehicle/area, and LATW TH rolls only (as exceptions usually modify the immediate preceding rule).

ground_truth_answer:
Fun fact: if a friendly unit advances into CC with an already-Encircled enemy unit, and the CC becomes a Melee, the friendly unit is also considered Encircled*, and will remain Encircled until they leave the Location (or fulfil one of the other conditions as described in A7.7). query:
Is an AFV, which ran out of fuel, immobile?: Still playing scenario 232 (Chance d'une Affaire), where SSR3 requires a secret dr to define the number of MPhs where each german AFV may move (low fuel).

Now my only AFV left has run out of fuel. Do I have to mark it as "Immobilized"? I guess not, because the amount of fuel left is secret.

And what happens when this AFV gets recalled (D5.341)? Does the crew have to abandon it, because it is immobile, or not? Of course, the definition of "mobile/immobile" (e.g. D.7) does not include this SSR case.
title: Is an AFV, which ran out of fuel, immobile?
raw_question:
Still playing scenario 232 (Chance d'une Affaire), where SSR3 requires a secret dr to define the number of MPhs where each german AFV may move (low fuel).

Now my only AFV left has run out of fuel. Do I have to mark it as "Immobilized"? I guess not, because the amount of fuel left is secret.

And what happens when this AFV gets recalled (D5.341)? Does the crew have to abandon it, because it is immobile, or not? Of course, the definition of "mobile/immobile" (e.g. D.7) does not include this SSR case.
ground_truth_answer:
SSR3 of 232 concerning the fuel-dr: "...the resulting value is the number of Movement Phases in which that vehicle may enter a new hex."
My understanding is that I would still be able to change VCA, when out of fuel, because I don't enter a new hex. This is also different to a "real" immobile/bogged vehicle, which confused me here.

The entire point of an SSR is "this is a rule that is different to the normal rules".  Complaining that an SSR doesn't comply with the rules is kind of wasted effort.

In general, it's best to take the text of a rule (whether in the rules book itself or in an SSR) as literally as possible.  (This doesn't always work, which is why there are questions.)  The SSR doesn't say anything about marking the vehicle with any kind of counter when it's "out of fuel" -- so don't.  As you note, the SSR prohibits entry of a new hex -- so the vehicle can do any type of movement it likes when it's "out of fuel" so long as it doesn't enter a new hex.  It is (on the face of it) in no way treated as being Immobile -- it can for instance happily remain in Motion.

If the vehicle is Recalled but is unable to enter a new hex (a basic requirement for Recall!) then it only seems logical that the inherent crew must abandon it as per D5.341 even though the vehicle is neither Bogged nor Immobilized.  However, you can argue that is "stretching" the intent of the SSR.  Since the SSR fails to cover the point, you and your opponent would need to mutually agree on how to resolve the problem.

The core of your (perfectly reasonable) uncertainty here is that the SSR is attempting to be "clever" but has failed to address all of the possibilities.  A well-written SSR would tell you exactly what all the consequences of being "out of fuel" are (possibly the simplest approach being to state "as soon as the vehicle is no longer able to enter a new hex, it is treated as being Immobilized for the remainder of the game").

ground_truth_answer:
I have posted this on a different forum, but the discussion is the same. 

This came up in at scenario we currently play (DTF 15 Storming Lommel) where the brits set up two abandoned AFVs in road locations with the crews in buildings. 
If the crews can move or advance out into the road, and recrew them in the CCPh, the AFV come into play almost a full turn earlier, and have a much better chance to avoid being shot up. 
The rules on the subject are somewhat contradictory, and I do not find that the above mentioned Q&A solves the issue. 

First of all the Q&A above has a couple of mistakes. 
1)An Abandoned vehicle is a Unit, as it is normally capable of movement. If it had not been a unit, it would not be possible to capture an Abandoned vehicle in CC at all, as A11.1 specifically states that "CC is a form of attack which can occur .... between opposing units ....".
2)A Friendly AFV may obviously not be crewed in this way, as it is not Abandoned, and the A) here is not absolute, as it has the exception "unless actually in CC".
(BTW, where is this Q&A to be found - I'm not able to locate it.... )

To recrew an Abandoned vehicle, an infantry unit have to start the MPh in the same location (D5.42), but rule A21.2 is cited as a specific exception. 
A21.2 states that an Abandoned enemy AFV may be captured automatically by any Infantry unit in the same location at the end of a CCPh, if there are no enemy Personnel in the Location. 
It also states that "Otherwise", i.e. if enemy Personnel are present, "an Abandoned AFV can be captured only by a CC attack capture attempt in a CC Location", and that both sides could attempt capture. 
Here A21.2 is a specific exception to A11.1, as the Abandoned AFV is clearly not opposing neither your own nor your opponents infantry unit, but is quite passive until actually recrewed.

Now there is another interesting Q&A to A7.4 and D5.4
Q: Is an abandoned vehicle still a unit? If it is a unit, is a previously friendly vehicle which was abandoned still a friendly unit, thus preventing another friendly unit to fire on it? If it is not a unit, may an abandoned vehicle be fired upon?
A. An Abandoned vehicle is a unit, but it is neither friendly nor enemy and can be attacked by either side.

This makes it quite plain; an Abandoned vehicle is a unit, but neither friendly nor enemy, which makes sense to me, as it is not capable of any kind of action or combat. 
In other words; You cannot hug it, nor will it fight back if attacked…. 😉

Still, things are not crystal clear, as A21.2 uses the expression "Abandoned enemy AFV". 
To me it seems the better solution to ignore "enemy" in this sentence, as it otherwise would contradict the above Q&A (7.4&D5.4).

Imagine the following: 
1) A German PzI is immobilized in a hex with an Abandoned French B1-bis and an Abandoned German PzIII. The crew fail their TC and exit the vehicle. Now, if they survive until the CCPh and there are no enemy infantry units in hex, per the Q&A in the above post, they could neither recrew their own vehicle nor the other German Panzer, but they could recrew the B1-bis with which they are totally unfamiliar.
2) A German PzIV is immobilized by enemy prep fire. Per the Q&A in the above post they could not recrew their own vehicle in the CCPh, unless an enemy infantry unit actually advances in for CC (and they make the capture DR), which in my view would make things harder, not easier /possible.
Both 1) and 2) are nonsensical IMO.

OH

Half hexes, ASLSK and VASL scenarios: Half hexes are considered playable when there is no adjacent board (2.3).  In ASLSK Scenario 1 it has units enter along east, west or north edge.  I thought that per 2.51 units that enter a mapboard have to setup off board.

title: Half hexes, ASLSK and VASL scenarios

ground_truth_answer: It's really just a VASSAL artifact - you are setting up your units in the off-board half-hex, and they still have to pay normal movement costs to enter the on-board half-hex. So when you set up your units they are still off-board even though on VASSAL they are partially onboard.  Hope that makes sense.

query:
Second Crack At Caumont concealment SSR question: Hi there,

I'd like some clarity on SSR 2. which states: "German units which set up in Concealment Terrain may begin the scenario concealed." 

At what point is the scenario deemed to 'begin' and therefore at what point do this additional level of concealment get applied? 

Many thanks!
title: Second Crack At Caumont concealment SSR question
raw_question:
Hi there,

I'd like some clarity on SSR 2. which states: "German units which set up in Concealment Terrain may begin the scenario concealed." 

At what point is the scenario deemed to 'begin' and therefore at what point do this additional level of concealment get applied? 

Many thanks!
ground_truth_answer:
A12.12 specifically mentions concealing ALL units before the opponent sees the setup.

Sure but that applies for the case when the opponent starts with no pieces on board!

The issue about this scenario is that the opponent does start with units on board.

There would be no need for a SSR if the general rule in A12.12 applied. In this case that specific provision of A12.12 does not apply because both sides start with units on board. 

So the questions that arises from the SSR is whether a defending stack, in concealment terrain, has a concealment marker placed on top of it before the opponent gets a shot at checking LOS or not. If the answer is yes, then the opponent never gets to see the top unit of that stack. If the answer is no, then the opponent does see the unit on top of the stack but before the first rally phase a concealment marker is anyway placed on top of the unit. 

My interpretation is that it is the first case. The opponent never gets to see what is in that stack.

This is A12.12:

The player setting up first in a scenario does so out of
vision of his opponent, and after setting up his regular units may place only
scenario OB-designated “?” at first—but only in Terrain listed in red in the
Terrain Chart/Desert Terrain Chart/PTO Terrain Chart. After his opponent
sets up in the same manner, each unconcealed unit (of both sides) which is
either out of the LOS of all unbroken enemy ground units within 16 hexes
of it, or at ≥ 17 hexes from all of them, may have a “?” not designated by the
OB placed on it [EXC: only one non-OB-designated “?” can be placed per
stack of units and not on top of any previously placed “?”]. Therefore, if one
side begins with no forces on board, the other side will be able to place “?”
on all of its non-Dummy units after placing those units (before the opponent
may look at the board).

So, which is legal for an AFV:  1) Motion attempt then sM use, 2) sM use then motion attempt...both? 

D2.401 A vehicle may attempt Motion status only once per enemy MPh and may not attempt it at all if already marked with a First Fire(or Final/Intensive Fire) counter.

D13.2 During the opponent's MPh, a smoke dispenser usage attempt can be made...as if it were intervening with Defensive First Fire.

The rules don't appear to clearly specify whether an AFV that makes a smoke dispenser attempt in DFF is marked with a First Fire counter or not, but I would interpret this as saying the AFV is marked, and therefore cannot subsequently make a motion attempt.

C8.5 Smoke may be placed by ordance/OBA only at the start of the owner's PFPh/DFPh.

C8.6 Unlike Smoke, WP may be fired by ordnance during (but prior to any friendly unit firing anything other than SMOKE) any friendly fire phase--not just the PFPh/DFPh...

So yes, it must be fired before all non-smoke shots, but remember that bazookas firing WP can also fire in DFF or the AFPh.

It's a great question.  Hillock rules SUCK!  You are exactly right that when originally introduced, they were always on little overlays and the hillocks were "enclosed" on the overlay.  You were either ON the hillock or next to it.

The way I play it:
Each railroad hex should be envisioned as a 1-hex completely 'enclosed' hillock.  If you treat every hex as such, then you can start to count how many hillock hexes you're crossing.  If you're LOS crosses the number of hillock HEXES as described in the rules, then LOS is blocked when it gets to that number (isn't it 3 if you're next to a hillock and 4 if you're on top of one?).  

If you're IN the railroad hex, you are ON the hillock.  If you're next to the hillock hex, you're adjacent to the hillock.  Count accordingly.

Does that help?  
The Hatten situation is not unique.  Almost all of the HASLs now use these hillock rules for railroads or in ABTF for the bridge ramp.  So now knowing these rules is essential.  I used to skip them when they only applied to Africa.

query:
When all the enemy units are HIP can you set up concealed?: If both sides set up with units on the board, but all units of one side are HIP, does the non-HIP side get to conceal all their units?

Thanks.
title: When all the enemy units are HIP can you set up concealed?
raw_question:
If both sides set up with units on the board, but all units of one side are HIP, does the non-HIP side get to conceal all their units?

Thanks.
ground_truth_answer:
Keep in mind that the Q&A that Klas compiles are not "official" and don't constitute errata (further, they only rarely state something that isn't in the rules already).

The specific wording in A12.32 is

A hidden unit may sacrifice its hidden status and become concealed to prevent an opposing unit in LOS from gaining concealment

I don't see any "only once play has begun" statement there.  However, remembering that HIP is just a special case of concealment, A12.14 has

The owning player can voluntarily remove any concealment at any time during his or his opponent's Player Turn [EXC: between when a Sniper target hex Random Location DR (14.2) is made and the Sniper counter is relocated].

which is much more explicit in terms of timing, although it could be argued that "voluntarily removing concealment" and "voluntarily dropping HIP status" are not exactly the same action.

The final arbiter of timing is the ASOP, and in this case we need to examine the "Pre-Game Sequence" section.  As far as I can tell the only comment on HIP loss is near the end of the sequence where it says

As determined by LOS/range, reveal hidden Fortifications (A12.33) [EXC: E1.16; G.2], then place "?" if/as allowed (A12.12).

which has nothing about voluntary (or even involuntary) loss of HIP for units.

So you can arrive at the conclusion that Klas states above without ever needing to reference a Q&A.

query:
Putting Guns in buildings—The story of the Soviet 76.2 obr. 36: There are two rules I frequently see missed by Soviet players. The first is that the T-34es up until the T-34/85 and the KV-1es are all RST AFVs. I frequently walk up to games and see T-34es zipping around CE like they were Israeli tank aces in '67 Sinai. Stop it! You must be BU to fire the main armament.

The second is placing the 76.2 obr. 39 Gun [Soviet Ordnance note 15] in a building. These are great light field guns, especially in the early war. But in ASL they are classed as ART ordnance. Per B23.423 a Gun may set up in a building if it is *small* (the Soviet 76.2 obr. 39—and the 76.2 obr. 36, the real topic of this post—is a normal-size Gun) or it must be an AT/INF Gun that is not large (as said before, it is classed as ART). So the 76.2 obr. 39 cannot set up in buildings.

The 76.2 obr. 39 is so common in Soviet service that it is nearly universal in scenarios on the Eastern Front. Not so the 76.2 obr. 36, most instances of which were captured by the Germans early in Barbarossa. The Germans saw that the obr. 36 was a potent anti-tank weapon (16TK in ASL terms), so they re-issued them to their own troops [German Ordnance Note 11] and gave some to Romania too [Axis Minor Ordnance Note 5]. In the change of ownership the Guns are reclassed as AT Guns in ASL terms, so now they may set up in buildings. I'll leave you to ponder how the same Gun can fit in buildings when used by one side but not by the other.

As a final note, I'll point out that the 76.2 obr. 39 is also used by the Romanians [Axis Minor Ordnance Note 12], but it remains classed as ART and so can't be put in a building.

JR

The second is placing the 76.2 obr. 39 Gun [Soviet Ordnance note 15] in a building. These are great light field guns, especially in the early war. But in ASL they are classed as ART ordnance. Per B23.423 a Gun may set up in a building if it is *small* (the Soviet 76.2 obr. 39—and the 76.2 obr. 36, the real topic of this post—is a normal-size Gun) or it must be an AT/INF Gun that is not large (as said before, it is classed as ART). So the 76.2 obr. 39 cannot set up in buildings.

The 76.2 obr. 39 is so common in Soviet service that it is nearly universal in scenarios on the Eastern Front. Not so the 76.2 obr. 36, most instances of which were captured by the Germans early in Barbarossa. The Germans saw that the obr. 36 was a potent anti-tank weapon (16TK in ASL terms), so they re-issued them to their own troops [German Ordnance Note 11] and gave some to Romania too [Axis Minor Ordnance Note 5]. In the change of ownership the Guns are reclassed as AT Guns in ASL terms, so now they may set up in buildings. I'll leave you to ponder how the same Gun can fit in buildings when used by one side but not by the other.

As a final note, I'll point out that the 76.2 obr. 39 is also used by the Romanians [Axis Minor Ordnance Note 12], but it remains classed as ART and so can't be put in a building.

query:
Trucks: 1. What is used to represent a Truck Inherent Crew when Routs?
2. A MMC/SMC can "drive" an Abandoned Truck?
title: Trucks
raw_question:
1. What is used to represent a Truck Inherent Crew when Routs?
2. A MMC/SMC can "drive" an Abandoned Truck?
ground_truth_answer:
Check D5.1 Only armed vehicles are maned by inherent crews. AFV have elite morale crews and unarmored vechiles have first line morale crews. Both of them exit the vehicle as vehicle crews (with lower strength than gun crews).

Unarmed vehicles have an inherent driver that never has a counter representation.

So your truck would have an inherent crew if it is an armed crew. Unarmed trucks don't have crews.

To man abandoned vehicles that need crews, check A21.22. That applies only to armed vehicles. Unarmed vehicles do not have a crew and its inherent driver never leaves the vehicle, so they cannot be manned by other units except by capture, in this case a MMC provides a driver at no cost or it it is an SMC it is removed from play until an MMC can provide a driver or the SMC leaves the unaremd vehicle (A21.21).

query: Pillbox and Fire Group: I have this feeling that a pillbox is never allowed to participate in a fire group with a unit not in the pillbox. Is this correct or am I imagining this?
title: Pillbox and Fire Group
raw_question: I have this feeling that a pillbox is never allowed to participate in a fire group with a unit not in the pillbox. Is this correct or am I imagining this?
ground_truth_answer:
I agree that this seems to be the intent of the rules, the text itself is not so clear. Sure, a unit in a bunker can't form a firegroup with an other unit in the same hex, since the bunker is treated as a pillbox, and the pillbox rules forbid this explicitly.

But: A unit in a bunker and a unit in a trench in an ADJACENT hex are ADJACENT, so, according to the rules, CAN form a firegroup. The pillbox rules only forbid same-hex FGs. I think. But I'm not sure.

Well.  You have a point.  However, unless that trench is within the pillbox's CA, there is no LOS between the two Locations (B30.2).  They're Accessible, but not ADJACENT, because ADJACENT requires a LOS.

So I'd say that IF the trench and the pillbox counter are in adjacent hexes and IF that trench is within the CA of the pillbox then yes, units in the trench and units in the pillbox can form a FG, under the rules as currently written.  However, in practice, I should think the chances of that setup actually occurring in a scenario would be quite small, because it would seriously compromise the defensive value of the pillbox.

Only one attempt per unit, so if the leader attempted self-rally, then a later rallied leader cannot attempt to rally that leader again in the same RPh.

If the Commissar fails self-rally, then he is done for the RPh, no other leader can attempt to rally him. "Each unit may attempt only one type of action in a RPh." (A3.1)

ground_truth_answer:
E7.401 ... The aircraft repeats this procedure (henceforth referred to as a Strafing Run) in every hex traversed until it occupies the target hex of its initial target. At this point it cannot attack again during that Player Turn, but must attempt to continue moving along that Hex Grain to receive all possible Light AA fire until it occupies the last hex it attacked. You got it right!

title: Human Wave Attacks
raw_question:
As I've read elsewhere in the forums, the Human Wave rules are kind of dense. I am having a hard time figuring out what the purpose of some of the specifics are, although I'm sure there's a perfectly logical explanation for why they're written the way they are. Here's the way I interpret 25.23 to 25.233. 

1. Pick a target hex
2. Pick the HW participants (at least 3 hexes and an average of 2 per hex, plus the leader from one of the hexes). 

3. The HW participants move toward the target hex in impulse fashion as per the rules with each using movement cost of the unit that has to expend the most MF. 

4. Each HW unit can move into a forward/side hex headed toward the target hex but in the process will  move into another forward/side hex containing a (armed, non disrupted) KEU but no (armed) friendly unit. 

I know in this description I'm leaving out lots of little details such as no HW participant can be guarding prisoners. 

Also, I don't understand the point of the whole range aspect (25.2321). Does it just mean that no HW participant can move in a way that increases the number of hexes from the unit to the target hex? 

I also don't get the purpose of the direction counters. Just move toward the target hex would seem to be the logical thing to do. What have I missed (I'm sure it's something). 

What have I gotten wrong about all of this?
ground_truth_answer:
IMO, if there's one thing that players new to Human Waves miss when reading the rules is that necessity to select a single (alternate) hex grain that defines the direction that the HW will move in.  A lot of folks think that "direction" is being defined for multiple hex grains simultaneously.  There is only one hex grain used to define direction.  All movement in the HW is either (a) towards that single hex grain; (b) parallel to that hex grain; or (c) away from that hex grain (which is limited in that the placing of the range counter means that you can't keep moving away).

To put it another way, while a HW can operate as multiple units moving in parallel, it will tend to converge on a point, with very limited ability to diverge away from that point.  The reason why you select a hex grain and not a single target hex is to avoid the problem of multiple units all trying to squeeze in to the same target Location; the HW thus has restrictions in the way it operates but retains some flexibility.

As JR points out, the reason the current HW rules seem a little ... mechanical ... in their operation is because the original HW rules barely defined anything, meaning that the HW could mean whatever you wanted it to mean, leading to general confusion.  Hence the point of the updated rules was to try and make sure that everything was defined.  The original rules were so poor that most players probably never, ever bothered performing a HW with Russian troops (thus depriving themseles of a potentially valuable tool); when the Japanese were introduced the Banzai ability made a lot of people take another look at the rules and really notice their limitations -- or alternately kept on ignoring them and never did a Banzai charge either, which seriously limits the effectiveness of Japanese troops.

raw_question: I have a question about the SPW 251/2 (the Half-track carrying the German 81mm mortar).  The chapter H note says to treat it as a normal OT SP gun for To Hit purposes.  Does it still have to use area fire like a normal mortar, or can it use direct fire and use the infantry target type?
ground_truth_answer:
That's ... a really perceptive question, actually.  There is no rule that I could find that says "a MTR mounted on a vehicle must obey all of the normal rules applicable to MTRs (C7.345, C9, etc.)".  Indeed German Vehicular Note 59 kind of implies the opposite.  I believe that the intent behind that note is "treat it as a normal vehicular weapon (that can only fire on the Area Target Type, has a minimum range, etc.)" but it is true that this is not what it actually says.

Certainly I've never played them any other way, nor have I ever heard of them being played any other way.  This is I think an example of the rules forgetting to spell out something because "everybody just knows".

The equivalent US vehicles (Notes 31-33) don't even get the blanket statement applicable to the German vehicles [EXC: The M4A1 gets a "treated as a normal NT AFV" comment].  Ditto for the MTR-armed Carriers (British Vehicle Notes 66-67).

So, um, yeah.  There ought to be some errata added somewhere (not sure where would be best -- probably C9, rather than add an errata item to multiple individual vehicles) -- but MMP have historically been very reticent to add errata for stuff that "everyone already knows already", so good luck with that ....

raw_question:

ground_truth_answer:
Well, this has been answered in many other threads.  A little time searching would answer your questions very comprehensively.

The Pocket edition does not have Chapters H, J or K.

The Pocket edition does not have 99.9% of the charts and tables required for play.

The Pocket edition does not have the binder's summary display of different counter types and what the various factors and markings represent.

However:

The Pocket edition does come with Chapter F, currently otherwise unavailable.

The Pocket edition does come with Chapter G, otherwise available only in Rising Sun (which is currently unavailable).

The Pocket edition does include all of the replacement pages for Chapters A-G from various products (which are mostly otherwise unavailable, although several of the replacement pages are available for download from the MMP site).  This includes the replacement pages provided in H-P (at the time of writing, no more recent replacement pages for these chapters have been released).

The Pocket edition does include a summary of all of the errata applicable for Chapters A-G.  This list covers up to ASL Journal #10 (more errata has subsequently been provided in #11 and #12).  Note that the errata is listed, it is not integrated into the text (so you still have to do your own manual markups).  Note also that no errata for anything other than these chapters is provided -- for the "complete" listing you need to hunt around the MMP website (it's not very well organised).

Therefore: the Pocket edition cannot in any reasonable sense be considered a replacement for the full ASL rules binder.  It is, however, an excellent supplement to the rules binder and is strongly recommended as such.

From reading rules and FAQ this is my interpretation.

Am I wrong on this?  Thanks.
title: VBM and Level 1
raw_question:
A T34 closed top is using VBM around a building (remains in motion) with a squad at Level 1 (second floor).  

From reading rules and FAQ this is my interpretation.

If the T34 is CE then the squad can use TPBF and therefore can only fire at the tank.

If the T34 is BU then the squad has no valid target and therefore can fire at more distant hexes.

Am I wrong on this?  Thanks.
ground_truth_answer:
Yes, you have interpreted the rules (A7.212) correctly.

Note that this is a special case of the usual rule (more commonly known as "VBM freeze"). (I.E., the vehicle is at ground-level with vulnerable PRC and the enemy infantry is in a higher-level Location within the same hex.)

If the vehicle and the infantry were at the same level, the infantry is prevented from firing at a different Location even if the vehicle has no vulnerable PRC (the more usual example of "the freeze").

query: M3 75mm vs 76mm M1: New to ASL. From what I gather in the rules, the only thing that matters for the HE TK# is the caliber. Is that correct? That seems way off for almost all American AT guns as the 76mm M42 projectile had much less TNT than the 75mm M48 projectile due to its much higher velocity. Am I missing something?
title: M3 75mm vs 76mm M1
raw_question: New to ASL. From what I gather in the rules, the only thing that matters for the HE TK# is the caliber. Is that correct? That seems way off for almost all American AT guns as the 76mm M42 projectile had much less TNT than the 75mm M48 projectile due to its much higher velocity. Am I missing something?
ground_truth_answer:
Essentially they are saying the only thing that matters is the size of the HE round and that the ratio of propellent to explosive is always constant - and that is patently false. There are plenty of other HE rounds that would not conform to that blanket treatment. As a retired armor officer, I must say this is really befuddling...

Just wait until you examine the destructive power of a Goliath vs. the destructive power of an AVRE mortar round vs. the destructive power of a shell from the Stürmtiger -- and then compare the real-world weight of explosives used in each.

Also consider the amount of HE that you can throw at an (ordinary) building -- e.g., by repeatedly firing 75mm rounds into it -- and yet the chances of the building rubbling or catching fire are usually tiny.  (Also not forgetting that there is one and only one way of breaching a wall or hedge -- the afore-mentioned AVRE -- and yet there are a few ways of breaching bocage.)

You can use a DC to blow a hole in the exterior wall of a fortified building -- or the interior wall of a rowhouse -- but not to blow a hole in the exterior wall of an ordinary building.

There are plenty of weirdnesses in the ASL rules if you want to find them, and they're all there for the sake of "keeping the regular game moving".  Everything is abstracted.

There are lots of folks that claim that ASL is "very realistic".  Sadly, even though most of those folks are fans of the game, they're quite mistaken.  ASL is the ultimate embodiment of "design for effect" and any time some particular rule fills you with rage for being contrary to your understanding of How Things Work -- just remember, if you enjoy the game, just roll with it.  If you're not enjoying the game, there are many alternatives that may suit you better.

ASL is a realistic abstraction of a 1950-60's war movie

query:
Concealment moving in open: should be an easy question but after reading the rules and all the FAQ I am still not sure......................

A concealed squad moves from a building to the open.  one hex.  neither hex is in LOS of the enemy.  The enemy is 3 hexes away behind some other buildings.

Do I keep concealment?
title: Concealment moving in open
raw_question:
should be an easy question but after reading the rules and all the FAQ I am still not sure......................

A concealed squad moves from a building to the open.  one hex.  neither hex is in LOS of the enemy.  The enemy is 3 hexes away behind some other buildings.

Do I keep concealment?
ground_truth_answer:
So, to be clear:  A unit assault moving within LOS AND into open ground does lose concealment, right?  (Absent snow and winter camo rules, of course.)

Yes.  Remember, however, that "open ground" is relative to the observer; more specifically, it's only "open ground" if the unit could be affected by the -1 FFMO DRM if it was being fired upon.  A normal hindrance, for instance, between the observer and the target is sufficient to prevent the application of FFMO and therefore the unit would not be in "open ground" for purposes of concealment loss.

This is all spelled out in A10.531.

This applies even if the unit is only in open ground "momentarily".  For instance, a unit advancing from one hex of a rowhouse building to an adjacent hex of the same rowhouse must "bypass" the building during the advance via a vertex (B23.71).  That vertex may well be treated as open ground to an enemy unit and if so the advancing unit would lose concealment.

Flamethrowers and FFMO: I couldn't find (though it might be somewhere in the forum) an answer to this stipulation/question concerning FFMO and FTs.

A22.2 DRM states that, in general, TEM does not apply to FT attacks.

FFMO is defined as being applied as a -1 DRM to an IFT attack during defensive fire unless combined with an *effective protective* TEM.

If a FT fires at a unit moving through a hex with no TEM, the -1 would apply.

If a FT fires at a unit moving through a hex with a TEM of +2, e.g. wooden building, would the FFMO -1 modifier be directly applied and the TEM ignored?

For Orchard, B14.3 states that is has no TEM, but is treated as non-open ground so subsequently negates FFMO.

*not* ignored and therefore does affect FT attacks, negating the FFMO -1 and adding the TEM of the terrain occupied, such as +2 for a wooden building?

What say ye?
title: Flamethrowers and FFMO
raw_question:
I couldn't find (though it might be somewhere in the forum) an answer to this stipulation/question concerning FFMO and FTs.

A22.2 DRM states that, in general, TEM does not apply to FT attacks.

FFMO is defined as being applied as a -1 DRM to an IFT attack during defensive fire unless combined with an *effective protective* TEM.

If a FT fires at a unit moving through a hex with no TEM, the -1 would apply.

If a FT fires at a unit moving through a hex with a TEM of +2, e.g. wooden building, would the FFMO -1 modifier be directly applied and the TEM ignored?  

Since, according to A22.2, TEM does *not* apply to FT attacks, it would not be considered "effective protective TEM" and therefore *not* affect the -1 FFMO modifier.

For Orchard, B14.3 states that is has no TEM, but is treated as non-open ground so subsequently negates FFMO.

Hmmm, special disturbing case for Orchard, or hint at precedent that TEM is 
*not* ignored and therefore does affect FT attacks, negating the FFMO -1 and adding the TEM of the terrain occupied, such as +2 for a wooden building?

What say ye?
ground_truth_answer:
OK, to address your points, though you haven't gone completely point to point to show where any of my 1-4 steps is incorrect ;) ...

Rule 10.531 fails on two accounts, one is that it is circularly defined, being effectively wherever one could apply the -1 FFMO is considered open ground, and wherever there is open ground is where we apply the -1 FFMO, which is actually the crux of what we are trying to determine and so therefore of no help.  

Secondly, this rule applies to "rout determination, Dash, concealment gain/loss, and Interdiction", no mention of attacks on the IFT and certainly not helpful specifically for FT attacks.

I have two rulebooks, the "latest" being the pocketbook 2nd edition purchased less than one year ago with no errata indicated for Index item Open Ground which references A4.6 which states: 

"A further -1 First Fire DRM applies to units moving in the open (FFMO), but whenever such movement is combined with another effective protective TEM or LOS hindrance feature (such as SMOKE or an AFV/wreck) between the target and firer or in the target Location itself, the -1 FFMO DRM does not apply."

So, points 1-4 still hold, being rephrased as...

Against FT attacks a unit moving does not have access to a TEM modifier A22.2, a lack of "effective protective" TEM defines the movement to be in open ground as per A4.6, without such TEM, the open ground FFMO modifier is applied and there is no TEM as per the A22.2 aforementioned:

"DRM:  FT attacks vs. non-Armored units are resolved on the IFT but receive no DRM due to leadership/heroism or defender's TEM except for non-CA attacks on a pillbox (B30.113), LOS hindrances and the +1 DRM for CX usage apply to IFT attacks."

So I am becoming more convinced that players are applying TEM to FT attacks, as respondents hint that they are presently doing, to avoid applying the -1 FFMO, but then somehow at that point forward deciding not to apply it any more to the attack, effectively deciding on their own that the TEM *does* apply to prevent FFMO, but *doesn't* apply to enable the moving unit to benefit from the TEM due to the terrain. 

I have yet to see any answer be able to justify the use of the rules in this way and so suspect that I am correct in my reading, but it goes against current accepted play for some reason.

query:
BPV Allotment Quwstion: What is the typical total BPV allotment for each side In a DYO scenario using 1 board, 2 boards, 3 boards, etc.

By year, per opponent (Germany v Russia) (German v France, etc) Britain vs Italy/ Germany, USA v Germany

Just want to get an average sense before I start a DYO game.
title: BPV Allotment Quwstion
raw_question:
What is the typical total BPV allotment for each side In a DYO scenario using 1 board, 2 boards, 3 boards, etc.

By year, per opponent (Germany v Russia) (German v France, etc) Britain vs Italy/ Germany, USA v Germany

Just want to get an average sense before I start a DYO game.
ground_truth_answer:
There is no "typical allotment".  The DYO system in ASL has never been subject to much analysis or criticism because the vast majority of players never make any use of it, preferring to play prepared scenarios instead.

It's a fairly straight-forward system to use, but it will generate some weird results (e.g., if you purchase assault engineers you will get a truly staggering number of DCs and FTs).  Some nationalities get heavily penalised in terms of numbers of leaders and basic SW while others might end up with more gear than they can easily carry.  It's difficult to get "balanced" forces as a consequence, and that's before you consider what the effects of different board combinations can be.

IMO the best way to make the DYO system "work" is for a third-party to adjudicate everything (i.e., determine the board layout, determine the VC, decide on any special rules, etc.).  That person allocates the points to each side who go off and buy their forces (within the conditions specified by the referee).  THEN the referee examines each side and makes adjustments to try and keep each side "reasonable".

It's a lot of trouble to go through and it still won't come close to guaranteeing that the game will be "balanced".  Most of the time, it's just not worth the effort.

The bridge in question was two hex long (but could have been more in a different context). We played it as not setting up on the bridge but this in itself posed further queries with other SSR.

title: Set-up Clarification
raw_question:
When a scenario card says eg "...set up within 2 hexes of..." does it include the location/s also. I always thought the wording should be "...on or within..." if the location/s themselves were included.

The bridge in question was two hex long (but could have been more in a different context). We played it as not setting up on the bridge but this in itself posed further queries with other SSR.

ground_truth_answer:
In every game I can recall (not just ASL), phrases like "within 2 hexes" mean "within a distance of 2 hexes".

So in the same hex = distance 0 = within 0 hexes; in an adjacent hex = distance 1 = within 1 hex; and distance 2 = within 2 hexes; etc.

In all these distances, the hex itself is certainly within N hexes of itself.

Agreed, and if you did set up on either bridge hex, you would still be setting up within two hexes of it.

ground_truth_answer:
See A16.1 Integrity Base
The integrity Base is the number of MMC points a side can lose before it must check for Battlefield Integrity. Some Guns have a negative M#.

From memory you need a towing vehicle with a T# equal to or less than the Gun's M# to tow it.

query:
Using a malfunctioned Gun as shield: My Gun (40L AT, T-type) got a hit with a K-result, which malfunctioned it and eliminated the crew. In the next turn I moved a HS there, which recovered the Gun, only to find out that they cannot repair it (according to A9.72).

Now, I assume the HS could still use the Gunshield's TEM for protection in the otherwise Open Ground hex. But can they also change the CA of a malfunctioned Gun, at the end of a friendly fire phase (C3.22)?
title: Using a malfunctioned Gun as shield
raw_question:

ground_truth_answer:
I'll cite two rules to try to answer your question
C11.5 "All AT and INF Guns have gunshields which help protect their manning crew"

D5.1 "A vehicle-crew counter has all the capability of an infantry-crew counter......"
 
A crew (infantry or vehicular) who man a gun, benefits from Gunshield protection.
ONLY the crew that mans (possesses/recovered) the gun benefits though. No other infantry in the hex (other crews included) can benefit of that.

query:
How I (mis)interpret A11.2 Infiltration, or how I would like it to be. A useless-or-not analisys of that dark paragraph.: Following my last thread.

So the TWO rolled by Infiltration rule looks like a real benefit ONLY if rolled by the ATTACKER and, being a roll low enough to harm (eliminate etc...) his enemies, it looks like a mean to advance one location more during CC. Was this the real intent of this rule?
I'm not completely convinced on this. Why Infiltration should advantage the ATTACKER more than the DEFENDER?
If this was the intent I think the rule would have been written using more likely the terms ATTACKER and DEFENDER in capital letter. It would have been much more clearer. The fact it is not so, makes me having some doubts. And going deeper into the words makes my doubts growing.
The matter is only about the DR of TWO, the 12 is easier because being implemented by the enemy units, can take less into account the "dice roll sequence".
I don't know Who wrote this rule in the depth of time, but I THINK it was made to give some more unpredictabilty to CC and a chance to survive for the poor hopeless units attacking with low odds.
The following analisys can be quite useless, having Klas already kindly answered to my questions and Alan pointed me to an interesting article, but you are welcome to spend two minutes in reading it.

A11.22 INFILTRATION
"The simultaneous nature of CC is momentarily suspended following an Original CC DR of 2/12."....
It makes no references to ATTACKER or DEFENDER, so if either make one of those rolls, CC is not simultaneous anymore, and, I THINK this means the 2 or 12 take the precedence on the "other" results: If the ATTACKER rolls a 12, the DEFENDER can withdraw before rolling his dice, if the ATTACKER rolls a 2, he can withdraw before the DEFENDER rolls his dice. In the majority of the CCs the ATTACKER would eliminate the DEFENDER with the 2, and, having he advanced in the now CC location most likely with favorable odds, why should he take/hope-in the benefit of Infiltration? To "jump off" the enemy unit? It could be, but the chances to roll 2 are too low to rely on this. It looks like the infiltration following the 2 DR has been tought for the DEFENDER, not for the ATTACKER, allowing he (the DEFENDER) to withdraw from desperate CCs.
..."Provided it has not been eliminated/captured/pinned, any Infantry/Cavalry unit which rolls an Original 2 CC DR may withdraw from CC/Melee immediately thereafter in the same CCPh without being attacked...."
This is the tricky part. IF the simultaneous nature has been suspended, as stated above, the unit which rolls 2 cannot have been "already" eliminated, so it looks like this line refers to the 11.3 sequential CC provisions. Otherwise there are some contraddictions: Note that the words "without being attacked" and "provided it has not been eliminated[...]" are in contrast if this rule takes into account only the ATTACKER DR rolled before the DEFENDER's: - if the ATTACKER eliminates the DEFENDER and the DEFENDER rolls 2, the DEFENDER "has been eliminated" but he can withdraw "without being attacked". But the DEFENDER was already been "attacked" rolling he after the ATTACKER. So why write this rule this way? You can answer that "without being attacked" refers only to the fact that if the ATTACKER rolls its 2 he can withdraw before the DEFENDER rolls its dice, but in this case it is not possible he(the ATTACKER) "has already been eliminated" since no dice are rolled by the DEFENDER yet. So again,  why write this rule this way? 
Further thoughts: assuming that to implement the 2 result the DEFENDER should have not been already eliminated, what is the real benefit in withdrawing, since in the most cases this low roll harms (eliminates etc...) the enemy leaving him in the location with no/less enemies?
The common interpretation makes this rule giving more the benefit of moving one location further in CCPh, more than allowing units to save themselves, as I noted above. But if this is the intent, why use the word "withdraw" instead of "move, advance or better INFILTRATE"?
Last note: A11.3 SEQUENTIAL CC begins with the words: "There are three OTHER (my capital) instances in which CC is not considered simultaneous"... Doesn't this should mean the preceding paragraph is about one OTHER instance of sequential CC?

Perhaps my english knowledge is confusing my understanding of the rule, perhaps not.
With only 40 games under my belt, I have most likely not experienced all the application of this rule. 
Feel free to point out all my misinterpretation. 
Be merciful.
Thanks for your time.

query:
Concealed unit with Prisoners: Do I lose concealment when I take prisoners, or when I move with them?
I didn't find any rule. So probably not?
title: Concealed unit with Prisoners
raw_question:
Do I lose concealment when I take prisoners, or when I move with them?
I didn't find any rule. So probably not?
ground_truth_answer:
The Prisoners are not treated like an enemy unit for "?"-gain purposes.

Prisoners are not treated like an enemy unit for any purpose [EXC: berserkers (A20.4)].

It is more productive to think of prisoners as a weird kind of SW that the guards are dragging around wherever they go.  Prisoners do not prevent concealment gain any more than a portaged MG or DC prevents concealment gain.

Note that I am talking about prisoners, i.e., enemy units that have been captured and are currently under guard.  Unarmed enemy units (whether they are ex-prisoners who have escaped or been released, or unarmed for some other reason) are a completely different thing.

Prisoners -- NOT a type of unit.
Unarmed units -- ARE a type of unit (as the name suggests).
