In the beginning I was always confused that a unit under DM can rout out of a building into the open, but not out of woods, and often played it wrong. So in the first example I may not rout the American unit from Z1 back into the woods at X1, but the only valid rout location is Z0. Or stay where it is. Right?

you can ignore Z0 because it is no farther than your starting hex Z1 from the german unit in CC2 (last lines of the A10.51 EXC ). So you can rout to X0 or X1.

In the second example CC9 is not a valid rout destination for the broken German unit in DD8, because it would be closer to the Americans. I remember there was a rule which says that a unit can always leave its current location when under DM? So, as CC9 is not valid, am I allowed to choose EE7 as my rout destination, moving through the brush? Or may I never leave the woods?

If it has a clear LOS to the americans in Y9, it can rout to FF7 or stay where it is. If it has no LOS to any american unit at the start of its RtPh, and it wants to rout, it MUST rout to CC9 because it is the closest wood/building hex. 
 
10.5 "A broken unit may rout if currently unde DM". A unit MUST rout if it is in OG and within normal range and LOS of a known enemy unit not in melee. And MUST rout if ADJACENT to or in the same location with an enemy unit both unbroken and armed. If neither of this conditions are in effect at the start of a units' RtPh, it may rout only if under a DM and cannot rout if not under a DM.

About leaving a building and not a wood, it's just a wording matter. I'll try to explain. You can ignore other hexes of the same building choosing another (closest) destination also if this makes you move through OG to reach the new destination. This because buildings are often formed by more than one hex, so you can ignore adjacent hexes of the same building but If your building is sourrounded by OG you are forced to rout through OG.
Wood hexes are never intended as part of a larger wood, so you can't ignore wood hexes which are part of "the same wood". So actually you should always consider the wood hex you are adjacent as the closest legal destination. .....mmmm......not sure I was totally clear...

ground_truth_answer:
Which is why I would not marked the Location in the described situation (because I don't think there is any rule calling for it [granted, I could be missing something]), because should the units remain in that Location until the next Russian APh, the 6-2-8 and the Hero should not be prohibited from advancing.

Well, certainly in the case of concealed units that is correct: A11.15 explicitly states that concealed units are not marked as being in Melee and are free to leave in their next MPh/APh.  If the concealment is lost (for any reason) then the units are immediately locked in Melee if it's already a "Melee Location" but are apparently not otherwise marked or affected.  There's no reference to placement of a CC marker in lieu of the Melee marker.

For units that are not concealed, however, the issue is, there really isn't a general rule about when to place a CC marker, just a handful of specific circumstances.  A15.432 refers to berserk units entering enemy Locations and requiring placement of the CC marker.  A25.233 refers to placement of the markers  during a Human Wave and A25.234 refers to the inability to advance when so marked.  D7.21 refers to the placement following a CC Reaction Fire attack.  (I don't think that the E7.22 placement of a CC marker for Aerial Combat is relevant here.)

D7.22 does add the interesting twist that placement of a CC marker also prevents Non-CC Reaction Fire (I'm sure I've played that wrong in the past!), which is certainly a good reason to not place one if it's not explicitly called for.  This is particularly relevant in Qwirz's example that started this thread.

So I guess I'm wrong in saying you should place one when not explicitly required to, and yet I still think it's a good idea to mark Locations where enemy units are co-habiting.  I guess that I would like a "this is a potential CC Location but this isn't a CC marker" marker!

ground_truth_answer:
F12.42.....

When a sand dune overlay has been selected, an extra, Final dr of ≤ 1 must be made in order to place it. Each already-selected sand overlay adds a -1 drm to that dr, as does each already-selected sand dune overlay [EXC: this drm becomes -2 if the already-selected sand/dune overlay is on the same half-board as, or on a half-board adjacent (even diagonally) to, the half-board being rolled for]. If the Final dr is ≥ 2, no overlay is placed. 

If it is ≤ 1, place the overlay and then make another dr; a Final dr ≤ 1 
makes the dune a High Dune (7.5), while any other result yields a Low Dune. 

Each already-selected High Dune adds a -1 (or -2, as given above) drm to this dr.

title: A7.9 cowering
raw_question:
Ok...question time!!! I'm reading the comprehensive example on journal #6 and it is a good way to (re)read some paragraphs.
A7.9 last sentence: "if a FG cowers, Random Selection is used to determine the unit(s)....that becomes marked with a Prep or Final Fire counter."
Does this mean that in PFph a FG which fires and cowers is not marked Prep as a whole? Just the selected unit(s)......others can fire again?
Does this mean that in enemy MPh a FG which use SFF and cowers is not marked FINAL as a whole? etc...etc...
I think this is not the rule intent....
Help please!
ground_truth_answer:
Guessing this would apply to inherent SW e.g PF / Mol ….?

Yes.  (Although actually NA for MOL, since you can't make a MOL attack separately from your inherent FP.)

One of the ASL "tricks" quickly learnt by experienced players: cowering does not apply to any attack that must make a "To Hit" DR.  So if you have a squad armed with a BAZ, maybe you want to fire the BAZ before using the squad's inherent FP; if you do it the other way around, the squad may cower and you won't get to fire the BAZ at all.  (Obviously, this is only a general rule; the specific situation may dictate a different approach.)

SW MTRs throw in an extra twist.  By the principle above, a squad armed with a MTR may wish to fire the MTR first before using his inherent FP.  However, if gaining and keeping acquisition is important, he may want to do it the other way around -- or not even use his inherent FP at all; because acquisition is lost if the firing unit makes any other attack (including Interdiction!) (C6.5).

title: Concealment loss
raw_question: so I’m trying to get a handle on the concealment gain/loss chart and I’m a little confused. Case A says “Non-Assault Movement”. So if my infantry uses Assault Movement it’s good to keep concealment. Case B though reads “moves/advances”. So does “Assault Movement” count as “moves”?  So does my Assault Moving infantry into Open Ground concealment or not. Seems like both cases apply here.
ground_truth_answer:
Check the definition of Open Ground - it isn't just a hex without TEM or hindrance terrain - the LOS of enemy units _to_ that hex is also a factor (for retaining concealment while assault moving).

-N
Here is the rule :
A10.531 OPEN GROUND: For purposes of rout determination, Dash, concealment gain/loss, and Interdiction, an Open Ground hex is any hex in which the particular enemy unit(s) could apply, during a hypothetical Defensive First Fire opportunity (regardless of what attacks it actually made in previous phases), the -1 FFMO DRM.

ground_truth_answer:
Hello again-
 Please look at board Z (If you have it) from the starter kit #1. I know there's no 1st level rules in SK#1; my question is: 
- Does hex L6 have LOS to M5?  ...due to the building touching that vertex.
 

The answer is "no", because the building art is not touching the vertex, it is crossing the hexside L5/M6.  Only by a tiny amount, sure, but that's enough.

If the building art was drawn in such a way that it truly did only touch the vertex, then the LOS would not (could not) be blocked, because the obstacle art has to show on both sides of your LOS string (A6.1).

This does not make the board "crazy" or illustrate some weirdness in the ASL LOS rules (that are plenty of other examples for those sort of issues).  It's perfectly straight-forward.  The only thing that makes it stand out in any way is that you have to take a good close look to see what's going on.  That does not make it unique in ASL in any way.  (It's maybe a poor choice for a Starter Kit board, but the kids have to grow up and learn the facts of life at some point ....)

ground_truth_answer:
Please look at board 1, hex W5.
 
 -If a squad is on level 3 (or maybe on the roof tops as per a SSR)

Level 3?  Such a location would only exist by SSR.  Ground, 1st and 2nd are the default levels that exist in this building.  However, I'll take your question at face value.  (A Rooftop location would be at Level 2.5.)

can they see hex's U6, U5 and U4 over the wood bldgs?

U6 -- no.  The minimum amount of Blind Hexes created by a building (or almost any other type of obstacle) is "1" (A6.42).  It doesn't matter how great an elevation advantage you have.  Only crest lines can potentially have their Blind Hexes reduced to "0" (B10.23).

U5 -- from W5, there is no blockage of LOS at any level.  It's a completely open LOS.  I don't understand why you might think otherwise?

U4 -- same as U6.

From W5, at Level 2 (or higher), you can see OVER the building in W5 and therefore can see T5, T6, etc.

The requirement is that at least one unit in the HW chain has a LOS to a target.  No LOS = no HW.  Nothing happens, false alarm, go about your business.

Any activity that requires a LOS before it can occur must implicitly involve a "free" LOS check.  The issue is whether the activity in question still occurs if the LOS check comes up bad.  Attacks on enemy units is an example of "yes, the activity still happens"; the rules for each particular activity will specify (or not).  Since nothing in A25.23 mentions any penalties for "attempting" an illegal HW, there are no penalties.

ground_truth_answer:
If a MMC throw a smoke grenade in an Internal Building Hex of a multi-level building and there is no stairs in the Internal Building Hex. Will Smoke spread to the higher-level Internal Building Hex？

Yes.

Why?  Because no EXC is provided in A24.4 for Interior Building hexes.  The presence of absence of a Stairwell is irrelevant.  (SMOKE does not use the stairs.)

[Aside from Sniper attacks (A14.22) and Indirect Fire attacks (B23.32), "interior building hexes" -- as defined in the Index -- are not treated differently to other building hexes.]

Regarding cellars, you should be specific about what sort of cellars you're talking about.  Cellar rules are only found in certain HASL modules, and the cellar rules for one HASL are not necessarily identical to the cellar rules of a different HASL.  In any case, you don't need a Stairwell (printed or inherent) to "permit" Smoke (or flames) to rise to a higher elevation in any building hex, cellar or otherwise.

All of that may offend your personal sense of "realism".  On behalf of the rules, I apologise for that.  The rules don't apologise, because they don't care.  They just are.

ground_truth_answer:
I ran into an interesting situation today, which I was not completely sure about. I had a building with a FG on two different levels:

Level 1: 447 squad A.
Level 2: 447 squad B with 5-12 MMG (ROF 2) and a 8-1 Leader

An enemy unit moved for 2 MF into a hex in LOS and Normal Range and I First Fired all my units in this building as a FG. To my understanding the Leader DRM cannot be used in this FG over two Locations. But nevertheless I declared that my Leader directs the Fire of his squad and MMG.

You are not eligible to make that declaration.  The Leader directs everything in the FG or nothing.  There is no in-between possibility.

The DR was 4 with cdr 2 (which means ROF for the MMG). It also means that my FG is Cowering. So the attack would be on the 8 FP column, instead on the 12 FP (shift left by one).

Yes, but ....

In my opinion the Leader-directed squad B does not cower, so I won't do Random Selection but mark squad A with a Final Fire counter. Squad B gets a First Fire counter and the MMG can still fire.

... incorrect on all counts.  The FG had no Leader direction, and all involved units are eligible to cower.

As the enemy expended 2 MF I fire the MMG again (alone). Now I think that I can apply the leader's -1 DRM to the shot, because he was directing this local group from the beginning. Correct?

No, as above.  Even if Squad B did not cower, and thus kept the ROF, the Leader was not involved with the initial FG and so cannot just insert himself into the action.  This remains true for the remainder of Defensive Fire (First and Final).

At last I wondered whether I can also fire squad B's inherent FP as SFF after the second MMG attack, but I guess that would be illegal because of Mandatory FG (A7.55)? Squad B would have to attack together with the MMG. But then the MMG would have to use SFF (Sustained Fire) as well (A8.3)...?

No, if the MMG still has ROF, SFF is n/a.  However, as soon as the manning unit uses SFF, it and all of its SW are marked with Final Fire (whether they are used in the attack or not), so the MG would not be eligible for any further ROF.

The issue of when Leaders do and do not participate in a FG is one of the more fundamental rules in ASL, so it's worth taking the time to read the rules and absorb them until they become second-nature.  Points to note:

1 - as I stated above, the Leader directs everything in the FG or he directs nothing.  There are no EXC to this!

2 - once a FG has formed, the Leader has to participate in the initial attack in order to participate in any subsequent attacks of that FG.  You are allowed to drop units from a FG after it has made any attack, but you are not allowed to add units to an existing FG (and that includes Leaders).

3 - "Leader directs fire" and "Leader applies his DRM to an attack" mean the same thing at all times.  The only EXC to that is firstly, a MMC using a FT can be directed by a Leader (to prevent cowering), even though the Leader's DRM cannot be used to modify the attack; and secondly, in CC/Melee attacks, a Leader's DRM can be declined if desired (although strictly speaking, Leaders don't "direct" CC attacks, they "participate" in them).

May they continue to move as a stack after this action?

Yes.  Yes.  Per A24.1, each squad must pre-designate the hex they are attempting to place SMOKE in before making the dr, but they can wait to see the results of each attempt before making their own attempt.  So it is legal to say "these three squads moving as a stack will each attempt to place SMOKE in an adjacent hex" (so they all spend 2 MF simultaneously) and then you make the dr for each squad, only picking the hex for each attempt just before rolling the die.  A couple of points to note:

1 - All of the attempts, collectively, have to be pre-designated.  So if you say all three squads are making the attempt, then you must make three dr (even if the first one succeeds and you don't need any more).  (Of course you can put multiple SMOKE counters in a single hex; but you can't decide to have one or more of the units not bother to roll at all);

2 - this is pretty much the only way outside of a Human Wave for an infantry unit to expend MF "doing nothing"; you can pre-designate that 2 out of 3 squads make SMOKE attempts, but maybe the 3rd squad doesn't have a SMOKE exponent; if you want him moving as part of the stack, he still has to expend the MF even though he isn't actually doing anything.  If there was something else he could expend MF doing, though (e.g., attempting to recover a SW), he could do that.

query: question about routing in  desert  battles.: So you can not rout toward an enemy, or in open ground in front of any fire. What about Desert battles? There's not cover at all. So are squads just dead?
title: question about routing in  desert  battles.
raw_question: So you can not rout toward an enemy, or in open ground in front of any fire. What about Desert battles? There's not cover at all. So are squads just dead?
ground_truth_answer:
In addition to the rule J.R. quoted, there is also the extremely important:

F.5 SURRENDER: In all scenarios set in North Africa (as defined in F11.2), Surrender may not be refused -- i.e., a surrendering unit may not be eliminated thereby invoking No Quarter (A20.3).

If you don't have F11.2 handy, North Africa is defined as: Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Morocco and Algeria.

This is one of ASL's infamous "hidden rules".  It's not really hidden, of course, it's right there in plain sight, but a lot of players forget that it exists.  While almost all scenarios set in Egypt and Libya (and there are many) are desert scenarios (so the application of a Chapter F rule is hardly surprising) there are several scenarios set in Tunisia that do not "look like" desert scenarios and therefore it's easy to forget that this Chapter F rule can apply.

Some questions, which I noted down during my last session:

1. An AFV has AAMG as its MA, with a note "AAMG NA VCA":
a) The VCA includes the hexsides of the covered area(C3.2). Does that mean "NA VCA" covers all the rest, but excluding these hexsides?

Yes.

b) A11.62 states that a CMG cannot be used in CC when it has a restricted CA. But what about a restricted CA of an AAMG? Can I use it in CC?

Yes, unless the specific vehicle note says something different.

c) Are there any restrictions in CC for a remote controlled AAMG, when the crew is BU?

Only whatever restrictions are noted in the specific vehicle note (if any).  Are you talking about German MAVN O?  It specifically says "treated as a normal AAMG" for any purpose other than the listed specific restrictions.  If there was meant to be an EXC for CC, it would say so.

2. The AFV has an MG as MA and can use ROF with it. As far as I understand there is no IF for an MG MA, so I can do SFF and FPF with it, like with a SW MG?

No.  A vehicular MG may use Sustained Fire as per the last sentence of A8.41 if it is the vehicle's MA (A9.3).  That is, if already marked with a First Fire counter, it may fire again during the DFPh using Sustained Fire, but only vs. adjacent/same-hex targets.

SFF/FPF are options only available to Infantry.

3. A Squad is in a hex adjacent to an AFV, which has put an Acquired Target counter on it during DFPh. In the APh the Squad advances (after passing PAATC) into the AFV's hex.
a) Does the Acquired Target counter still move with the Squad, into the firer's hex?

Yes, unless it's a 5/8" acquisition, or unless the acquired weapon is unable to fire at range 0.

b) Assuming both units survive CC unharmed, can the AFV fire into its own hex, using the Acquired Target? C5.5 makes me think that Case E and Case N must be used together.

Yes.  Yes (all DRM are cumulative except where specifically indicated otherwise).

c) When I fire into my own hex during PFPh with HE, then all units are affected? Also the firing AFV's crew, when they happen to be CE? (Probably not. That would be really strange.)

All enemy units, and all units in melee can be affected.  Remember that a vehicle is never held in melee (A11.7).  With a couple of specific EXC (e.g., Thrown DC) you can never affect yourself with your own attack.

OK, trying to get this nailed down.

Trenches and Foxholes are separate locations for very specific actions within a hex location, I've got that figured out.

Almost.  DO NOT describe them as "separate Locations", because "Location" has a very specific game meaning.  Better to say that they are separate positions within the hex.

Assuming a very basic case, clear LoS throughout, level ground, etc. I move an MMC during the MPh from an adjacent hex into a trench. It costs 1MF if I'm *not* going into the trench, and obviously there are DFF opportunities as a result, one per firing defender because the move only cost 1MF. FFMO/FFNAM would apply (or not) as usual. For our purposes, the trench is in OG and this is not an assault move. 

Now let's say the unit wants to enter the hex and move into the trench. 1MF for moving into the hex, 1MF for jumping into the trench. 

As I'm reading it, DFF can occur, applying FFMO/FFNAM, for the first MF expended in the hex, then again for the trench jumping into, but without the FFMO/FFNAM for the second MF. Let's leave rout out of it for now, the interdiction rules seem clear to me. I know! When Rout seems clearer than, oh, anything else, I must be very confused. 

Well, I think one source of your confusion is that you are treating the two different choices as if they were  two different types of movement.  They are not.

The unit expends 1 MF to enter the hex.  That is true regardless of the existence of the trench, and regardless of the unit's intentions.  That 1 MF expenditure can trigger Defensive First Fire in the usual manner, and FFMO/FFNAM can apply as usual.

THEN -- only then -- the moving unit, if able, may expend an additional MF to enter the trench.  Or, of course, he could expend additional MF to leave the hex, or make a smoke grenade attempt, or whatever.

Entering the hex and entering the trench are separate, distinct activities during the MPh.  Do not conflate them into a single action!

This is a bit confusing to me because I've played Red Barricades scenarios with printed shellholes (same for polder in the SK Decision at Elst set), and those assume you go directly into the shellholes and get their benefit immediately if you play 2MF to enter the hex, but OG if you pay 1MF. Once you stop moving in that hex, you are considered to be in the shellhole because there isn't any way to track that.

Correct.  Shellholes are not entrenchments and don't use the same rules.  A shellhole hex is a special type of terrain where, during the MPh, the TEM it offers differs depending how many MF you expended to enter the hex.  This is completely different to the way entrenchments work.

If Defender is ALL HIP setup..........the Attacker setup is then onboard................Can the defender prevent Concealment gains for Attacker units in LOS during Setup????

To deny concealment (at setup or at any other time) there needs to be an unbroken unit with LOS (so even a dummy stack is sufficient).  The A12.121 Concealment Loss/Gain Table is one of the most important tables in the entire game.  Study it.

Which part of the rule you quote is unclear?  It states exactly which units gain concealment!

My AFV Intensive Fired during the PFPh and rolled an original DR of 12 for its TH, which is the X# for Intensive Fire. So I placed a MA Disabled marker.

The 'good' news is you picked about the best time to disable your MA.  You may indeed fire your remaining weapons this fire phase, and you may also do so during your opponent's player turn.  On the movement phase of your next player turn, you must exit the board using the fewest MPs possible, but that still allows you to use motion bounding fire on your way home.  Good luck!

query:
Concealment at Setup: Setup procedure is incorrect.

Russian sets up, using only provided concealment counters (and only in Concealment terrain).

Then German sets up, using only provided concealment counters  (and only in Concealment terrain).

Then Russian and German units out of LOS gain concealment, no matter what the terrain.

If one side has no units on-board, then they may place non-provided concealment counters on unit when they setup and before the opponent looks at the board.
title: Concealment at Setup
raw_question:
Setup procedure is incorrect.

Russian sets up, using only provided concealment counters (and only in Concealment terrain).

Then German sets up, using only provided concealment counters  (and only in Concealment terrain).

Then Russian and German units out of LOS gain concealment, no matter what the terrain.

If one side has no units on-board, then they may place non-provided concealment counters on unit when they setup and before the opponent looks at the board.
ground_truth_answer:
Brian's summary is correct.

The important things to remember are that during setup, "?" counters provided in the scenario OB may only be placed in Concealment Terrain (the terrain types marked in red on the Terrain Chart); and, during setup, units that qualify for concealment gain, either because they are out of all enemy LOS (even if in open ground), or because they are in LOS but in Concealment Terrain at extreme range (typically > 16 hexes) do not have to make a Concealment dr.

Neither of the above rules apply once play of the scenario begins.

To check the nitty-gritty details, consult the Concealment Loss/Gain Chart (learn it, love it, make it your best friend) and the Advanced Sequence of Play (the scenario setup section).

Incidentally, I know it's a suggestion printed in the rules, but the give-the-enemy-lots-of-dummy-counters-when-playing-solo rule is not very effective if you're actually playing solo.  ASL is not really geared for solitaire play (not counting the actual Solitaire ASL expansion, which is a different kettle of fish altogether) and lots of enemy concealment is not going to do much to make the play interesting, although your plan is about as good as you can make it.  If you had a live opponent, he would be planning all sorts of things with his dummies that you can't reasonably replicate in solo play.  In general, you'll get a better solo game by picking scenarios that don't make use of lots of dummies.

The FP for the OVR is 20.5 FP.
BMG is 3 FP and CMG is 8 FP. MGs fired as TPBF/BFF are ((3+8)*3)/2 = 16.5 FP. Adding the base value of 4 FP for my AVF yields 20.5 FP.

The DRMs are:
- Motorcycle (D15.5) -1 (there is no FFMO -1 for it)
- Motion Vehicle +2
- Armor Leader -1

The Attacker's DR is 10, which is a 1MC.

The 447 rolls 9, Breaks, and has to Bail Out, because the Cycle is in Motion.

The Bail Out DR is 7, so it barely avoids elimination. The 447 is placed in broken state with a DM counter below the Cycle.

There will be no CC RF, because the 447 is now broken. There would also be no CC RF if it were pinned.

The AFV is marked with a Bounding Fire Counter and spends another MP to leave the OVR-Location.

query: Leadership bonus: Very new ASL player with a quick question.  If a squad is in a hex with both a +1 and a -1 leader and is firing do they get the better -1 leaders bonus?  Thanks!

ground_truth_answer:
An EXC to the above replies is when an unpinned, Good Order Commissar and a normal leader are together in a hex.  The Commissar pulls rank over any other leader and prevents the application of another leader's modifier (even if the Commissar isn't otherwise involved!), and if it's the RPh and there are broken units present, the Commissar (and no other leader) must attempt to rally them. A25.222:
"A Commissar must attempt to rally broken units in its Location..."

There might an exception if said broken unit is itself a Commissar - I think they always have to Self-Rally.

This has some implications for Japanese leaders; since all Japanese leaders are Commissars,...
G1.41:
"A Japanese leader [EXC: Inherent armor leader] is equivalent to a Commissar for all rally and berserk purposes; i.e., he bestows all the same benefits and penalties given in A25.222-.223...."

So there are some subtle difference between a Russian Commissar and a Japanese leader:
A Japanese leader increases the Morale Level of all other non-berserk Japanese Infantry/Cavalry units, even if he is pinned, a Russian Commissar needs to be unpinned to do that.

Also, I think a Japanese leader can receive the leader DRM of another leader when performing any action, a Russian Commissar can't.

I think those are the two difference.

B12.2 "... it is only the presence of brush in a same-level hex between the same-level firing (or observing/spotting) and target hex that forms a LOS Hindrance ...."

Whenever any terrain type is described as having some LOS effect (whether it's a Hindrance or an Obstacle) that only affects same-level LOS then you can assume (barring some explicit statement to the contrary) that the terrain type is only a half-level high.

Yes, but that is the only movement option for the unit in that MPh.  You can't combine regular movement (of any sort, for any purpose) with sewer movement.

query:
Routing adjacent to a known enemy unit: I have a unit that wishes to rout out of hex K19 on the Red Barricades board. There are enemy units in hexes J18 and L19, meaning that the unit is surrounded. However, there is a black bar between J18 and K19, so J18 is out of LOS of K19 and thus not a known enemy unit at the start of the rout phase. J19 is the only possible rout direction, but once entering that hex, the broken unit is in the LOS and ADJACENT to the enemy unit in J18. Is the broken unit allowed to rout from K19 to J19?

Argument for allowing it: the enemy unit does not become known until after the routing unit enters J19, so the initial move from K19 to J19 is not considered routing ADJACENT to a known enemy unit

Argument against allowing it: the timing of when the enemy unit becomes known not mentioned in the rules, so once the routing unit enters J19, it is in a hex ADJACENT to a known enemy unit, and since it is not leaving J18, the rout is not allowed

Obviously, if routing into J19 is allowed, the routing unit must continue to rout because it cannot end the rout phase ADJACENT to J18.

Advance and Concealment: Does an Advance is considered "Non-Assault-Movement" ?

Do I loose a concealment marker if I do advance in the APh ?
title: Advance and Concealment
raw_question:
Does an Advance is considered "Non-Assault-Movement" ?

Do I loose a concealment marker if I do advance in the APh ?
ground_truth_answer:
To a concealment terrain, no. To open ground yes.

Not quite.  The issue is "open ground vs. not open ground", NOT "open ground vs. concealment terrain".  Never confuse "concealment terrain" with "not open ground", they are different concepts.  (So different that there is even one type of concealment terrain that is also treated as open ground!  Anyone care to guess what it is?)

If your advancing unit is in open ground vs. any good order enemy unit within 16 hexes with a LOS to it, then it will lose concealment (Case B on the Concealment Loss/Gain Table). [EXC: Winter Camouflage (E3.712) can negate this.]

Remember hindrances cancel open ground consideration.

Terrain hindrances, yes.  LV Hindrances, no.

ground_truth_answer:
The current scenario that I'm playing features gullys.

The way I am playing them, is that a same level adjacent hex, cannot see units that are actually in an adjacent gully. They have to wait for the units to crest or exit to some other ground level hex.

Does this sound right?

Uh, no.  The best way to play LOS into gullies is the way the rules describe in A6.3.

The general rule is, to see INTO a gully, the observing unit must have a height advantage >= the range in hexes.  So a unit one level higher at a range of one hex (i.e., in an adjacent hex) can see INTO the gully.  If you are 2 hexes away, the height difference must be at least two levels, and so on.

There are many exceptions to this general rule.  E.G., units in adjacent gully hexes do not have LOS to each other if their respective gully hexes do not share a common gully hexside (i.e., they do not "connect"). (A6.8, first EX)  However, units can see INTO depression hexes without necessarily having the height requirement described above, if they are looking along a depression (A6.3 EX).

Hi all!
This is one of the rules I still can't grasp.
Reading and re-reading rules and Backblast #2 wonderful article "Dance with the Tiger", I still have doubts.
D7.2 last lines "Reaction Fire vs an OVRing vehicle is resolved immediately after the resolution of that OVR"
Pag. 29 Backblast #2, CC Reaction Fire paragraph "If an infantry or cavalry unit is unbroken, unpinned, armed, not in melee, and in a moving vehicle's location, it may attempt to attack the vehicle using the CC rules. This is true whether the vehicle is overrunning the location or not."
Now, playing 137.Italian Brothers the following occurred.

L3 is about to OVR the 8-1 and three 4-3-7 in N9. 
Being not able to harm the BU AFV with fire, can the Infantry units attack the vehicle when it enters the hex, BEFORE the OVR resolution????
Are there other means of defence?
Any help is much appreciated.
Thanks!!!

EDIT: Sorry for the poor focus of the picture.
ground_truth_answer:
It means you may conduct Defensive Fire that is not CC RF on the MP expenditure announced for the OVR. So if the unit being OVR has an LATW, it may use it.

A Gun has a special rule for OVR prevention, enabling it to fire one more time on the onrushing tank before the OVR is resolved. Note that this always counts as an intensive fire shot, regardless of wether the Gun has fired before. So it can easily break during the attempt. If a kill is scored, the OVR will still take place, but FP is halved.

5.64 OVR PREVENTION: Regardless of the number of shots a non-vehicular Gun has already taken during a Player Turn (including Intensive Fire), it is entitled to the possibility of one more Intensive Fire shot at a target in its own hex if it is about to be OVR [EXC: OVR Prevention cannot be used by a Gun with a "No IF" listing on the back of its counter; 5.63]. Immediately after the OVR MP expenditure (D7.1) is announced (but before the OVR is resolved) the Gun makes its To Hit DR vs the vehicle making the OVR, but not until its CA covers the hexside entered by the OVR vehicle. If a Gun has already fired from woods/building/rubble, it is not allowed to change its CA (5.11) and is not eligible for OVR Prevention vs an AFV entering its hex from outside the Gun's CA. A Gun which has already Intensive Fired during that MPh suffers only one set of Intensive Fire penalties (i.e., the Intensive Fire DRM and B# reductions of the two Intensive Fire shots are not cumulative). The Original To Hit DR of the firing Gun also acts as a NMC vs its own manning Infantry. If the manning Infantry is pinned or broken as a result of that NMC, the To Hit attempt is voided (except for any Gun Malfunction or Low Ammo (D3.71) it may have caused) and the OVR vehicle resolves its OVR. If the NMC is passed by rolling < the manning Infantry's Morale Level, the To Hit DR is resolved vs the OVR vehicle and may possibly lessen the OVR attack (D7.11). Regardless of the outcome of the To Hit DR, the Gun is marked with a "No Fire" counter to indicate that it may not fire again during that Player Turn—even if it is about to be OVR again.

Finally remember that berserkers must move first in the MPh before any non-berserker unit (A15.43 and the ASOP).

Further clarification: FPF is a type of attack that can only occur during the MPh, and never during the DFPh (A8.31).

SAN target determination with multiple LOCATIONS: My nemesis Bill (!) and I are playing Pavlov's House and I activated his Sniper.  He rolled for the target hex but since there were no eligible targets, we triggered 14.21 "ALTERNATE TARGET: 14.21 Should greater than or equal to 2 such hexes be equidistant, the Location with the lowest TEM is the target." and moved the Sniper to the closest hex that contained enemy units. I had Russians on the Ground floor (fortified stone building TEM +4) and 1st floor (stone building +3 TEM).

There was only 1 eligible HEX for the Sniper to hit but it had 2 Locations.  We weren't sure if the sniper attacked the +3 Location or we triggered 14.2 that says "if that new target hex Contains greater 1 Location occupied by an eligible enemy unit, the Sniper player selects which of those Locations to attack".  So, we let the Sniper select the Location.

Did we play this correctly??
title: SAN target determination with multiple LOCATIONS
raw_question:
My nemesis Bill (!) and I are playing Pavlov's House and I activated his Sniper.  He rolled for the target hex but since there were no eligible targets, we triggered 14.21 "ALTERNATE TARGET: 14.21 Should greater than or equal to 2 such hexes be equidistant, the Location with the lowest TEM is the target." and moved the Sniper to the closest hex that contained enemy units. I had Russians on the Ground floor (fortified stone building TEM +4) and 1st floor (stone building +3 TEM). 

Here is our question - 14.21 specifically uses the term 'hexes' not 'Locations' being  equidistant to select the 'Location' with the lowest TEM.  There was only 1 eligible HEX for the Sniper to hit but it had 2 Locations.  We weren't sure if the sniper attacked the +3 Location or we triggered 14.2 that says "if that new target hex Contains greater 1 Location occupied by an eligible enemy unit, the Sniper player selects which of those Locations to attack".  So, we let the Sniper select the Location.

Did we play this correctly??
ground_truth_answer:
There's a lot of confusion here which would go away if you pay attention to what exactly it is that you're doing each step of the way.

A14.21 is all about selecting the target HEX.  The first sentence of A14.21 makes this clear.  Everything in A14.21 is about determining which HEX you're moving the Sniper to.  First choice: nearest hex with eligible targets.  If there's still more than one choice, you choose the hex that has the lowest TEM.  If you still have more than one choice, then the player decides which hex the Sniper is moved to.

Congratulations!  You now know which hex the Sniper is attacking.  Now you actually move back to A14.2 to determine WHO in that hex is actually being attacked.  This is where we see the rule "If that new target hex Contains > one Location occupied by an eligible (14.22) enemy unit(s), the Sniper player selects which of those Locations to attack."  The Location with the lowest TEM is completely irrelevant to this choice.  The Sniper player can choose the Location with the highest TEM, if he wants to!

In other words:

1 - Select the target hex per the criteria specified in A14.21.

2 - Having selected the hex, if you have a choice of multiple Locations, the Sniper player chooses which Location to attack.  That's all it is -- a simple choice!

3 - Having at last decided which Location is being attacked, you then select the actual target of the attack, if there is more than one eligible target.  Usually this will be by Random Selection (but A14.21 lists the EXC that enables the Sniper player to bypass RS and just pick a particular target).

In the entirety of the above procedure, the only time "lowest TEM" comes into the picture is in step 1, and even then, only when there is more than one possible hex to attack.

query:
Advanced squad leader starter set 2. Rallying in close combat/melee: I have a broken SMC in a combat situation.
Cannot find the rule about weather or not he can rally during the "Rally Phase" at the beginning of the next turn, whilst still in combat. 

What is the definition of "Eligible" that would define what units can be rallied.
title: Advanced squad leader starter set 2. Rallying in close combat/melee
raw_question:
I have a broken SMC in a combat situation.
Cannot find the rule about weather or not he can rally during the "Rally Phase" at the beginning of the next turn, whilst still in combat. 

What is the definition of "Eligible" that would define what units can be rallied.
ground_truth_answer:
Broken units can certainly appear in CC situations.  An important consideration is whether a Melee exists or not.

As stated above, broken units must attempt to Withdraw from a Melee in the CCPh (and cannot move in the RtPh).  If it is not a Melee, then they have no options in the CCPh at all -- they must sit and take whatever is coming to them -- but will usually rout in the preceding RtPh.  There are EXC, typically if the enemy units are concealed and the broken unit is not under DM, they can move up to the broken unit and advance in (with a very good chance of scoring an Ambush).

None of the above tells us much about what a broken unit in CC's options during the RPh are, though.  There are a couple of clues:

A10.6 tells us that a Good Order leader can attempt to rally broken units in his Location.  If there's a Melee going on, the leader will not be Good Order, unless he is not involved in the Melee somehow -- e.g., if he is concealed.

Fairly definitively, A11.15 tells us that "Units locked in Melee may not Interdict routing units nor conduct any other activity other than CC or Withdrawal from Melee."

So, if the broken unit is actually held in Melee, no form of (deliberate) rally attempt can be made -- the broken unit is forbidden from such activity (and any leader present would also be similarly forbidden if he is also locked in Melee).

What if the broken unit is not in Melee, though?  For example, if the only enemy unit in the Location is a non-stopped vehicle, then there is no Melee.  "Other activities" (such as rally attempts) then seem to be allowed.

There is an (unofficial) Q&A from MMP that says:

A10.6 & A11.15
Can a broken unit be rallied while in CC or melee?
A. Only via HOB.

That's pretty definitive, but the "CC" portion is not (as above) actually supported by existing rules text (unless there's some other buried rule that I've missed, which is always possible).  As such, it constitutes errata-in-waiting.  It would be up to the players to decide whether to accept it in their game.  Personally I don't really see a problem with it, but if my opponent didn't want to accept it, it would be hypocritical of me to argue against him, given my prior public statements concerning unofficial Q&A. :D

query:
Skulking question, with apologies: I hate to bring this old thing up but Ive been away from ASL for almost 15 years and am wondering what the current thinking is in the industry. Recently I got the notion to revisit this old favorite of mine and picked up the various Starter Kits, New RuleBook and Beyond Valor.(I sold off my entire collection years ago, unwisely it appears)

Skulking was a 'no-no' in our group back in the day. Absolutely legal but unethical and frowned upon. Ive been reading around the net and see that opinions still vary however. 

One that bothers me a bit is the notion that scenario designers assume Skulking and to eliminate it (through rule change or simply a gentleman's agreement) may unbalance scenarios.

Is this true? Has it therefore always been an accepted tactic, even among the developers? Did I and my buddies have it all wrong back then?

Recently I got the notion to revisit this old favorite of mine and picked up the various Starter Kits, New RuleBook and Beyond Valor.(I sold off my entire collection years ago, unwisely it appears)

Skulking was a 'no-no' in our group back in the day. Absolutely legal but unethical and frowned upon. Ive been reading around the net and see that opinions still vary however. 

One that bothers me a bit is the notion that scenario designers assume Skulking and to eliminate it (through rule change or simply a gentleman's agreement) may unbalance scenarios.

Is this true? Has it therefore always been an accepted tactic, even among the developers? Did I and my buddies have it all wrong back then?
ground_truth_answer:
Good answer but it's not realistic to consider ASL covering 2 minute gaps of time per turn. It's highly variable.... consider turns in Red Barricades... cheers :) 
Note the Rulebook Section A3, first sentence, "Each game turn represents 2 minutes of actual time..." 

This is a pretty clear statement of design intent. ASL was designed to represent a quick clash between two small forces, usually a mere slice of the action. 

Over the years designers have really stretched this original concept, especially in big CGs. Many players really enjoy large CGs and I'm fine with that because it keeps the game active.  

But I also like Bruce's concept of "cinematic time" since ASL is a really great dramatization of WWII action. And two minutes of cinematic time can represent almost anything. :)

We know what it says in the hallowed book. Regardless, I don't think even early on that the designers ever met this intent.

But the development of RB threw that baby out with the bathwater in an obvious way and it became a big discussion with Kibler during our playtests. Finally he stated that the scenario action was to represent the most intense fighting of the day -- as if to justify that these turns really are only two minutes long. 

Does anyone really think action in Stalingrad only lasted 12-18 minutes and after that, nothing? It should be clear to everyone that ASL is much too bloody for it to only portray two minutes of real time each turn and always has been, except on 'mad minute' occasions, regardless of design intent, which is mostly a residual 'appendix' from the old Squad Leader. 

In general, most wargames are too bloody to represent what actually occurred in real time situations, but gamers aren't interested in the hours of lulls to bring up reinforcements, get commands from HQ about objectives, truces to pick up the wounded and dead, etc... they just want to go directly into the battle parts.

It means that the dr number is also the number of SWs that may be scrounged.

HIP foxholes and ? units clarification needed: Hi all!
I'm playing Le Manoir. German Foxholes are set up Hidden.
According to rules when an enemy unit is in LOS (regardless of range) I have to reveal them.
What about units inside (HIP as well)? Do I place them too under a "?" Counter beneath the foxhole?
Or do I reveal them per HIP units rule?
What about units in foxholes NOT in concealment terrain? Should I reveal them with no "?" Counter since FHoles are not concealment terrain?
Thanks
title: HIP foxholes and ? units clarification needed
raw_question:
Hi all!
I'm playing Le Manoir. German Foxholes are set up Hidden.
According to rules when an enemy unit is in LOS (regardless of range) I have to reveal them.
What about units inside (HIP as well)? Do I place them too under a "?" Counter beneath the foxhole?
Or do I reveal them per HIP units rule?
What about units in foxholes NOT in concealment terrain? Should I reveal them with no "?" Counter since FHoles are not concealment terrain?
Thanks
ground_truth_answer:
Yes, but 12.33 says "Fortifications set up in non-Concealment terrain are treated as if set up in Concealment terrain [exc: They also lose their HIP status due to enemy LOS regardless of range].
And here start my doubts........

Right.  Units are not Fortifications.  The rule permits the foxholes to be HIP.  The guys in the foxholes are not HIP, unless you have an SSR explicitly permitting this!

The only Fortification that grants "free" HIP status to the units within it is a pillbox (B30.7, last sentence).

If a unit is granted HIP by SSR, then generally it must be set up in Concealment Terrain.  There are EXC, but they are not important right now.  Fortifications may be set up HIP regardless of the terrain, but usually they will lose that HIP status very easily, as per A12.33 and the Concealment Loss/Gain Chart.

If a scenario granted you the ability to HIP a unit in Concealment Terrain, and you placed a foxhole in that same hex, then the foxhole will be revealed as per A12.33, but the unit will only be revealed via the normal rules for Concealment Loss.

Does that make it clearer?

And yes, the fact that the foxhole will lose HIP much more easily than the unit inside it means that the sudden appearance of a seemingly- empty foxhole may make your opponent suspicious.  Use that to your advantage.  The possibility of a hidden unit may make your opponent nervous about moving close to it.  Alternately, he might waste a lot of time trying to deal with it.  But is your HIP unit actually there?  If you can send your opponent on a wild goose chase, or make him scared of shadows, then you chances of winning the scenario are improved.

Non-CC reaction fire is firing on IFT, using LATW, or a gun.

CC-Reaction fire is attacking the vehicle with the CC table while the vehicle is spending MP.

Confusion with A7.212 Target Selection Limits: The rule text seems clear. When I have a known enemy unit, or an armed or armored vehicle, in my location I cannot attack anything outside of it.

But the example below confuses me.

1. When the squad is in the upper location, then it is in a different location. But still unable to fire outside? Why? The rule only mentions its own location. TBPF is also strange, while the PRC can only use PBF.

2. Why on earth can the HT suddenly start firing outside when becoming CE? They should be even more vulnerable to fire from the squad than in its current BU state. Or does it mean that they could theoretically always fire outside, but being BU they cannot fire at all?

title: Confusion with A7.212 Target Selection Limits
raw_question:
The rule text seems clear. When I have a known enemy unit, or an armed or armored vehicle, in my location I cannot attack anything outside of it.

But the example below confuses me.

1. When the squad is in the upper location, then it is in a different location. But still unable to fire outside? Why? The rule only mentions its own location. TBPF is also strange, while the PRC can only use PBF.

2. Why on earth can the HT suddenly start firing outside when becoming CE? They should be even more vulnerable to fire from the squad than in its current BU state. Or does it mean that they could theoretically always fire outside, but being BU they cannot fire at all?

Is this just a special case for OT HT, which can exchange fire through their open top against a unit with elevation advantage, which isn't mentioned in the actual rule?
ground_truth_answer:
When the HT is CE? And they can use TPBF when it is BU? (Still confused.)

The HT, like any other OT vehicle, must be CE in order to fire any weapons other than bow-mounted MG/FT (D5.3).

Passengers of the HT must normally be CE in order to fire (D6.62) but as that rule notes Reciprocity (A6.5)applies, so any enemy unit that can attack the Passengers even when they're BU (A7.211) can be attacked by those Passengers.

Except that the A7.212 EX states that BU Passengers can't attack back, which seems at first to be a contradiction; but Reciprocity is specifically discussing high-to-low shots (and the reverse), and D6.61 explicitly states that BU Passengers can attack back when their CE DRM has been reduced to < its normal value due to elevation advantage.

So the summary is, if the HT and the enemy unit are in the same Location, the enemy unit can attack the HT's Passengers with TPBF even if the latter are BU; but in that case the BU Passengers may not attack back.  (The BU HT itself can't attack anything anywhere [EXC: OVR].)  If the enemy unit is in the same hex, but in a different, higher Location, the enemy unit still qualifies for TPBF vs. the HT, the CE DRM is reduced by 1 for every full level of elevation difference, the HT is treated as an unarmoured vehicle if the CE DRM is so reduced, but the BU Passengers may attack back (but not with TPBF) at that enemy unit.

For the HT/PRC to qualify for TPBF, they must be CE (and the target must be in the same Location -- since HT are not known for their ability to climb stairwells) [EXC: if the HT is at ground-level and the target is in a Cellar Location (e.g., RB, FB, etc.) then the HT might be able to get TPBF vs. the unit in the different Location -- but I don't have any of those rules handy and there might be a Cellar rule that prevents that.]

OK?

5b. Vehicle is in VBM movement on a hexside. When I stop and then start Reverse Movement in VBM, my new CAFP is immediately the Rear CAFP? I don't have to drive the hexside, which I currently straddle, backwards first?

6. A 16 MP halftrack is unloading an infantry unit for 4 MP, whereby the infantry expends 1 MF. How much Defensive Fire do they have to endure? First four shots for 4 MP, then one shot for 1 MF? And will both units (halftrack and infantry unit) be attacked together, as their movement is more or less connected? Or first the halftrack and then the infantry?

7. I'm still wondering that infantry fire on moving targets is not penalized in any way. Or did I miss a rule?
ground_truth_answer:
1. I fire my MG as Ordnance on the VTT. As far as I understand it can keep ROF while doing so. Assuming I still have ROF after that VTT shot, may I switch to normal Small Arms fire for the next shot? And switch again?

Yes.  There's no rule explicitly stating it, it is more the absence of any rule prohibiting it.

2. The Terrain Chart shows "COT" for tracked vehicles into Shellhole hexes. When I move (CE) into a Road / Open Ground hex with Shellholes, is the COT 0.5 or 1 MP?

0.5.  The "COT" designation on the chart essentially means "pay whatever you would pay if this terrain feature was not present".

3. Can I attack unmounted horses? In OVR? In CC?

Well.  An interesting question.  Horse counters, by themselves are one of those great ASL mysteries.  The Index, under Unit, states: "Any game piece or counter with its own MF/MP allotment and normally capable of movement without being portaged, pushed, or towed.  Cavalry [but not horses], ... are all different types of units."  This makes sense: a horse counter, by itself, is incapable of movement.

Then we get to A13.7 HORSES: "Horses are units, but are never considered enemy units."

Uh ... what?  Which rule do you believe?  There's also A13.34 MF ALLOTMENT: "A Horse counter's basic MF allotment is 12 MF."  If a Horse is not a unit, then by definition it has no MF allotment at all; it would be Cavalry that has a basic MF allotment of 12 MF ("Cavalry" defined as per A13.1).  It's a bit confusing.

So let's consider the two possibilities.

(i) Horse counters ARE NOT units.

A7.1: "Fire attacks are the main process by which a unit attacks enemy units."  So does this mean that if you're not a unit, you can't be "attacked"?  Generally that's true -- other things like various terrain types and unpossessed SW can be affected as the result of certain types of attacks, but those attacks are not targeting those things specifically.  We have the first sentence of A13.511 "Horses, whether mounted or not, are attacked using the  Vehicle Line of the IFT in addition to, and at the same time as, fire against any Cavalry unit(s) riding them." (My emphasis.)  Uh, what?  If the horse counters aren't mounted, what "Cavalry unit(s) riding them" are being attacked as a pre-requisite?  The sentence doesn't make much objective sense.  It's my guess that the sentence is trying to indicate that yes, you can shoot at an unmounted horse, but that's not actually what it's saying.  A7.308 actually says something very similar, but uses "Personnel target in the same Location" instead of "Cavalry", which is a better way of expressing the idea.  In that case you always have the "I am testing to see if there is a HIP unit in that hex" excuse to fall back on; of course such a shot would be Area Fire.

(ii) Horse counters ARE units.

Does that help?  Actually no, since by A13.7 they are very explicitly not the enemy.  So the A7.1 comment applies again.  Of course forms of attack that don't distinguish between friendly and enemy units (e.g., OBA) would certainly affect them.  We also have the same A13.511 dilemma as above.  But otherwise, in general, non-enemy units are not affected by fire, with specific EXC (A7.4).

All of the above, which interpretation you want to follow, applies equally to OVR as to other fire attacks.

As for CC, the answer is pretty clearly "no".  Horses have no CC value (not even a "(1)") and are not vehicles, so are not attacked with CCV.  A13.7 tells us that Horse counters are "captured in the same manner as a SW via Recovery".  But further on you get "A unit leading a Horse counter may eliminate that counter as if it were a SW."

After all that, note of course that the only reason you might have to want to eliminate a Horse counter is to prevent an enemy unit from using it.  They are not otherwise any sort of impediment or worth any VP.

4. Do I still have the option for a BFF or BF attack after an OVR? As I understand there is no fire marker on the unit after OVR, so the answer is probably yes?

Good lord, no.  D3.3 BOUNDING FIRST FIRE: "... Any vehicle that fires during its MPh is using Bounding First Fire and is marked with a Bounding Fire counter ..." and D7.1 "An OVR is a form of Bounding First Fire ...".

5a. D2.21 states that Reverse Movement quadruples the entry costs for an AFV. How about the MP for changing VCA in a VBM vertex? Is it quadrupled too?

No.  VCA change is a separate MP expenditure to the hex/hexside entry cost (D2.11, D2.33).

5b. Vehicle is in VBM movement on a hexside. When I stop and then start Reverse Movement in VBM, my new CAFP is immediately the Rear CAFP? I don't have to drive the hexside, which I currently straddle, backwards first?

I never thought of it that way before, but yes, in a way.  See the second EX on p.D6 -- having traversed (but not exited) the hexide in one direction, you don't need to (indeed, cannot) traverse it again, no matter which direction you choose to move in.  However, your CAFP does not change -- that's determined by the VCA while you're using VBM (D2.32).  Switching to Reverse Movement does not change your VCA, and hence does not change the CAFP.

6. A 16 MP halftrack is unloading an infantry unit for 4 MP, whereby the infantry expends 1 MF. How much Defensive Fire do they have to endure? First four shots for 4 MP, then one shot for 1 MF? And will both units (halftrack and infantry unit) be attacked together, as their movement is more or less connected? Or first the halftrack and then the infantry?

The vehicle is expending 4 MP, and hence can be shot at a total of 4 times (by any 1 firer).  The infantry has expended only 1 MF, and thus can be fired at only once.  The MP and MF are expended simultaneously.  If the attack can affect both targets, then yes they will both be affected (to a maximum of 1 time).  Of course if the attack is using the VTT it cannot affect the infantry, and similarly if it's using the ITT it cannot affect the vehicle.  Note that D5.43 explicitly defines the target status of the infantry.  In essence, as soon as PRC declares the exit from the vehicle, that exit is automatically successful (although the now-infantry unit might not survive the process!).  The reverse is not true -- an infantry unit trying to become PRC must first survive all attacks "unpinned and in Good Order".

7. I'm still wondering that infantry fire on moving targets is not penalized in any way. Or did I miss a rule?

I don't understand the question.  Why would stationary firers be penalised?  Bullets and fragments from exploding grenades move a heck of a lot faster than men, even men riding in a truck.  Enough bullets and grenade fragments in a given space are difficult to dodge -- the best defence is to lie as flat as possible, behind cover -- not normally compatible with the idea of "moving".  Sometimes you get away with it -- and sometimes you don't.  If you roll a high number on your IFT attack, does it represent that your men are bad shots, or that the enemy unit was doing a fantastic duck-and-cover routine?  You decide!  If you rolled a low number -- then clearly they weren't dodging well enough.

ground_truth_answer:
Now that you've pointed that out, it makes me want to check what the index has as the definitions for routing and movement.  NRBH, or I'd do it myself.

No definitions, as such, just references to applicable rules.

Generally speaking, Infantry Movement (A4) just uses the terms "moving", "movement", "moved", etc.  Routing (A10.5) predominantly uses the terms "rout", "routing", etc., although the occasional use of "move" occurs -- but usually in combination with "rout" (e.g., "A routing unit may never move ADJACENT to a Known enemy unit ...".

Similarly Advance (A4.7) predominantly uses "advance".

In all cases some allocation and expenditure of MF is involved, which ties them all together, but generally the Rout rules go to a fair amount of effort to distinguish the act of "routing" from the act of "movement".

The german squad in T4 is firing at the bypassing russian 227 and aims at the vertex S7S8R7. The wreck is an inherent hindrance, so its hexsides belong to that hindrance.

Do I have to apply this +1 hindrance DRM, because the aimed vertex touches it? Or may I ignore it, because the 227 in reality bypasses in hex S8 and not directly on its hexside?
title: Attacking a Bypassing unit with an adjacent Hindrance

The german squad in T4 is firing at the bypassing russian 227 and aims at the vertex S7S8R7. The wreck is an inherent hindrance, so its hexsides belong to that hindrance.

ground_truth_answer:
Yes. A bypassing unit is always IN the hex of the obstacle which it is bypassing and not straddling the hexside.
The Wreck, if it were in the hex bypassed, would actually not count as a hindrance but would give a TEM protection.

In the present case, it has no effect on the DFF shot - and certainly not a hindrance, as the LOS of the firer doesn't go through its hex to the target.

Can Cavalry attack in the PFPh, MPh (Bounding Fire?), AFPh?

Cavalry may fire like any other unit as Mounted Fire (halved) - this is in Prep Fire, Defensive Fire, or First Fire vs moving units and so on.  It can also fire in the Advanced Fire Phase though it will be halved again in that case.  

The only way it can fire during its own Movement Phase is with a Charge (A13.6).  It does so as Triple Point Blank Fire (TPBF) with no halving for being mounted; however, it has to survive all defensive fire first.  Read the paragraph carefully as there are extra MF expenditures, a Gallop requirement, and so on.  Good luck!

What would be the DRM, when the 747 fires at the 447?

+2 for the wall: B9.3 "Fire traced through a wall/hedge hexside or hexspine may be subject to a TEM for that wall/hedge if the target is in the Location formed by that hexside/hexspine."  (My emphasis.)

I don't know that there is any option to decline a better TEM that is available to you (WA being an EXC as it is the mechanism to determine whether the wall TEM is available/applicable).  In the specific case of a wall hexspine, the only reason I can think of to decline it would be to negate a HEAT attack (if the American possessed a BAZ, for instance) -- but I don't believe that there is any choice involved, the Wall TEM is available so it applies.

Both B9.31 and C8.31 specify that a HEAT attack requires that the target be "receiving Wall TEM".  "Receiving" is unfortunately a bit of a wishy-washy term in this specific case, since it seems to imply a choice on the part of the target, but I don't believe that it really comes down to "choice" when WA is not an issue -- the Wall TEM exists whether the target wants it or not.

2.  No, it doesn't apply to Interdiction.  Among other things, by A10.531 FFMO must apply in order to invoke Interdiction, and FFMO is disallowed for Snap Shots (A8.51).

3a. I have a Hero with a 4FP MMG and a MMC with 4FP in the same location. 15.23 states that the Hero applies -1 DRM to its IFT DR as well as a +1 DRM, because the SW requires two men. The +1 DRM is "negated by the heroic DRM". Is the before mentioned -1 DRM the heroic DRM, or another -1 DRM? So the attack together with the MMC would be 8FP-1 or just 8FP?

3b. Assuming the attack was 8FP-1, what happens when I add a 8-1 leader in that location? Will his leadership modifier add to the attack as well, i.e. 8FP-2?

3a.  Just 8FP, no DRMs.
3b.  With an 8-1 leader, you'd have 8FP with a -1 DRM, aside from FFMO/FFNAM, TEM, etc.

4. Is an Assault Move into a Foxhole allowed? If yes, is it possible to DFF on that unit without Foxhole TEM before it is entered?

4.  You may Assault Move into a Foxhole assuming you meet the normal conditions (less than normal MF), but you would be subject to possible First Fire in the hex before you enter the Foxhole itself.

5. CA for MMG and HMG confused me. When I shoot and keep ROF I am restricted by the CA. What happens when I lose ROF and make a SFF shot? Is it still restricted? What about FPF? It is always restricted until  the DFPh begins? And then again, provided I have multiple ROF shots in the DFPh?

5.  The CA holds for the rest of the phase, regardless of SFF or FPF.  You may change CA for the DFPh (unless you're pinned, A9.21), however - the new CA will apply for the duration of that phase.  Note you only suffer a fixed CA when firing from woods/buildings/rubble. 

6. A broken/wounded/etc. unit always loses Concealment. Does it only lose Concealment in the moment it is broken, and can regain it later? Or can it generally not gain Concealment or be concealed when broken?

6.  A unit cannot gain Concealment unless it is Good Order.

query:
Allowed LOS Checks?: I'm not sure if I understand when it is legal to check LOS. Some rules are driven by LOS and seem to require lots of LOS checks, while at the same time, particularly when firing, it seems one should not be allowed to check LOS without risk (e.g. you may waste a shot if it turns out LOS does not exist).

It is my understanding that during a scenario one cannot first check LOS and then decide whether to fire or not. You must declare the attack, then check LOS, and if there is no LOS, the attack still takes place but has no effect. This implies you should not be allowed to check LOS whenever you want and that whether two locations have LOS to each other is a bit of a guessing game until you actually take an action.

However, there are other things that require LOS checks. For example, route paths and interdiction. When routing can either player check LOS whenever they want, or does the non-routing player declare things like "I think this unit can see your routing unit, let me do a LOS check?"

Similarly, concealment/loss gain. As units move or take actions, can you be constantly checking LOS, or does a player have to say "I think this unit can see that unit, let me check if it has LOS to remove your concealment?"

Thanks!
title: Allowed LOS Checks?
raw_question:
I'm not sure if I understand when it is legal to check LOS. Some rules are driven by LOS and seem to require lots of LOS checks, while at the same time, particularly when firing, it seems one should not be allowed to check LOS without risk (e.g. you may waste a shot if it turns out LOS does not exist).

It is my understanding that during a scenario one cannot first check LOS and then decide whether to fire or not. You must declare the attack, then check LOS, and if there is no LOS, the attack still takes place but has no effect. This implies you should not be allowed to check LOS whenever you want and that whether two locations have LOS to each other is a bit of a guessing game until you actually take an action.

However, there are other things that require LOS checks. For example, route paths and interdiction. When routing can either player check LOS whenever they want, or does the non-routing player declare things like "I think this unit can see your routing unit, let me do a LOS check?"

Similarly, concealment/loss gain. As units move or take actions, can you be constantly checking LOS, or does a player have to say "I think this unit can see that unit, let me check if it has LOS to remove your concealment?"

Thanks!
ground_truth_answer:
The Index is your friend.  Look up the various rules covered in "LOS Checks".  Most rules explicitly label "free" LOS checks (e.g., in A12.14, the last sentence in the second column of p.A35; C6.51); at other times, the free LOS is implied (and necessary) to make the rule work (e.g., Case J1 and J2 Limited Aim -- those are mandatory DRM if they apply, but some times you'll need to check LOS to various hexes to see if they do actually apply).  In the case of hidden fortifications (A12.33) the LOS checks are not only free and mandatory, but since it might be revealing information to just string the LOS in front of your opponent, such LOS checks are done secretly.  The same is true of, say, a concealed Gun changing CA -- if it's done in LOS of an enemy unit the concealment loss is automatic, but you might need to string the LOS to see if that's the case.

Generally speaking, the context of a rule (or action) that might invoke concealment loss will guide you as to whether the LOS check is "free" or not.  Take note of the "honor system House Rule" discussed in A12.16 and apply the same principles -- which is basically "Trust but Verify".

By B23.71, the black bar between the rubbled hex and the adjacent rowhouse hex is still there.

query:
CC random selection and leader creation: As the ATTACKER in a simultaneous CC, my unit gets a Casualty Reduction result against two enemy MMCs. I roll RS to see which are affected.

The DEFENDER then rolls a natural 2, decides not to withdraw, and a leader is created. The presence of the leader doesn't change the result of my original DR, so the result of my attack is still a CR.

The question is, do I reroll the Random Selection to take account of the fact there are now 3 defending units?
title: CC random selection and leader creation
raw_question:
As the ATTACKER in a simultaneous CC, my unit gets a Casualty Reduction result against two enemy MMCs. I roll RS to see which are affected.

The DEFENDER then rolls a natural 2, decides not to withdraw, and a leader is created. The presence of the leader doesn't change the result of my original DR, so the result of my attack is still a CR.

ground_truth_answer:
IIRC, the Field Promotion rules say you re-calculated as if the leader was present all the time.
Yes, at least my eASLRB says the following:

Unless one or both sides Withdraw due to Infiltration (11.22), both attacks are re-figured using both of the originally-rolled Original DRs and the new leader's FP/Leadership just as if he had been there all along.

Yes, that's a good point. The correct rule is A18.12 here. So that last bit would mean that the original RS would be tossed out, and a new RS for three units be made.

Notice that there is a recalculation ONLY if one or more sides don't take advantage of withdrawal. Which covers the case mentioned by Russell, the defender, if they do stick around, -- well it looks like they need to reroll the RS.

Not that I can get technical with you Klas, but if a unit wishes to move to a new hex in its MPh, must roll at the start of it's Mph
Not necessarily.

E1.53:
"At the start of its MPh, each onboard ground unit or stack wishing to move to a new hex in that MPh [EXC: 1.531] must first make a Movement DR (Δ)...."

I.e., if one of the conditions/exceptions in rule E1.531 applies in the hex I start in, I do not have to make a Movement DR. E.g., I am on a road and move only along road hexes - no need for a Movement DR at all then.

E1.531:
" A unit or stack that, at the start of its MPh, wishes to enter a sewer/tunnel, or move within the same hex or along a TB, or can see a Known enemy unit, or is currently on or ADJACENT to a trench/bunker/road/path/gully/stream/river bank or Illuminated Location, does not make a Movement DR until such time as it is no longer in or ADJACENT to such terrain (at which point it must immediately make a Movement DR if still moving)...."

query:
long range fire during AFPh: Is the FP halved TWICE?

thx 
Bill
title: long range fire during AFPh
raw_question:
Is the FP halved TWICE?

thx 
Bill
ground_truth_answer:
Is the FP halved TWICE?

Or even more, depending on the circumstances.

Any application of Area Fire (i.e., halved FP) is cumulative with any other application of Area Fire.

So: if your unit is a Passenger on a truck, is pinned, is firing in the AFPh, at long range, and the truck is in Motion, and the target is concealed, your FP is divided by 64!

A funny little fact about Assault Fire: it can only apply when the target is within normal range, but aside from that, if you qualify, then your minimum FP will be 2, no matter how many times you are halved.  The reason is that after all halving is applied, the result (which will be a number > 0, even if it's only a tiny fraction) is FRU (to at least 1) and then you add 1.  So: minimum of 2 FP -- even if your unit is a Passenger on a truck, is pinned, is firing in the AFPh, and the truck is in Motion, and the target is concealed -- but NOT at long range.

ground_truth_answer:
what you have to understand is that units in CREST status are in a very specific position close to that side of the hex that is higher than the level IN the hex. 

if they move out of the hex on the other side, they first go down INTO the hex to then go up the other side to exit it which results in much more movement within the same hex, while units IN the hex already start down there so it takes them less movement.

also, while thus changing position, those units in CREST status do so in the view of the enemy, while units IN the hex are generally out of sight.

compared to a building, the units are expected to start their movement in the middle of the hex so again there is no extra movement from the side of the hex to the middle of the hex.

query:
Tank trying to overrun and go HD on slope at the same time.: This cropped up during a game yesterday - an AFV on a level 1 hill moved into the slope hex of the hill and wanted to try to go hull down but was also attempting to overrun an infantry squad (already broken) in the same hex.

How does this work through - is it possible? Does the AFV spend the HD manoeuvre MF's before the overrun or after? Does it get HD (if successful) against defensive fire it takes in the hex?

Thanks.
title: Tank trying to overrun and go HD on slope at the same time.
raw_question:
This cropped up during a game yesterday - an AFV on a level 1 hill moved into the slope hex of the hill and wanted to try to go hull down but was also attempting to overrun an infantry squad (already broken) in the same hex.

How does this work through - is it possible? Does the AFV spend the HD manoeuvre MF's before the overrun or after? Does it get HD (if successful) against defensive fire it takes in the hex?

Thanks.
ground_truth_answer:
I was wondering if I was missing something, and thought that these would be discrete, separate expenditures, until I had a closer look:

There are four things happening as the AFV enters the hex:

* It's expending MP to enter the Location.

* It's expending MP to perform an OVR.

Per D7.1, these are a combined expenditure, unless all of the enemy units in the hex are unknown (A12.41) (which was obviously not the case here, since the enemy unit was broken).

* It's expending 2 additional MP to perform a HD Maneuver attempt.

D4.22 makes it clear that these are spent as additional MP when entering the Location.  So it's actually combined with the above.

* Finally it's expending a MP to stop (if able) (required by the HD Maneuver attempt).  This is definitely a discrete, separate expenditure, but doesn't answer the question of the timing of the other events.

Since all Defensive First Fire must await the outcome of the HD attempt, and the resolution of the OVR must await the outcome of any DFF attacks, and the MP for the HD attempt and the OVR are simultaneous with the entry of the hex, then it seems to me that the rules are crystal clear: roll for the HD attempt, resolve any DFF attacks, resolve the OVR (which as noted, will still happen even if the vehicle has been eliminated; D7.11).  Then, finally, assuming the vehicle has not already been immobilised, it expends a MP to stop.  If it still has MP available, it must then expend them either in Delay or further movement. and ends its MPh.

I don't see any need for a Q to MMP.  The situation is a little convoluted, but it doesn't throw up any questions that the rules can't already answer.

Note that if the enemy unit was unknown, the sequence would be different.  The entry of the Location and the HD attempt are still a combined expenditure, and are still resolved first (because of the no-DFF-until-HD-attempt-completed rule).  Then the enemy unit must either drop its concealment voluntarily or take a PAATC (unless exempt) (because that's done instantly per A12.41; I guess that means it must happen before any DFF).  Then the vehicle must expend the Stop MP (D4.22 says it's immediate), and only then (after any DFF provoked by the Stop MP) does it decide whether it will declare an OVR or not (and if so, that is then a separate MP expenditure, which of course may provoke further DFF).

title: Throwing Smoke from Bypass on board 3

ground_truth_answer:
In playing Gavin's Take on Board 3, a US elite infantry unit is bypassing the woods in J2 (on the hex side next to the hill).  Can it place smoke in K3 while bypassing the woods?  Or does the woods depiction in the middle of the hex block the ability to throw the smoke into the adjacent location (K3)?

The answers you've received about the LOS requirement are correct (assuming that the statement about SMOKE placement requiring ADJACENT is correct; I'm NRBH, so cannot confirm; see below).  However, when posing questions like this, it helps considerably for you to be precise with the details.  There are two hexsides "next to the hill" in hex J2, and the answer to your question is different depending on which hexside(s) you're talking about.

If you're bypassing only the I2/J2 hexside, then the answers already posted are correct; at no point does the squad have LOS to K3, and thus cannot attempt to place SMOKE in that hex.

If you're bypassing only the I3/J2 hexside, OR if you're bypassing both hexsides, then the squad does have a LOS to K3, from the I3-J2-J3 vertex.  Thus, it is ADJACENT and can attempt to place the SMOKE.

Now, all of that being said: do you actually require ADJACENT Locations?  Certainly not always, as you can place SMOKE from an upper Level building Location (or across a Cliff hexside) to an adjacent (but not ADJACENT) Location.  It depends on the exact wording of the rules.
If it turns out the rule does NOT require ADJACENT, then the whole question of LOS becomes moot.
