query: What changed from 1st Edition?: The question is exactly what it says on the tin. I might be getting my hands on a 1st Edition rulebook and would like to know if I will have any problems playing an opponent with a later edition. In other words, are there significant innovations I have missed?
title: What changed from 1st Edition?
raw_question: The question is exactly what it says on the tin. I might be getting my hands on a 1st Edition rulebook and would like to know if I will have any problems playing an opponent with a later edition. In other words, are there significant innovations I have missed?
ground_truth_answer:
IIRC, the only thing that really changed is the Human Wave rules. 

Technically they changed in the errata pages originally included in Doomed Battalions -- but that didn't predate the 2nd ed. rules by very much.

The 2nd ed. rules attempted (and almost succeeded) to include every official Q&A that had been published up until that point.  (A couple were missed by accident, and have been added to 2nd ed. via errata; one or two were deliberately omitted because it was decided to overturn them.)

In addition, an unknown (but quite large) number of additional changes were made because of unofficial Q&A (that had not previously been published widely, if at all), as well as some improvement in the rules language here and there.

The most "obvious" changes were moving the Collateral Attacks rule from Chapter A (where it confused new players) to Chapter D (where it makes more sense); improved Wall Advantage/Bocage rules; and the additions of Chapters E and K (and dropping of Chapter N).  Some sections got new/better Examples.  The IIFT was added as an official option, and the OBA and OVR flowcharts were added.  There were several new/improved charts and tables added to the rules dividers.

To answer the original question: the game still played fundamentally the same, but there are some detail differences here and there.  Every now and again you might trip up on something specific but mostly you'd never notice.  That being said: there is no reason to go out and spend money on a used copy of 1st edition.  That money would be better invested in a copy of the 2nd ed. rules (the Pocket version, at the very least).

title: MGs and FF, SFF, FPF
raw_question:
I am not sure if I understand the rules for machine guns (MGs) and first fire (FF), subsequent first fire (SFF) and final protective fire (FPF).

I believe a MG that is NOT marked FF can continue to fire at moving targets with full fire power (FP) until it fails a rate of fire (ROF) roll, even if its manning squad is marked FF. As soon as it fails the ROF roll, it too is marked FF. True?

I believe a MG MUST fire with the squad that mans it if the squad chooses to SFF or FPF. It would fire at half FP and would be considered sustained fire. True?

I believe a MG CANNOT fire alone for SFF or FPF. It only takes part in SFF or FPF if the squad that mans it is firing. True?

Any other subtleties I might be missing?

Thanks!
ground_truth_answer:
Full squad with MG fire MG only in the first fire phase at a target that is two hexes away.
MG is marked with FF, but not the squad.

Q1.Can the squad FF at a target more than two hexes away?

Yes. To count as SFF the unit/weapon (either SW or inherent FP) has to be already marked with a first-fire counter [A8.3]. Unless the MG cowered the inherent FP would still be unmarked. The counters that come with Beyond Valor aren't sophisticated enough to make this distinction. Players often put the MG to the side and mark it alone to indicate the current state. Later modules come with "SW first fire" & "Inherent first fire" counters. Later versions of Armies of Oblivion have them. Despite not having a perfect system for marking a squad and MG firing separately, the squad may use its inherent FP (or a second MG, or a second ordnance SW) as first fire at any range otherwise allowed.

Q2.If the squad did not FF, I assume that in the SFF, it can on,y fire at adjacent target as the MG is marked with
An FF counter?

Once a unit/weapon is marked with a first fire counter and using SFF, the unit/weapon can fire at any target in normal range and no farther than any Known enemy unit [A8.3]. That might be adjacent, but in your example (as far as you have stated) the target for SFF would have to be at range less-than-or-equal-to two hexes.

Comment: I am not 100% sure what you mean by, "in the SFF." I assumed you meant, "as SFF," i.e. during the enemy MPh. It is possible you are asking about the DFPh instead. If so there is still no restriction on the use of the inherent FP of the squad as long as it is not marked. If it is marked with first fire, it can only fire at ADJACENT targets [A8.4].

query:
Hazardous movement for manhandling a gun: when does it stop?: Manhandling a gun is a hazardous movement. Hazardous movement applies a -2 DRM to fire on the manhandling unit. At which moment does the DRM ceases to apply?

The A4.62 rules say that the manhandling unit receives a -2 DRM to any fire attack regardless of fire phase until it is pinned. 

Also, the C11.3 EX makes clear that a unit firing during the DFPh on a gun that has been manhandled during the previous MPh still applies the -2 DRM as Case O.

ASL SK EP#1 rules go further to say "[...] any fire attack directed at it that player turn regardless of fire phase [...]". Note that it is said explicitly that the -2 applies during the whole player turn.

Now, searching on the Internet I've found some GS threads that settle on the contrary, that the -2 applies only during the manhandling unit's own MPh and no further. That is based on a 2003 Q&A from Perry that says that the -2 DRM for manhandling applies only during its MPh, no further.

The Index adds no information to the description of Hazardous Movement, and there are no changes on these particular rules from the 1st Ed rules.

Now, what is your take on this? When does the Hazardous Movement penalty ceases to apply to units that have Manhandled a Gun?
title: Hazardous movement for manhandling a gun: when does it stop?
raw_question:
Manhandling a gun is a hazardous movement. Hazardous movement applies a -2 DRM to fire on the manhandling unit. At which moment does the DRM ceases to apply?

The A4.62 rules say that the manhandling unit receives a -2 DRM to any fire attack regardless of fire phase until it is pinned. 

Also, the C11.3 EX makes clear that a unit firing during the DFPh on a gun that has been manhandled during the previous MPh still applies the -2 DRM as Case O.

ASL SK EP#1 rules go further to say "[...] any fire attack directed at it that player turn regardless of fire phase [...]". Note that it is said explicitly that the -2 applies during the whole player turn.

Now, searching on the Internet I've found some GS threads that settle on the contrary, that the -2 applies only during the manhandling unit's own MPh and no further. That is based on a 2003 Q&A from Perry that says that the -2 DRM for manhandling applies only during its MPh, no further.

The Index adds no information to the description of Hazardous Movement, and there are no changes on these particular rules from the 1st Ed rules.

Now, what is your take on this? When does the Hazardous Movement penalty ceases to apply to units that have Manhandled a Gun?
ground_truth_answer:
Solid and interesting reasoning, but why ignore A4.62, which clearly delineates that pushing a gun results in hazardous movement (HM), hence application of the -2 DRM, regardless of fire phase? That much seems very clear. A4.62 does not stipulate that any of the listed activities are exempt in other fire phases...other than whence pinned. Now, pin status is removed at the end of the player turn, giving us a hint that HM DRM goes away only at the end of the player turn, not the end of a unit's MPh.

I agree that the HM DRM applies regardless of phase, but only while a unit is so engaged. Perhaps it is worth posting the entire Q&A in order to provide more context.

A4.62, A23.7, B8.3, B21.41, B23.41, B24.7 & C10.3
Q. Do all Clearance attempts receive the Hazardous Movement penalty until the Clearance DR is made?
A. The appropriate Clearance attempts do.

Q. Does Pushing a Gun (C10.3), Setting a DC, or Crew exiting a Cellar (B23.41) receive the Hazardous Movement penalty only
during the applicable MPh?
A. Yes.

Q. Does the Hazardous Movement penalty apply to Sewer Movement and Fording as long as the unit is in that terrain?
A. Yes.

Is it your suggestion that E.2 be invoked, so that C10.3 supersedes A4.62?

No. Unless a unit is actually "engaged" in a dangerous activity that warrants the application of the HM DRM, the DRM is NA. 

Pushing a Gun, Setting a DC, and exiting a destroyed vehicle are special cases. The latter can occur during any phase in which the vehicle is destroyed (including falling into a cellar), hence the stipulation in A4.62 that the HM DRM can any apply "regardless of fire phase." (Note the wording. The rule does not specify that the HM DRM applies in any/all fire phases, only that it applies "to any attacks against units so engaged [in HM] regardless of fire phase.")

I also agree, for example, that a unit that Sets a DC is only subject to the HM DRM during its MPh.

23.7 SET DEMOLITION: A DC which is neither Placed nor Thrown is considered a Set DC and has special advantages and requirements. A Set DC is one which has been Set prior to play by SSR, or which was Set and declared during play by an Infantry unit which spent all of its MF (using Hazardous Movement) to Set the DC in its Location during its MPh and made a dr ≤ its US# (subject to leadership drm by any leader assisting the unit to Set the DC) without being pinned or broken.

The problem seems to be unclear language in reference to the sequence of play; the rulebook indicates 'engagement' in activity, also, 'having just pushed.'

Agreed. Some rule sections such as C10.3 could use a clarification. Others, already make it quite clear that the HM DRM only applies during a specific time period. Take, for instance, paratroops, which are only subject to this DRM during DFF, i.e. when they are considered to be Aerial targets.

9.3 DEFENSIVE FIRST FIRE: After the Drift of all parachutes has been resolved, the DEFENDER may use Defensive First Fire and Subsequent First Fire vs them—even if they have drifted offboard (9.41). Aerial paratroops are subject to Hazardous Movement DRM, and can claim neither Height Advantage, TEM, concealment (9.11), nor any Hindrance other than LV/SMOKE (E.6). Hazardous Movement DRM even apply to an attack (only) on an Aerial SW in an attempt to destroy/malfunction it (A9.74) although such attacks will usually be caused by mistaken identity due to Random Selection.

Putting a labor status marker could indicated ongoing 'engagement' until it is pinned by fire. There is nothing in the rulebook exempting that interpretation because the rulebook does not define 'engagement' -- at least not anywhere I have found so far. Not that I have gone over it with a fine-tooth comb, but nothing in my ASOP (not sure which version it is other than 'rev') explains when the HM DRM goes away.

Which brings us back to the Q&A above, and which helps delineate when HM ends wrt A23.7, B23.41*, and C10.3.

*FWIW, my version of B23.41 includes this info.

23.41 CELLARS:...If the AFV rolls an Original 6 on the colored dr of the Bog Check DR, the AFV has fallen through the floor to the cellar and is removed. Should the AFV crew survive, it is automatically placed at ground level subject to Hazardous Movement for any subsequent fire during that phase (D5.6).

query: Concealment placement during setup: Just when I think I have it, I don't.  In Commando Schenke the Russians set up first out of sight of Germans and have OB designated ? counter to put on.  Now the German sets up (I assuming out of sight of opponent) on board.  Does he get to place ? counters on his units in concealment terrain that are out of LOS before Russian player gets to look at the board?
title: Concealment placement during setup
raw_question: Just when I think I have it, I don't.  In Commando Schenke the Russians set up first out of sight of Germans and have OB designated ? counter to put on.  Now the German sets up (I assuming out of sight of opponent) on board.  Does he get to place ? counters on his units in concealment terrain that are out of LOS before Russian player gets to look at the board?
ground_truth_answer:
I thought units under ? counters are not considered, "known enemy units" and therefore do not prevent ? counter gain.

You are correct that they are not "known enemy units".  However, "known" is not a requirement for preventing concealment gain.

It's worth spending a little time studying the Concealment Gain/Loss Table.  It will tell you many things that the text of the rules barely mention (or sometimes don't even mention at all).

The core rule to remember is that "unbroken unit" is sufficient to DENY GAIN, but "Good Order" is required to CAUSE LOSS.  Thus dummies can stop you from becoming concealed, but your opponent has to reveal a real unit to make you lose concealment that you already have.

The other important thing to remember is to note the difference between "Concealment Terrain" and all other types of terrain.  Just because a hex has positive TEM does not make it "Concealment Terrain" (e.g., graveyards).  Only the terrain types listed in red on the Terrain Chart are Concealment Terrain.

Note also the different effects of long range (> 16 hexes).  Your infantry can become concealed at long ranges even if someone has LOS to them.  They can also move without losing concealment if the only LOS to them is long-range.

Emplaced Guns (and their crews) have their own special rules about concealment loss, of course.  Vehicles, in general, don't keep concealment very easily, and are not that good at getting it either.  It is often not even worth the effort of rolling to see if a vehicle gets concealed when it's out of LOS -- if it's not in Concealment Terrain, it will lose the concealment as soon as an enemy unit has LOS to it (at any range).  Also remember that (with a very few unusual exceptions) PRC keep or lose concealment per their vehicle.

Finally, probably the number one concealment rule most frequently played incorrectly: if you are provided with "?" counters in your OB, these counters can ONLY be placed in Concealment Terrain -- regardless of whether they are being used to conceal a real unit, or being used to create a dummy stack.  Again, just having positive TEM, or being completely out of enemy LOS is not good enough: it MUST be Concealment Terrain.  Remember that this rule ONLY APPLIES to "?" counters supplied in the OB.

query:
Regarding the CA rules: Before formulating a question to MMP regarding the following rules problem I wanted to hear your opinions.

Rule C3.2 defines the Covered Arc (CA). In the rules text it is obvious that the hex of the vehicle (or gun) is not included in the CA. This is also consistent with legacy rules from the Squad Leader system (SL 29.4) and ASLSK#2 and ASLSK#3 rules.

There is however an example text under the illustration in C3.2 that is ambiguous (should it be regarded as an exception rather than an example?). Added to this there is a Q/A in J1 that clearly states that a gun's own hex IS included in the CA.

Note that several other rules will depend on how CA is defined. Here are a few:
A11.62
C5.51
D3.1, 3.11 and 3.12
D1.81 (with errata in J7) and 1.82
title: Regarding the CA rules
raw_question:
Before formulating a question to MMP regarding the following rules problem I wanted to hear your opinions.

Rule C3.2 defines the Covered Arc (CA). In the rules text it is obvious that the hex of the vehicle (or gun) is not included in the CA. This is also consistent with legacy rules from the Squad Leader system (SL 29.4) and ASLSK#2 and ASLSK#3 rules.

There is however an example text under the illustration in C3.2 that is ambiguous (should it be regarded as an exception rather than an example?). Added to this there is a Q/A in J1 that clearly states that a gun's own hex IS included in the CA.

Note that several other rules will depend on how CA is defined. Here are a few:
A11.62
C5.51
D3.1, 3.11 and 3.12
D1.81 (with errata in J7) and 1.82
ground_truth_answer:
The C3.2 example is not ambiguous; it's clear the Gun's own hex includes the CA. The example also clarifies that during the Movement Phase, a vehicle enters the CA only through the two relevant hexsides. 

There is nothing in the rules stating that the text of an example is not part of the alphanumeric rule  -- as far as I am aware. Cite me a rule number that states that! :) I would concur that it's not good form for an important rule interpretation to be found in an example; but it all fairness, the example is embedded into the structure of C3.2. 

It's the incorrect assumption that such text is not part of the rules that leads to what appears to be a rules problem. 

A11.62 is not relevant to defining CA because E.2 applies to the definition of the CA being formed by the higher alpha-numeric rule C3.2 and there is no specific exception to C3.2 in A11.62.

C5.52 supports the example in C3.2 by referring to C3.2 as the fundamental rule for CA.

D3.1 referes to C3.2 as defining CA.

D1.81 and 1.82 refer to special conditions of covered arc known as VCA and TCA, which are still defined under the auspices of C3.2; that is, no exceptions to C3.2 are stipulated or overwritten by these rules.

Thanks for everyone's consideration.
title: Vehicle in Melee
raw_question:
Lets say you have a Sherman in Melee w/a German 4-6-8.  Rules say the 468 is held in Melee but a mobile vehicle is never "held" in melee.  Does that mean the Sherman can TPBF the 468 in Prep or Defensive Fire while the 468 needs to wait for CC??  

Thanks for everyone's consideration.
ground_truth_answer:
That may be a good idea. But first I would like some help listing all the cases when same hex fire could be an issue.

The cases that come to my mind are:
- Berserk units entering the tank's (or gun's) hex in the MPh
- A tank entering another unit's hex during the Mph
- Any unit still in the tank's (or gun's) hex during Prep Fire or Defensive Fire
- Close combat

A lot of rules affect these cases. Any help listing them would also be appreciated.

I think a more simple question would be: when/if is a Gun's/vehicle's own Location within its weapon's CA.

Is that not what you think C3.2 is unclear about ?

But it seems it has already been asked before, old official Q&A on the matter:

C3.2 & D1.81-.2, D8.5 Can a Gun fire in its own hex (i.e., is its own hex considered in its CA)? Do the same principles apply to BMG/CMG?
A. Yes; except during the MPh if the hex is entered from outside the CA, when, even if the moving target now expends MP for some other
purpose (e.g., firing sD or stopping and unloading Passengers), the Gun would still have to turn its CA to include the direction from which the hex was entered, or if the bow-mounted weapon of an Immobile vehicle (D8.5). Yes.

ground_truth_answer:
Is a broken unit in a building that previously lost DM put back under DM when a flame in it's hex becomes a blaze?
I think so yes, since only DM units can rout, IIRC.

ASOP, Step 6.11B
"...Place DM counter on each non-DM unit/stack that must rout (A10.62)."
We went with the section in B25.4 that says that units which are unable to voluntarily break (which would include already broken units)may move during their rout phase into an accessible location just as if withdrawing from melee. 

Although it seemed odd to have a broken unit move at all without going back under DM. The ASOP you quoted certainly overrides when combined with A10.4 which says that broken units cannot move in any way except to rout or to withdraw from CC. 

So the broken unit must "leave" the blaze location but he can only leave by routing per A10.4 and the ASOP says that units that must rout go back under DM. Problem solved :) Though a bit convoluted.

My gaming associate and I played our first game of Rising Sun the other day and had a few questions. 

1. Paths. So this seems like an easy one but the scenario stated that all roads were to be treated as paths. The only real difference between roads and paths is line of sight, yes? For example you could shoot down a road but due to the winding nature of a path that doesn't apply.
You still thread LOS as normal.  If the art allows the shot, the LOS is good, even though the LOS is along a Path.  Use of Path movement rate incurs no FFMO risk, though, because the zero-TEM Path portion is not Open Ground.  G.1.

EDIT:  No, the Path art in Dense Jungle is in fact Jungle terrain (and TEM) as per application of B13.6.  As Dense Jungle is Inherent terrain, I suppose you may not trace LOS through it's Path art any more than you could trace LOS along an Open-Ground land hexside.  (Re Light Jungle, I think you could trace LOS down a Path, though.)

2nd EDIT:  It occurred to me later that there can be no LOS down a Path at all.  B13.6 says Path art is Woods (usually).  A Woods is an LOS obstacle.  So, no down-Path LOS, and I was twice wrong today.  Sorry for leading any reader down a bad Path, earlier.

And is it possible to move into a path hex but remain in the woods/jungle along the path and not lose TEM?
Versus D1F, if not moving at the Path rate, then the non-Path TEM would apply.

2. Berserk units. We had a Japanese squad go berserk under FPF from the Marines. So the Japanese unit gains additional MF, can move into the occupied hex in the Mph, then TPBF and engage in H2H?
Correct.

3. And finally, mortar placement in the PTO. We were playing Cibik's Ridge, and had a hell of a time trying to figure out where to place our mortars. Since dense jungle prohibits mortar fire, even on paths, and the jungle blocks line of sight, how do you work around the mortar's minimum firing range? My Japanese light mortars had some success in pinning Marines but they were fired from practically point blank in the open. My opponent couldn't figure out where to place his Marine mortars so they practically went to waste. 

Looks like a tough problem.  Note that use of C9.31 Spotted Fire would effectively shave one hex off MTR Minimum Range.  The penalty is offset a bit by the SSR-granted Bore Sighting for eligible US weapons.  HTH.

ground_truth_answer:
Yes it can. There are two contiguous hexsides in AA7 and AA8 each, which is normal 1MF bypass. (If for example the unit would start movement from BB6 and bypass AA7 and AA8 to AA9, it would have to pay 2MFs for AA7, because that bypass would exceed the two contiguous hexsides rule.)

Forcing rout: I'll rephrase the questions in my previous thread, since I'm a little bit wiser now:

1. Does an adjacent, broken, known enemy unit force a broken unit to rout?

2. Does a pinned, known enemy unit which has one of your broken units in open ground within it's LOS and normal range force it to rout?

Regarding the first question, the rules seem to me to say no, but there's a Q&A from rule 10.5 about what happens when to broken units are adjacent to each other, and whether or not the defender has to rout after the attacker routs away first. If broken units don't force routs, this shouldn't even be a question.

Regarding the second question, the rules in 10.5 (routing) and 10.62 (DM) refer to 10.532 (interdictor) when they mention normal range. Also, the starter kit rules state clearly that it is units which could interdict your broken unit which force it to rout, and a pinned unit (or a unit with any other halving or positive DRM) can't interdict.

I think the answer is 'no' to both questions, but the rules seem a bit vague on the second question. It should be stated clearly in 10.5 and 10.62 that units must be able to interdict to force non-adjacent units to rout, or to give them DM. This is not stated clearly in the flowchart on routing I found on the Texas-ASL site either. A possible 'interdictor' is more than an unbroken enemy unit which has your unit in LOS and normal range. If the answer is 'yes' to the second question, then the flowchart is very clear.

ground_truth_answer:
checking the rules A10.5;
"a broken unit cannot remain in an open ground hex within LOS and normal range of a known non-melee enemy unit, nor may it END its routphase adjacent to a known enemy unit that is both unbroken and armed"

so, for open ground purposes a "known enemy unit" is sufficient to force it to rout (so even broken units and pinned units can force it to rout).
while for "adjacent" purposes, it must be a known,unbroken armed unit that would cause failure to rout" (ending the rout phase adjacent to a broken or unarmed unit does not cause failure to rout)
broken units of both sides can remain adjacent to each other as long as they are both not in open ground.

to be able to inderdict, a unit must be able to fire with at least 1FP into the routing unit's open ground hex at normal range ( with either inherent FP or any sw) and may not be affected by any form of area fire, regardless whether the unit has already exhausted all of its firing options for the turn.
given that a pinned unit halves its fire, it cannot interdict.

the reference to 10.532 is only to indicate how "normal range" is determined/defined, so while a pinned unit cannot interdict, it still has a normal range.

the rules often differentiate many situations as such; the possible threat of being fired upon is sufficient to affect enemy units (instill fear) in some way, while only actual fire will cause casualty losses. so a pinned unit can threaten broken units but doesnt cause actual losses

'During the RtPh a broken unit not in Melee may not end a RtPh adjacent to or in the same location as an unbroken Known Enemy Unit and may not remain in the same Open Ground location in the normal range and LOS of a Known Good Order enemy unit that would be able to interdict it if it were routing in that hex.'

But I guess that this could mean 'able to interdict unless prevented because of having halved FP or positive DRM'. After all, the rule says 'Good Order enemy unit', which should include pinned units, etc. I don't think there is supposed to be different interpretations of rules in starter kits and full ASL, it's just that full ASL has more rules.

I guess this means the Texas-ASL flowchart is correct, which is nice to know, since it gives a good summary in case I forget something again.

Not sure about this. What about this? If a pinned unit is the interdictor, then Open Ground is not invoked per 10.531. That rule is very specific how Open Ground is defined in this case. Even if the pinned unit is in normal range (by itself or with a SW), as far as the routing unit is concerned, it's not in open ground because the pinned unit cannot interdict.

I don't have time to check if the comprehensive routing example covers this situation.

What is marked with Prep Fire?

John

The correct answer during Prep Fire (PFPh) has been mentioned above and applies similarly to Defensive Fire (DFPh).

However, the multifarious affect of random selection and cowering is more pronounced during Defensive First Fire (MPh):

'A' is marked with a first fire counter (but not the LMG as yet since it may retain ROF). 

'B' is marked with Final Fire and if it also possessed an LMG, then that weapon  would also be marked with Final Fire. 

Residual firepower in the target hex would be reduced for the cowering (and likely even more if a conscript/green unit B was the cowered) and would not include the firepower of the LMG belonging to 'A' (unless ROF were forfeited).

After that, there are different ramifications for SFF, FPF, TBPF, etc. for each unit depending on marked fire status -- as the ATTACKER  continues his MPh.

Hidden unit attacks AFV in open ground: Hi folks,

Let's say my hidden squad with an ATR advances into CC with an AFV in open ground after passing his PAATC. Is he eligible for an ambush? He loses concealment for advancing into open ground, but does that happen before or after the ambush opportunity?

Let's assume both the squad and the AFV survived CC. Now the squad is trapped in melee and can't use his ATR at any point during the turn unless the AFV chooses to leave the hex. The AFV is not trapped in melee, but must fire all its weapons at the squad, unless it wants to leave the hex and risk being shot in the rear by the ATR. Is this correct?

If the AFV fires its MGs using TPBF and eliminates the squad, can it then fire its MA outside the hex?

Thanks for your help!

              --David H.
title: Hidden unit attacks AFV in open ground
raw_question:
Hi folks,

Let's say my hidden squad with an ATR advances into CC with an AFV in open ground after passing his PAATC. Is he eligible for an ambush? He loses concealment for advancing into open ground, but does that happen before or after the ambush opportunity?

Let's assume both the squad and the AFV survived CC. Now the squad is trapped in melee and can't use his ATR at any point during the turn unless the AFV chooses to leave the hex. The AFV is not trapped in melee, but must fire all its weapons at the squad, unless it wants to leave the hex and risk being shot in the rear by the ATR. Is this correct?

If the AFV fires its MGs using TPBF and eliminates the squad, can it then fire its MA outside the hex?

Thanks for your help!

              --David H.
ground_truth_answer:
Before he advances anywhere, your HIP unit is placed on board, concealed.  He then advances into an open ground hex in the LOS of an enemy unit (the tank!) which causes him to lose concealment (unless some other condition permits him to keep concealment, e.g., winter camouflage).  So with no concealment on either side, there is no possibility of ambush.

If the AFV is Stopped, then yes, the squad is held in Melee, and cannot use his ATR.  Note that the Melee condition is removed as soon as the vehicle is non-Stopped (not "leaves the hex").  However, with an ATR, the squad would probably be better off waiting until the AFV has left the hex before taking the shot (because of the Case E penalty).

You have the vehicle's choices essentially correct: it is not held in Melee, but cannot fire at any target outside of its own hex so long as the enemy unit is still there.  If it eliminates the squad with MG fire, then yes, the MA could fire at a different target.

(2) Sighting TC vs. a dug-in tank

Is a dug-in tank considered a vehicular target for purposes of a sighting TC? Typically, armored cupolas are represented by smaller turret counters, so I was wondering if that might change the answer.

According to E7.421, a near-miss vs. an AFV results in the Basic TK# being halved, although cases A and B (C7.21-7.22) still apply. My question is: do cases A and B apply before or after the TK# is halved? According to C7.23, for a CH, the TK# is doubled before modifiers, so I was wondering if the near-miss case should be treated similarly. Unfortunately, the rule is unclear to me as written.

(4) Recall

As far as I can tell, the only way a Stuka gets recalled is on an original sighting TC of 12. Otherwise, once they enter, I'm stuck dealing with them until the end of the scenario unless I can shoot them down with AA fire (of which I have very little). Is that correct?

(1) If the factory hex is roofed, then the Stuka has no LOS to the interior hex.  If the factory hex is roofless, then there is a LOS.

ground_truth_answer:
Here are the most useful rules paragraphs.

A4.4 PORTAGE: A SW may not move by itself; it must be carried or placed on a vehicle by Infantry/Cavalry at some cost to the latter's MF allotment. The various SW portage costs are listed on each SW counter in the form "#PP". Portage cost is assessed per item carried, not distance traveled; even if a unit carries a SW during only one MF expenditure before dropping it, that unit may not recoup the portage cost used for that SW for use in the remainder of its MPh. Otherwise, an unbroken Infantry unit can pick up and drop items at any point in its move provided it has sufficient MF to do so (subject to 4.431 & 4.44). No item can be portaged more than once per phase except as allowed by combined Infantry and vehicle portage within a single phase.

A4.42 INHERENT PORTAGE CAPACITY (IPC): A MMC has an IPC of three PP, and a SMC has an IPC of one PP.5 An Infantry unit loses one MF for each PP carried in excess of its IPC. A SMC may never portage more than two PP although one SMC can add its IPC to that of any one Good Order Infantry unit to increase the IPC of the latter, provided the two units start the phase together and move together as a stack. Otherwise, Infantry units may not combine their IPC. A broken unit may not portage anything in excess of its IPC (see 10.4) even if accompanied by a leader.

A4.52 PORTAGE EFFECTS: CX Infantry have an IPC one < normal. Each PP carried in excess of this reduced IPC is deducted directly from their increased MF allotment.

  	
EX: A squad carrying four PP has > a squad's IPC. However, if that squad Double Times, its MF allotment is increased to four (4 MF + 2 MF  - 2 MF [2 PP > CX IPC] = 4).

  	
EX: A HS carrying five PP has only two MF; if accompanied by a leader, they would have five MF (4.12, 4.42). If the HS (only) Double Times with the leader, they have six MF. However, if the leader also Double Times, then they have only five MF.

title: Casualty reduction vs broken squad

ground_truth_answer:
1. When a squad suffers casualty reduction it must still take the morale check, right? It says 'other squads' in the rules, but then it also says 'any just-reduced HS'.

2. If the squad which suffers casualty reduction was already broken, then fails the morale check, is it then casualty reduced again, i.e. eliminated?

Correct.

Situation 1 - unbroken squad suffers a k/2.  It is immediately reduced to an unbroken half-squad, and that half-squad takes a 2MC.  If that half-squad breaks, it remains on-board under a DM counter.

Situation 2 - broken squad suffers a k/2.  It is immediately reduced to a broken half-squad, and that half-squad takes a 2MC.  If that half-squad breaks, it is removed from the map (breaking twice = eliminated).

Hope that helps!

Case B & C gives me a headache: I can't get a handle on how or why the Firer-based hit determination DRM Case B & C works. 

CASE B; FIRE IN AFPh: All ordinance which did not enter their current hex during that Player Turn (Only during the MPH?) and are not using OP fire are subject to Case B.

So if you didn't move during the MPH there's a penalty?  Why?

CASE C; BOUNDING FIRER: A vehicle which HAS (Emphasis mine) entered a new hex during its MPH but does not fire until its AFPh is using Bounding Fire and always uses Case C DRM (i.e. it must add the +2 DRM of Case B to the...(Is this an example or an addition?) applicable Gun Type DRM of Case C) as Bounding Fire Fire for shot it takes.

Can you see why I find all this confusing?  One thing it seems to say is B is one case, but if you're C you're also B even though the conditions of having moved is different.

title: Case B & C gives me a headache
raw_question:
I can't get a handle on how or why the Firer-based hit determination DRM Case B & C works. 

CASE B; FIRE IN AFPh: All ordinance which did not enter their current hex during that Player Turn (Only during the MPH?) and are not using OP fire are subject to Case B.

So if you didn't move during the MPH there's a penalty?  Why?

CASE C; BOUNDING FIRER: A vehicle which HAS (Emphasis mine) entered a new hex during its MPH but does not fire until its AFPh is using Bounding Fire and always uses Case C DRM (i.e. it must add the +2 DRM of Case B to the...(Is this an example or an addition?) applicable Gun Type DRM of Case C) as Bounding Fire Fire for shot it takes.

Can you see why I find all this confusing?  One thing it seems to say is B is one case, but if you're C you're also B even though the conditions of having moved is different.

Can anyone make sense of this for me?
ground_truth_answer:
If they haven't moved that turn and they have an op fire token on them neither B nor C apply.

D3.3 Vehicles cannot opportunity fire. they can bounding fire.

Yes it is confusing, and annoying, but in the end it makes sense.

Case B. If your vehicle has not moved or fired that turn, but all of a sudden you want to fire in the AFPh, that is +2 TH. Why is there a penalty? Because other moving friendly units may have forced the enemy to expose themselves, but you don't have as much time to fire if you had prep fire. 

Case C. If you do move, then you are stuck with Case B (+2 for firing in the advance Fire phase, as usually the case, all modifiers are cumulative), plus an additional penalty for moving around, usually +2 for a turreted tank, and +3 for a NT, so total +4 or +5. This is the usual case. The best way to mitigate that, is to move to point blank range, and get an additional -2, to reduce those heavy modifiers. 

Very rarely you might have a stabilized gun. Like in 2 scenarios out of 1000. Then the total is +3. 

Basically the idea is to fire your tanks while not moving, esp at infantry, but sometimes bounding fire the tanks at enemy vehicles in the AFPh or even the MPh is a very good idea esp if the enemy is locked into place having already fired on you as you approach. 

hope this helps.

query: Off boared artillery advanced squad leader: It seems to me that it is better to call down OBA during the Def Phase VS the Prep phase. title: Off boared artillery advanced squad leader
raw_question: It seems to me that it is better to call down OBA during the Def Phase VS the Prep phase. If done in the Prep phase, enemy has a chance to move during their own movement phase. If called down during Def Phase, the FFE1 is resolved during the enemy prep phase and no chance of movement. Correct?
ground_truth_answer:
Prep Fire Phase OBA is best time to use SMOKE to significantly hinder the enemy fire for two fire phases and moderately so for another two (second ATTACKER game turn). This allows attacking troops to close with a dangerous enemy position. Not only that, the FFE can be cancelled in the next ATTACKER fire phase to make ready for a new FFE draw, with the possibility to land elsewhere one phase sooner. 

Often anything less than 120mm isn't going to much affect enemy in buildings or entrenchments as much as the attacker would like with a standard FFE, so better is use of SMOKE.

Def Fire Phase OBA is not as effective for laying a SMOKE. To get decent smoke, such an FFE is better to land in the Prep Fire Phase. 

So, as you say, DFPh is a better time to torch FFE to disrupt an enemy concentration for a back to back pounding in DF and Prep. Could be a good time to bring down Rocket FFE for maximum pounding (hoping it won't drift on top of your own stacks!)

Harassing Fire is mentioned above. Harassing Fire OBA is good to lay down in Prep, in order to block enemy attacker movement -- on their turn -- through and within the zone of effect, as they try to come to grips with the defender. This won't work as well if used in the Prep fire phase, although there will be an FFE C lurking around anyway if Harassing Fire is brought down then. However, if the Attacker has good cover on the way in, Harassing fire can be a waste of black card.

Hovering SR is a good tactic as suggested. esp with a bad ammo card hand and/or scarce ammo; once the atty comes down, could be tough to get that next black cbit draw.

I'm sure there are more ideas. Unmentioned are the best times to lay down barrages. I would think Prep to lay down a nice smokescreen.

Cloaking loss at night: My buddy, Bill, and I are starting the Edson's Ridge campaign game. He's the Marines on Hill 100 and I'm the cloaked Japanese moving thru light and dense jungle to take the hill (hai!).  

Bill has sent up some starshells to light up the area during Japanese movement.  1 or 2 of my groups has reached the edge of the woods, is illuminated and has taken fire.  Our question is whether a cloaked group moving into an illuminated hex loses cloaking even though the enemy has no LOS into the hex. 

(E1.31 LOSS: An Infantry unit loses Cloaking/"?" at night if it uses Non-Assault Movement in a Location that is already Illuminated when that unit expends MF in it. Otherwise, it does not lose Cloaking/"?" at night when moving/advancing.)

There no mention of enemy LOS into the hex when the unit moves. Bill believes it's implied but I'm taking it more literally and say I lose cloaking.  I'd rather not but rules are rules.  Help!
title: Cloaking loss at night
raw_question:
My buddy, Bill, and I are starting the Edson's Ridge campaign game. He's the Marines on Hill 100 and I'm the cloaked Japanese moving thru light and dense jungle to take the hill (hai!).  

Bill has sent up some starshells to light up the area during Japanese movement.  1 or 2 of my groups has reached the edge of the woods, is illuminated and has taken fire.  Our question is whether a cloaked group moving into an illuminated hex loses cloaking even though the enemy has no LOS into the hex. 

(E1.31 LOSS: An Infantry unit loses Cloaking/"?" at night if it uses Non-Assault Movement in a Location that is already Illuminated when that unit expends MF in it. Otherwise, it does not lose Cloaking/"?" at night when moving/advancing.)

There no mention of enemy LOS into the hex when the unit moves. Bill believes it's implied but I'm taking it more literally and say I lose cloaking.  I'd rather not but rules are rules.  Help!
ground_truth_answer:
Personally, I think it is more or less clear that the intention of E1.31, is that there needs to be an enemy unit in LOS - otherwise Concealment would be lost easier at Night, and I have a hard time seeing that, that is the intention of the rule.

Chapter E is, unfortunately, not the best written chapter in the ASL rulebook.

If the ASLRB were to be associated with interpretation of poorly clarified intentions, I'd be happy with your remarks as closure to the issue. 

That may be is true of many more poorly developed wargames, but has not been the norm in ASL over the years. People are asking questions because they want clarity; e.g., the OP opened this topic for that reason. Perhaps the OP is indeed satisfied with the interpretations, but that won't prevent another OP from asking these same question(s) due to lack of rules clarity. 

Most people, but not all it seems, would agree that rulebooks should be about clarity of how to play, not about intentions or interpretations of what should be done in a given instance. Ambiguous situations are resolved with rules re-writes in serious games (e.g. the National Football League rules of play).  

Apparently some here are happy with admittedly brilliant interpretations of the intentions of the night rules in ASL, then stick with such positions as being sufficient (perhaps with a pat on the back) ... 

rather than possibly admit some change is needed.

The interpretations look to be accurate; regardless, A12.121 contradicts itself and E1.31 is poorly written. 

Are we to end on that 'triumphant' recognition of Chapter E -- as if we are newly seized with some stunning realization that we don't already know about the dubious writing therein? 

Do people want a set of night rules that are contradictory and incomplete regarding concealment/cloak loss? 

Or do people want it fixed properly with some errata adjustments? Clearly this is where I stand.

Try these on then take a whack at them:

12.121 CONCEALMENT LOSS/GAIN TABLE: The specific situations that allow"?" gain (or cause "?" loss) are given in the Concealment Table [EXC: Night (E1.3)]. ...  ... The Concealment Table always takes precedence over the body of the rules (EXC: E1.31, moving Infantry concealment loss occurs in  more restrictive circumstances than indicated; other uncommon causes e.g., an uncommon cause] of "?" loss might be mentioned in the Concealment Table even though it is omitted from the rules proper for the sake of brevity)."

{Note: the specific change for night looks awkward because of the insistence on referring to the concealment table as an additional 'rules body.' It's a bit puzzling speaking of 'brevity' in the written rules for ASL (in itself a haha)  -- this is the first rules mistake about concealment, to have done so -- as the rules should always clarify the contents of any tables, not the other way around}

1.31 LOSS: An Infantry unit loses Cloaking/"?" at night if it uses Non-Assault Movement in a Location that is already illuminated (in the LOS of a Good Order Enemy ground unit as per the concealment loss/gain table) when that unit expends MF in it, or if it enters an enemy-occupied Location during the MPh. Otherwise, it does not lose Cloaking/"?" at night when moving/advancing.

title: Human Wave example in Rule Book: Understanding Range
raw_question:
I have a question on the Human Wave example in the rule book (page A53, my version ©2014). I’m having trouble understanding Range. 

The example says that the “units that entered N1 and O2 are marked with a Range counter since they increased the range to the HW alternate Hex Grain…” It looks to me that after they move they stayed the same range from the HW alternate Hex Grain of P1-P2-PO3-O4 – the unit in P1 moving to O2 is one hex away and staying one hex away from the HW alternate Hex Grain of P1-P2-PO3-O4, and the unit in O1 moving to N1 is two hexes away and remaining 2 hexes away. To my eyes, the unit in R2 moving to Q5 is in the same Range from the HW alternate Hex Grain as the unit in P1, but it doesn’t get marked. 

Any help grasping Range?
ground_truth_answer:
In the example given the Alternate Hex Grain selected is P1-P2-O3-O4.

The unit that starts out in P1 is 0(zero) hexes off the Alternate Hex Grain since it is sitting in P1 which partly makes up the Hex Grain. When he moves to O2 he increased his range from the Hex Grain to 1. So he is marked with a Range Counter.

Similarly the unit starting in O1 began the human wave 1 hex off the Alternate hex grain since O1 is one hex away from P1. When he moved to N1 he increased his range to 2 so he is marked with Range Counter. 

Your confusion seems to be from imagining that the Alternate Hex Grain is made up partly of the hexspines between hexes. But it's not. It is a series of four full hexes in this example.

Size and weight of support weapons, ordnance, and vehicles is factored throughout the rules. The PP ranking for s/w accounts for the weight as well as other factors in moving and prepping the weapon to fire. For ordnance, the QSU feature and Manhandling also have reflect to some degree the weight.

I suspect the OP is regarding the fact that the bridge and ice collapsing rules ignore the weight of personnel, ammo and guns and only factor in vehicle weights.

Consider this example: a squad moves in Open Ground for four hexes during its MPh. Then on its APh it advances in a bamboo hex one level higher.

I don't really find this to be absurd at all. In both examples, once you climbed up the hill through the bamboo you were so exhausted you were essentially done for the turn. The fact that, in one example, you had an easy walk on the flat before the exhausting bamboo does not change the fact that the uphill bamboo is totally exhausting and ends your movement. 

In both cases you end your turn CX. In both cases you can't move further after going uphill into the bamboo. 

That being said, it's far the best to not get too bound up in making reality based arguments against the workings of your boardgames. It will never end and it will impact your enjoyment. It's all just a very rough abstraction designed to support challenging and fun game play.

Offboard AA against Gliders: I'm playing through scenario 93 (Tavronitis Bridge) right now. One of the SSRs is that the British get 2 free AA shots against the incoming German gliders. I'm a bit confused with the AA-against-gliders rules, and want to make sure I'm doing things right.

First, I use the * column on the IFT. So, if the SSR says I get a "4 FP attack", would that mean I use the *4/30mm/2FP column? Or the *5/37mm/4FP column?

Next, the rules seem to indicate that I compare my result with the * number on the glider counter. But... the German glider has a * number of 1? I'm not entirely sure how I could possibly hit it? Or do I use the IFT result (e.g. KIA, K/, etc.)?

I'm confused. Thanks in advance for any guidance!
title: Offboard AA against Gliders
raw_question:
I'm playing through scenario 93 (Tavronitis Bridge) right now. One of the SSRs is that the British get 2 free AA shots against the incoming German gliders. I'm a bit confused with the AA-against-gliders rules, and want to make sure I'm doing things right.

First, I use the * column on the IFT. So, if the SSR says I get a "4 FP attack", would that mean I use the *4/30mm/2FP column? Or the *5/37mm/4FP column?

Next, the rules seem to indicate that I compare my result with the * number on the glider counter. But... the German glider has a * number of 1? I'm not entirely sure how I could possibly hit it? Or do I use the IFT result (e.g. KIA, K/, etc.)?

I'm confused. Thanks in advance for any guidance!
ground_truth_answer:
IIRC, gliders are attacked using the *-row on the IFT, exactly as if they were unarmored trucks.

The number in the star in the glider counter is a positive DRM to this attack. 

So, in your scenario, you have two 4FP attacks. The number in the *-row of the IFT is 5, and since you have a +1DRM (due to the number in the star in the counter), gliders are damaged on a 4 and destroyed on a 3. Also, 4 and 5 force evasive action.

Hope this helps. Enjoy the scenario, it's really fun!

"to have a professional tech writer review the rulebook"

Don't pin your hopes on a "tech writer". The ones I have met, they are paid based on volume, not accuracy. 

And before I get beat about the head and shoulders, I am sure there are some out there that have to met accuracy standards, but I have never met one.

McK

Well, since this would be an independent contractor situation, the metric of quality would be whatever MMP chose to use. The writing in the ASL rulebook can be improved for clarity without being simplified.  E.g., B23.22 -- it currently reads in part, "a multi-hex building which contains no stairwell symbol is considered a 1-1/2 level obstacle to LOS despite also having another vertical level in each hex besides the ground level in the form of a level 1 capacity." query: SPW 251/21: This halftrack (Veh. Note 66.1) has a puzzling note. Three TK DR are made on the MG column (TK 4) as opposed to the 20L table I would expect to use (TK 6). Why is this the case?
title: SPW 251/21
raw_question: This halftrack (Veh. Note 66.1) has a puzzling note. Three TK DR are made on the MG column (TK 4) as opposed to the 20L table I would expect to use (TK 6). Why is this the case?
ground_truth_answer:
This halftrack (Veh. Note 66.1) has a puzzling note. Three TK DR are made on the MG column (TK 4) as opposed to the 20L table I would expect to use (TK 6). Why is this the case?

Mark,

A proper answer to this question probably requires input from an armorer, but from the ultimate source, Wikipedia:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MG_151_cannon

Production of the MG 151 in its original 15 mm calibre format began in 1940. After combat evaluation of the 15 mm cartridge as the main armament of earlyMesserschmitt Bf 109F-2 fighters, the cannon was redesigned as the 20 mm MG 151/20 in 1941 to fire a 20 mm cartridge. Combat experience showed that a more powerful explosive shell was preferable to a higher projectile velocity. The MG 151/20 cartridge was created by expanding the neck of the cartridge to hold the larger explosive shell used in the MG FF cannon, and shortening the length of the cartridge case holding the longer 20 mm shell to match the overall length of the original 15 mm cartridge. These measures simplified conversion of the 15 mm to the 20 mm MG 151/20 simply by changing the barrel and making other small modifications. A disadvantage of the simplified conversion was reduction of projectile muzzle velocity from 850 metres per second (2,800 ft/s) for the 15 mm shell to 700 metres per second (2,300 ft/s) for the larger and heavier 20 mm shell. With an AP projectile the new 20mm cartridge could only penetrate around 10-12mm of armor at 300m and at 60 degrees, compared to 18mm penetration for its 15mm predecessor in the same conditions, but this was not seen as a significant limitation. The 20 mm version thus became the standard inboard cannon for the Bf 109F-4 series onwards. The 20 mm MG 151/20 offered more predictable trajectory, longer range and higher impact velocity than the 580 metres per second (1,900 ft/s) cartridge of the earlier MG FF cannon. The MG FF was retained for flexible, wing and upward firing Schräge Musik mounts to the end of the war.

Still, it would seem that even with a reduced penetration capability, maybe a TK=5 would be more appropriate as this is the 15mm/12.7 TK column.

Bill

title: Walls, hedges, wall advantage--my head hurts
raw_question:
I'm a SL player from the early 80s who got ASLSK#1 last year and futzed around with it a little.  I decided to go whole hog and a buddy and I have jumped into ASL feet first.  I'm a dedicated rules reader and have also watched a number of instructional videos from Russ, idjester and Joe Steadman.  But I'm struggling with B9.  I have trouble telling when a shot is blocked or simply a TEM and I really don't understand wall advantage.  

Can anyone point me to what they think is the best training--written or video--that might clear this up for me?
ground_truth_answer:
Note that when a positive inhex TEM is applicable, WA can be chosen or not (thus forfeiting the in hex TEM or not):
B9.31 The wall/hedge TEM is not cumulative with positive TEM of other terrain in that hex, although it is cumulative with LOS Hindrances and SMOKE. A target unit claiming WA (9.32) does not receive in-hex TEM [EXC: Runway (7.3); Air Bursts (9.34)], but receives wall/hedge TEM if applicable [EXC: it may elect instead to receive appropriate TEM for Emplacement or for a friendly AFV with which it shares WA (D9.3)].

But if in OG, WA is mandatory :
B9.323 MANDATORY WA: A unit unable to claim in-hex TEM of at least +1 must claim WA as soon as possible (even if having in-hex Hindrance), and cannot voluntarily forfeit it. Neither Emplacement, Gun-shield, Height Advantage, nor a friendly AFV with WA are considered to provide an in-hex TEM for this purpose. A "Wall Advan" counter is not necessary in this case, unless there is an enemy unit sharing one or more of the unit's wall/hedge hexsides.
I personally like to mark such units nevertheless, just to make it easier when a situation implies the WA to be contested.

Note that a vehicle which is HD behind a wall/bocage can claim either the Q TH DRM (i.e. TEM) or the HD status at the moment it is fired upon :

D4.2 ...A HD target may not also claim a Case Q TH DRM but it may claim a Case Q TH DRM in lieu of HD status.

Chapter T, Tarawa, 22 pages
Chapter V, Valor of the Guards, 36 pages
Chapter Z, Other Campaigns, 86 pages
Chapter FB, Festung Budapest, 54 pages
Chapter dividers are 2-6 pages for each chapter

A few comments regarding each chapter:

Index: The index actually contains some definitions and rules that are important, but you don't need to memorise it.

Chapter A, Basic Rules: As with most of the core chapters you don't need to read all of chapter A to play ASL. Some rules are only applicable to specific scenarios (cavalry will not be in every scenario for example). A few rules are optional.

Chapter B, Terrain: This chapter should probably be treated as a glossary - you only need to know the rules for the terrain that is on the maps of the scenario you are playing.

Chapter C, Ordnace: Again you only need to read what is relevant (off board artillery is not in every scenario for example).

Chapter D, Vehicles: Only applicable for scenarios with vehicles in them. 

Chapter E, Miscellaneous: This chapter is labelled as optional. It has rules for rare situations (like scenarios with aircraft or night scenarios).

Chapter F, North Africa: Only applicable for scenarios set in North Africa (the desert).

Chapter G, Pacific: Only applicable for scenarios set in the Pacific theatre.

Chapter H, Vehicle and ordnance notes: Conatins some rules pertaining to specific vehicles and guns, but mostly historical notes. Should be used as a reference and only consulted to determine specific rules for equipment used in the scenario at hand.

Chapter I, Campaign game - never published

Chapter J, Deluxe ASL: This chapter was actually 4 pages in the first edition if memory serves. It actually has one rule that is implemented in some of the campaign games (hth close combat).

Chapter K, Training manual: This was the first attempt at a simple way to learn ASL. This chapter is mostly superceded by the Starter Kits, but can be a fun read nevertheless.

Chapter L, Online ASL - never published

Chapter M, ASL Analysis - never published: A few old Generals had a series of articles which apparently were intended to be developed into this chapter, but that never happened.

Chapter N, Armory: This is just a list of all counters from all modules. This chapter is only published as a pdf.

Chapter O, Red Barricades: A campaign game (a BRILLIANT campaign game). The rules are only relevant to the campaign and the associated scenarios.

Chapter P, Kampfgruppe Peiper: Similar to chapter O.

Chapter Q, Pegasus Bridge: Similar to chapter O.

Chapter R, A Bridge too Far: Similar to chapter O.

Chapter S, Solitaire: Solitaire ASL is almost a completely separate game. 

Chapter T, Tarawa: Similar to chapter O.

Chapter V, Valor of the Guards: Similar to chapter O.

Chapter Z, Other Campaigns: This chapter collects the rules for a number of smaller campaign games that don't have their own chapters.

Chapter FB, Festung Budapest: Similar to chapter O.

All in all, even if the game has 1000 pages of rules, I think you would be able to play some basic scenarios after only reading 20 to 30 pages. If you want to add ordnance you would probably need to read a further 20 and perhaps another 20 for the vehicle rules. This means that only about 5-10% of all the rules are important to know in order to play vast amounts of scenarios. The remaining 90% of rules can be treated as something you look up when you need it for a specific scenario.

query:
The ★ Vehicle Line: You are shooting a MMG at a Truck, perform a RTC (Rules Task Check), dig around in the MG rules and all A9.6 says is "...otherwise it is resolved on the ★ Vehicle line...". You look up "★", "Vehicle line" and "Star Vehicle line" in the Index and find nothing. If you continue to Search the Index, you will find "Unarmored" is (somewhat) synonymous with ★, but there is no reverse citation.

The ★ Vehicle Line is the row of horizontal numbers on the IFT (or IIFT) underneath the FP row (confusingly displayed as DR/FP, where DR refers to the column of Dice Roll (DR) results and FP refers to the horizontal row of numbers). This ★ Vehicle Line can be read in a somewhat similar fashion to the Close Combat Table, with a Burning Wreck for a DR less than half this number, elimination for a DR less than this number and immobilization for a DR equal to this number. There is also a maximum number of vehicles that can be eliminated on the ★ Vehicle Line; a RTC can be performed for the (odd) situation of more than one vehicle unit in the hex. 

Rules citing the ★ Vehicle Line include A7.308, A7.309, A9.6, A9.61, A13.511 (Cavalry), D6.7 and E7.511; D15.5 (Motorcycles) - ★ Vehicle Line NA.

I was fortunate enough to persuade MMP to include "Pivot" in the 2nd Edition ASLRB; I'll lobby for "★ Vehicle Line" should there be another edition.

Dismounting Cavalry: What exactly are the penalties for dismounting cavalry riders (I'm sure FFNAM applies) that dismounted at the start of their MPh in an OG hex? Are the dismounting cavalry riders governed like unloading from a vehicle (D6.5)? Does any First Fire effect the now unmounted horse counter as well?

title: Dismounting Cavalry
raw_question:
What exactly are the penalties for dismounting cavalry riders (I'm sure FFNAM applies) that dismounted at the start of their MPh in an OG hex? Are the dismounting cavalry riders governed like unloading from a vehicle (D6.5)? Does any First Fire effect the now unmounted horse counter as well?
Thanks in advance! :)
ground_truth_answer:
Cavalry spends MF instead of MP, so dismounting cavalry units just spend the required 1 MF to dismount and go on.

It's not allowed to use Assault Movement when dismounting (or riding), so FFNAM will apply.

If there's D1F against a unit that has just dismounted, fire will affect both the (now) Infantry and the unmounted horses at the same time, as usual when firing on the IFT. See A13.511 for the details on the attacked horses. Basically, they are treated like unarmored vehicles.

query: SW Recovery & Concealment Loss: It doesn't say in the rules, or on the Concealment Loss/Gain table, but does a unit attempting SW recovery lose its concealment? Thanks again!

raw_question: It doesn't say in the rules, or on the Concealment Loss/Gain table, but does a unit attempting SW recovery lose its concealment? Thanks again!
ground_truth_answer:
Yes

See "C" in the Loss/Gain Chart  - since recovery is "Any other action" and it not one of the excepted ones, it loses conceal if less than or equal to 16 hexes in LOS of a GOOD ORDER enemy unit.

C If it engages in any other action [EXC: using a radio/field phone; Spotting; taking a PAATC (and Leader DRM applied to such a PAATC) not caused by a vehicle entering its Location; SW/Gun repair attempts]; e.g., attempts to entrench, kindle a Fire, Deploy, Recombine, make a Sniper/PF/MOL/ATMM Check, rally a broken unit, apply Leader DRM [EXC: PAATC; Armour Leader],use Clearance, place SMOKE grenades/DC, etc.

A10.531 Open Ground: For purposes of rout determination, Dash, concealment gain/loss, and Interdiction, an Open Ground hex is any hex in which any Interdictor could apply, during a hypothetical Defensive First Fire opportunity (regardless of what attacks it actually made in previous phases), the -1 FFMO DRM.

All same-level Direct Fire and spotting attempts traced through (not just into or out of ) an effective LOS Hindrance hex are modified by a +1 DRM to either the IFT or To Hit DR, or the Artillery Initial Accuracy dr. E3.1 Low Visibility (LV):...A LV Hindrance [EXC: Fog] is treated exactly like a LOS Hindrance except that a LV Hindrance DRM is cumulative with other Hindrances regardless of range and does not by itself negate the FFMO DRM or Interdiction, or affect the placement of (or attack by) Residual FP (A8.26), or prevent concealment loss [EXC: Winter Camouflage].

query:
Cavalry, break, bail out...: Imagine a cavalry unit. For some reason or another, it must make a MC. It fails the MC and breaks. Per A13.51, the horse counter is removed. Also per A13.51, the infantry unit must "Bail Out(D6.24)" and must immediately make an other MC.

title: Cavalry, break, bail out...
raw_question:
Imagine a cavalry unit. For some reason or another, it must make a MC. It fails the MC and breaks. Per A13.51, the horse counter is removed. Also per A13.51, the infantry unit must "Bail Out(D6.24)" and must immediately make an other MC.

Regardless of the outcome of this MC, any SW carried by that unit is removed. (D6.24)

Is this correct? Is there anything else to consider?
ground_truth_answer:
Here is the rule that mentions Cavalry double time:

A13.36 GALLOP: Cavalry may increase its MF allotment by eight (to 20) by declaring a Gallop at the start of its MPh, or by four by declaring a Gallop during its MPh, and placing a CX counter on the Horse counter [EXC: Gallop declaration is NA while in a marsh, deep stream, or ford-able Water Obstacle, or if the Cavalry/Horse is currently CX].

Note the exception that I underlined.

Then, in the Advanced Sequence Of Play, Movement Phase, article 3.22A you can read "Cavalry may declare Gallop for 8 extra MF unless Cavalry is CX)".

Part of A4.51 states when to remove a CX counter:

A unit's CX counter is removed if the unit breaks; or in its next Player Turn as soon as it: has completed all of its Prep Fire, or is designated as an Opportunity Firer, or moves (unless due to a Minimum Move or Deep Stream Entry it becomes CX again), or becomes TI; or at the conclusion of its next MPh -- whichever comes first. A CX counter is removed at the start of a MPh and does not affect that unit during that MPh other than prohibiting its use of Double Time during that MPh.

title: About Slopes...
raw_question:
Hi everybody,
I'm focusing on Slopes rules, since I own several historical modules involving these.
Even if I'm not a very experienced ASL player, so maybe I'd just better shut up, I must say that I'm a bit puzzled about these rules.
First of all, if the main reason for their introduction is to counteract the "plateau effect", I don't think the goal is reached.
After all, I think the Alpine Hill Option provided by standard rules may reveal much more effective.

Also, look at this example taken from "Slopes in ASL" article by Chas Smith:

Well, this seems to me a very unrealistic situation.
We see that L2 is higher than M2 (3/4 of level higher), but at the same time, it is lower than L1 (say 3/4 of level lower). Intuitively, I would think that L1 is 1,5 levels higher than M2, but it's not: it's at the same level.

ground_truth_answer:
You are correct in a purely logical sense. L2 can't be both lower than L1 and higher than M2 if L1 and M2 are level with each other. 

But this is only true if you conceptualize all the hexes as perfectly flat hex shaped segments of separate terrain. In reality the terrain would be undulating, ridged and irregular and, in a general sense, these areas could have this kind of a relation to each other. 

My advice is to not analysis ASL too much. It's a great game that's surprisingly fun and rewarding to play and has a great community. But if you start picking at the rules and attempting to apply a lot of logical analysis you will just drive yourself nuts. 

Don't question the inconsistencies... just play and SHUT UP!! :D

query:
Green or Conscript: Hi,
    I know you can tell if a MMC is a Conscript by the "C",  but I was wondering.  Do all nationalities have Green Units(how can you tell on the counter) as well as Conscripts?

Thanks for the help, :)
E Burden
turks1966
title: Green or Conscript
raw_question:
Hi,
    I know you can tell if a MMC is a Conscript by the "C",  but I was wondering.  Do all nationalities have Green Units(how can you tell on the counter) as well as Conscripts?

Thanks for the help, :)
E Burden
turks1966
ground_truth_answer:
When HP is published the Finns will have both types.

Personally I've always wondered why the Allied Minors have Green instead of Conscripts.

I thought it was because the Allied Minors were overrun too quickly to have significant numbers of true "conscripts" in the sense of impressed troops, penal units, and other types of either unwilling and/or untrained troops.  Allied Minor green units I thought typically represented reservists, military cadets, or police units, i.e., troops with some training and mostly recruited voluntarily.

Conscription is a method of recruiting, it doesn't mean lack of motivation, will or training. I think most of the countries in WW2 had a conscription system, at least Finland had (and still has) universal conscription.

In ASL green, conscript, 1st line, etc. status is just a way to have some differences between untried, veteran and unmotivated/untrained troops.

An enemy hero is held in melee in the same hex as a stopped friendly AFV.

It's the MPh and a friendly MMC moves into the above hex to infantry OVR the hero. The hero presumably cannot defensive first fire as he is held in melee.

title: Infantry OVR against unit already in melee

ground_truth_answer:
The AFV has no effect on the Infantry OVR.

And note that since the SMC is already in Melee, it does not have the option to enter an Accessible Location.

~Rob
title: SW/Cowering
raw_question:
The rules say any MMC that cowers has a Final Fire marker immediately placed over the light mortar/crew. My question is: Does that Mortar actually fire, or no? Thanks,
~Rob
ground_truth_answer:
Just to step back here ... doesn't the rule state that a Final Fire marker is placed on a LIGHT mortar?  And then, what is the definition of a LIGHT mortar?
See C9.2:
"...Any mortar ≤ 60mm is a light mortar and is treated as a SW because it is on a ½" counter...."

The Cowering rule (A7.9) says:
"...In addition, any unit that cowers (as well as all of its SW/Guns regardless of whether it was using its inherent FP) is automatically marked with a Final or Prep Fire counter as appropriate...."

It doesn't really say the red part today, but it probably should to be complete.

1) To see behind an obstacle the firer has to be one level higher than the obstacle (i.e. a wood hex on level 0 is a level 1 obstacle and you have to be on level 2 to see past it).

4) There is an additional blind hex for every full five hexes the firer is away from the obstacle.

6) There is one less blind hex for every level the firer is higher than he has to be to look over the obstacle, to a minimum of 1. (i.e. if you are 7 hexes away from a wood on level 0, and you are on level 2, behind the wood are two blind hexes. If you climb to level 3, there is only one blind hex)

title: Beginners question about LOS and blind hexes
raw_question:
I have difficulties parsing the rules for LOS and blind hexes (english is not my first language). So did I get this right?
1) To see behind an obstacle the firer has to be one level higher than the obstacle (i.e. a wood hex on level 0 is a level 1 obstacle and you have to be on level 2 to see past it).
2) Even if the firer is higher, there are blind hexes behind the obstacle that are not in LOS.
3) Normally, there is one blind hex behind an obstacle.
4) There is an additional blind hex for every full five hexes the firer is away from the obstacle.
5) There is an additional blind hex for every level that the obstacle is higher than necessary to be an obstacle. (i.e. a level 2 obstacle has two blind hexes behind it, if those hexes are level 0)
6) There is one less blind hex for every level the firer is higher than he has to be to look over the obstacle, to a minimum of 1. (i.e. if you are 7 hexes away from a wood on level 0, and you are on level 2, behind the wood are two blind hexes. If you climb to level 3, there is only one blind hex)
7) This all is somehow different for hill crest line.
ground_truth_answer:
1) To see behind an obstacle the firer has to be one level higher than the obstacle (i.e. a wood hex on level 0 is a level 1 obstacle and you have to be on level 2 to see past it).
You just have to be higher - not necessarily a full level higher. A 1/2-level higher will do. So e.g., being on level 1.5 is enough see past a level 1 woods.

A6.4:
"...unit is at an elevation > the height equivalent of any intervening full level obstacle..."

2) Even if the firer is higher, there are blind hexes behind the obstacle that are not in LOS.
Correct.

3) Normally, there is one blind hex behind an obstacle.
Behind an obstacle that is 1 level high, that is correct.

4) There is an additional blind hex for every full five hexes the firer is away from the obstacle.
Correct. 5-9 - 1 extra Blind hex, 10-14, 2 extra, etc.

5) There is an additional blind hex for every level that the obstacle is higher than necessary to be an obstacle. (i.e. a level 2 obstacle has two blind hexes behind it, if those hexes are level 0)
Correct, though I would not call it an "extra" Blind hex - more like a normal (per A6.4) Blind hex.

6) There is one less blind hex for every level the firer is higher than he has to be to look over the obstacle, to a minimum of 1. (i.e. if you are 7 hexes away from a wood on level 0, and you are on level 2, behind the wood are two blind hexes. If you climb to level 3, there is only one blind hex)
Pretty much.

7) This all is somehow different for hill crest line.
Yes, there are some differences.

Thanks to Wu Wei and Klas for this nice summary of q&A:D

ground_truth_answer:
Hello All.  Say I have a German squad with a MMG in a level 2 bldg , that has a FF counter on it.  The Americans have a concealed half squad 6 hexes away that moves using assault movement into a open hex that is a level 2 hill and behind a bocage hexside, they then claim wall advantage.   The Germans have a LOS to this hex which is 5 hexes away. I want to shoot at the American squad using SFF. Is the fire halved for SFF and then halved again for concealment(for being behind Bocage ) and then with a DRM of +2 for Bocage  ? Am new to ASL and just starting out.  Hope this question has not been asked before.  Have I played this right? Thanking all who reply. 

Tommy - the bocage grants a +2 DRM as you note, but it does not automatically grant concealment status.  **IF** the unit was already concealed when it moved behind the bocage (and was otherwise out of LOS for its entire move) THEN it does in fact retain concealment (even if it used non-assault movement).  If it wasn't, it won't gain concealment until the CCPh and then only if it remains where all LOS to it is through a bocage hex side.

In answer to your question, yes, your unit will be halved for SFF* and halved again **IF** the target started concealed and never lost concealment during its move. Further, no, the -1 FFMO would not apply to the shot since it's being traced through a hex side that gives a positive DRM.  If it weren't assault moving, however, it would be subject to FFNAM (combined with the bocage TEM).

Bocage is a little twitchy, but it's a fun terrain in which to fight.

-N

*RE: SFF - be sure there aren't other KEUs closer than the target.  If there are, they can't fire at the unit behind the bocage anyway - always restricted to the nearest/equidistant target with SFF.

ground_truth_answer:
Robin & Luke are right.

The answer to your question though ..

C6.4 talks about boresighting LOCATION

Location (in the index) defined as: 
"a hex as well as any of the following sub-divisions of that hex: sewer, upper or lower building or bridge level, pillbox, cave"

Note also that under C6.41
"Bore Sighting may be used only by a Scenario Defender (see Index)"
Scenario Defender defined as: 
"The Scenario Defender is the side that sets up wholly or partly on-board and does not have to capture terrain (on other than its setup board) in order to fulfill its Victory Conditions, while facing an opposing side that enters wholly from offboard."

ie.. if the both sides start onboard, no one gets to boresight.

Regards, 
Jack

query:
Portage Points and Passengers: OK, So I've read through the various bits of the rules, and it seems like this is one of those moments where the apparently exhaustive ASL manual doesn't actually specify something quite simple and important.

Do support weapons count against a transport's PP? IE if a halftrack can carry 15 PP, does an LMG of 1PP count against that 15?

Seems a bit dumb if a machine gun takes up more room than a leader counter...
title: Portage Points and Passengers
raw_question:
OK, So I've read through the various bits of the rules, and it seems like this is one of those moments where the apparently exhaustive ASL manual doesn't actually specify something quite simple and important.

Do support weapons count against a transport's PP? IE if a halftrack can carry 15 PP, does an LMG of 1PP count against that 15?

Seems a bit dumb if a machine gun takes up more room than a leader counter...
ground_truth_answer:
Thanks! You'd think in amongst all the exceptions in all the rules that refer to PP they could have just said "SW PP count against vehicle PP capacity."D6.1 : "Thus a vehicle with Transport Capacity can carry any combination of MMC/SW, provided the transport's PP capacity is not exceeded."
The word combination seems to clearly allude to the PP value of SWs and passengers being added one to the other.

6.2 : "therefore, a dm 76-82mm mortar is transported by Riders at its normal five PP cost." is an indirect allusion that the SW PP do count against the vehicle's PP capacity.

A4.4 PORTAGE: A SW may not move by itself; it must be carried or placed on a vehicle by Infantry/Cavalry at some cost to the latter's MF allotment. The various SW portage costs are listed on each SW counter in the form "#PP". SW PP are clearly linked to the fact that they can be placed on a vehicle.

I have a question.
At the end of B13.6, I read: "...a path has no other effect on a hex (i.e., inside the woods contour the path is woods; outside the contour it is not).".
Instead G.1 says: "No road exist (all brush-roads and woods-roads are Paths, with no Open Ground in the brush-/woods-road portion of those hexes;".

No. It means that in PTO, when LOS only goes through a road depiction in brush/woods, that portion of the LOS is not Open Ground. That road depiction is also not a road, but is instead a path.

Path depictions are always paths, and are identical in PTO and ETO.

Routing non-DM units: A situation came up in a current game of mine, where my opponent says I couldn't rout a unit without DM markers. Rule A10.5 says you may rout units which are DMd, but it does not mention units without DM markers. I was under the impression that all broken units may rout normally in the rtph. Have I missed a rule somewhere? 

Thanks.
title: Routing non-DM units
raw_question:

Rule A10.5 says you may rout units which are DMd, but it does not mention units without DM markers. I was under the impression that all broken units may rout normally in the rtph. ground_truth_answer:
See:

Rule A10.5 Routing: "A broken unit may rout if currently under DM."

Rule A10.6 Desperation Morale: "[EXC: A unit may opt to retain its DM status provided it is not in a woods/building/pillbox/trench so as to guarantee its ability to rout again in the next RtPh. If overstacked in a woods/building, it may also opt to retain its DM status]."

So only units under DM may rout.

I had a situation in which I had a broken unit in a woods hex under DM which failed to rally so it lost it's DM marker and was unable to rout in the subsequent rout phase unless fired on or an enemy unit moved adjacent thus putting it back under DM. It was likely that this unit would surrender so I took the risky measure of firing at it with my own men with a low FP shot - just enough to get  it back under DM and hopefully not CRing it. Well, it worked and the unit went under DM and I could rout it out of the woods in the next RtPh. :D

You cannot target your own units unless specifically allowed. See A7.4.
