query: Smoke on the Water: Can you place ordnance smoke on a bridge over a water obstacle?
title: Smoke on the Water
raw_question: Can you place ordnance smoke on a bridge over a water obstacle?
ground_truth_answer:
Can you place ordnance smoke on a bridge over a water obstacle?

If using the Area Target Type, No.  The game treats Ordnance SMOKE differently from Infantry SMOKE grenades.

C8.52 says to place Ordnance SMOKE at ground level.  In the case of a bridge over Water, that would be in Water, a place SMOKE may not be placed (A24.1).

There is this Q&A:
A24.8 & C8.52 C8.52 states that when using the Area Target Type, SMOKE ammunition is placed at ground level of the target hex hit. If placing SMOKE in a Gully hex with Area Target Type (Crest status is Level 0, IN the Depression is Level -1), is the SMOKE counter placed IN the Depression, to be at Level -1, with a two level Hindrance measured from -1? Or is the SMOKE counter placed at Crest status, to be at Level 0, with Hindrance measured from 0?
A. IN; from -1. 

Separately, HoB has ruled Ordnance SMOKE =may= be placed on a bridge in at least one of their game products.  Treat that as a special rule, if applicable.

Otherwise, the answer is No.

ground_truth_answer:
A few rules queries came up in our PTO game tonight, surrounding some Japanese units that went berserk.

A moving Japanese stack with a 10-1 leader, a crew, and a squad moved into a hex where there was already a Japanese squad which had completed its movement earlier in the MPh. Residual fire made the leader roll HOB and he went berserk. 

1. Did the non-moving squad have to make a NTC to see if it went berserk? (We thought yes: A15.41, and applied the leadership DRM to the NTC, but did not give the non-moving squad the +1 Morale bonus for being in the same stack as a moving leader.) 

No NTC was required because all (except those Immune to HoB) go Berserk automatically (G1.41, penultimate, points to A25.223).

2. It seemed to be impossible to mark the Japanese crew as Berserk in VASL-- is that right?

Yes, because a Crew is not susceptible to HoB.  A15.1, 3rd.

3. The moving Berserk units charged with the MF remaining from their new 8 MF allowance. But we thought the non-moving Berserk unit could not move as it had finished its MPh. Is that right?

Yes.

4. The moving Berserk units moved into the same hex as my American 6-6-7, and survived TPBF, and I survived the AFPh. Could I voluntary break in the RtPh, and rout the usual 6MF away through non-open ground?

Yes, because the 6-6-7 is in CC but not yet Melee, it may voluntarily break so as to rout away.  A10.41 & A10.5.  NB:  If you are going to voluntarily break, you must declare it at the beginning of the RtPh.  A10.41, 1st.

5. I didn't voluntary break, and the hex with the berserkers and my squad were joined by another Japanese squad Advancing in. Was it correct to roll for Ambush?

If otherwise applicable, Yes.  Note that the IJA player will suffer a pair of  adverse Ambush +1 drms owing to the presence of Lax Berserkers in his force.  Table A11.4, and Berserk are always Lax in CC (A15.432, last).

How do I resolve an IFT attack of 4 FP factors on an unarmed and unarmored truck, if the final DR is 6, NMC?

The 'star' vehicle number for this column is 5.

I am guessing that the truck takes the NMC, and if it fails it is abandoned with no crew counter.

Thanks,

John
ground_truth_answer:
A7.308 vs UNARMORED VEHICLES: All non-ordnance Direct Fire attacks vs unarmored vehicles/horse counters are resolved on the  Vehicle line of the IFT using the same IFT DR (after any applicable modification) for any Personnel target in the same Location. Unless using Defensive First Fire, non-ordnance attacks vs unarmored vehicles/horses affect all occupants of the Target Location including Infantry and other vehicles/horses which are present in the same Location [EXC: a vehicle in Bypass and out of the firer's LOS cannot be affected, nor can more vehicle/horse counters be affected by a DR than the highest KIA# of that column as randomly determined (e.g., a 6, 8 or 12 FP attack vs the  Vehicle Line could affect no more than three vehicles; a 2 or 4 FP attack could affect only two vehicles; a 1 FP attack could affect only one vehicle)]. If that Final DR is < the Kill Number listed for the IFT FP column used, the vehicle is eliminated [EXC: Unlikely Kill; 7.309]; if it equals the Kill Number, the vehicle is immobilized [EXC: if HD the vehicle is unaffected by an Immobilization result]; if the Final DR is ≤ half of the Kill Number, the vehicle is eliminated as a burning wreck and all of its PRC are eliminated. Otherwise, the PRC of an eliminated vehicle must check for survival (D5.6). The surviving PRC of an eliminated vehicle are not subject to further effects from that attack. However, the Vulnerable PRC of a vehicle that has not been eliminated may still be subject to a Collateral Attack (D.8).

So if the final DR is higher than the star number, there is no effect.

query:
Missing Rules for CH extension Panther Line: Hi everyone,
I just bought ASL Comp Panther Line from Critical Hit.
I noticed that Slope Hexsides rule are required (Rules O2, P3). I really don't have any idea of what these rules are and where to find them. Anybody can help me?
Thanks, really!!!!
title: Missing Rules for CH extension Panther Line
raw_question:
Hi everyone,
I just bought ASL Comp Panther Line from Critical Hit.
I noticed that Slope Hexsides rule are required (Rules O2, P3). I really don't have any idea of what these rules are and where to find them. Anybody can help me?
Thanks, really!!!!
ground_truth_answer:
3.1 A slope hexside5 represents an undulation in the terrain substantial enough to give an Up-Slope (3.2) unit a LOS advantage. On the PB map a slope hexside is represented by brown hash-marks along that hexside (EX: PBK5-L5). The entire hexside (inclusive of vertices) marked by a slope, but not the slope artwork itself, is considered part of that slope hexside.

  	
3.2 UP-SLOPE/DOWN-SLOPE: A Location whose hex contains one slope hexside is either Up-Slope or Down-Slope to LOS drawn across that hexside to or from that hex. If the slope lines are in the Location's hex, the Location is defined as being Down-Slope across that hexside; if the lines are in an adjacent hex along the hexside common to both hexes, the Location is Up-Slope across that hexside. A Location can be both Up- and Down-Slope across two different slope hexsides.

  	
3.3 LOS: Slopes are neither obstacles nor Hindrances.6 Being Up-Slope affects LOS only in that an Up-Slope Location is treated as being ¾ of a level higher than normal to LOS that begins or ends in that Location and crosses an Up-Slope hexside of that Location. Thus, barring other obstructions to LOS, an Up-Slope unit - even if not in a hill Crest-line hex - can trace a LOS across an Up-Slope hexside of its hex to a lower elevation (i.e., across a hill Crest Line) and/or over (B.4) obstacles and Hindrances whose topmost obstacle/Hindrance height is < the Up-Slope elevation of the viewing unit [EXC: entrenched LOS restrictions would still apply as per B9.21, as would wall/hedge TEM as per B9.31. Otherwise, being Up-Slope or Down-Slope itself has no effect on LOS (e.g., slopes are ignored if the LOS goes through their hex or along their hexside, and also when calculating an A6.41-.43 increase or decrease in the number of Blind Hexes caused by an intervening obstacle). Being Up-Slope itself can neither grant HA nor allow an Up-Slope unit to make a HD attempt. The presence of one slope hexside does not change the elevation of that hex's Base Level.

3.31 FIRE LANE: For the purposes of Fire Lane LOS/LOF drawn across one slope hexside, assume that the term "same-level" means "same-Base-Level". See also 3.42 and its example.

  	
3.4 COVER: A slope can, in certain instances, provide a +TEM (3.41) or a +DRM (3.42).

  	
3.41 DIRECT-FIRE TEM: Ground-level Infantry in a hex containing three (or two non-contiguous) Down-Slope hexsides may claim a +1 slope DRM vs Direct Fire [EXC: FT], provided the attack originates from a non-adjacent firer whose elevation advantage (if any) over that of the target is < the range of the attack and the attacker's LOS crosses one of the target hex's Down-Slope hexsides. (A.5 applies to a FG attack.) Slope TEM is Cumulative with no other +TEM [EXC: Mud/Deep-Snow TEM]). Being Up-Slope itself provides no TEM, does not negate the FFMO/FFNAM DRM, and does not affect Wall Advantage rules.

Moving Infantry in EE14 (assuming there is a LOS) would not receive the Slope DRM because CC12 is not Up-Slope to FF14, nor (for the same reason) would the slope DRM apply to lnfantry attacked by a Fire Lane Snap Shot at hexside DD14-EE14.

  	
3.5 ENTRY: A unit crossing if slope hexside that it is Down-Slope from is moving Up-Slope. A unit crossing a slope hexside that it is Up-Slope from is moving Down-Slope.

Infantry on skis would receive a ½-MF bonus for each Down-Slope hexside they cross (cumulative with any bonus received for moving to a lower elevation). Crossing a slope hexside while moving on a road does not negate the B3.4 MF road bonus.

  	
EX: See the 3.3 illustration. Looks like -3, as senseless as it seems. Unfortunately, E3.731 outranks B27.3 & B27.5. Instead of the +1 TEM, they should have gone with a one-IFT-column-shift-left, which is effectively a +1 TEM. Note that Sand halves HE IFT except for CH, which is doubled normally (F7.4).

query:
Heterodox routing - what do you think?: A recent thread on the facebook ASL list has made me question whether my understanding of the rout rules is at odds with orthodox interpretation.  In an effort to better isolate to what extent I may or may not be failing to grok the system, I have created several scenarios below.  Each scenario involves one broken squad attempting to rout.  

Do you agree with my interpretations or not?  Please indicate what you think happens, and why.  

Scenario 1 - "Crawling Cover"

Until today, I would have said the broken unit has two choices:
1) declare the woods in 33H7 its rout target and rout F5, G6, H6, H7, taking interdiction in F5, G6, and H6, or 
2) low crawl into low crawl to F5 without suffering interdiction.

After re-reading A10.5 today, I wonder though whether this sentence --
"A broken unit may end its RtPh in an Open Ground hex in the LOS and Normal Range of a Known enemy unit without Interdiction only if it has used Low Crawl (10.52) to increase the distance between itself and the nearest Known enemy unit during that RtPh" means that the broken unit either takes interdiction even if it chooses option 2) above or is not even allowed to choose option 2.  Thoughts?

Scenario 2 - "Shellholes or Potholes?"

SSR: 33E6, F6 and G6 contain shellholes.

I believe the broken unit in this case has essentially four options (although option 1 below seems pointless in light of option 2):

1) Rout directly to 33H7 via E6, F6, G6, paying the open ground 1MF cost in each, and suffer interdiction 3 times.  
2) Same as above, but pay the shellhole 2MF cost for one of E6, F6 or G6, and suffer interdiction twice.
3) Pay the 2 MF cost in each of E6, F6, and G6 and end the RtPh in G6, suffering no interdiction.   
4) Low crawl to E6 and suffer no interdiction.  

Scenario 3 - "Back to the Future"

SSR: Grain is in season.  No quarter is not in effect.  

I'm fairly certain of the rules here, although it does make it seem as if the routers are able to see into the future.  

I believe the broken unit is required to surrender to the unit in 33U3.  

Why?  I believe R6 is the only valid rout target, and the only path to that target will subject the unit to interdiction crossing the S hexrow.  The only way to avoid that is low crawl, but since it is adjacent to a KEU it will surrender instead.  

Scenario 4 - "Grain is out of season!"

SSR: Grain is out of season.  

Until today my understanding was that the broken unit had a bunch of options here.  

1) Don't ignore 33Y1 and rout there via Y4, X3, X2, X1, and take a bunch of interdiction along the way. 
2) Ignore 33Y1, and rout to X0 instead, again via Y4, X3, X2, X1, and again taking a bunch of interdiction.  
3) Low crawl to Y5, Z5, or AA5, taking no interdiction. 

Per the facebook thread mentioned at the beginning of this post, option 3 does not appear to be one that is accepted by most players (including at least one ASLOK three-peater), but I can't figure out why.  Give me some quotes if you can figure this one out.  

My reasoning is that a unit only has to rout towards the nearest building/woods if it is able to reach that building/woods in that RtPh.  If the unit low crawls it obviously cannot reach a non-adjacent but otherwise nearest building/woods in that RtPh, and therefore is merely bound by the first strictures of A10.51 -- i.e. can't rout towards a KEU, nor adjacent to a KEU (unless leaving their hex).  

The alternative reading seems to be that a unit using low crawl may only do so into the first of hex of a hypothetical shortest (in MF) rout path towards the nearest building/woods.  I don't understand this reading though, since it seems to turn the "to" in "a routing unit must move to the nearest (in MF) building or woods hex (even if overstacked)" into a "towards".  

Scenario 5 - "4 MF Down the Lane"

SSR: Grain is in season.  No quarter is not in effect.

43Z8 is only 4 MF away "as the crow flies", but that 4MF path is not a legal rout path for the broken unit.  

My interpretation is that the routers can go pretty much anywhere they like in the Z4 or AA8 grain fields.  Alternately they could even low crawl to Z4 or AA8 (although why would they want to when they could rout further free from interdiction?) 

I'm frankly uncertain whether they could rout down the road starting in AA7 (towards DD3)... on the one hand they have legal rout options that do not require interdiction or low crawl, so they should not surrender via RtPh method... however, does that mean that a unit is obligated to exercise a legal rout path that doesn't involve low crawl/interdiction even if another otherwise legal rout path exists that involves low crawl/interdiction when they start the RtPh adjacent to a KEU?  My guess is that the rout down the road is not legal in this case, but it seems like a gray area.  

Scenario 6 - "A Similar Scenario"

SSR: Grain is in season.

This time the broken unit is 5MF down the lane from a woods hex, but that path would not be a legal rout (since it would require going adjacent to the KEU in 43Y6).  I think the routers in this case could go pretty much anywhere north-east of a line running W2-AA4-AA7-W9, taking any applicable interdiction if they leave the grain fields e.g. crossing the road in AA5.  

Scenario 7 - "Routs Yours is Mined"

SSR: Grain is in season.

The building in 16O4 is obviously the closest woods/building for the broken unit (3 MF direct route). Obviously one option is to rout N4-O4, and eat a minefield attack.  However, routers are not required to rout through known minefields.  There is a 6 MF route to 16O4 (via L4, L3, M3, N3) that gets them there without going through a minefield.  The question is, may the routing unit instead rout to the woods in M2 for 5 MF (L4, L3, M3, M2)?  I am agnostic on this question.  If I had to rule, I'd actually say that if the unit chooses not to rout through the minefield it is obligated to choose the then shorter route to the woods in M2.  

Wow.  My thanks if you made it through all that, and even more thanks if you've got some opinions (or even better, citations).  Oh, and if you Schwerpunkt guys ever need some scenario names, call me!  :whistle:

I believe the broken unit is required to surrender to the unit in 33U3.  

Why?  I believe R6 is the only valid rout target, and the only path to that target will subject the unit to interdiction crossing the S hexrow.  The only way to avoid that is low crawl, but since it is adjacent to a KEU it will surrender instead.  

Scenario 4 - "Grain is out of season!"

SSR: Grain is out of season.  

Until today my understanding was that the broken unit had a bunch of options here.  

1) Don't ignore 33Y1 and rout there via Y4, X3, X2, X1, and take a bunch of interdiction along the way. 
2) Ignore 33Y1, and rout to X0 instead, again via Y4, X3, X2, X1, and again taking a bunch of interdiction.  
3) Low crawl to Y5, Z5, or AA5, taking no interdiction. 

Per the facebook thread mentioned at the beginning of this post, option 3 does not appear to be one that is accepted by most players (including at least one ASLOK three-peater), but I can't figure out why.  Give me some quotes if you can figure this one out.  

My reasoning is that a unit only has to rout towards the nearest building/woods if it is able to reach that building/woods in that RtPh.  If the unit low crawls it obviously cannot reach a non-adjacent but otherwise nearest building/woods in that RtPh, and therefore is merely bound by the first strictures of A10.51 -- i.e. can't rout towards a KEU, nor adjacent to a KEU (unless leaving their hex).  

The alternative reading seems to be that a unit using low crawl may only do so into the first of hex of a hypothetical shortest (in MF) rout path towards the nearest building/woods.  I don't understand this reading though, since it seems to turn the "to" in "a routing unit must move to the nearest (in MF) building or woods hex (even if overstacked)" into a "towards".  

Scenario 5 - "4 MF Down the Lane"

SSR: Grain is in season.  No quarter is not in effect.

43Z8 is only 4 MF away "as the crow flies", but that 4MF path is not a legal rout path for the broken unit.  

My interpretation is that the routers can go pretty much anywhere they like in the Z4 or AA8 grain fields.  Alternately they could even low crawl to Z4 or AA8 (although why would they want to when they could rout further free from interdiction?) 

I'm frankly uncertain whether they could rout down the road starting in AA7 (towards DD3)... on the one hand they have legal rout options that do not require interdiction or low crawl, so they should not surrender via RtPh method... however, does that mean that a unit is obligated to exercise a legal rout path that doesn't involve low crawl/interdiction even if another otherwise legal rout path exists that involves low crawl/interdiction when they start the RtPh adjacent to a KEU?  My guess is that the rout down the road is not legal in this case, but it seems like a gray area.  

Scenario 6 - "A Similar Scenario"

SSR: Grain is in season.

This time the broken unit is 5MF down the lane from a woods hex, but that path would not be a legal rout (since it would require going adjacent to the KEU in 43Y6).  I think the routers in this case could go pretty much anywhere north-east of a line running W2-AA4-AA7-W9, taking any applicable interdiction if they leave the grain fields e.g. crossing the road in AA5.  

Scenario 7 - "Routs Yours is Mined"

SSR: Grain is in season.

The building in 16O4 is obviously the closest woods/building for the broken unit (3 MF direct route). Obviously one option is to rout N4-O4, and eat a minefield attack.  However, routers are not required to rout through known minefields.  There is a 6 MF route to 16O4 (via L4, L3, M3, N3) that gets them there without going through a minefield.  The question is, may the routing unit instead rout to the woods in M2 for 5 MF (L4, L3, M3, M2)?  I am agnostic on this question.  If I had to rule, I'd actually say that if the unit chooses not to rout through the minefield it is obligated to choose the then shorter route to the woods in M2.  

Wow.  My thanks if you made it through all that, and even more thanks if you've got some opinions (or even better, citations).  Oh, and if you Schwerpunkt guys ever need some scenario names, call me!  :whistle:
ground_truth_answer:
On scenario 1 I believe that errata has removed the need to low crawl farther away.

Correct, from ASL Journal 5:
A10.5 Errata: In lines 15-16 delete “to increase the distance between itself and ≥ 1 nearest Known enemy unit(s)”.

Is this also true at Night?

And if so, you may simply stay where you are, ADJACENT to the enemy rather than Rout at all?
I've always played it (and mostly seen it played) that one has to rout if one can even at Night (in a situation normally requiring a rout), but if unable to, one is not eliminated for failure to rout.

But there is an unofficial Q&A that says a broken unit is never required to rout:

E1.54 At night, is a unit that begins the Rout
Phase in a building, under DM and adjacent to a
Known enemy unit forced to rout? Is the answer
the same for any type of concealment terrain?
How about open ground?
A. No unit is ever forced to rout at night (E1.54).

Hi guys.

The text reads: "a squad carrying five PP has only two MF and must expend them both to enter that Open Ground hex and load onto the vehicle unless it is accompanied by a SMC (A4,12, A4.42) carrying no PP of its own, thereby leaving the vehicle with one-fourth of its MP remaining for that MPh.".

ground_truth_answer:
Gents would I be right in thinking that if the attacker had a roll of 2 in close combat
They can attack the defender and then withdraw and if the defender rolled 
A 12 the attacker would attack then could withdraw but if the attacker rolled a twelve would the defender be able to withdraw I don't think it can but I wanted to make sure, 
many thanks in advance.

Phil, 2s and 12s temporarily suspend the simultaneity of CC - if the Attacker rolls a 2, the effects are applied and he may immediately withdraw.  If he doesn't withdraw, surviving Defenders (if any) may attack.  If the Attacker rolls a 12, the Defender may withdraw, but must forgo making a CC roll of his own.  If the Attacker rolls something other than a 2 or a 12 and the Defender then rolls a 12, the Attacker may withdraw, and finally, if the Defender rolls a 2, he may withdraw.  We always have the Attacker roll first for this reason - it's the possibility of snakes and boxcars that might scramble the results.

Here's the rule, just for completeness:

11.22 INFILTRATION: The simultaneous nature of CC is momentarily suspended following an Original CC DR of 2/12. Provided it has not already been eliminated/captured/pinned, any Infantry/Cavalry unit which rolls an Original 2 CC DR may withdraw from CC/Melee immediately thereafter in the same CCPh without being attacked, even if it did not eliminate the defenders (see also Field Promotions; 18.12). Any Infantry/Cavalry unit(s) attacked by an Original 12 CC DR may likewise withdraw from CC immediately thereafter, assuming it has not been eliminated by that 12 CC DR. If the option to withdraw is taken, it must be done immediately; the unit cannot wait to make its own attack (if it has not yet done so) or see the outcome of other attacks before leaving. See also Ambush Withdrawal (11.41).

query:
Rout with No Quarter penalties in effect: Hi everybody. I need advice from ASL experts.
Referring to the Comprehensive Rout Example (page A28 in ASL rules 2nd edition):

The text reads (first paragraph, second sentence): "The broken squad in L8 would rout in L7 and suffer interdiction there and any survivors would be unable to rout further without moving closer to the KEU's in K6 and Q8: unable to rout away from the ADJACENT unbroken KEU in L8, the broken unit would be eliminated for Failure to Rout."

Now, there's something I don't get here.
First: what does KEU in Q8 have anything to do, since it's never in the LOS of the broken unit? I think the broken unit in L8 could rout in L7 suffering Interdiction and, if survives, could then enter M7 building...
Second: the broken unit could also try to rout in K8, since it's not getting closer to any enemy unit in LOS...

Am I missing something?
Thank you for any counseling!
title: Rout with No Quarter penalties in effect
raw_question:
Hi everybody. I need advice from ASL experts.
Referring to the Comprehensive Rout Example (page A28 in ASL rules 2nd edition):

The text reads (first paragraph, second sentence): "The broken squad in L8 would rout in L7 and suffer interdiction there and any survivors would be unable to rout further without moving closer to the KEU's in K6 and Q8: unable to rout away from the ADJACENT unbroken KEU in L8, the broken unit would be eliminated for Failure to Rout."

Now, there's something I don't get here.
First: what does KEU in Q8 have anything to do, since it's never in the LOS of the broken unit? I think the broken unit in L8 could rout in L7 suffering Interdiction and, if survives, could then enter M7 building...
Second: the broken unit could also try to rout in K8, since it's not getting closer to any enemy unit in LOS...

Am I missing something?
Thank you for any counseling!
ground_truth_answer:
First up I has to rout towards woods or building and the first non-ignoreable woods/building is M7 ( since that building will bring it farther away from all KEUs (in J9, L8 and M9) [10.51].)
Thus the prohibition of routing to K8.
Now whether the LOS from L7 to Q8 is clear is something I am not sure about from the picture but given the example I would expect it to have been checked.
Remember you are above thehedges in L7 so can see over them. You might clip the M8 woods but are unlikely.

Now if you are adjacent to a KEU and unable to rout away without using low crawl or suffering interdiction, you will surrender.
The Rout to L7 can be interdicted.
( squad in M9 as well as the AFV MG in L8 can Interdict the rout to either K8 or L7 because the +1 Height Advantage TEM does not apply when the LOS crosses the Crest Line traversed by the moving unit [B10.31])
Thus he will surrender to the adjacent unit.

I attatch the full paragraph:

The broken squad in L8 must rout since it is in the same hex as an unbroken KEU and not in Melee. It must rout towards building M7 since that building will bring it farther away from all KEUs (in J9, L8 and M9) [10.51]. The first hex it enters while routing cannot be L9 or M8 since that would be moving ADJACENT to the unbroken KEU in M9. It cannot enter K9 from L8 since that would be moving closer to the KEU in J9. Therefore, the first hex it routs through must be K8 or L7. It cannot Low Crawl when leaving an enemy-occupied Location [10.52] and the squad in M9 as well as the AFV MG in L8 can Interdict the rout to either K8 or L7 because the +1 Height Advantage TEM does not apply when the LOS crosses the Crest Line traversed by the moving unit [B10.31]. Therefore, the broken unit cannot rout without being subject to Interdiction and since No Quarter is not in effect, it Surrenders [20.21], and the squad in M9 accepts the Surrender.

query:
Hooking a gun vs loading passengers: In D6.4 we can read that:

6.4 LOADING: A vehicle must be stopped to embark Passengers/Riders. It may move in the same MPh after they load, but it may not move in that MPh prior to their loading (including the expenditure of a MP to bring a Motion vehicle to a stop) [EXC: Infantry hooking up a Gun, C10.11]. 

If we check C10.11,

10.11 HOOKING UP: A Stopped vehicle not in Bypass may hook up a Gun (if the vehicle's T# ≤ the Gun's M#) by spending half (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment [EXC: if the Gun's M# is circled (e.g. M(6), the vehicle must expend two-thirds (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment] in that Gun's hex (in addition to any required MP/MF cost to enter the hex), provided a crew (as per 10.111) is on foot in that hex. This expenditure does not itself qualify that vehicle as a moving target, but does allow Defensive First Fire opportunities against it (that Gun shares its target status and is destroyed or missed depending on the fate of the vehicle). That Gun is then placed on top of that vehicle to indicate that it is in tow. Neither that Gun, its crew, nor that vehicle/its PRC can fire during that PFPh/MPh and all are TI for the rest of that Player Turn. That crew may also load into that towing vehicle at no extra MP/MF cost as it hooks up that Gun, but if it expends > half its MF allotment in pushing/entering that Gun's hex, that Gun cannot then be hooked up by that unit in that MPh. A non-QSU Gun (10.23) must first be limbered (10.21) before it can be hooked up. See 10.31 for pushing and hooking up a Gun in the same MPh.

And 10.31,

10.31 A Gun can be pushed and then hooked up during the same MPh, but only if its pushing Infantry can still attempt to push that Gun another hex in that MPh (i.e., can attempt another Manhandling DR), and only if the vehicle has not yet exceeded the specified MP/MF expenditure for hooking up (10.11). No Manhandling DR is actually required for hooking up or unhooking.

As I read it, it means that a vehicle that starts its turn in Motion is forbidden to load passengers, but it can hook a gun and load its crew.

Isn't that strange?
title: Hooking a gun vs loading passengers
raw_question:
In D6.4 we can read that:

6.4 LOADING: A vehicle must be stopped to embark Passengers/Riders. It may move in the same MPh after they load, but it may not move in that MPh prior to their loading (including the expenditure of a MP to bring a Motion vehicle to a stop) [EXC: Infantry hooking up a Gun, C10.11]. 

If we check C10.11,

10.11 HOOKING UP: A Stopped vehicle not in Bypass may hook up a Gun (if the vehicle's T# ≤ the Gun's M#) by spending half (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment [EXC: if the Gun's M# is circled (e.g. M(6), the vehicle must expend two-thirds (FRU) of its MP/MF allotment] in that Gun's hex (in addition to any required MP/MF cost to enter the hex), provided a crew (as per 10.111) is on foot in that hex. This expenditure does not itself qualify that vehicle as a moving target, but does allow Defensive First Fire opportunities against it (that Gun shares its target status and is destroyed or missed depending on the fate of the vehicle). That Gun is then placed on top of that vehicle to indicate that it is in tow. Neither that Gun, its crew, nor that vehicle/its PRC can fire during that PFPh/MPh and all are TI for the rest of that Player Turn. That crew may also load into that towing vehicle at no extra MP/MF cost as it hooks up that Gun, but if it expends > half its MF allotment in pushing/entering that Gun's hex, that Gun cannot then be hooked up by that unit in that MPh. A non-QSU Gun (10.23) must first be limbered (10.21) before it can be hooked up. See 10.31 for pushing and hooking up a Gun in the same MPh.

And 10.31,

10.31 A Gun can be pushed and then hooked up during the same MPh, but only if its pushing Infantry can still attempt to push that Gun another hex in that MPh (i.e., can attempt another Manhandling DR), and only if the vehicle has not yet exceeded the specified MP/MF expenditure for hooking up (10.11). No Manhandling DR is actually required for hooking up or unhooking.

As I read it, it means that a vehicle that starts its turn in Motion is forbidden to load passengers, but it can hook a gun and load its crew.

Isn't that strange?
ground_truth_answer:
The sequencing is an obvious artifice:  move then hook up for Guns; load up then move for infantry.

Neither is "correct".  Both are an attempt to roughly model fluid events in a structured turn.

There are good reasons for the differences (in terms of game mechanics) because of the differences in the way Guns and infantry move without vehicles:  if a vehicle could only hook up before moving, in practical terms the vehicle would usually need to drive to the Gun's location the turn before [EXC:  Guns manhandled into the vehicles hex].

That consideration does not apply to infantry:  they are highly mobile on foot, so getting vehicle and putative passengers into the same location before the vehicle moves is much easier (EX: after the vehicle's previous turn's movement is finished the infantry could use its MPh and APh to reach the vehicle's location).

I think that is enough to justify the different mechanics for loading (and the hooking up of Guns comes up rarely enough that the scope for confusion is limited).

ground_truth_answer:
Is there really anything new here from when the late Ian Daglish wrote his article about vehicles in woods for VFTT #45?

http://www.vftt.co.uk/vfttpdf/vftt45.pdf

Finally, a few unrelated points which have certainly confused me in the past. When a crest line runs through a woods hex, all woods in the hex are considered to be at the higher level. In other words, treat the entire woods depiction as if it were sitting on the higher side of the crest line. This is true also for other terrain types: e.g., grain, brush, building, but not for Inherent Terrain which in effect follows the contour of the crest line (see B10.1 for Examples). In other words, all of the woods depiction in a hex always rises to the same height, but the height of Inherent Terrain depends on the crest line.

Also remember that any unit bypassing the woods in a hex is assumed to be moving through the higher level of the hex, and expend MF/MP accordingly, even if no crest line appears to be crossed. You can bypass the woods in the hex, but if you enter the hex you must do so at the highest level. 

Look at the B10.31 Example on page B13. If there were woods in the center of hex BB1, either German unit could bypass them, but the 4-6-7 would have to pay the doubled MF to ascend the crest line (though it would still be subject to FFMO/FFNAM as HA would not apply). Odd though it might sound, the 4-6-7 would still be visible over any half-hex obstacle such as a wall or hedge, but would not qualify for HA. 

Philippe Leonard’s “Look at Bypass” in Annual ‘93a addresses this and other issues.

A vehicle starts its turn under a motion counter, and wants to move one hex forward, and take the best bounding first fire shot it can.

You're basically right, except that you can't actually spend delay while in motion. You can, however, always pay "extra" to enter a hex, so in this case (and many others) it's a distinction without a difference.

So whether you over-spend to enter and then stop or you stop and then delay, it's going to work out the same. And, yes, you will need to stop before bounding firing to get the best odds.

I assume you're just coming into LOS of the target? That's the only reason the MPs spent would matter at all.

ground_truth_answer:
Someone please provide me with a rational system for plotting who has aquired who.
Hmmm... I've never had any problems using Acquisition counters.

Let's look at "Paw of the Tiger" as an example:

The Russians have 18 T-34s, 6 each of three different models, with IDs from "A" to "F". You obviously can't use a single color for all 18 Russian tanks, so instead each T-34 model gets its own color.

Once the Acq counters come into play, most players can remember which color goes with which T-34 model. If necessary, you can also jot down the assignments on a piece of paper (blue = T-34 M41, etc.), but I've never had to do this.

The Germans have two Tigers, two Pz IIIs, and an AT Gun, so they have a couple of options. They can carefully select their five units so that each one has a different ID, allowing them to use a single color of Acq counter. Or, like the Russians, they can assign a different color to each of the three types: Tiger, Pz III, AT Gun.

If you are just a starting out in ASL and only have Beyond Valor, then you might not have enough different colors of Acq counters to handle a scenario with a lot of different units. But many of the add-on modules include additional Acq counters, so as you expand your ASL system you should eventually have plenty of different colors to use.

Lock n Load gets round this by providing PAIRS of markers, each sharing a letter or number. One is marked Aquiring and is placed on the shooting counter and the other is marked either - 1 or -2 to indicate hit modifiers and is placed on the target.

why didn't ASL do this?
For ASL, this sounds like overkill that would just clutter up the map with unnecessary counters. ASL's single Acq counter system seems to work fine for most players.

Technically it costs 0.5 MP for a vehicle to cross a road hexside, and here you're not crossing a road hexside, you're bypassing an hex using village terrain.

ground_truth_answer:
Entering a multi hex building is what makes this confusing. So if the building in question is a 5 hex sized building and I had two MMC's in only two of those hexes, the enemy can just walk right in on any of the other three hexes of my Fortified Building? So a Breach is not needed in this case?

In ASL the status of "fortified building" is per building Location, which is every Level in an hex. To have upper levels fortified you have to fortify its lower levels first.

But to make things easier, imagine a multi hex building with no upper levels. It has five hexes, all of them fortified. If you have a squad equivalent in two of those five hexes, the enemy won't be able to move or advance into them. But they can surely enter the empty hexes, even if fortified.

The effect is that your occupied fortified hexes are secure both from outside the building and from inside the building proper.

query: Smoke on the water.: I really thought you couldn't put smoke into a stream. In Journal 10 the beginners article had smoke being thrown by infantry into and Effluent hex. I looked and couldn't find a reason why not. Have I misunderstood this all these years?
title: Smoke on the water.

ground_truth_answer:
I really thought you couldn't put smoke into a stream. In Journal 10 the beginners article had smoke being thrown by infantry into and Effluent hex. I looked and couldn't find a reason why not. Have I misunderstood this all these years?

Yes. You can place (and fire) SMOKE into a stream hex.

A24.1...A squad may not place SMOKE in Water Obstacles [EXC: Bridges (not foot bridges)], sewer, or marsh hexes (and neither may ordnance). 

B21.1 A Water Obstacle is a body of water large enough to stop the normal movement of men and vehicles, which cannot enter without special assistance. Any non-stream hex whose center dot is emplaced in a blue background is a Water Obstacle hex. 

8.52 SMOKE ammunition is always placed at ground level in any target hex which is hit on the Area Target Type, except Interior Building hexes, even if the only visible part of that hex is the upper level of a building. A Gun cannot place SMOKE in its own hex, although some AFV may place smoke in their own hex without their Gun (D13).

query: Do the 3 Starter Kits add up to the complete 3 Ring Binder contents?: And does the 2nd ed binder still contain the graphic images inside the covers, like the AH version?  That would be the only reason to get the empty binder.
title: Do the 3 Starter Kits add up to the complete 3 Ring Binder contents?
raw_question: And does the 2nd ed binder still contain the graphic images inside the covers, like the AH version?  That would be the only reason to get the empty binder.
ground_truth_answer:
Do the 3 Starter Kits add up to the complete 3 Ring Binder contents? 

No - not by a long shot.  The Rules for ASLSK are an excellent complete game - and could be played and enjoyed alone as a complete game forever.  IMHO - they compare favorable to any other tactical WWII game system in existence.

The difference in the two systems is scope.  Full ASL is MASSIVE.  

ASLSK is not simpler than Full ASL (neither are difficult); but rather, it's just (a whole lot) smaller.

Full ASL:  A Humvee with a warehouse full of gear and attachments.

ASLSK:  A Smart Car.

You need to know how to drive to do either, and the details of that are the same.  However, the Humvee (+ gear) gives you a lot more options.

Basically, SK#1 presents a simplified version of chapter A, SK#2 is a simplified chapter C, and SK#3 is a simplified chapter D, and all three have rules on terrain, obviously, but there are far more terrain types in full ASL. 
 
This is a nit - but I'd call it a streamlined version of Chapters A, C and D.  Nothing is changed or dumb-down.   Instead, extra detail is left out.  

Examples of detail left out: 

Chapter A: concealment, bypass movement, dash movement, Machine Gun Fire Lanes, prisoners;  
Chapter B: Building levels, exotic terrain; 
Chapter C: Off-board Artillery, towing Guns
Chapter D: crew survival, platoon movement, bypass movement.

Chapter E is essentially a collection of special rules that are only used in certain scenarios when the are specifically called for, and never when they are not.  Example: Night, Weather, Air Support, Paratroop and Glider Drops, River Crossing (Boats).  Its contents are completely absent from ASLSK.

Other Chapters that are included in subsequent modules (not in the ASL rulebook) add rules for other nationalities and new terrain types (Desert, Jungle, the Japanese etc.).

What this means is that if you graduate to full ASL - you add to what you already know, rather than having to re-learn basics.  The scope expands (massively) in two ways:

:d6-1:  The theaters of war and types of scenario situations you can model,

:d6-2:  Your options during play: rules are added that let you do stuff that you could do (or that could happen, or that exist) in real life, but for which ASLSK does not have the "software" to model.

As far as I know there is only one difference between full ASL and SKASL and it is an obscure minor thing that is easy to learn "the new way" if you move up to the big game.

The SK don't give many counters.  I kind of like to do points based encounters more than scenarios.
Full ASL has a lot of support for DYO (Design Your Own) scenarios: point values for the various units, rules for generating leaders and support weapons based upon the number and quality of troops that you purchase, and rarity factors for guns and vehicles (so a given gun/vehicle may not be available for purchase in a DYO scenario, depending upon how rare/common it was). But I don't hear about many players who actually play DYO scenarios regularly.

The Starter Kits don't really support DYO scenarios: they include the point values and rarity factors for the various units, but none of the required rules, charts, and tables are included.

I'm a miniatures guy.  What I'd really like is really large hexes so I can use the current generation of 20mm miniatures made for Flames of War.
The Deluxe maps were designed for 1/285 scale miniatures, although that idea never caught on. Most players just use the regular counters on the Deluxe boards.

The Deluxe modules have been out of print for a long time, but Deluxe isn't dead: there's often at least one new Deluxe scenario in each issue of the ASL Journal, and some third party publishers also release Deluxe scenarios on occasion.

MMP has considered reprinting the Deluxe boards (along with some new ones), but it will be a long time before this happens... if it ever happens.

How about rolling a die each turn for LOS when it goes thru building hex(es)?  It represents the squad maneuvering a little within their own hex (& the target also) to see past the building.  The LOS can change from turn to turn because the enemy might shift away, successfully getting out of sight.
ASL players tend to frown on house rules like this, so while it's an interesting idea, don't expect anyone else to be willing to use it in a game.

You can always draw up your own maps to get buildings sized the way that you want; there's even a software program specifically created to make it easy to create ASL maps:

ground_truth_answer:
I am not sure you can do this, I believe you have to pre-declare stack MF expenditure ("my stack moves to zB3 for 2MF", or "my stack attempts to drop smoke in zB3 for 2MF").
But the members of a stack can do different activities with a given MF expenditure: "Units moving as a stack expend MF simultaneously and need not spend MF for the same purpose, but must designate at the same time all actions for the same MF." (A4.2)

So while you can make three attempts in a single ADJACENT hex, I don't believe you can attempt into 3 separate ADJACENT hexes - as long as you are spending it as stacked.
"Units attempting to place SMOKE grenades must specify the hex they wish to place them in before rolling the placement dr, but are otherwise free to observe the placement attempts of previous moving units before designating their own placement attempts." (A24.1)

The rule clearly states that the target is designated before the placing unit rolls its placement dr, but it does not require that a target be designated before any other unit in the stack makes a placement dr, nor does it require that a target be designated at the time that the MF expenditure is announced. Indeed, the last part of this rule, about observing other placement attempts, only makes sense for units moving as a stack... as units moving individually, or making smoke placement attempts on different MF expenditures of a stack, would of course know the results of any previous placement attempts before they have to designate their target.

I can't find any Perry Sez or errata that changes or contradicts these two rules, so I believe my answer was correct.

motion tank firing on moving tank: I'm trying to get to grips with the armour rules and finding my brain is turning to cardboard left out in the rain.

It is the Russian movement turn, one of their T34's moves into the sights of a Tiger which is under a motion counter. I can see how BFF applies to a firing tank in it's movement phase but this is the movement phase of the Russians. Motion DRM apply to the target but what applies to the attacker?

I'm trying to get to grips with the armour rules and finding my brain is turning to cardboard left out in the rain.

It is the Russian movement turn, one of their T34's moves into the sights of a Tiger which is under a motion counter. I can see how BFF applies to a firing tank in it's movement phase but this is the movement phase of the Russians. Motion DRM apply to the target but what applies to the attacker?

thanks
ground_truth_answer:
Pup, the rules in this case are ok. There is just a problem of interpretation. 
I disagree. This section of the rules is a disaster and desperately needs to be revised.

 C5.35 states that for Motion/Non-Stopped vehicles case C4 applies, along with cases C, or C1, or C2 "as applicable".
The key is "as applicable". If you then read C5.31 and C5.32 it says that C1 and C2 apply to vehicles firing during their MPh. So, "not applicable" to a D1F from a Motion vehicle. 
You are saying that cases C1 and C2 are not "applicable" because they state that they apply to vehicles firing during their MPh. But in C5.3 it also states that vehicular ordnance firing during it's MPh uses the Case C DRM. It's the exact same statement that is made for cases C1 and C2.

If you exclude C1 and C2 because of the statement about it's MPh then you have to exclude C also. This would make section C5.35 absolutely meaningless. 

But the fact is that C5.35 says that you apply C4 to a Motion Firer and then apply C, C1 or C2 as applicable and even defines what "as applicable" means in parentheses as "depending on MP expended..."

 So, you see, no contradictions, no changes, no nothing. It's there in the rules. You can show it to your opponents. 
What I see in the Rules is that C, C1 or C2 apply to a Motion firer as applicable depending on the MP expended by the target just prior to the shot. That's what the rule book says in a muddled and confused fashion. 

But a poorly thought out and arbitary Q&A has been issued from on high so the loyal team of ASL oldtimers rally around the flag and try to pretend that nonsense makes perfect ASL sense.

C1 and C2 apply specifically to Bounding Firers only.

Angry much?  :)

I am going to agree with ASLNoob - the rules for C4 are written poorly. C4 is written well for Bounding Fire, but not for defensive Motion firers. Cases C, C1, and C2 all apply specifically to Bounding Firers, not defensive Motion firers. I could argue both sides of this, but I believe the intention is for case C to apply to the defensive Motion firer, but not C1 nor C2.

ground_truth_answer:
You are right.  Once broke they lose CX.  If they rally they are eligible for Double Time.

Here is something that you can do with SS.  Take a stack of 3 SS squads and a -1 or -2 leader.  Double time them, run forward as far as you can to a position that will allow you to rout 'forward', voluntarily break them, rout them 'forward', They have a broken morale of 9 so with rally terrain and -1 leader they rally  on a 7 or 8 with a -2 leader.  Declare Double Time again and repeat.  Finding the spot that allows a rout 'forward' is the tricky part.

I think you can only voluntarily break if you have LOS to a Known enemy unit, so finding the spot that allows this is very tricky. Commissars also help when doing this trick.

Third, the most usefull AA is light AA : if your guns are in AA mode, you simply fire at the plane, using the IFE, the plane's DRM (in the black star) and remember that range is counted double (1hex = 2 hex).
Swinging the gun will add some CA DRM.
Fourth, as the aircraft can attack at any moment during MPh, about any unit, the placement of your AA resources never will be ideal.
At last, the Sighting TC is quite easy to compute : roll the dice, look up the DRMs : 8 or less, OK. 12 original : recall, 12 final : mistaken attack...

The ASL rulebook is singularly terrible at these 'bare-bones' systematic, procedural examples, because it's all about the exceptions. But I feel like you have to learnt he rule before you worry about the exceptions.The word that "you play 10% of the rules 90%" proves quite true.
When you are accustomed to the bulk of the rules, you will mostly look into the rulebook when special occurences happen - which are covered by the "exceptions".

Now, to get a grasp of the rules, a good way to go is to play along the Starter Kit rules : they are a simplified set of rules, which mostly don't conflict with the full thing.

I hope I helped a little...

title: Have tanks LOS over hedges/walls?

ground_truth_answer:
Yes, LOS is blocked for everything on the same level as the wall/hedge.

Note that a tank adjacent to a wall or hedge cannot fire its BMG though the hexsides with the wall or hedge. These are not 'short' (2'-3') walls, but 'tall' ones (4'-5')!
A BMG could fire through the hexside if it is a hedge - not wall/bocage though.

Per D4.223 firing a non-MA is only NA if the vehicle is Hull Down, and a hedge does not bestow HD status.

title: Concealed unit entrenching
raw_question:
guyz

does a concealed MMC in the act of entrenching (i.e., it has a labor -1 counter) lose its concealed status when a moving enemy unit moves into its LOS?

thanx and cheers
-Lamskiy-
ground_truth_answer:
Case C on the Concealment Loss/Gain table: 

An infantry unit in either concealment or non-concealment terrain that is in LOS range 16 or less will lose concealment for attempting "any other actions; e.g. attempts to entrench."

As the OP pointed out, its not the TI marker that would make him lose concealment but the attempt to entrench (die roll) during that phase. 

If your unit is out of LOS, attempts entrenchment and gets a TI marker, he does not lose concealment.

If you unit is in LOS and attempts entrenchment, it gets a TI marker and loses concealement.

8. After determining the hit location, the AF listed on the Tiger counter is inserted into one of many mathematical equations dependent on the combination of symbols on the counter.

9. The result of this equation is AF of the particular location that the T-34 has just hit.

10. The Russian player consults the appropriate To-Kill table for the type of ammunition they used.

11. The AF of the particular location hit by the T-34 is subtracted from number taken from the To-Kill Table. This is the To-Kill number.

12. The Russian player then tries to roll under this number. What happens if their roll equals the To-Kill number exactly?

Thats as far as I've been able to get. I'm guessing that a successful roll on step 12 leads to something on the AFV Destruction Table (C7.7) but I can't read the table at all. The combined usage of algebra, abbreviations, color codes, various symbols, superscripts and footnotes absolutely boggles my mind. Can someone set me straight on what I'm supposed to be doing here?

I've got the latest version of BV and the Big Orange Rulebook sitting right in front of me with the play aids for armor spread out over the floor. I still can't figure out what happens when a tank shoots another tank. Heres what I (think) I understand so far.

1. In the German Mph, a Tiger drives into the LOS of a T-34.

2. The Russian player states that they are firing at the Tiger with their T-34 along with what kind of ammunition they are using.

3. The Russian player rolls for ammunition availability and/or depletion if applicable.

4. The Russian player uses string to confirm that the T-34 does indeed have LOS to the Tiger.

5. The Firer-Based Hit Determination DRM's (as listed on Table C5) are calculated and then added to the Target-Based Hit Determination DRM's (as listed on table C6). The result is the final To-Hit DRM.

6. The Russian player consults the To Hit Table (C3). They find the appropriate column for the range, and row for Target Type (Vehicle). How do you know when to use the red numbers? They add the final To-Hit DRM to the number taken from the To-Hit Table and attempt to roll under this number on 2 Dice. What happens if the DR is exactly equal to the target number?

7. Assuming the result is a hit, the Russian player then compares the colored and uncolored die to determine the location of the hit.

8. After determining the hit location, the AF listed on the Tiger counter is inserted into one of many mathematical equations dependent on the combination of symbols on the counter.

9. The result of this equation is AF of the particular location that the T-34 has just hit.

10. The Russian player consults the appropriate To-Kill table for the type of ammunition they used.

11. The AF of the particular location hit by the T-34 is subtracted from number taken from the To-Kill Table. This is the To-Kill number.

12. The Russian player then tries to roll under this number. What happens if their roll equals the To-Kill number exactly?

Thats as far as I've been able to get. I'm guessing that a successful roll on step 12 leads to something on the AFV Destruction Table (C7.7) but I can't read the table at all. The combined usage of algebra, abbreviations, color codes, various symbols, superscripts and footnotes absolutely boggles my mind. Can someone set me straight on what I'm supposed to be doing here?
ground_truth_answer:
Here's some detailed notes, but yes, you've got the essentials.

1. In the German Mph, a Tiger drives into the LOS of a T-34.
Okay...

2. The Russian player states that they are firing at the Tiger with their T-34 along with what kind of ammunition they are using.
Technically, he also specifies if he is using Vehicular, Infantry or Area Target Type. Since it is a vehicular target, VTT and AP ammo are assumed if it is not otherwise stated. ITT will not do anything here (though it could be used to fire on Riders or a CE crew), and ATT is mostly meant for concealed targets, but can be useful if the Gun is not able to penetrate the target's armor (immobilization and shock).

The only special ammo available to a T-34 will be APCR (noted by an 'A' and numbers on the back of the counter).

3. The Russian player rolls for ammunition availability and/or depletion if applicable.
Yes. But this is the To Hit DR. If he uses APCR and rolls under his depletion number (should be the same for all T-34s, but the depletion number will vary by year), then it is a normal To Hit roll (though using the APCR To Kill table if it hits). If it is equal to the depletion number, then proceed with APCR, but that T-34 has no more available for the rest of the scenario. If the roll is equal to the B#/X#, then the Gun malfunctions. Otherwise, there was no APCR for that tank, which cannot try for APCR for the rest of the scenario, and the To Hit DR is repeated, using normal AP this time.

4. The Russian player uses string to confirm that the T-34 does indeed have LOS to the Tiger.
Yes. In many cases, this will be obvious and can be skipped, just as in infantry fire.

5. The Firer-Based Hit Determination DRM's (as listed on Table C5) are calculated and then added to the Target-Based Hit Determination DRM's (as listed on table C6). The result is the final To-Hit DRM.
Yes. In this case, the Tiger is moving, so Case J will apply, and J1/J2 may apply because of lack of MP spent in LOS of the T-34. Case L cannot apply because of the Motion target. A Tiger I is a large -1 target (Case P). Cases Q or R (TEM & Hindrance) could apply.

Assuming the T-34 is not in Motion, the likely Firer-based mods are Case A (if it needed to turn the turret, or even body to make the shot), Case F (it had already fired and exhausted ROF, getting a First Fire marker for the MA), and Case L (Buttoned Up).

6. The Russian player consults the To Hit Table (C3). They find the appropriate column for the range, and row for Target Type (Vehicle). How do you know when to use the red numbers? They add the final To-Hit DRM to the number taken from the To-Hit Table and attempt to roll under this number on 2 Dice. What happens if the DR is exactly equal to the target number?
Note that you usually calculate the TH# and DRM before declaring the shot (possibly guessing on the Hindrances and the like), so you have an idea if it's worth taking.

7. Assuming the result is a hit, the Russian player then compares the colored and uncolored die to determine the location of the hit.
Yes.

8. After determining the hit location, the AF listed on the Tiger counter is inserted into one of many mathematical equations dependent on the combination of symbols on the counter.

9. The result of this equation is AF of the particular location that the T-34 has just hit.
Not really an equation. If it was a hull hit, use the number for front or side armor as appropriate. Rear armor is one point less than side.

A turret hit modifies the AF up if the appropriate AF is in a square, AF is modified down if it is in a circle. If neither, it is the same as the hull.

The possible AFs are given in D1.6. Adjust up and down the list of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11, 14, 18, 26 as needed above.

10. The Russian player consults the appropriate To-Kill table for the type of ammunition they used.
Right. Adjust for range, if needed.

11. The AF of the particular location hit by the T-34 is subtracted from number taken from the To-Kill Table. This is the To-Kill number.
The Final TK number (C7.11).

12. The Russian player then tries to roll under this number. What happens if their roll equals the To-Kill number exactly?
See the AFV Destruction Table (C7.7). Generally, in this case, a hull hit will Immobilize the target (C7.5), and a turret hit will Shock it (C7.4).

ASL is all about forcing your opponent to make hard choices.

Rout question from a blaze to an upper level encirclement predicament: All,
If a squad enters a building that has a flame marker in it in the movement phase and the flame turns to blaze in the Adv Fire phase it must rout out or be eliminated. When it entered the blaze it was adjacent to an enemy unit. The only legal rout is upstairs in the same building. Does the squad surrender instead since it will be routing to a location that will be an upper level building encirclement? Assume the building is only occupies one hex. In effect the squad is routing to a location that it could never escape from due to the blaze in the ground floor.
Thanks for your help in advance.
title: Rout question from a blaze to an upper level encirclement predicament
raw_question:
All,
If a squad enters a building that has a flame marker in it in the movement phase and the flame turns to blaze in the Adv Fire phase it must rout out or be eliminated. Does the squad surrender instead since it will be routing to a location that will be an upper level building encirclement? Assume the building is only occupies one hex. In effect the squad is routing to a location that it could never escape from due to the blaze in the ground floor.
Thanks for your help in advance.
ground_truth_answer:
Martin, I think there are two questions here: if a unit can choose or not to rout, and if a unit in a blaze can choose it or not.

For the second one, just expand your own quote another sentence:

A10.5 Broken units must rout away (ATTACKER first—one unit at a time [EXC: Voluntary Rout; 10.711]) during that RtPh or be eliminated for Failure to Rout [EXC: Surrender; 20.21]. Otherwise, a broken unit must rout only if in a Blaze (B25.4).

For the first question, yes, it seems that I read it wrong: a unit could refuse routing and be outright eliminated (or surrender if the conditions apply). But I've never seen anyone refuse a rout and prefer being eliminated. Maybe in some weird ASL situations it could be the better choice, of course.

The rules I cited for surrender only say that surrender is forced if certain conditions apply.

So, my take:

1. When in a Blaze, a unit MUST rout.
2. If the only possible rout (in any case) is trough Interdiction or Low Crawl and ADJACENT to Known, Good Order, armed enemy Infantry/Cavalry, the unit MUST surrender.
3. If not in a Blaze, a unit has the option to refuse rout and either surrender or be eliminated if no enemy can capture the unit.

OBA rules to read are little hard to conceptualize :soblue:and the rulebook locations can be little difficult (For example the ASLRB index doesn't include the information found on ASL Rulebook 2nd dividers)

Basically alot of #$%! events happen for a typical OBA attack (Different for NOBA Chapter G14.6 Rising Sun rules & Rocket Artillery C 1.9) :
1. Contact attempt (C1.2)
2. Battery access  (C1.21)
3. Contact access + Battery access then place AR counter
4. LOS check to AR counter placement (C1.3)
5. Accuracy roll for SR (C1.3)
6. LOS check for SR (1.3) 
   * Note placing SR ends actions for observer/battery OBA actions      
     (C1.322 End of actions) 
7. Correct -or- convert SR into FFE:1/2 (C1.33)

To start with you need to have someone (1 of the following in your forces OOB for the scenario) to call in the OBA:
* Observer + Radio (C1.2)
* Observer + Field Phone (1.23)
* Off Board Observer (C1.63)
* OP Tank/Observation Post Tank (C1.2,C1.6, H1.45-1.465)

Then you have the different types of Fire Missions:

* HE concentration           C1.72 Player decision
* Smoke concentration        C1.72 Player decision
* WP/White Phosphorus        OBA Nationality chart either- SMOKE in OBA
* Harassing Fire             C1.72 Player deicsion
* Pre-Registered Fire        C1.73 SSR or DYO
* Bombardment                C1.8  SSR or DYO
* IR/Illuminating Rounds     E1.93 OBA Nationality chart
 

So you have type of observer, then type of fire mission and THEN 'conditions' of artillery like:

Plentiful ammo (C1.21 + add black chit to draw pile)
US Plentiful ammo (A25.33) US always plentiful ammo unless SSR otherwise

ground_truth_answer:
What rule covers this in the main rule book.

B23.25 (with the Journal 5 errata in red):

23.25 ADJACENT BUILDING HEXES: A unit in a building is ADJACENT to an adjacent building level of the same building only if both are either on the same level [EXC: Rowhouse; 23.71], or are vertically connected by a stairwell (printed or inherent). Otherwise, no LOS exists between adjacent units in the same building, nor does a LOS exist between non-adjacent units in the same building, unless a LOS clear of the building depiction can be traced through intervening hex(es)—such as from 1M5 to N3 (see 23.1 illustration). LOS to a unit in a building Location [EXC: rooftop Location] can exist only if drawn to an ADJACENT unit or (for LOS between different hexes) if the LOS as it enters the hex does not cross a hexside within the building depiction (e.g., in contrast to 1X3/X4).

ground_truth_answer:
The actual wording is ...receiving Dummy counters equal to the number of squad-equivalents in his OB...

The key is is "squad-equivalents".  10 full squads means 10 Dummy counters.  8 squads and 2 half-squads would be only 9 Dummies.  No Dummies are received for AFV or Guns.  A12.2 allows for replacing any number of 1/2" Dummies with 5/8" Dummies, however.

A24.1 reads, "Placement in an ADJACENT hex of higher elevation is only allowed across a single crest line or building level stairwell..."  Does that mean they can't?
If it's a single crest line, yes, they can try.  After getting SMOKE, they can, on a subsequent dr of 1..3, place the SMOKE at the higher level (up and over).  If the subsequent dr is 4..6, their SMOKE usually ends up in their own hex (rolls back downhill to them).

A24.1,  for the subsequent dr rule.  B10.11, 1st, for the definition of a Crest line.

query:
Rooftop Concealment Question: Question: A 5/8” mortar is on a rooftop location. There are unbroken enemy units with a LOS to the rooftop location at a lower elevation within 16 hexes to the mortar. Can the mortar can concealment? 

Situation: The situation arose during a playing of Festung Budapest CG II between two teams of players. The Axis team has 82mm mortars on rooftop locations of several buildings (L29, L33, N31 I believe). After loosing both their HIP status and concealment (as per A12.34), the axis team automatically grew concealment at the end of their player turns for all revealed mortars. The Russian team believes this is incorrect and the mortars should not be able to grow concealment. 

Axis argument: The Axis teams justification for the automatic gaining of concealment is:
	B23.82 CONCEALMENT: … A unit can remain hidden or concealed on a rooftop if there are no Good Order enemy ground units within 16 hexes of it 	that are at the same or higher level with a LOS of it; these same restrictions 	apply to gaining “?” on a rooftop [EXC: the enemy units need only be unbroken 	(as opposed to Good Order) to prohibit such gain]. 

The Axis player interprets this to mean that so long as there are no unbroken enemy units at ≥ level to the mortar, concealment gain is automatic.

ground_truth_answer:
First, the Concealment table ALWAYS takes precedence.

B23.82 CONCEALMENT: … A unit can remain hidden or concealed on a rooftop if there are no Good Order enemy ground units within 16 hexes of it that are at the same or higher level with a LOS of it; these same restrictions apply to gaining “?” on a rooftop [EXC: the enemy units need only be unbroken (as opposed to Good Order) to prohibit such gain]. 

O.5 ROOFTOPS (B23.82 & B23.83): A Rooftop Location is Concealment Terrain only for setup purposes. Once the first RPh has been completed B23.82 comes into effect. A Rooftop Location is not considered a building Location for rout and Victory Condition purposes. A Gun may never be Emplaced (C11.2) on a Rooftop.

The roof is Concealment Terrain for Set-up purposes, which is what it means.  For set-up, it's like Woods when you set up.  (duh!)

In RB, since roofs are in play, you can set up Concealed on the Roof.  And so can anyone else.  Then, when you look at the ASOP, when the game starts that RPh, you lose concealment as per the Table.

And that's what Rule B23.82 is talking about.

And as the game progresses, if you are still the only unit on a roof and no one is higher, you gain/loss your concealment as per the table (as if you were in woods).  If you're on the roof, and no enemy has a LOS to you, you'll gain concealment, just like Woods. (their is no automatic gain, just like in Woods if you are in LOS).

As another example, if an HIP Spotter is on a Roof, and no one is higher, then he stays HIP.

Actually, pretty simple and very clear.  Not sure why some are not understanding the rule.  Granted, I've played the CG for Red Barricades over 10 times.

[12.06] Area Target Type vs. Area Fire
These are easy terms to confuse, but they are separate concepts and actually refer to different things.

Area Target Type is an Ordnance TH procedure. MTRs always fire with ATT, and any weapon attempting to lay SMOKE must also use the ATT. Otherwise, use of ATT (as opposed to Vehicle Target Type or Infantry Target Type) is optional. Use of ATT consumes all of a unit's available ROF [EXC: MTR fire], and, if a hit is secured, the normal FP of the attack is halved. The advantages of ATT are that it's often easier to obtain a hit, at the penalty of reduced attack effectiveness. ATT is also the only way to gain acquisition against a concealed target.

Area Fire refers to any circumstance that causes your normal FP to be halved, e.g., firing at a concealed unit, firing in the AFPh, firing at long range are all examples of Area Fire. Ordnance is affected by Area Fire differently; it must add +2 to the TH DR, but if it hits, it attacks at normal strength *for the chosen Target Type*. Note that this means that *if* you are using the Area Target Type vs. a concealed target, you will have a +2 TH DRM *and* attack at half strength.

Basically the sniper attacks any units (with certain exceptions) in the target hex you rolled for. If there are no enemy units in the target hex the sniper will target the nearest (in hexes) enemy unit, ie move the sniper counter to the closest hex with enemy unit/s in it. ground_truth_answer:
Hi Matt - first off, great to see you here and let me know if/when you're free for another face-to-face session - I promise it'll help! :D  See my comments in italics within your quote.

Allowed AFV ranged fire/attacks?

Fire during (PFPh)
    Check!

Bounding Fire (during AFPh after movement into hex hex during MPh)
    As alluded to in Eddy's post, two types: (1) what you're describing, and (2) what Eddy mentions - firing during the AFV's movement phase.  The unique aspect of #2 compared to most other shots with main armament, is that AFV firing with Bounding *first* fire will NOT gain acquisition.  The only exception is a gyro-stabilizer-equipped vehicle (if you have one of these it will be noted in the scenario SSR).

Fire during (AFPh if didn't fire during PFPh & NO Bounding fire)
     Firing during the AFPh would still count as Bounding Fire (i.e. +2 TH DRM 

Fire during (Defensive Fire Phase)
     Which also includes firing during the enemy's Movement Phase (aka "First Fire").

Intensive Fire
     Check! There are restrictions on when this can be done, however.

Attempt Deliberate Immobilization
      Check!  Note the limitations on range, caliber required in order to be effective, and acquisition.  Can be very effective, however. 

Form Fire Group (per A7.5)
     Off the top of my head, the only AFV that can form fire groups with other units are Half-tracks, and it's a special exception just for them.  They may form fire-groups with other half-tracks or other Infantry (including leadership modifiers if in the same hex with Infantry and the leader is either with the Infantry or with the Passengers).  Of course, any AFV may fire-group its own weapons (e.g. bow machine-gun plus Co-Ax machine-gun).

Gun Duel (Defender using C2.2401)
     Check, but a Gun Duel is often declared by the *attacker* after a Defender declares a shot.  They are only successful (i.e. attacker gets to shoot first - using Bounding First Fire) if the DRM paid by the Defender exceed those of the Attacker or if they're equal then the one with the lower *final* TH DR wins.  When you consider that covered-arc change costs are doubled if the shooter is firing from a building or woods, you can begin to see where this can work out in the attacker's favor, especially if he's equipped with gyro-stabilizers, which cut down on his DRM for this calculation only.

just trying to understand some of the difference between personnel counters and AFV. For example AFV cannot Opporunity Fire (A7.25) or Assault Fire (A7.36). Also AFV MGs cannot use Mandatory Fire Direction (A9.4 only Infantry Leaders allow this)

Next is MG on AFVs:
Can AFV MGs take Snapshots (A8.15)?
Yes, but only with Machine-guns - the rule states "Neither a MG that must change its CA (9.21), nor an ordnance weapon, nor a weapon using IFE/Canister can make a Snap Shot"

title: PzKpfw II (Fl)
raw_question:
OK, the PzKpfw II (Fl) has a special ability to place smoke at exactly 3 hexes inside the VCA. If you change VCA to use do this, then you used the same Case A penalties as if you were using a smoke mortar. There is a lot missing here from the rule, I am wondering if anybody has any thoughts on this.

For example is line of sight necessary to the hex where the smoke is placed?

If the PzKpfw II (Fl) is hull down, can it use this ability (i.e. similar to using other hull based weapons)?
ground_truth_answer:
The chapter H note says :

The smoke discharger, if successfully fired, allows the placing of a smoke counter at three (only) hex range within the tank's VCA. Any VCA change pertinent to using the sD is treated as per D13.32.

The VCA change penalty is the only concession to the sM rule.
Otherwise, it is a sD.

That means :
- range blocked at 3 hexes ("only")
- within VCA (and not TCA)
- LOS not needed (hey, it can fire over a building, woods or any obstacle... or even through one!):arrrh:
- no +2 moving/motion penalty
- no Hindrance penalty
- it can fire from a building or deep jungle (:D)

I understand that some people can feel their sense of reality deeply contradicted by those facts, but that is how the rule is displayed.

One could not argue that the vehicle note was written before the sM rules were, as it directly refers to them.
Rules' lawyering supplemental argument : chapter H comes after chapter D, so it supersedes the latter unless otherwise stated.

So, until there is an erratum about that vehicle note - and, frankly, I do think that something should be done about it, as my "feeling of reality" is ruffled to - I will play along the present rules.
ASL is to WW2 what D&D is to Middle Ages : I don't mind having a super duper smoke puffing dragon around.;)

Mph - 9 hexes (CX, Lder, Road bonus). - gets routed from defensive fire
RtPh - 6 hexes rout

Enemy Player turn
 - Our poor squadie gets fired at, DM'ed again
 - Enemy moves adjacent

Total = 21 hexes = 840 Meters
That makes it average 7 Meters/sec ...not near enough to sprint speeds but still faster than my normal walking speed at the games shop!!

hmmmm ...anyone else can add to that and see if we have potential olympic champions in our ASL Squads?
ground_truth_answer:
While the rules officially define a turn as being two minutes in duration, this definition can be fudged quite a bit by various parts of the game system. Here's how Squad Leader designer John Hill explained it in his Designer's Notes to the original game:

The given time span of "two minutes" is actually not a hard and fast rule. With the given movement of 4MP per unit, we have a squad covering only 160 meters in two minutes. In reality, even carrying the usual assortment of equipment, you could go farther, if all you did was move. But, if you consider all the possibilities: rally, move, fire, counterfire, fire again, and close combat, then maybe each turn is really four minutes long. So, there is a possible internal contradiction. Then, throw in the whole problem of, "How long would it take for the actual platoon leaders to decide to do this?" and you begin to see how really "fudged" two minutes are.
With regards to the original question, issue #36 of View from The Trenches ran an interesting article by Wayne Hadady entitled "The Physics of ASL" which stated the following:

A hex is 40 meters across [A2.1]. A Game Turn represents two minutes of real time . Given a run of dice on steroids, an Infantry unit could conceivable spend those two minutes as follows:

* move 9 hexes (CX, Leader and Road bonus) in its MPh
* rout 6 hexes, ending in Capture (a move of one more hex)
* Withdraw one hex with a CC-winning guard
* be moved 9 hexes by the guard
* rout 6 hexes with the guard
* defeat the guard in CC and Withdraw one hex

Total hexes/distance traversed: 33h/1320m (about a 2:30 mile pace)
Back issues of View From The Trenches can be downloaded from:

http://www.vftt.co.uk/index.asp

query: Hill Movement: OK, how many MP/MF does it cost to go from I1 to Y1 along the road?
title: Hill Movement
raw_question: OK, how many MP/MF does it cost to go from I1 to Y1 along the road?
ground_truth_answer:
It just so happens that I was reading about this this afternoon, so I'm sure that this is a case of an Abrupt Elevation Change (A10.5). So:
1. Infantry: 3MF (1 [each intermediate level descended] plus 2 [COTx2 to ascend 1 level] [each intermediate level ascended]).
2. Vehicle: 5MP (2 [each intermediate level descended] plus 2 [ascending 1 level via road] [each intermediate level ascended] plus 1 ).

The 15BB8 to AA9 reference in the A10.51 example is to a situation of exactly this kind (without the road). :)

EDIT. Minor but important correction: ascending 1 level to enter Y1 is not an intermediate level. Oops. :shake:
EDIT #2. Corrected the vehicular MP cost for ascending 1 level via road (thanks Chuck). ;)

You can also streetfight (A11.8) an adjacent AFV in a road hex as it moves past you if there is a building on the other side of the road.

Generally you have to take a PAATC
If you pass it you can generally take out a tank on fours or less..

title: Is the squad inherent firepower includes the LMG of that squad?
raw_question: I remembered I read somewhere in the rulebook that it includes the LMG but I found it's weird that the German LMG has FP of 3 while the German squad has FP of 4 only. Anyone confirms if I'm correct?
ground_truth_answer:
I rather would refer to the preliminary paragraph of chapter A9 :
[A LMG counter represents a weapon additional to the inherent complement of such weapons present in a squad and accounted for by that squad's FP. The inherent LMG of a squad counter is not subject to any of the following rules, nor can it ever be turned into a LMG counter.]

The Inherent FP of a squad never includes an LMG in counter form.

Spraying Fire is not only linked to the presence of a "ghost" LMG:

A7.34 SQUAD SPRAYING FIRE: Spraying Fire is limited to those squads with an inherent LMG, multiple SMG, and/or superior tactical training. 

Counter MGs can use spraying fire.
But a squad with spraying fire only can fire at about the range of an SMG.
The example in the rule shows a 628 Russian squad, which typically represents the "SMG only" squads that were part of SMG companies.

ground_truth_answer:
After some further research, I think I'm going to have to disagree with you guys. I'm pretty sure you're supposed to refer to both the Russian and the British notes. 

First of, BV (even 3rd edition) doesn't even come with Lend-Lease vehicles (Russian note numbers 48-58). In page H28F, under Lend-Lease Vehicles it says the following:
"For DYO purposes use British counters to represent the following vehicles in the Soviet service. All pertinent Vehicle Notes apply normally."
(underline by me)

Interestingly Starter Kit 3 comes with 6 Russian colored Sherman IIIs (unique in the system?) and its Vehicle Note is a mix of both nationalities. Its fluff text is of the Russian note, but it has a special note of using Black TH numbers after 1943, which is lifted straight from the British notes. It doesn't mention Gyros or Multiple hits, but those concepts are not in Starter Kits so that's easily explained. They still have the white ROF indicating Multiple Hits, and a big G in the back for the Gyros, even in Russian colors.
