Tactically, should I use area fire in the above case? ..and if so, which column of the IFT should be used if a hit is achieved?
ground_truth_answer:
I think Binko has the right DRMs; Ben makes a good point re ATT and acquisition.

Area fire attacks at half the FP. So the only time you would want to use Area Fire is probably at long range when the To Hit chance is much better. 

Normally I'd agree but the sIG IB is a gnarly beast, with a 150mm MA.  Even at halved firepower it still hits on the 12 column.  Let's look at your chances either way, in the upcoming DFPh:

Infantry Target Type:  Base 8 To Hit, with +2 DRM for Concealment and a further +3 for Stone Building TEM - you need to roll a three or less (8.3%); success brings a roll on the 30 column with no DRMs, where any result is a 1MC or better.  So, overall you have an 8.3% chance of inflicting a result.

Area Target Type:  Base 7 To Hit, with -1 DRM for Acquisition, +2 for Concealment, and no TEM DRM for an ATT shot - you need to roll a six or less (41.7%); success brings a roll on the 12 column where the +3 TEM DRM now applies - you have a 41.7% chance of an NMC or better (58.3% chance of a PTC or better).  Here you have an overall chance of 17.4% of inflicting at least a normal morale check.

So, you have an interesting choice - ITT allows you to bring the pain in  a serious way (KIAs on the 30 column up to 5) but the ATT doubles your chance of a meaningful result.  The sIG IB has a circled B9 Ammo Depletion number, meaning it won't be around long - you need to make every shot count.  In this case you might forgo the 30 column jackpot in exchange for a much better chance of making the French roll a morale check.  

Thanks to all who clarified. Learnt something new here. The big surprise for me was acquisition cannot be earned against concealed targets (gotta check the ASLRB).

All the while, i suspected that using ATT would give me better chances of doing some damage, or to wait for concealment to be stripped from targets before blasting them; i.e. using infantry to fire at them first and then the SIGs if they lose concealment.

I am normally conservative with vehicles and support them with infantry close by to ensure that them no good frenchies don't pop up and CC them while in urban areas.

Cheers
-Lamskiy-

ground_truth_answer: I know the question is from years ago, but it's there so others like me can find answers about a game they've grown to love. This is my opinion, having played far fewer games than the person asking and always playing solo: concealment is essential. You can't enjoy being a defender without it. The attacker will know everything about you and will simply make you look like a fool. As an attacker, not using concealment is advantageous (you'll most likely win), but you won't feel the uncertainty or the doubt of sending your men to their deaths, you won't think about how and where to attack, you won't enjoy trying to WIN. You'll be a no-brainer. The axis of attack, the main effort, thinking... all pointless. Just put all your forces on this point (the least defended) and roll the dice... you'll be playing a kill-or-be-killed game (if so, Warhammer 40,000 is better; the miniatures are bigger and cooler), and since you choose where, you'll kill more and better. Regarding POWs, I'm only giving an approximation due to lack of experience. I don't play with this rule either. It took me quite a while to feel comfortable with the rest of the rules, and I was overwhelmed by the number of pieces on the board to even be interested in it. However, despite having enjoyed it a lot, I feel that in some games one side won or lost simply because of the absence of this rule. That's how it is; the scenarios assume you'll use this rule, and that's why they give you more or less AFV, MMC, or fill it with HT or trucks. CVP, POW... the scenario was tested that way. If you don't use this rule, you'll enjoy it as much as I did at the beginning, without getting a headache from so many pieces on the board or even more doubts about the rules. But now I feel comfortable with the rules, and I think I've played some great scenarios without really perceiving all their nuances. That my victories and defeats were faked. I wonder if it was all just like a fool looking at a Velázquez painting and saying, "What a beautiful painting, I wouldn't mind putting it in my living room." Now I want to learn that rule and replay those same scenarios in all their glory. Something tells me that what I took for granted as the winning tactic for that scenario for one side or the other—or what I assumed would inevitably be the winner—will be put to the test. In short, use concealment ASAP, use POW when you can play by new rules without having a nervous breakdown.

I know the infantry that possesses the SW can fire a 2nd shot using subsequent first fire at half FP but can the machine gun fire at full strength for the 2nd MF shot and if that retains ROF can it fire at other units that move in its LOS until ROF is lost and RF is left at that site?
ground_truth_answer:
Now, a question: 

Why did I italicize the last phrase in the MMG/HMG rule (which is A9.21 IIRC)?

MMG/HMG that hold Rate of Fire and are firing from a woods, rubble or building hex would not be able to fire outside the covered arc established by their first shot for the remainder of that phase.

Remember, Defensive First Fire takes place during the Movement Phase, is a DIFFERENT phase than the Defensive Fire Phase, which occurs after the Movement Phase is completed. (See A3.3 and A 3.4)

So what does that mean? Since I can only fire at units MOVING using First Fire and Subsequent First Fire in the Movement phase, what happens to my unused rate of fire if everyone has finished moving?

IF I still have ROF with my LMG/MMG/HMG, I can wait for Def. Final Fire Phase, and since I had ROF, my MG is NOT marked with a First Fire, so I can NOW fire again - and this time, at ANYONE in my LOS, because the covered arc goes away at the end of the Movement phase! 

(There is an exception for pinned units, but that's a different learning moment!) 

Hope this is helping! If it is confusing, just ignore me!

    ---Russ

query:
Concealed Units: 1.  Does a concealed unit prevent an enemy unit from gaining concealment?

2.  If a concealed unit moves in LOS of a concealed enemy unit does it   lose concealment?

3.  Can a unit gain concealment if in LOS of a concealed enemy unit?

The way I look at it, a concealed unit is not a known unit and may contain only Dummy counters. So in order to prevent or cause an enemy unit to lose its concealment it would have to reveal at least one of its concealed units (perhaps by random selection if more than one concealed unit in the stack). If this is the case, does the unit that just revealed itself return to its concealed state or remain unconcealed?
title: Concealed Units
raw_question:
1.  Does a concealed unit prevent an enemy unit from gaining concealment?

2.  If a concealed unit moves in LOS of a concealed enemy unit does it   lose concealment?

3.  Can a unit gain concealment if in LOS of a concealed enemy unit?

The way I look at it, a concealed unit is not a known unit and may contain only Dummy counters. So in order to prevent or cause an enemy unit to lose its concealment it would have to reveal at least one of its concealed units (perhaps by random selection if more than one concealed unit in the stack). If this is the case, does the unit that just revealed itself return to its concealed state or remain unconcealed?
ground_truth_answer:
1. Yes. This is one reason to keep your dummies alive and hunt down the opponent's dummies.

See the Example in A12.121. It specifically mentions a Dummy stack.

2. Only if it is a non-dummy unit, which must be momentarily revealed to force loss of concealment (most guys I've played with just need a verbal, 'yup, it's real'). The enemy unit retains its "?" after this momentary revelation. The one that gets revealed is the owner's choice. However, machanics are different when you try to enter a Location with a "?" or Hidden enemy unit.

See A12.14. Middle of paragraph before the Example.

query: Point Attack: Does an aircraft continue to fire at its initial target every time it moves into a hex towards it (sort of like Strafing except shooting at the same target) and then once it reaches the initial target hex it may no longer attack (targets outside the initial target hex I suppose)?
title: Point Attack
raw_question: Does an aircraft continue to fire at its initial target every time it moves into a hex towards it (sort of like Strafing except shooting at the same target) and then once it reaches the initial target hex it may no longer attack (targets outside the initial target hex I suppose)?
ground_truth_answer:
Does an aircraft continue to fire at its initial target every time it moves into a hex towards it (sort of like Strafing except shooting at the same target) and then once it reaches the initial target hex it may no longer attack (targets outside the initial target hex I suppose)?

Yes, but you only get two attacks versus the Point target:

7.402 POINT ATTACKS: A FB makes a Point Attack in the same manner as a Strafing Run with the following differences. After a FB has made its initial attack from four hexes away and has moved toward that target to the next hex along the predesignated Hex Grain, it may attack the same target hex again. Moreover, because it is now attacking from only three hexes away (six-hex Aerial Range), any To Hit DR is based on the 0-6 column of the To Hit Table instead of the 7-12 column. After this second attack, the FB must still attempt to continue moving along the predesignated Hex Grain until it occupies its target hex for purposes of receiving Light AA fire, but cannot make any additional attacks during that Player Turn.

Hope this helps,

JR

ground_truth_answer:
1. yes, tanks can First Fire.  Note that their MG are not Infantry and the tanks may not Subsequent Fire Fire or Final Protective Fire their MG.  However, they can Subsequent First Fire their MA (which may result in Intensive Fire or normal SFF if IFE).

2. Motion requires all MG/IFE to fire at half FP.  And a tank's MA firing when in Motion gets gets the +2 (Case B), +1 or +2 for restricted(C1) or limited(C2) aim, and finally +2 for T/ST and +3 for NT (+1 if stabalized) for Case C.  And finally the lower dr is x2.

And if the AFV is BU, that is afurther +1 (Case I).

So a normal CE "tank" has a turreted main weapon, which results in a total of +5 DRM with and the lower dr is doubled.  An SP has NT and would be +6.

Examples:
Assume a Motion CE AFV with turreted MA.

DR: 4, 2 results in double lower dr to 4 which is a total of 8 +5 is a Final TH of 13.

DR: 1, 2 results in double lower dr to 2 which is a total of 4 +5 is a Final TH of 9

Mortars Firing on Open Top Halftracks Transporting Troops?: First it is not AF added up to 4, just having ALL AF being less than 4.  Same is true for the +1 DRM.

Yes, even large AFV can be destroyed by mortars.  But only the big ones.

I agree it is strange that mortars aren't allowed to target passengers of a half-track from a reality point of view.  But this ain't reality.  It's ASL.

Everything else looks good.

For your "Why can't a mortar get a direct hit and wipe out the passenger squad" question, look at rule C3.7, Critical Hits.  That blows up the whole thing.

Also remember that a halftrack with a BU counter is quite vulnerable to CC.  It will be OT and have no usable MG.  And the passengers can not participate.

Mortars are strange things.  They either do great things or nothing.  The following mantra is quite common, "Hit, rate.  No effect.  Hit, rate.  No effect.  Hit, rate.  No effect."

David, I agree with you that the attack is resolved using C1.55 which references C7.345 which details the attack resolution. I also agree with you that it seems logically that there SHOULD be a -1 DRM for OT. But I can't find it.  

I'm really working hard to get this portion of the rules clear in my mind and if you can cite the specific rule that gives a -1 DRM for a mortar attack on an OT AFV I'd really appreciate it. This doesn't only apply to Halftracks but would also affect stuff like OT Tank Destroyers. 

C7.22B provides an additional -1 DRM for Aerial attacks or MOL/DC attacks from a higher elevation against OT vehicles. D6.61 provides for attack even against BU passengers in an OT Armored Halftrack if the firer has an elevation advantage. But I can't find anything that provides a -1 DRM for being OT when Armored Halftracks come under regular mortar fire. 

Logically there should not be a penalty for an OT vehicle being fired on by a mortar. Unless the mortar round lands inside the vehicle (which is handled by the critical hits, I believe) then the mortar bomb is landing at ground level outside of the vehicle and the armored sides of the halftrack provide protection to the crew and passengers.

The other cases (elevation advantage or air attacks) involve direct fire against the passengers and crew that bypasses the protective side armor of the half track or other OT vehicle. Likewise the DC/MOL are being tossed down into the vehicle

It's not that players think the game is perfect and cannot be improved; there's just a strong desire to have everyone playing by the same exact set of rules.I think this would be the major motive for not tweaking the rules too much.
The size of the rulebook has also an impact on the situation : learning it already takes a lot of time - not speaking of mastering most of it ¨
Imagine that any guys comes around and wants to change this or that detail (among hundreds of them)...
It easily would generate into a global mess.

And there is the real risk that the proposed variant does not take in count many effects on other rules : that impact can reveal itself as disastrous - but only after some months or years.
How can one go back, if such a modification has been adopted ?

There was the case of the bridge -1 TEM, additional to the FFMO one.
The erratum (which tried to be consistent with the Terrain chart), created such a mess among the community, that it had to be annulated by a subsequent erratum.

For the veteran ASL players maybe this is simply a reaction to the "bad old days" of Squad Leader, where all of the rules published in the three SL expansions were optional rules. Just imagine trying to play ASL if most of the rules could be used only if both players agreed to use them!I agree.
The simple size of the Rulebook speaks about the risks of major modifications.

it might make a fine SSR for a particular situation, if the scenario designer could provide any sort of verifiable historical justification for it.I agree. An SSR is the best way to go.
Now, it is important to be able to write an SSR that covers all the rules' interactions...

As it seems, the rallying rule variant is more a "realism argument" thing than a minor variant that could be limited to an SSR.

In the ASL community, "realism arguments" are considered as total "BS" (pardon me for the rudeness of the expression, but it will be the common answer one would have to read on some active forums).
ASL is a game, which is by definition an approximation - and thus uses abstractions.
ASL is not reality, nor a very precise simulation (although, among wargames, it is among the most detailed ones). So trying to "change" it to something "more realistic" is an illusion that leads nowhere.

title: Next n00b question -- where does defensive fire occur?
raw_question:
This is an issue we keep going back to the rules on (using ASL SK 2), and we keep getting flummoxed. 

A unit is in a hex, say, A002 or whatever.It is moving to, I dunno, B003. The attacker announces "I am moving this unit from this hex to that hex, expending 2 MF to do so". The defender says "I am using Defensive First Fire on that unit."

Does the fire "land" in the hex the unit was IN, or the hex the unit is moving TO? If the unit breaks, does it stop moving in A002 or is it in B003?

For any other "You expend MF (placing a DC, using smoke, etc), I shoot" scenario, does the shooting take place BEFORE or AFTER the effect of expending the MF? Is the smoke placed no matter what, in other words, or can firing on the unit cancel the smoke placement attempt (by breaking or eliminating the unit)?
ground_truth_answer:
Fire always takes place AFTER the MF are expended. So you would fire after the smoke is placed. Using the AFTER reasoning, you see that the fire is directed at the new hex. A unit moving from a5 to a6 is fired on at a6, because it is after the MF is spent that they may be fired on.

Note p.10 of the SK2 rulebook, 1st column: "Units expend MF based on the terrain that is entered...whenever a player moves a unit he states out loud the MF expended by that unit in entering that hex..." And also on p. 10, line 8 of 3.3.1: "Any time a unit or stack expends MF in the LOS of a Good Order Defender unit, the DEFENDER has the option to temporarily halt movement while he fires at it..."

Basically, you haven't moved unless you've spent MF, you haven't spent MF unless you've entered a new hex (or placed smoke, etc.), and the defender can't fire unless you've spent MF.

The defender cannot prevent movement into a hex or cancel smoke placement by defensive firing. If a unit breaks, they are broken in the new hex.

query:
N00b question -- fire groups with different DRMs: So, I'm still learning this using ASL SK 2. A question came up in the last game we couldn't figure out.

If you have two units form a fire group, and one's LOS passes through two grain hexes, and one passes through one, how do you handle the different DRM for the combined group? (Or any other situation where one group has one DRM and another has another, but you're combining firepower.)
title: N00b question -- fire groups with different DRMs
raw_question:
So, I'm still learning this using ASL SK 2. A question came up in the last game we couldn't figure out.

If you have two units form a fire group, and one's LOS passes through two grain hexes, and one passes through one, how do you handle the different DRM for the combined group? (Or any other situation where one group has one DRM and another has another, but you're combining firepower.)
ground_truth_answer:
Actually, it comes down to being the worst of all possible worlds.

In a multi-hex fire group:
Use the worst possible TEM (generally caused by a wall or hedge).
Use the worst possible Hindrance
Use the worst applied leadership modifier.
If any one unit is CX, apply the +1 for that.

There's probably a few other individual modifiers, but you get the idea. And you take all of those components individually, and add them up. So, if you have two squads in a multi-hex firegroup, and one unit is firing through two hexes of grain (+2 Hindrance), and the other is firing through one hex of grain, but is CX (+1 Hindrance, +1 CX), you add the +2 Hind to the +1 CX for a +3 DRM.

title: OBA questions
raw_question:
My friend and I are playing our first scenario with OBA, and I have a couple questions.  

The Germans get one 80+mm module of HE.  It is the beginning of the German prep fire phase.  FFE:2 is on the board.

First, does each OBA attempt begin with a Radio Contact check, regardless of Battery Access being previously established?

Second, if my FFE:2 is not in position to do any damage, I will correct it.  But after reading the rules it seems to me that with an FFE, as opposed to a SR, I cannot correct AND attack in the same phase.  Is this true?  If it is, will it convert to FFE:C at the end of the phase, or will I get another chance to use the FFE:2 next turn?

Thanks in advance for the help, folks!
ground_truth_answer:
From FFE:C there are three different paths you can follow but they all require you pull another chit for Battery Access.
With a FFE:C on the map, here's the short version of your three options (assuming that you maintain contact and draw a black chit for a new fire mission):

(A) Place an AR anywhere on the map, which will be subject to normal extent of error, to place a new SR.

(B) Place an AR within 18 hexes of the FFE:C, with the extent of error limited by the distance from the FFE:C, to place a new SR.

(C) Leave the FFE:C in place, convert to FFE:1, resolve, and then convert to FFE:2.

All of these options, of course, have various restrictions/requirements.

What you *can't* do with a FFE:C is correct your aim and continue firing; you either continue firing at the same location, or you correct your aim and go back to just a SR on the map.

You can also usually assault move into a non-open ground hex without losing concealment.

Note that if you advance into terrain that could not have assault moved into (for example, terrain that takes more than 3MP for a squad without a leader) you will lose concealment too.

Or into a space that takes three MPs and you're green/conscript, you lose it. Basically, if it takes your normal full MP to move into a space (not advance) then you lose concealment. 

One trick on the defense is to alternate a guy moving forward and backwards during your MPh/AdvPh, so the enemy doesn't get a shot at him during DfPh. This is called "skulking". To elaborate this, have two units to do this. One moves back and gains concealment, while the other one, which gained concealment last round, moves forward during AdvPh to start the dance again.

Okay it says "A unit's CX counter is removed...as soon as it:...or moves."

CX come off at the start of the Mph though, so how would it end up moving with a CX marker if it comes off at the start of the Mph? Moving comes after the start of the Mph, where the CX is removed.

ground_truth_answer:
Okay it says "A unit's CX counter is removed...as soon as it:...or moves."
I don't see the contradiction here. Moving is one of many triggers for removing a CX counter.

CX come off at the start of the Mph though, so how would it end up moving with a CX marker if it comes off at the start of the Mph? Moving comes after the start of the Mph, where the CX is removed.
If you're going to be very precise about it, no - this is not the correct formulation. Refer to the Extended Sequence of Play on the red binder divider. The "Beginning of THE MPh" is extremely limited and includes actions for only a few rare cases. CX status will be removed when the unit moves during ITS MPh. So, as you say, a unit will never move with CX the turn after it gained it.

I can't see how a unit would have a CX DURING the Mph since the CX comes off at the START of the Mph.
Because the unit could have declared Late Double Time - see the EXC to A4.5.

It says that the CX comes off at the end of it's next Mph.
Read the whole sentence - that's the fallback case for a whole list of possibilities. The CX is removed whenever any of them occur. So if you Prep Fire a CX unit, the CX is removed. If you decline Prep and move, the CX is removed then. If you decline Prep and also decline to move (maybe because another Prep didn't work out), then the CX is removed at the end of the MPh. 

The very next sentence says it comes off at the start of the Mph.
Actually, it says "a Mph", which is different. The CX counter is removed (if the unit moves) at the beginning of ITS MPh, and thus does not affect the unit during that MPh.

query:
Hexgrains?: I'm relatively new, and am looking for lots of good examples of hexgrains and alternate hexgrains, with graphics to show explanations. I'm mainly looking for help with Firelanes and Human Waves.

Thanks!
title: Hexgrains?
raw_question:
I'm relatively new, and am looking for lots of good examples of hexgrains and alternate hexgrains, with graphics to show explanations. I'm mainly looking for help with Firelanes and Human Waves.

Thanks!
ground_truth_answer:
In this case.

At the risk of over-explaining:

The particular point is that a hexgrain is just that. A... grain (see definition 6).

When you look at a hex grid, you can see straight rows of hexes going in three directions.

If you look at any particular hex in the above illustrations, as you move through any particular side to an adjacent hex and keep going in that direction, you are following a hex grain. So, in this case the hexgrains go up-down, upper left-bottom right, and lower left-upper right, and any particular hex will have these three grains passing through it.

To preserve players' sanity, the firelane rules generally just allow you to follow the hex grain when setting one up. This makes siting of MG especially important on the defense.

However, the FL rules also allow for 'alternate' hexgrain use. This is based off of the six hexspines radiating out from a hex (these are the same lines that separate the six adjacent hexes from each other). See the Covered Arc discussion in chapter C for a better idea of what is meant.

So here, you're allowed to fire down the junction of two adjacent hexes to set up your FL. Past that, you go to another hex, and then down the next hexspine, and so on. So, obviously the actual hexes are affected by the FL, but what happens in between? (On the hexspines?) There, you have to choose one side or the other to be affected by the FL. Pick a hex in the above illustration, and pretend you have a good amount of flat clear ground to work in. You can set up an alternate hexgrain FL firing directly to the left or right, but for the alternate hexes (where you're firing along the hexspine), you have to choose whether you're affecting the hexes above or below the spine. You get to make this choice once, when you set up the FL, and the entire FL follows that choice. You can't affect the adjacent hex above the hexspine, and then affect the hex below the hexspine 3 hexes away.

Yes, the negative effect of desperation morale is considered once, and then removed (although there are some circumstances in which the counter may remain).

title: Learning Concealment
raw_question:
My friend and I have worked through ASLSK1-3, and now are learning the full ASL system.  The second scenario we are attempting is Scenario B from the 'Classic' batch of scenarios that originally were for Squad Leader.  This one brings up some questions about concealment, since I don't fully comprehend how this all works yet.

My questions are:

When a unit sets up under concealment, it remains concealed until it moves/fires/etc, regardless of being in LOS of enemy units, right?

After all the ? counters are placed from the scenario card, any other units out of LOS of any enemy revealed, Good Order unit get a free ? counter, right?

Concealed units DO force Loss of Concealment for enemy concealed units that move in the open, fire, etc, right?

I think I've answered most of these questions by discussing with my friend and repeatedly re-reading the concealment rules, but I'd like some clarification from all-y'all.  Thanks!
ground_truth_answer:
But I think I figured out that a ? unit is NOT a good order unit, but DOES still have an effect on concealment.
Well, not exactly. A Dummy unit/stack (multiple ?'s) is not Good Order. A (real) unit under a ? counter is Good Order. However, you must momentarily reveal it (lift up the ? counter) in order to strip enemy concealment. This is primarily a matter of verification - since ASL's rules attempt to be rigorous enough for tournaments, you can't simply say that a concealed unit is real without proving it. However, there are also some gameplay ramifications here as well. It's sometimes a better idea not to momentarily reveal your own unit and let the enemy keep his concealment in order to keep him in the dark about where your own real units are. What you choose depends on how valuable that knowledge would be in that situation.

Because the rule about momentary reveals is primarily a verification issue, some people consider it "gamey" and house-rule it in friendly play. A number of players I've met will "show a boot" without revealing the exact stats of the unit. A few will simply go by one another's word without any verification at all. However, the rules as written are quite clear that the unit must be completely (though only momentarily) revealed.

query:
Wall/Hedge LOS question: B9.2 states:

"A wall/hedge lying lengthwise (on a hexspine) exactly along a LOS is a Half-Level LOS obstacle only if ... touching one of the viewing/target hexes and the vertex opposite of the viewing/target hex has walls/hedges on all of its three hexspines." (Emphasis in Original).

I'm struggling with the precise definition of the word "one" as used in the above sentence. 

Does "one" mean:
A. At least one; or
B. One and only one.

It makes difference if the wall/hedge lies along a hexspine that connects both the viewing and target hex.  Look at page B9 for an example.  If the rule means "at least one," there would not be an LOS between P4 and Q6 on the examples in the right hand column, because at least one of the viewing/target hexes is touching the hedge, and the opposite vertex has hedges on all three hexspines.

But, if one means "one and only one," then there would be an LOS between P4 and Q6, because the hegde is adjacent to both the viewing and target hexes; it is not merely adjacent to only ONE of them, it is adjacent to TWO of them, therefore LOS would not be blocked.

I admit, that the "one and only one" definition makes less sense.  For that reason my gut tells me that "one," as used in B9.2, means "at least one."  But I'm usually wrong on these things, so I thought I'd put it out there.  It doesn't help that the rule decided to put the word "one" in italics, which lead me to consider that perhaps "one" means "one and only one."

What constitutes a leader action?: As detailed as the rules to this game are, I'm having dificulty locating a specific list of things that constitute an action taken by a leader.

When I was taught the game, I was told that generally a leader can only do one thing per phase.

Some of the rules bear this out.  For example, A3.1 clearly states "RALLY PHASE (RPh): Both players may attempt to repair weapons, rally broken units, etc. Each unit may attempt only one type of action in a RPh."

So, during the RPh, can a leader attempt to recover a SW from a broken squad (A4.44), and then attempt to rally the broken squad?

Clearly the leader attempting recovery is an action for the leader, but is the act of rallying the unit an action for the leader, or is it just an action for that unit?  A10.71 makes reference to leaders attempting to rally broken units.  Put in those words, it makes it seem like the leader is trying to get the units to rally, and it would therefore be an action on the leader's part.  That being said, A10.6 states that "Broken units of both sides may attempt to rally during any RPh if a Good Order friendly leader is present in the same Location."  This seems to imply that it doesn't matter whether the leader has acted in the Rally Phase or not, pointing to the conclusion that it is not an action for the leader.

So I ask again, does using a leader to rally troops in the same Location constitute an action for that leader, such that it would preclude him from attemping recovery or repair in that same RPh.

As a corollary question, would attempting to deploy good order squad(s)during the RPh count as an action for a leader?  Would recombining constitute an action for a leader?

query: Self-rally without the ability...: I was reading in a strategy forum today that "the attacking player may self-rally one MMC during the rally phase, even if it doesn't have self-rally capability." Is this true? If so, can anyone quote section in the book that this rule is contained in?
title: Self-rally without the ability...
raw_question: I was reading in a strategy forum today that "the attacking player may self-rally one MMC during the rally phase, even if it doesn't have self-rally capability." Is this true? If so, can anyone quote section in the book that this rule is contained in?
ground_truth_answer:
Yes
In your half player turn, as the FIRST rally attempt of the rally phase, you may attempt to self rally one unit not capable of typical self rally.  Its called Field Promotion (18, pg A37 in RBV2).

From the RBV2:

18. FIELD PROMOTIONS
18.1 Leader creation during play may occur in either of two ways.

18.11 SELF-RALLY: The first MMC Rally attempt of a player’s own
RPh may be performed as Self-Rally regardless of Self-Rally capability
(10.63) in an attempt to rally that MMC, provided there is no Good Order
leader in that Location and the broken unit is not Disrupted (19.12). If this Self-Rally attempt results in an Original 2 DR, the MMC is rallied and, in addition, the ATTACKER may roll on the Leader Creation Table with a +1 drm for having been broken prior to the Self-Rally 2 DR. Any Original DR other than 2 during the Self-Rally attempt is handled as a normal Self-Rally attempt, so the broken unit can still rally without a Field Promotiontaking place even if it is not normally capable of Self-Rally.

query:
1987 and 89 Upgrades to ASL 1st Edition...?: Hi,

   Can anyone tell me if the 1987 and 89 upgrades to the first edition effectively update it to second edition?  If not, what changed from 1st to 2nd?  Are the second edition rules a must have to play today, or is the first edition w/ '87 & '89 compatible?

Bruce
title: 1987 and 89 Upgrades to ASL 1st Edition...?
raw_question:
Hi,

   Can anyone tell me if the 1987 and 89 upgrades to the first edition effectively update it to second edition?  If not, what changed from 1st to 2nd?  Are the second edition rules a must have to play today, or is the first edition w/ '87 & '89 compatible?

Bruce
ground_truth_answer:
One of the Journals does have a writeup from MMP that states the changes and additions to the RB.
It is in ASL Journal #3: "First Do No Harm – Designer's Notes on the 2nd Edition" by Perry Cocke.

The Wall Advantage, Hedge/Bocage, and Human Wave rules apparently had the most major changes, but off-hand I couldn't say exactly how much difference there is between the 1st edition and 2nd edition versions of these rules. One example that I can give is that the 2nd edition added a step to the Advanced Sequence of Play (ASOP) for declaring Wall Advantage that was not present in the 1st edition ASOP.

The changes to the rest of the rules were primarily incorporating existing errata and Q&A's, and some wording changes for better clarity in some areas.

Are the second edition rules a must have to play today, or is the first edition w/ '87 & '89 compatible?
The 1st edition rules, even with all of the published errata for them, are not equivalent to the 2nd edition rules... and the 1st edition is no longer being supported with errata. But the 1st edition rules are still quite usable: the vast majority of the rules work exactly the same way in both editions.

The 2nd edition rulebook is a much-improved rulebook in many ways, and a recommended purchase if you can afford it, but, unless you are planning to compete seriously in the top tournaments, it is not required. The 1st edition rules will still work fine for casual gaming with friends, and for beginners looking to move to ASL from the Starter Kits.

The leader DRM is mandatory only for morale checks. The owner may choose to use it for a fire attack. If the units in a hex spit their firepower between several attacks against different targets, the leader can be used for only one of these. 

When a firegroup fires, it will get the leader modifier from the hex with the worst leader modifier in that attack. If one +1 leader is included in the attack from one hex, and a -1 is included in the attack from another hex the total modifeier will be +1. If the owner attaced without the +1 leader taking part in that attack, the total modifeier would be 0, since the hex holding the +1 leader would now be without any leader modifier.

query: Snipers: Does any one have a blow by blow example of how snipers work?  I understand when they are activated, but how do they determine their target, etc.
title: Snipers
raw_question: Does any one have a blow by blow example of how snipers work?  I understand when they are activated, but how do they determine their target, etc.
ground_truth_answer:
without going to far into the rules...

1. At the start of the game each player places the sniper counter within 6 hexes of 6 enemy occupied hexes.....5 occupied hexes...4 occupied hexes....

2. On activation a die is rolled, 1 or 2 indicates a possible hit.
   

3. Target hex dr like a spotting round to determine target.
   Sniper counter moves to target hex.

4. sniper selects target if multiple targets or an alternate 
   target closest to  initial hex.

5. to resolve attack roll a die, roll of 1 breaks MMC or eliminates SMC
   roll of 2 pins MMC or wounds SMC. 3-6 no effect.

It's all in rules section A14

Very close, but  no extra dr is needed as stated in #5. 

When sniper is activated and you roll the 1 or 2 for a possible hit (meaning eligible targets are available), resolution of the attack takes place when you roll the first 1 or 2.  You don't roll again.  

i.e.  you don't need to roll the DR = SAN then roll a dr=1,2 and again a dr=1,2  (ASLese) Just DR then dr...and determine via #3

Yeah, that's a pretty huge difference in terms of game effect as well there, basically accidentally requiring another roll with only 33% odds to do anything.

One of those things that ASL does; it took us awhile to be comfortable we were getting the spotting round movement part right (I think those rules are very oddly written for such a simple concept).  Would have been nice if rather than cross-referencing to Chapter C, they would have just said in the sniper rules something like roll one die for direction, another die for number of hexes.

title: [Fun] Rules for making coffee in ASL
raw_question: That is beautiful.
ground_truth_answer:
Excellent!

The corollary to this in  is:

E78. Making Coffee

"One lump or two?"

- Bugs Bunny

When this event occurs, the receiving player must determine a Random Hex [1.8]. That player may select one unit in or adjacent to that hex and have it try to make coffee. The player then makes a Making Coffee Roll [O20.2.4].

If the Making Coffee Roll exceeds the Coffee/Tea Rating for that nation and year then coffee is made. If the unit is broken, unbreak it. If the unit is suppressed, remove the suppression marker. If the unit already has a veteran marker on it, take no further action. Otherwise, place a Veteran marker on it.

If the Making Coffee Roll equals the Coffee/Tea Rating for that nation and year, then it becomes Suppressed, unless the unit is British, in which case it becomes Broken.

If the Making Coffee Roll equals the Coffee/Tea Rating for that nation and year, then it becomes Broken.

If an unmodified 12 is rolled, then the game ends and whoever was the acting player wins.

query:
Difference between SMOKE and WP placement?: Hi,

Under the rules section A24.SMOKE it states:"Units attempting to place
SMOKE grenades must specify the hex they wish to place them in before rolling the placement dr, but are otherwise free to observe the placement attempts of previous moving units before designating their own
placement attempts."

Whats the sense of the underlined phrase. It seems logical that one unit after the other makes a move. Or does this phrase count for a stack of units?

And so the next question comes up; under A24.3 WP it states:"The rules for placement of WP grenades are identical to those of conventional smoke except that such use must be announced prior to the Placement Attempt dr."
But where is the exception in that. I see no difference between SMOKE and WP Placement.
Maybe it could count for a stack of units, but nothing seem to indicate
that. 
I hope you know what I mean and can answer my questions.
Thanks in advance.

Greetings,
Chris
title: Difference between SMOKE and WP placement?
raw_question:
Hi,

Under the rules section A24.SMOKE it states:"Units attempting to place
SMOKE grenades must specify the hex they wish to place them in before rolling the placement dr, but are otherwise free to observe the placement attempts of previous moving units before designating their own
placement attempts."

Whats the sense of the underlined phrase. It seems logical that one unit after the other makes a move. Or does this phrase count for a stack of units?

And so the next question comes up; under A24.3 WP it states:"The rules for placement of WP grenades are identical to those of conventional smoke except that such use must be announced prior to the Placement Attempt dr."
But where is the exception in that. I see no difference between SMOKE and WP Placement.
Maybe it could count for a stack of units, but nothing seem to indicate
that. 
I hope you know what I mean and can answer my questions.
Thanks in advance.

Greetings,
Chris
ground_truth_answer:
Forget my question, now it's clear.
I was a little bit confused.
:) actually, it turns out that you're not the only one that has been confused by this...

I decided to look into this matter further. I could not find any "Perry sez" or 2nd ed. Q&A/errata for this, but I did find a debate between Ole Boe and Bruce Probst – both well-respected rules experts – from Aug 2005 on ConsimWorld:

A24.1 says quite clearly "Units attempting to place SMOKE grenades must specify the hex they wish to place them in before rolling the placement dr, but are otherwise free to observe the placement attempts of previous moving units before designating their own placement attempts."
Yes, and "previous moving units" are units that moved previously, but have now finished their MPh, i.e. units that are not part of the moving stack.
In other words, it's legal to say of a stack consisting of two squads moving together: "Squads A & B will both attempt to place SMOKE in adjacent hexes. Squad A wants to try for hex 1." (Rolls die) "OK, since that worked, Squad B wants to try for hex 2." (Rolls die)
No, because A is not a previously moving unit when moving stacked with B. This is clear from A4.2 which says: "Units moving as a stack ... must designate at the same time all actions for the same MF." So you can clearly not designate the placement hex of squad B after having seen the result of squad A.
If this were not true, the "otherwise free to observe" clause would be so trivial as to be pointless (of course you observe the activities of units that moved previously!). (There was an old unofficial 1st ed. Q&A which did exactly support what you wrote above, but clearly the current 2nd ed. text of A24.1 overrules it.)
I checked this, and the text of the 1st ed. A24.1 uses the same wording, so Bruce's claim that the 2nd ed. text overrules the 1st ed. Q&A has no logical basis: the text didn't change!

I agree that the sentence in question is so trivial as to be pointless. That doesn't allow you to act as if it means something else than it actually says though
This was the end of their discussion. I don't think Ole managed to change Bruce's mind on this, but apparently neither one felt strongly enough about it to ask for a ruling from MMP (a "Perry sez").

I agree with Ole here, and disagree with Bruce: The "otherwise free to observe" part of A24.1 does not constitute an exception to units moving as a stack, which is ALWAYS simultaneous. This is exactly what the rules say, and the 1st ed. Q&A is powerful evidence that this is the correct interpretation. 

But, given that two rules experts couldn't agree on what this rule is saying, perhaps someone really should ask Perry for a ruling...

query:
Escaping POW's: I've started a campaign where I'm playing one scenario for each month of WW2. Recently I've been playing 'Bitter defense at Otta' from Journal 3 as the Brits and captured a German squad. My opponent lacking any moral scruples opened fire and broke both the prisoners and the guards.

Despite some 30 or so games to date this particular issue had never really come up...the prisoners don't break but casualty reduce to a half squad. The guard breaks, routs and the prisoners travel with the guard. In the close combat phase the prisoners pass a task check, attacking the guard at 1:4 odds but with -2 against broken units and miss. The guards cannot attack back as they are broken.

My questions are:
1) Can the British squad rally in close combat/melee? I've looked at A10.6 and there doesn't seem to be any restriction on doing this, but I seem to remember reading somewhere that you can't rally if a known enemy unit is  adjacent, or in same hex (not sure where and could be wrong). 

2) A10.62 A broken unit is put under DM when a known armed enemy unit is adjacent to it...a) do prisoners count as known armed enemy units for this purpose? (It seems common sense that they are not armed but I have read a VFTT article that says they do put DM onto broken units)
b) Does being in close combat/melee count as being adjacent (strictly speaking not...but c'mon I'd be more scared if someone was engaing me with fisticuffs than gesturing rudely 40 metres away).

If I can't rally, then the prisoners will kill my guards unless I withdraw from melee which gives them a -2 against broken, -2 withdrawing, base chance of seven that quite frankly offends me! Any ideas?

The game in question is two thirds of the way through with the positions recorded. 

It's only the second game...without having the Allied minor module, there's only about five fighting months before the invasion of Russia in 1941, and about 25 scenarios before VJ day using all the scenarios in my collection. I'm 1-0 down so far after losing the Borders are Burning...those Finns are lethal!

2) A10.62 A broken unit is put under DM when a known armed enemy unit is adjacent to it...a) do prisoners count as known armed enemy units for this purpose? (It seems common sense that they are not armed but I have read a VFTT article that says they do put DM onto broken units)

If I can't rally, then the prisoners will kill my guards unless I withdraw from melee which gives them a -2 against broken, -2 withdrawing, base chance of seven that quite frankly offends me! Any ideas?

The game in question is two thirds of the way through with the positions recorded. 

It's only the second game...without having the Allied minor module, there's only about five fighting months before the invasion of Russia in 1941, and about 25 scenarios before VJ day using all the scenarios in my collection. ground_truth_answer:
1) Can the British squad rally in close combat/melee? I've looked at A10.6 and there doesn't seem to be any restriction on doing this, but I seem to remember reading somewhere that you can't rally if a known enemy unit is  adjacent, or in same hex (not sure where and could be wrong).
No rally allowed in a Melee: (A11.15) "Units locked in Melee may not Interdict routing units nor conduct any activity other than CC or Withdrawal from Melee."

2) A10.62 A broken unit is put under DM when a known armed enemy unit is adjacent to it...a) do prisoners count as known armed enemy units for this purpose?
Prisoners are never armed: (A20.5) "... a white unarmed counter..."

(It seems common sense that they are not armed but I have read a VFTT article that says they do put DM onto broken units)
A10.62 requires that a unit be armed to put a broken unit under DM, but note also that the errata for this rule specifies that DM is placed when a broken unit is "attacked by CC/WP,..." (red shows the errata change), so the Guards are now under DM.

b) Does being in close combat/melee count as being adjacent (strictly speaking not...but c'mon I'd be more scared if someone was engaing me with fisticuffs than gesturing rudely 40 metres away).
No, as per the Index definitions units in the same hex are not adjacent.

If I can't rally, then the prisoners will kill my guards unless I withdraw from melee which gives them a -2 against broken, -2 withdrawing, base chance of seven that quite frankly offends me! Any ideas?
I'd say things look pretty bleak... and those former prisoners may be in line for some medals. And what do you want to bet that after killing off their Guards, they'll add insult to injury and make the DR necessary to re-arm?

:)

I just startet playing the sk, but i looked at some rules from the
rulebook(2nd). And now a bypass question comes up.
Look at example 4.31: How much are the MF when moving along the D4-C4, D4-C5 and then the D4-D5 hexside to enter e5? I assume 3MF.
And D4-C4, D4-C5, D4-D5, D4-E5 to enter E4 (even it doesn't make sense)? I assume 4MF.
And D4-E4 to enter E5? I assume 3MF.
Is that right?

Thanks in advance

Greetings,

-Chris
title: Bypass question
raw_question:
Hi!

I just startet playing the sk, but i looked at some rules from the
rulebook(2nd). And now a bypass question comes up.
Look at example 4.31: How much are the MF when moving along the D4-C4, D4-C5 and then the D4-D5 hexside to enter e5? I assume 3MF.
And D4-C4, D4-C5, D4-D5, D4-E5 to enter E4 (even it doesn't make sense)? I assume 4MF.
And D4-E4 to enter E5? I assume 3MF.
Is that right?

Thanks in advance

Greetings,

-Chris
ground_truth_answer:
No, there is no need to expend 1 more MF to cross the wall at the D4-E4-D5 [edit: D4-E4-E5] vertex (this is just like the 4.3 example discusses at the other vertex). Think of the unit as being slightly inside hex D4 and so it can move along the open ground into E5 going around the wall rather than crossing it.

To clarify a bit more, the reason you need to pay 1 MF to cross the wall into D5 is that moving directly from D4 to D5 requires crossing the wall. Moving directly from D4 to E5 does not require crossing a wall.

query:
Terrain Question: It's been a while since playing ASL and now I'm getting back into it.  Unfortunately, I left my rulebook in another state!  Yeah, I need to get that back here ASAP.

Meanwhile, a question came up.  I'm playing against some Finns in the snow and I think we're doing the IFT modifiers incorrectly.  We're combining all the modifiers and it gets pretty crazy.

For example, let's say I'm firing at the following hex:

- a Finn (in a snow smock) +1
- up a hill +1
- in a foxhole +2
- in woods +1
- through a LOS hindrance +1

Should this really be a +6 attack???  Are all of these items cumulative?  I'm guessing we're doing this wrong and some items are not cumulative.  Please let me know!

Thanks,
Jason
title: Terrain Question
raw_question:
It's been a while since playing ASL and now I'm getting back into it.  Unfortunately, I left my rulebook in another state!  Yeah, I need to get that back here ASAP.

Meanwhile, a question came up.  I'm playing against some Finns in the snow and I think we're doing the IFT modifiers incorrectly.  We're combining all the modifiers and it gets pretty crazy.

For example, let's say I'm firing at the following hex:

- a Finn (in a snow smock) +1
- up a hill +1
- in a foxhole +2
- in woods +1
- through a LOS hindrance +1

Should this really be a +6 attack???  Are all of these items cumulative?  I'm guessing we're doing this wrong and some items are not cumulative.  Please let me know!

Thanks,
Jason
ground_truth_answer:
1) Foxholes are not cumulative with any terrain in the hex such as woods, shellholes, walls, etc...
Correct, see B27.3

2) Height advantage is also not cumulative with any positive modifier in the hex.
Correct, see B10.31

3) Hinderances will always add a modifier. I thought so on this one...it certainly makes sense.
Correct. A6.7 is the rule, although it does not contain any completely explicit statement saying that LOS Hindrances ALWAYS apply... but the key point is that it does not provide any exceptions in which a LOS Hindrance would not apply.

Note, however, that the Hindrance must be between the firing unit and the target in order to apply; Hindrance terrain in the firing unit's hex, and/or in the target unit's hex, never adds a modifier to a shot.

4) Snow smocks will always count unless specifically mentioned as an exception (I believe the rules note that they don't get the +1 in a building, for instance).
Hmmm... the Winter Camouflage rule, E3.712, doesn't exactly say this.

If the Winter Camouflage rules apply (that is, if the "snow smocks" are not a SSR applicable only to that scenario), and if snow is present (of course), then the Finnish infantry will receive a +1 LV (low visibility) Hindrance DRM if:

* the shot is at a range greater than 8 hexes, and

* there is no positive TEM other than SMOKE

(I think the main advantage of Winter Camouflage, for infantry, is that it allows you to Assault Move or advance into open ground and still retain concealment.)

In your example, the foxhole TEM would prevent you from claiming the Winter Camouflage LV Hindrance DRM.

So the shot would be a +3: +2 for the foxhole, and +1 for the LOS Hindrance.
